## original-en · diogenes-of-babylon · 103:181

“But, at such an age, you will never return from so long a journey.” What care I for that? I neither undertake it to return, nor to finish it my business is only to keep myself in motion, whilst motion pleases me; I only walk for the walk’s sake. They who run after a benefit or a hare, run not; they only run who run at base, and to exercise their running. My design is divisible throughout: it is not grounded upon any great hopes: every day concludes my expectation: and the journey of my life is carried on after the same manner. And yet I have seen places enough a great way off, where I could have wished to have stayed. And why not, if Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes, Zeno, Antipater, so many sages of the sourest sect, readily abandoned their country, without occasion of complaint, and only for the enjoyment of another air. In earnest, that which most displeases me in all my travels is, that I cannot resolve to settle my abode where I should best like, but that I must always propose to myself to return, to accommodate myself to the common humour.

The Stoic, named in the succession of the sourest sect — Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes, Zeno, Antipater — all of whom readily abandoned their country for the enjoyment of another air. Not the Cynic, nor the atheist, nor the Apolloniate.

## original-en · saturninus-general · 103:255

I am seldom called to it, and as seldom offer myself uncalled; liberty and laziness, the qualities most predominant in me, are qualities diametrically contrary to that trade. We cannot well distinguish the faculties of men; they have divisions and limits hard and delicate to choose; to conclude from the discreet conduct of a private life a capacity for the management of public affairs is to conclude ill; a man may govern himself well who cannot govern others so, and compose Essays who could not work effects: men there may be who can order a siege well, who would ill marshal a battle; who can speak well in private, who would ill harangue a people or a prince; nay, ‘tis peradventure rather a testimony in him who can do the one that he cannot do the other, than otherwise. I find that elevated souls are not much more proper for mean things than mean souls are for high ones. Could it be imagined that Socrates should have administered occasion of laughter, at the expense of his own reputation, to the Athenians for: having never been able to sum up the votes of his tribe, to deliver it to the council? Truly, the veneration I have for the perfections of this great man deserves that his fortune should furnish, for the excuse of my principal imperfections, so magnificent an example. Our sufficiency is cut out into small parcels; mine has no latitude, and is also very contemptible in number. Saturninus, to those who had conferred upon him the command in chief: “Companions,” said he, “you have lost a good captain, to make of him a bad general.”

Who said to those that had conferred upon him the command in chief: companions, you have lost a good captain, to make of him a bad general — which Montaigne offers as the excuse of his own principal imperfections. A third man of the name.

## original-en · lansac · 104:10

The Parliament of Bordeaux chose me mayor of their city at a time when I was at a distance from France, and still more remote from any such thought. I entreated to be excused, but I was told by my friends that I had committed an error in so doing, and the greater because the king had, moreover, interposed his command in that affair. ‘Tis an office that ought to be looked upon so much more honourable, as it has no other salary nor advantage than the bare honour of its execution. It continues two years, but may be extended by a second election, which very rarely happens; it was to me, and had never been so but twice before: some years ago to Monsieur de Lansac, and lately to Monsieur de Biron, Marshal of France, in whose place I succeeded; and, I left mine to Monsieur de Matignon, Marshal of France also: proud of so noble a fraternity--

Mayor of Bordeaux some years before Montaigne, and one of the two who had held the office twice before him.

## original-en · metrocles · 69:574

that swells thus, and thus fortifies itself by growing old. Do but consult the ancient considerations that gave the first motion to this famous torrent, so full of dignity, awe, and reverence, you will find them so light and weak that it is no wonder if these people, who weigh and reduce every thing to reason, and who admit nothing by authority, or upon trust, have their judgments often very remote, and differing from those of the public. It is no wonder if people, who take their pattern from the first image of nature, should in most of their opinions swerve from the common path; as, for example, few amongst them would have approved of the strict conditions of our marriages, and most of them have been for having wives in common, and without obligation; they would refuse our ceremonies. Chrysippus said, “That a philosopher would make a dozen somersaults, aye, and without his breeches, for a dozen of olives.” That philosopher would hardly have advised Clisthenes to have refused Hippoclides the fair Agarista his daughter, for having seen him stand on his head upon a table. Metrocles somewhat indiscreetly broke wind backwards while in disputation, in the presence of a great auditory in his school, and kept himself hid in his own house for shame, till Crates coming to visit him, and adding to his consolations and reasons the example of his own liberty, by falling to try with him who should sound most, cured him of that scruple, and withal drew him to his own stoical sect, more free than that more reserved one of the Peripatetics, of which he had been till then. That which we call decency, not to dare to do that in public which is decent enough to do in private, the Stoics call foppery; and to mince it, and to be so modest as to conceal and disown what nature, custom, and our desires publish and proclaim of our actions, they reputed a vice. The other thought it was to undervalue the mysteries of Venus to draw them out of the private oratory, to expose them to the view of the people; and that to bring them out from behind the curtain was to debase them. Modesty is a thing of weight; secrecy, reservation, and circumspection, are parts of esteem. Pleasure did very ingeniously when, under the mask of virtue, she sued not to be prostituted in the open streets, trodden under foot, and exposed to the public view, wanting the dignity and convenience of her private cabinets. Hence some say that to put down public stews is not only to disperse fornication into all places, that was confined to one, but moreover, by the difficulty, to incite wild and idle people to this vice:--

Who broke wind backwards somewhat indiscreetly while disputing before a great auditory in his school, and kept himself hid at home for shame until Crates came to visit him; and who slept in winter abroad amongst sheep and in summer in the cloisters of churches.

## original-en · cotys · 104:64

But souls that are to meet with adverse events and the injuries of fortune, in their depth and sharpness, that are to weigh and taste them according to their natural weight and bitterness, let such show their skill in avoiding the causes and diverting the blow. What did King Cotys do? He paid liberally for the rich and beautiful vessel that had been presented to him, but, seeing it was exceedingly brittle, he immediately broke it betimes, to prevent so easy a matter of displeasure against his servants. In like manner, I have willingly avoided all confusion in my affairs, and never coveted to have my estate contiguous to those of my relations, and such with whom I coveted a strict friendship; for thence matter of unkindness and falling out often proceeds. I formerly loved hazardous games of cards and dice; but have long since left them off, only for this reason that, with whatever good air I carried my losses, I could not help feeling vexed within. A man of honour, who ought to be touchily sensible of the lie or of an insult, and who is not to take a scurvy excuse for satisfaction, should avoid occasions of dispute. I shun melancholy, crabbed men, as I would the plague; and in matters I cannot talk of without emotion and concern I never meddle, if not compelled by my duty:

Who, having bought a great quantity of very fine earthenware, paid liberally for it and then broke it all himself immediately, to take away betimes the occasion of being angry with his servants.

## original-en · chremonides · 104:71

Let us not attempt these examples; we shall never come up to them. They set themselves resolutely, and without agitation, to behold the ruin of their country, which possessed and commanded all their will: this is too much, and too hard a task for our commoner souls. Cato gave up the noblest life that ever was upon this account; we meaner spirits must fly from the storm as far as we can; we must provide for sentiment, and not for patience, and evade the blows we cannot meet. Zeno, seeing Chremonides, a young man whom he loved, draw near to sit down by him, suddenly started up; and Cleanthes demanding of him the reason why he did so, “I hear,” said he, “that physicians especially order repose, and forbid emotion in all tumours.” Socrates does not say: “Do not surrender to the charms of beauty; stand your ground, and do your utmost to oppose it.” “Fly it,” says he; “shun the fight and encounter of it, as of a powerful poison that darts and wounds at a distance.” And his good disciple, feigning or reciting, but, in my opinion, rather reciting than feigning, the rare perfections of the great Cyrus, makes him distrustful of his own strength to resist the charms of the divine beauty of that illustrous Panthea, his captive, and committing the visiting and keeping her to another, who could not have so much liberty as himself. And the Holy Ghost in like manner:

The young man Zeno loved, at whose drawing near to sit down by him Zeno suddenly started up — and told Cleanthes, who asked why, that he heard the physicians prescribe rest above all things and forbid emotion.

## original-en · perrete · 104:107

Our people nowadays are so bred up to bustle and ostentation, that good nature, moderation, equability, constancy, and such like quiet and obscure qualities, are no more thought on or regarded. Rough bodies make themselves felt; the smooth are imperceptibly handled: sickness is felt, health little or not at all; no more than the oils that foment us, in comparison of the pains for which we are fomented. ‘Tis acting for one’s particular reputation and profit, not for the public good, to refer that to be done in the public squares which one may do in the council chamber; and to noon day what might have been done the night before; and to be jealous to do that himself which his colleague can do as well as he; so were some surgeons of Greece wont to perform their operations upon scaffolds in the sight of the people, to draw more practice and profit. They think that good rules cannot be understood but by the sound of trumpet. Ambition is not a vice of little people, nor of such modest means as ours. One said to Alexander: “Your father will leave you a great dominion, easy and pacific”; this youth was emulous of his father’s victories and of the justice of his government; he would not have enjoyed the empire of the world in ease and peace. Alcibiades, in Plato, had rather die young, beautiful, rich, noble, and learned, and all this in full excellence, than to stop short of such condition; this disease is, peradventure, excusable in so strong and so full a soul. When wretched and dwarfish little souls cajole and deceive themselves, and think to spread their fame for having given right judgment in an affair, or maintained the discipline of the guard of a gate of their city, the more they think to exalt their heads the more they show their tails. This little well-doing has neither body nor life; it vanishes in the first mouth, and goes no further than from one street to another. Talk of it by all means to your son or your servant, like that old fellow who, having no other auditor of his praises nor approver of his valour, boasted to his chambermaid, crying, “O Perrete, what a brave, clever man hast thou for thy master!” At the worst, talk of it to yourself, like a councillor of my acquaintance, who, having disgorged a whole cartful of law jargon with great heat and as great folly, coming out of the council chamber to make water, was heard very complacently to mutter betwixt his teeth:

The chambermaid to whom an old fellow, having no other auditor of his praises, boasted: O Perrete, what a brave, clever man hast thou for thy master! The modern edition spells her Perrette.

## original-en · henri-de-guise · 104:60

I would have the advantage on our side; but if it be not, I shall not run mad. I am heartily for the right party; but I do not want to be taken notice of as an especial enemy to others, and beyond the general quarrel. I marvellously challenge this vicious form of opinion: “He is of the League because he admires the graciousness of Monsieur de Guise; he is astonished at the King of Navarre’s energy, therefore he is a Huguenot; he finds this to say of the manners of the king, he is therefore seditious in his heart.” And I did not grant to the magistrate himself that he did well in condemning a book because it had placed a heretic amongst the best poets of the time. Shall we not dare to say of a thief that he has a handsome leg? If a woman be a strumpet, must it needs follow that she has a foul smell? Did they in the wisest ages revoke the proud title of Capitolinus they had before conferred on Marcus Manlius as conservator of religion and the public liberty, and stifle the memory of his liberality, his feats of arms, and military recompenses granted to his valour, because he, afterwards aspired to the sovereignty, to the prejudice of the laws of his country? If we take a hatred against an advocate, he will not be allowed the next day to be eloquent. I have elsewhere spoken of the zeal that pushed on worthy men to the like faults. For my part, I can say, “Such an one does this thing ill, and another thing virtuously and well.” So in the prognostication or sinister events of affairs they would have every one in his party blind or a blockhead, and that our persuasion and judgment should subserve not truth, but to the project of our desires. I should rather incline towards the other extreme; so much I fear being suborned by my desire; to which may be added that I am a little tenderly distrustful of things that I wish.

Whose graciousness a man may admire, Montaigne complains, and be called of the League for it — his instance of the vicious form of opinion that makes every judgment a party badge. Not the Duc de Guise who commanded at Dreux.

We are told by several examples, as Praestantius of his father, that being more profoundly, asleep than men usually are, he fancied himself to be a mare, and that he served the soldiers for a sumpter; and what he fancied himself to be, he really proved. If sorcerers dream so materially; if dreams can sometimes so incorporate themselves with effects, still I cannot believe that therefore our will should be accountable to justice; which I say as one who am neither judge nor privy councillor, and who think myself by many degrees unworthy so to be, but a man of the common sort, born and avowed to the obedience of the public reason, both in its words and acts. He who should record my idle talk as being to the prejudice of the pettiest law, opinion, or custom of his parish, would do himself a great deal of wrong, and me much more; for, in what I say, I warrant no other certainty, but that ‘tis what I had then in my thought, a tumultuous and wavering thought. All I say is by way of discourse, and nothing by way of advice:

Who tells of his father that, being more profoundly asleep than men usually are, he fancied himself to be a mare and served the soldiers for a sumpter — and was what he fancied himself to be.

## modern-en · montaigne · 28:2

[These — included in the 1588 edition — were twenty-nine sonnets of La Boétie, accompanied by a dedicatory epistle to Madame de Grammont. The sonnets, referred to at the end of Chapter XXVII, do not really belong to the book, and are of only slight interest now; the epistle has been transferred to the Correspondence. The author, who says his book and he are one thing, that he is himself the matter of it, and that he wants to be seen here in his simple, natural, ordinary fashion. ## modern-en · edward-black-prince · 1:1

Edward, Prince of Wales — the Black Prince, who long governed our Guienne, a man whose fortune and character carried much of the most striking grandeur — had been provoked beyond bearing by the Limousins. When he took their city by assault, no cries from the people, no prayers and tears of women and children flung at his feet, could stop his revenge. It was only further inside the town, when he came across three French gentlemen who alone, with unbelievable courage, were still holding off his victorious army, that consideration and respect for such valour first checked the torrent of his fury. His clemency began with these three knights, and from them spread to all the remaining inhabitants of the city.

Edward III’s eldest son, called the Black Prince, who governed Guienne for the English crown. He stormed the city of the Limousins and would not be stopped by the cries of the people or the tears of the women and children — and then spared three French gentlemen who were holding off his whole army alone, and after them the rest of the town.

## modern-en · scanderbeg · 1:2

Scanderbeg, Prince of Epirus, was chasing one of his own soldiers with intent to kill him. The soldier, having tried every form of humility and supplication in vain, resolved as a last resort to turn, plant himself, and wait sword in hand. The sudden steadiness brought his captain's fury to a stop, and seeing the man take so striking a stance, Scanderbeg pardoned him. The story could of course be read otherwise by anyone unfamiliar with that prince's prodigious courage and might.

The prince of Epirus, famous for prodigious force and valour. Chasing one of his own soldiers to kill him, he was stopped by the man turning to face him sword in hand, and pardoned him for the resolution.

## modern-en · conrad-iii · 1:3

The Emperor Conrad III, besieging Guelph, Duke of Bavaria, would accept no mean or unmanly satisfaction whatever as a condition for mercy, and would settle for nothing softer than this: that the ladies and gentlewomen with the duke in the town might walk out, unharmed in honour, on foot, carrying only what they could lift themselves. Whereupon they, magnanimous, hoisted their husbands and children — and the duke himself — onto their shoulders and carried them out. The emperor, ravished by the generosity of it, wept for joy, and the deadly hatred he had carried against the duke vanished on the spot; from that day on he treated the duke and his with full humanity. Either of those two methods would work easily on me, for I have an unusual leaning toward mercy and mildness — so much so that I think I would surrender my anger sooner to compassion than to admiration. Pity, of course, is reckoned a vice among the Stoics, who require that we help the afflicted but not be so affected as to suffer with them. I thought these examples not ill suited to the question at hand, all the more because in them we see great souls assaulted and tested by two very different means: resisting one without yielding, and being shaken and subdued by the other. It may be true that letting one's heart be wholly conquered by compassion can be put down to weakness, softness, and over-tenderness — which is why the weaker natures, women, children, and the common sort, are the most susceptible to it. But to have resisted and scorned the power of groans and tears, and then to yield only to the bare reverence of the sacred image of Valour — this can only be the work of a strong and inflexible soul in love with and honouring masculine, obstinate courage. Even so, astonishment and admiration may produce a similar effect in less generous minds. Witness the people of Thebes, who put two of their generals on trial for their lives for having kept arms past the precise term of their commission. They only just pardoned Pelopidas, who bowed under the weight of so dangerous a charge and offered no defence but prayers and supplications; while Epaminondas, by contrast, launched grandly into a recital of the great deeds he had done in their service, and reproached them haughtily and arrogantly for ingratitude and injustice — and they had not the heart to push the trial further, broke up the court, and went home, the assembly loudly praising the man's high courage.

Who besieged Guelph of Bavaria and would concede nothing but that the women in the town might walk out on foot with what they could carry — and wept for joy when they carried out their husbands, their children and the duke himself, and gave up the hatred he had conceived against him.

It may be true that letting one's heart be wholly conquered by compassion can be put down to weakness, softness, and over-tenderness — which is why the weaker natures, women, children, and the common sort, are the most susceptible to it. But to have resisted and scorned the power of groans and tears, and then to yield only to the bare reverence of the sacred image of Valour — this can only be the work of a strong and inflexible soul in love with and honouring masculine, obstinate courage. Even so, astonishment and admiration may produce a similar effect in less generous minds. Witness the people of Thebes, who put two of their generals on trial for their lives for having kept arms past the precise term of their commission. They only just pardoned Pelopidas, who bowed under the weight of so dangerous a charge and offered no defence but prayers and supplications; while Epaminondas, by contrast, launched grandly into a recital of the great deeds he had done in their service, and reproached them haughtily and arrogantly for ingratitude and injustice — and they had not the heart to push the trial further, broke up the court, and went home, the assembly loudly praising the man's high courage.

Besieged by Conrad III and carried out of his own town on the shoulders of the women, whose stratagem made the emperor his friend.

## modern-en · dionysius-elder · 1:4

Dionysius the Elder, after a long siege and great difficulty, took the city of Reggio and with it the governor Phyton, a very gallant man whose defence had been unyielding. Dionysius decided to make a tragic example of his revenge. He began by telling Phyton that he had, the day before, ordered his son and all his relatives drowned. Phyton's only reply was that they were by one day happier than he was. Dionysius then had him stripped and handed to the tormentors, who dragged him through the streets of the town and most cruelly whipped him, all the while heaping bitter insults on him. He kept his courage intact the whole way, voice strong and face undaunted, declaring out loud the honourable and glorious cause of his death: that he would not surrender his country into the hands of a tyrant. And he called down on Dionysius a swift punishment from the offended gods. Reading in his soldiers' faces that, far from being offended by the prisoner's haughty speech to the contempt of their captain and his triumph, they were struck with admiration for so rare a virtue and inclined to mutiny — even ready to rescue the prisoner from the executioner — Dionysius stopped the torture and, in private, had Phyton thrown into the sea.

The tyrant of Syracuse. He took Reggio and its governor Phyton, told him his son and kindred had been drowned the day before, and had him whipped naked through the streets — and when he read in his own soldiers’ faces that they admired the man and were ready to rescue him, stopped the torture and had him drowned in private. Montaigne returns to him among the men who died of joy.

Man, in truth, is a marvellously vain, fickle, and unstable subject, and one on whom it is very hard to form any certain and uniform judgment. ## modern-en · alexander · 1:6

And, directly contrary to my first examples, the bravest of all men, the one most famous for clemency to those he overcame — Alexander — after great difficulty stormed the city of Gaza. Entering, he found Betis, its commander, of whose valour during the siege he had had striking and repeated proof, standing alone, abandoned by his soldiers, his armour hacked to pieces, drenched in blood and wounds, and still fighting in a crowd of Macedonians striking him from every side. Alexander, nettled at so dear-bought a victory — he had two fresh wounds of his own — said to him: 'You shall not die as you intend, Betis. You shall suffer every torment that can be inflicted on a captive.' To which Betis answered only with a fierce and disdainful look. 'What,' said Alexander, watching his haughty, obstinate silence, 'is he too stiff to bend a knee? Too proud to utter one suppliant word? Then I will conquer this silence. If I cannot force a word from his mouth, I will at least extract a groan from his heart.' And turning his anger into fury, he ordered Betis's heels bored through and had him dragged alive, mangled and torn apart, at the back of a cart. Was it that the height of courage was so natural and familiar to this conqueror that, since he could not admire it, he respected it less? Or that he held valour to be so peculiarly his own that his pride could not, without envy, endure it in another? Or that the natural impetuosity of his fury was simply incapable of opposition? Surely, had it been capable of moderation, the sack and ruin of Thebes would have moderated it: to see so many valiant men, lost and without further defence, slaughtered before his eyes — above six thousand put to the sword, of whom not one was seen to flee or heard to cry for quarter, but every one running here and there to seek out the victorious enemy and provoke them to give him an honourable end. Not one was seen who, however weakened by wounds, did not in his last gasp still try to take revenge, and with all the weapons of a brave despair to sweeten his own death in the death of an enemy. Yet their valour drew no pity, and the length of one day was not enough to satisfy the conqueror's thirst for revenge. The slaughter went on to the last drop of blood that could be shed, and stopped only when it met none but unarmed people — old men, women, and children — thirty thousand of whom were carried away as slaves.

Alexander the Great, whom Montaigne calls the bravest of all men and who was reputed gracious to those he overcame — and who had Betis of Gaza’s heels bored through and the man dragged to death at a cart’s tail for refusing to speak. Montaigne asks whether valour was so familiar to him that he respected it the less, or so peculiarly his own that he could not endure it in another.

## modern-en · psammenitus · 2:1

The story goes that Psammenitus, King of Egypt, was defeated and taken prisoner by Cambyses, King of Persia. When his own daughter passed by him as a prisoner, in a wretched dress, carrying a bucket to draw water, his friends around him broke down in tears and lamentation; he himself stayed unmoved, said nothing, and kept his eyes on the ground. He kept the same face when, moments later, he saw his son led to execution. But when at last he spotted one of his own household friends being dragged off among the captives, he tore at his hair and beat his breast with all the extravagance of extreme grief.

The King of Egypt taken prisoner by Cambyses, who watched his daughter go by as a slave and his son led to execution without a word or a change of face, and broke down only at the sight of one of his own household among the captives — because, he said, that grief alone was small enough to be shown by tears.

Something like this may have been working in the imagination of the ancient painter who, in painting the sacrifice of Iphigenia, had to show the sorrow of those standing by in proportion to the interest each had in the death of this beautiful innocent girl. Agamemnon’s daughter, whose sacrifice the ancient painter painted by laying out all his art on the grief of the onlookers and then drawing her father with a veil over his face, no countenance being capable of that degree of sorrow.

## modern-en · ferdinand · 2:9

In Ferdinand's war against the widow of King John of Hungary, around Buda, a man-at-arms drew everyone's notice for his singular gallantry in a particular encounter; he was widely praised and mourned when he was left dead on the field — and by no one more than Raisciac, a German lord who had been deeply taken with so rare a valour. When the body was brought off and the count, out of common curiosity, came to look at it, the armour was no sooner removed than he recognised his own son — a thing that added a second blow to the compassion of all the bystanders. Without saying a word, without taking his eyes from the wretched object, he stood fixedly contemplating the body of his son, until the violence of his sorrow overcame his vital spirits and dropped him stone-dead to the ground.

Who made war about Buda on the widow of King John of Hungary — the campaign in which Raisciac lost his son.

## modern-en · sophocles · 2:21

Besides the Roman lady who died of joy when she saw her son safe back from the defeat at Cannae, and Sophocles, and Dionysius the Tyrant, who died of joy, and Thalna, who died in Corsica reading the news of the honours the Roman Senate had decreed in his favour — we have, even in our own time, the example of Pope Leo X, who on hearing of the taking of Milan (a thing he had wanted with all his heart) was seized with so sudden an excess of joy that he immediately fell into a fever and died. And for a more striking testimony to the weakness of our human nature, it is recorded by the ancients that Diodorus the dialectician dropped dead on the spot, from sheer overwhelming shame at not having been able, in his own school and in the presence of a great audience, to extricate himself from a nice argument that had been put to him. The Athenian tragedian, and one of Montaigne’s examples of men who died of joy. Montaigne cannot acquiesce in the judgment of the man who, against the accusation of Sophocles’s son, concluded him capable of managing his domestic affairs from having read one of his tragedies.

## modern-en · plato · 3:4

We find this great rule repeated often in Plato: "Do your own work, and know yourself." Each part contains all our duty between them, and each in its way involves the other; for whoever will do his own work properly will find that his first lesson is to know what he is and what is proper to him, and whoever rightly understands himself will never mistake another man's work for his own — he will love and improve himself above all else, refuse superfluous employments, and put aside all useless thoughts and propositions. As folly, on one side, even if it had everything it desired, would never be content, so wisdom, settling for what is present, is never dissatisfied with itself. Epicurus excuses his sages from all foresight and care of the future.

The Athenian philosopher, Socrates’s pupil, and with Cicero the writer Montaigne quotes most. He is an authority and an adversary in the same breath: Montaigne takes “Do thine own work, and know thyself” from him and calls a good deal of the rest of him poetry.

## modern-en · livy · 3:5

Among the laws relating to the dead, I think this a very sound one: that the actions of princes be examined after their death. They are equal with the laws, when not above them, and therefore what justice could not inflict on their persons it is only reasonable should fall on their reputations and on the estates of their successors — things we often value above life itself. This is a custom of singular advantage to the countries that use it, and one all good princes should welcome, for they have reason to be offended that the memories of the wicked should be treated with the same reverence as their own. We owe submission and obedience to all our kings, good or bad alike, for that has to do with their office; but esteem and affection are owed only to their virtue. Grant to political government that we endure unworthy rulers with patience, conceal their vices, and lend our recommendation to their indifferent actions while their authority still needs our support. But once the relation of prince and subject is over, there is no reason to deny our true opinions their voice, in the name of liberty and common justice; least of all to deny good subjects the glory of having served reverently and faithfully a prince whose imperfections they knew very well, since that would be to deprive posterity of a useful example. And those who, out of some private obligation, unjustly take up and defend the memory of a faulty prince serve a private interest at the cost of public justice. Livy says, very truly, that the language of men brought up in courts is always full of vain display and false witness: every one indifferently exalts his own master and stretches his praise to the utmost extent of virtue and sovereign greatness. Some may condemn the boldness of those two soldiers who answered Nero so roundly to his face. The one, asked why he hated him, said: "I loved you while you were worth it. Since you have become a parricide, an incendiary, a player, and a coachman, I hate you as you deserve." And the other, asked why he had tried to kill him, said: "Because I could think of no other remedy against your endless mischief." But the public, universal testimony given of Nero after his death (and which will go on being given of him, and of every other wicked prince like him, to all posterity) of his tyrannies and abominable conduct — who, in his sound judgment, can object to it?

The Roman historian of the city from its foundation. The older edition writes him Titus Livius at 66:0 and 73:70, and misprints him Titius Livius at 62:18, where the modern edition has the name right.

## modern-en · aristotle · 3:7

Aristotle, who must have a finger in everything, raises a question about Solon's saying that no one can be called happy until he is dead: whether someone who has lived and died according to his heart's desire, but has left a bad name behind him and a miserable line of descendants, can really be called happy. As long as we have life and movement we can carry ourselves in fancy and preoccupation wherever we please; but once we are out of being, we have no further communication with what is — and so Solon would have done better to say that no one is ever happy, since he cannot really be so until he is no more.

The philosopher of the schools, whom Montaigne calls the god of scholastic learning and who, he says, will still have a hand in everything.

## modern-en · bertrand-du-guesclin · 3:10

Bertrand du Guesclin, dying at the siege of the Castle of Rancon, near Le Puy in Auvergne, the besieged were ordered after surrender to lay the keys of the place upon the dead general's body. When Bartolommeo d'Alviano, the Venetian general, happened to die in the service of the Republic at Brescia, and his body had to be carried through the territory of Verona — enemy country — most of the army was inclined to ask the Veronese for safe-conduct. Theodoro Trivulzio opposed it, preferring to force a passage by arms and risk a battle, saying it was not fitting that one who had never feared his enemies in life should seem to fear them in death. Under Greek law, in fact, anyone who applied to an enemy for a body to bury it forfeited his victory and could no longer set up a trophy, while the one applied to was reckoned the winner. By this Nicias lost the advantage he had visibly gained over the Corinthians; and Agesilaus, by the same rule, secured an advantage over the Boeotians that he had only doubtfully earned in the field.

The French general who died at the siege of the Castle of Rancon, and on whose corpse the besieged were made to lay down the keys of the place when they surrendered.

## modern-en · edward-i · 3:11

These things might seem strange if it had not been the general practice in every age, not only to extend our concern with ourselves beyond this life, but to imagine that heaven's favour does not merely often accompany us to the grave but, after life is over, takes an interest in our ashes. There are so many ancient examples of this — leaving aside what we see in our own time — that I need not labour the point. Edward I, King of England, in his long wars against Robert, King of Scotland, had experience of how decisive his own presence in person was to the success of his enterprises, having always been victorious in whatever he undertook in person; when he was dying he bound his son by solemn oath that as soon as he was dead his body should be boiled until the flesh came off the bones, and the flesh buried while the bones were preserved to be carried with the army whenever it had to march against the Scots — as if destiny had inevitably attached victory even to his remains. John Zizka, the same man who, in defence of Wycliffe's heresies, threw the Bohemian state into turmoil, left orders that he be flayed after his death and his skin made into a drum to be carried in war against his enemies, in the belief that it would contribute to the continuation of the successes he had always had against them. In the same way, certain of the Indians, in their battles with the Spaniards, carried with them the bones of one of their captains, on account of the victories they had once won under his command. And other peoples in that same New World carry with them in war the relics of brave men who had died in battle, to fire their courage and improve their luck. In the first kind of example, what was reserved for the tomb was only the reputation earned by past achievement; in the others, an active power is still attributed to the dead.

Who had found in his long wars with Robert of Scotland that his own presence decided everything, and made his son swear to boil his body, bury the flesh, and carry the bones with the army whenever it marched against the Scots.

## modern-en · bayard · 3:12

Captain Bayard's behaviour is of a better grain. Mortally wounded by a harquebus shot and pressed to retire from the fight, he answered that he would not begin at the last gasp to turn his back on the enemy. Mortally wounded by a harquebuss shot and urged to retire, he answered that he would not begin at the last gasp to turn his back on the enemy, and had himself set down at the foot of a tree with his face to them. Montaigne asks in the chapter on names who would believe that Captain Bayard should have no honour but what he derives from the deeds of Peter Terrail — the two names being one man.

## modern-en · maximilian-i · 3:13

I must add another example, no less striking than any of the rest for the present matter. The Emperor Maximilian, great-grandfather of the present King Philip, was a prince in whom great and uncommon qualities were everywhere mixed, including a singular personal beauty; but he had one habit very contrary to that of other princes, who for the despatch of their most important affairs turn the close-stool into a chair of state. He would not let any of his bedchamber, however familiar, see him in that posture, and would steal aside to make water as scrupulously as a virgin, shy of letting his physician or anyone else see those parts we are accustomed to conceal. I myself — for all the unembarrassed way I talk — am naturally so modest in this that, except under the pressure of necessity or pleasure, I scarcely ever let anyone see those parts or actions custom requires us to conceal: I suffer here more constraint than I think is becoming in a man, and especially in one of my profession. Maximilian fostered this modest humour to a degree of superstition: he gave express orders in his last will that they should put drawers on him as soon as he was dead — to which, I think, he might as well have added that the man who put them on should also be blindfolded. The charge Cyrus left with his children, that neither they nor anyone else should see or touch his body once the soul had left it, I put down to some superstitious devotion of his; for both Cyrus and his historian were noted throughout their great qualities for a singular respect and reverence for religion.

A prince of great qualities and singular beauty of person, and so modest about his body that he would let nobody see him at the close-stool, and gave orders in his will that they should put drawers on him as soon as he was dead. Great-grandfather to King Philip of Spain, and father to Don Philip.

## modern-en · marcus-aemilius-lepidus · 3:15

Another, contrary curiosity (and there is no shortage of examples in my own family) seems somehow akin to this one: that a man should rack his brains in his last moments to plan obsequies of so peculiarly studied a frugality as to have one servant with a lantern. I see this humour praised, and the arrangement of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who forbade his heirs to spend on his funeral even the common ceremonies usual on such occasions. Is it really temperance and frugality to avoid expense and pleasure when the use and knowledge of them is imperceptible to us? An easy and cheap reformation. If guidance were needed here, I would say that in this, as in every other action of life, each person ought to regulate the matter according to his fortune. The philosopher Lycon prudently told his friends to dispose of his body wherever they thought best, and as for the funeral, to make it neither too superfluous nor too mean. For my part, I would leave the ordering of this ceremony entirely to custom, and shall, when the time comes, leave it to the discretion of whoever has to do me that last office. "Totus hic locus est contemnendus in nobis, non negligendus in nostris"; and a saint said this, very holily: "Curatio funeris, conditio sepulturae: pompa exequiarum, magis sunt vivorum solatia, quam subsidia mortuorum." Which made Socrates answer Crito, who asked him at his death how he wished to be buried: "However you like." If I were to occupy myself beyond the present with this affair at all, I should be most tempted, as the highest pleasure of this kind, to imitate those who in their lifetime entertain themselves with the ceremony and honours of their own obsequies in advance, and take pleasure in looking at their own dead face in marble. Happy are they who can gratify their senses by insensibility, and live by their death.

Who forbade his heirs to spend on his hearse even the ceremonies customary at a funeral.

I am ready to feel an implacable hatred for every form of popular rule, though I think it the most natural and equitable of all, every time I remember the inhuman injustice of the people of Athens, who, without any hearing or vouchsafing the men a word in their defence, put to death their brave captains just returned in triumph from a naval victory they had won over the Lacedaemonians near the Arginusae Isles — the bloodiest and most stubborn engagement the Greeks ever fought at sea. He asked the gods to turn this sentence to their good, and prayed that, for his and his companions' failure to fulfil the vows they had made (which he then named) in thanks for so glorious a victory, the gods' anger might not fall on them. One of the Athenian captains condemned after the victory at the Arginusae for not staying to bury their dead. Allowed to speak at last, he said nothing of his own cause or of the cruelty of the sentence, but asked the gods to turn it to his judges’ good and prayed that their neglect of the vows he and his companions had made might not be visited on the city; and went to his death.

## modern-en · augustus · 4:10

I remember a story going around when I was a boy — that one of our neighbouring kings, having received a blow from the hand of God, swore he would have his revenge, and to that end issued a proclamation that for the next ten years no one should pray to Him, or so much as mention Him throughout his dominions, or, as far as his authority went, believe in Him; by which they meant to paint not so much the folly as the vainglory of the nation the tale was told about. The two vices always travel together, but in truth such actions have in them still more presumption than want of wit. Augustus Caesar, having been tossed about by a storm at sea, took to defying Neptune, and during the pomp of the Circensian games, by way of revenge, removed his statue from its place among the other deities. In which he was still less excusable than the man before him, and less so than he was again later when, having lost a battle under Quintilius Varus in Germany, in rage and despair he ran his head against the wall, crying out, "Varus, give me back my legions!" These outdo all folly, since impiety is now added to them — invading God himself, or at least Fortune, as if she had ears subject to our batteries; like the Thracians who, when it thunders or lightens, fall to shooting against heaven with Titan-like vengeance, as if by flights of arrows they meant to bring God to reason. Even though the ancient poet in Plutarch tells us —

The first Roman emperor, Julius Caesar’s heir. ## modern-en · quintus-marcius · 5:0

Quintus Marcius, the Roman legate in the war against Perseus, King of Macedon, in order to gain time to reinforce his army, put out some openings for an accommodation, by which the king was lulled into agreeing to a truce of several days — long enough to give his enemy the opportunity and leisure to recruit fresh forces, which was the cause of the king's final ruin. Yet the elder senators, mindful of their forefathers' ways, condemned this procedure as a falling-off from their ancient practice, which, they said, was to fight by valour, not by trickery, surprises, or night-encounters; not by feigned flight or sudden rallies to overcome the enemy; and never to make war without first proclaiming it, often setting both the hour and the place of battle. It was on this generous principle that they handed Pyrrhus's treacherous physician back to him, and the Etruscans' disloyal schoolmaster back to them. This was a truly Roman procedure, with no resemblance to Greek subtlety or to Punic cunning, where it was reckoned a less glorious victory to overcome by force than by fraud. Deceit may serve in a pinch, but only that man can truly admit he has been beaten who knows he has been overcome neither by policy nor by accident, but by sheer valour, man to man, in fair and just war. It clearly appears from the talk of those good old senators that this fine line had not yet found its way among them:

The Roman legate against Perseus of Macedon, who opened sham overtures of accommodation to gain time to reinforce, and was condemned for it by the elder senators as degenerating from the Roman practice of fighting by valour and not by artifice.

## modern-en · lysander · 5:9

For our part, we are less scrupulous about such things, and grant the honour of war to whoever profits by it. We say, with Lysander, that "where the lion's skin is too short, we must eke it out with a piece of the fox's," and the most common openings for surprise come from this practice. There are no moments when a commander needs to be more on his guard than during parleys and negotiations for accommodation. From which it has become a general rule among the soldiers of recent times that the governor of a place under siege should never go out to parley. It was for breaking this rule that, in our fathers' day, the Seigneurs de Montmord and de l'Assigny, defending Mousson against the Count of Nassau, were so harshly criticised. Even so, it might be excusable in a governor who, when he goes out, does so in a way that keeps the safety and the advantage on his own side — as Count Guido di Rangone did at Reggio (if we believe Du Bellay; Guicciardini says it was Guicciardini himself) when the Seigneur de l'Escut came up to parley. He stepped so little away from his fort that, when a disturbance broke out during the parley, not only did Monsieur de l'Escut and his party — who had advanced with him — find themselves much the weaker (so much so that Alessandro Trivulzio was killed there), but l'Escut himself was glad to follow the count and, trusting to his honour, take cover behind the walls of the town from the danger of the shot.

The Spartan admiral, whose maxim Montaigne quotes for his own countrymen: where the lion’s skin is too short, eke it out with a piece of the fox’s.

Even so, it might be excusable in a governor who, when he goes out, does so in a way that keeps the safety and the advantage on his own side — as Count Guido di Rangone did at Reggio (if we believe Du Bellay; Guicciardini says it was Guicciardini himself) when the Seigneur de l'Escut came up to parley. He stepped so little away from his fort that, when a disturbance broke out during the parley, not only did Monsieur de l'Escut and his party — who had advanced with him — find themselves much the weaker (so much so that Alessandro Trivulzio was killed there), but l'Escut himself was glad to follow the count and, trusting to his honour, take cover behind the walls of the town from the danger of the shot.

The Florentine historian, who tells the Reggio story against Du Bellay’s version.

## modern-en · lucius-aemilius-regillus · 6:1

Lucius Aemilius Regillus, the Roman praetor, having wasted his time trying to take the city of Phocaea by force because of the extraordinary courage with which the inhabitants defended themselves, agreed at last to receive them as friends of the people of Rome and to enter the town as he would enter a confederate city, with no kind of hostility — and gave them all the assurances they asked for. But once he had, for the greater pomp, brought his whole army in with him, it was no longer in his power, however hard he tried, to restrain his men. Cleomenes used to say that whatever harm a man could do his enemy in wartime was above justice and not accountable to it in the sight of gods or men. Socrates’s disciple and a soldier — both a great captain and a philosopher of the first form, as Montaigne puts it. His licence about stratagems in war is more than Montaigne will follow.

## modern-en · aubigny · 6:5

Monsieur d'Aubigny, besieging Capua and pounding it with a furious battery, found that Signor Fabrizio Colonna, the governor of the town, had begun a parley from a bastion. And more recently, at Yvoy, Signor Giuliano Romero, playing the novice by going out to parley with the Constable, found his place taken at his return. But, that we should not get off scot-free, the Marquess of Pescara, laying siege to Genoa where Duke Ottaviano Fregoso commanded under our protection, had the terms between them so far advanced that the matter was looked on as done and on the point of being concluded — and then the Spaniards slipped in and used this treachery as an outright victory. And since, at Ligny in Barrois, where the Count de Brienne was in command, when the emperor in person besieged the place and Bertheville, the count's lieutenant, went out to parley, the town was taken while he was negotiating.

Who was battering Capua when his soldiers, slack in their guard during a parley, let the French into the place unawares.

## modern-en · chrysippus · 6:8

But the philosopher Chrysippus held the opposite view, and I share it. He used to say that those who run a race ought to put all their force into what they are doing and run as fast as they can; but that it is by no means fair to lay a hand on a rival to slow him, or stick out a leg to trip him up. And more generous still was the answer of the great Alexander to Polypercon, who urged him to take advantage of the night's darkness to fall on Darius: "Not at all," he said; "it is not for such a man as I am to steal a victory. Malo me fortunae poeniteat, quam victoria pudeat."

The Stoic philosopher who held that a runner should use every force he has, but may not lay a hand on his adversary to stop him or set a leg before him to throw him down. Montaigne agrees.

## modern-en · henry-vii · 7:0

There is a saying that death discharges us of all our obligations. I know some who have taken it in another sense. Henry VII of England agreed with Don Philip, son of the emperor Maximilian — or, to give him a more honourable title, father of the Emperor Charles V — that Philip should hand over the Duke of Suffolk of the White Rose, Henry's enemy, who had fled into the Low Countries. Philip duly did so, but on condition that Henry would not attempt the duke's life. But when Henry came to die, he commanded his son in his last will to put the duke to death as soon as he himself was dead. And lately, in the tragedy the Duke of Alva put on for us at Brussels in the persons of the Counts Horn and Egmont, there were several striking moments. One in particular: Count Egmont (on whose word and faith Count Horn had come and surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva) earnestly asked to be allowed to mount the scaffold first, so that death might discharge him of the obligation he had given the other. In that case it seems to me that death did not in fact acquit the former of his promise, and that the latter was discharged from it without dying. We cannot be bound beyond what we are able to perform, since effect and performance are not really in our power: indeed the only thing we are masters of is the will, and on the will, by necessity, all the rules and the whole duty of mankind are founded and established. Count Egmont, therefore, regarding his soul and his will as still bound by his promise even though he had not the power to make it good, would no doubt have been absolved of his duty even if he had outlived the other. But the King of England, who deliberately and with full intent broke his faith, was no more to be excused for putting off the execution of his infidelity until after his death than the mason in Herodotus, who kept the secret of his master the King of Egypt's treasure inviolate during his lifetime but at his own death revealed it to his children.

Who got the Duke of Suffolk delivered into his hands on condition that he attempt nothing against the man’s life, and then commanded his son in his will to put him to death as soon as he himself was dead. Montaigne will not allow that death excused the broken faith.

## modern-en · count-horn · 7:0

There is a saying that death discharges us of all our obligations. I know some who have taken it in another sense. Henry VII of England agreed with Don Philip, son of the emperor Maximilian — or, to give him a more honourable title, father of the Emperor Charles V — that Philip should hand over the Duke of Suffolk of the White Rose, Henry's enemy, who had fled into the Low Countries. Philip duly did so, but on condition that Henry would not attempt the duke's life. But when Henry came to die, he commanded his son in his last will to put the duke to death as soon as he himself was dead. And lately, in the tragedy the Duke of Alva put on for us at Brussels in the persons of the Counts Horn and Egmont, there were several striking moments. One in particular: Count Egmont (on whose word and faith Count Horn had come and surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva) earnestly asked to be allowed to mount the scaffold first, so that death might discharge him of the obligation he had given the other. In that case it seems to me that death did not in fact acquit the former of his promise, and that the latter was discharged from it without dying. We cannot be bound beyond what we are able to perform, since effect and performance are not really in our power: indeed the only thing we are masters of is the will, and on the will, by necessity, all the rules and the whole duty of mankind are founded and established. Count Egmont, therefore, regarding his soul and his will as still bound by his promise even though he had not the power to make it good, would no doubt have been absolved of his duty even if he had outlived the other. But the King of England, who deliberately and with full intent broke his faith, was no more to be excused for putting off the execution of his infidelity until after his death than the mason in Herodotus, who kept the secret of his master the King of Egypt's treasure inviolate during his lifetime but at his own death revealed it to his children.

Who surrendered himself to the Duke of Alva on Count Egmont’s security, and was executed with him at Brussels.

## modern-en · francis-i · 9:8

King Francis I boasted that he had by this means tied up Francesco Taverna, the ambassador of Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan — a man very famous in his day for his skill in talking. This gentleman had been sent to excuse his master to His Majesty in a very serious business, which was this: the king, in order to keep up some intelligence in Italy, out of which he had lately been driven, and particularly with the Duchy of Milan, had thought it convenient to keep a gentleman of his own on hand with the duke — an ambassador in effect, but in outward appearance a private person who was supposed to be residing there on his own affairs. The duke, being much more dependent on the emperor (especially while he was negotiating his marriage with the emperor's niece, daughter of the King of Denmark, who is now the dowager of Lorraine), could not show any open dealings or conferences with us without serious risk. For this commission, one Merveille, a Milanese gentleman and an equerry of the king, was thought very suitable, and was sent there with private credentials and instructions as ambassador, along with other letters of recommendation to the duke concerning his own private affairs, the better to mask and colour the business. He was so long at that court that the emperor at last got wind of his real employment there — which was the cause, we suppose, of what followed: under pretext of some murder, his trial was dispatched in two days, and his head was struck off in prison at night. Messire Francesco arrived in France prepared with a long counterfeit account of the affair (for the king had applied to all the princes of Christendom, as well as to the duke himself, to demand satisfaction) and was given his audience at the morning council. There, after he had laid out several plausible justifications of the fact in support of his case — that his master had never looked on Merveille as anything but a private gentleman and his own subject, who was there only on his own business, and had never lived under any other character; absolutely denying that he had ever heard he was a member of the king's household, or that His Majesty so much as knew him, so far was he from taking him for an ambassador — the king, pressing him in turn with several objections and demands and challenging him from every side, tripped him up at last by asking, then, why the execution had been carried out at night, and as it were by stealth. At which the poor confounded ambassador, the more elegantly to extricate himself, replied that the duke would have been very loath, out of respect for His Majesty, to have such an execution carried out by day. One can imagine how he was scolded when he got home, for having so grossly tripped in the presence of a prince of so delicate a nose as King Francis.

Francis I of France, a prince, Montaigne says, of so delicate a nostril that he caught Francesco Taverna out in a single question, and who was still keeping a secret agent in Milan when Merveille was beheaded there.

## modern-en · julius-ii · 9:9

Pope Julius II, having sent an ambassador to the King of England to stir him up against King Francis, had his ambassador heard. Before he would give an answer, the king urged the difficulties he would meet in setting on foot so great a preparation as would be needed to attack so powerful a king, and gave his reasons. The ambassador very unseasonably replied that he too had considered the same difficulties and had laid them before the pope. From this saying, so directly contrary to the matter in hand and the business he had come for (which was simply to incite the king to war), the King of England first drew the conclusion (which he later found to be true) that this ambassador, in his own heart, was on the French side. ## modern-en · clement-vii · 10:3

Just as we teach young ladies the sports and exercises best fitted to show off the grace and beauty of those parts where their chief charm and perfection lie, so it should be with these two advantages of eloquence which the lawyers and preachers of our age principally lay claim to. If I were worthy to advise, the slow speaker, it seems to me, would be better suited to the pulpit and the other to the bar — for the preacher's office naturally allows him all the leisure he might want to prepare himself, and his career runs in an even, uninterrupted line, with no break or stop, whereas the pleader's business and interest compels him to enter the lists on every occasion, and the unexpected objections and replies of his opponent throw him out of his course and force him, on the instant, to think up new and extempore answers and defences. Yet at the meeting between Pope Clement and King Francis at Marseilles, it happened quite the contrary: Monsieur Poyet, a man who had spent his whole life at the bar and had the highest reputation for eloquence, was charged with making the address to the pope. Having so long meditated it beforehand that, they say, he brought it ready-made with him from Paris, on the very day it was to be delivered the pope, fearing that something might be said that would give offence to the other princes' ambassadors who were attending him there, sent word to the king of the line he thought best suited to the time and place — quite another thing, as it happened, from what Monsieur de Poyet had taken so much trouble over. So that the fine speech he had prepared was no use, and he had to come up with another on the spot, which, finding himself unable to do, Cardinal du Bellay had to step in and perform that office. The pleader's part is no doubt much harder than the preacher's, and yet, in my view, we see in France more passable lawyers than preachers. It seems that wit's nature is to be prompt and sudden in its operations, while judgment is more deliberate and slow. But he who stays totally silent for want of leisure to prepare himself to speak well, and he whom leisure does not help to better speech, are equally unfortunate.

Who at the interview with King Francis at Marseilles sent word of the argument he thought suitable, and so wasted the harangue Poyet had been preparing since Paris.

## modern-en · severus-cassius · 10:4

It is said of Severus Cassius that he spoke best extempore, that he owed more to fortune than to his own diligence; that it was an advantage to him to be interrupted in speaking, and that his opponents were afraid to provoke him, lest his anger should redouble his eloquence. I know from experience a temperament of nature so impatient of any tedious and elaborate preparation that, unless it goes frankly and gaily about its work, it cannot do anything to purpose. We say of certain compositions that they smell of the oil and the lamp, because of a certain rough harshness that laborious handling stamps on whatever it has been used on. Beyond this, the anxiety of doing well, and the kind of straining and striving of a mind too far stretched and overbent on its task, breaks and frustrates itself like water that, by the force of its own pressing violence and abundance, cannot find a ready way out through the neck of a bottle or a narrow sluice. In the kind of nature I am now speaking of, there is this too — that it would not be disordered and stimulated by such passions as the fury of Cassius (such a motion would be too violent and rough); it would not be jostled, but coaxed; it would be roused and warmed by unexpected, sudden, and accidental occasions. Left to itself, it flags and languishes; agitation alone gives it grace and vigour. I am always at my worst in my own possession, and when wholly at my own disposal: chance has more claim on whatever comes from me than I do; occasion, company, and even the very rising and falling of my own voice draw more out of my mind than I can find when I sound and apply it by myself. So the things I say are better than those I write, if either were worth choosing where neither is worth much. This also happens to me: that I do not find myself where I look for myself, and I hit on things more by chance than by any active search of my own judgment. I sometimes happen to write something that strikes me as neat and lively, though it will appear dull and heavy to someone else — but enough of these fine compliments; every man talks like this of himself, according to his talent. When I come to speak, however, I am already so lost that I do not know what I was about to say, and on these occasions a stranger has often spotted it before me. If I made an erasure every time this inconvenience overtook me, I should leave nothing standing; occasion, on some other day, will lay the thought as plain to me as the light, and make me wonder why I should have hesitated.

Who spoke best extempore and owed more to fortune than to diligence: it was an advantage to him to be interrupted, and his adversaries were afraid to nettle him for fear his anger should redouble his eloquence. He is also the intimate friend who, seeing Labienus’s books burned, cried out that they would have to burn him too, since he carried them by heart. The older edition prints his name both ways round, Severus Cassius at 10:4 and Cassius Severus at 65:39.

## modern-en · francesco-saluzzo · 11:14

— yet they carry far less authority now than they used to. Which makes all the more remarkable the case of Francesco, Marquis of Saluzzo, lieutenant to King Francis I in his ultramontane army, much favoured and respected at our court, and beholden to the king's bounty for the very marquisate itself, which had been forfeited by his brother. With no real provocation given him, and with his own affection set against any such disloyalty, he let himself be terrified, as the report ran, by the fine forecasts that were being put out everywhere in favour of the Emperor Charles V, and to our disadvantage — especially in Italy, where these foolish prophecies were so far believed that at Rome large sums of money were being wagered on the returns when the prognostics came true, so sure were they of our ruin. Having often bewailed to those of his closest acquaintance the disasters he saw bound to fall on the Crown of France and on the friends he had at that court, he revolted and went over to the other side — to his own misfortune, however, whatever stars were ruling at the time. But he carried himself in this affair like a man pulled by different passions: with towns and forces in his hands, the enemy's army under Antonio de Leyva close by him, and we suspecting nothing of his design, it had been in his power to do far more than he did. We lost no men through this faithlessness of his, nor any town except Fossano, and that only after a long siege and a brave defence.

Lieutenant to Francis I in the army beyond the mountains, holding the marquisate by the king’s gift, with no provocation to turn and his own affection against it — and frightened into revolt, it was said, by the prognostics that everyone was spreading in Charles V’s favour. Montaigne notes that with towns and troops in his hands he could have done far more harm than he did.

## modern-en · tages · 11:27

The famous art of divination among the Tuscans began like this: a labourer, striking deep into the earth with his ploughshare, saw the demi-god Tages rise up, with an infant's face but armed with mature and senile wisdom. On the rumour of this, all the people came running to see the sight, and his words and science — containing the principles and means of attaining this art — were recorded and kept for many ages. A birth in keeping with its later course. For my part, I would sooner regulate my affairs by the throw of a die than by such idle and empty dreams. And indeed, in every republic, a good share of the government has always been left to chance. Plato, in the civil polity he models on his own fancy, leaves it to decide several matters of great importance, and is willing, among other things, that marriages should be assigned by lot; he attaches such weight to this accidental choice as to require that the children born in such weddings be brought up in the country, and that those born in any other wedding be cast out as illegitimate and base. He adds, however, that if any of those exiles, as they grow, give signs of merit, they may be recalled; and that some of those who were kept may, in the same way, be exiled if they show little promise as they grow up.

The demigod who rose out of a furrow with an infant’s face and an old man’s wisdom, and dictated the principles of Tuscan divination to the people who came running to look at him. Montaigne says the birth suits the art.

## modern-en · diogenes-the-atheist · 11:31

I think no better of them for some such accidental hit. There would be more certainty about it if there were a rule, and a truth, of always lying. Shown, in the temple at Samothrace, the offerings and painted stories of men saved from shipwreck by the gods’ especial favour, he answered that the pictures of those who were cast away are not here, and they are by much the greater number.

## modern-en · xenophanes-colophon · 11:32

Cicero observes that of all the philosophers who have acknowledged a deity, only Xenophanes of Colophon has tried to root out every kind of divination — which makes it less of a wonder if we have now and then seen some of our princes, sometimes to their own cost, lean too heavily on these vanities. I would have given anything to see with my own eyes those two great marvels: the book of Joachim, the Calabrian abbot, which foretold all the future popes, with their names and characters; and that of the Emperor Leo, which prophesied all the emperors and patriarchs of Greece. This much I have witnessed myself: that in times of public confusion, men astonished at their fortune abandon their own reason and superstitiously seek out in the stars the ancient causes and warnings of their present troubles. In my time they have been so strangely successful in this that it has made me believe — this being an amusement for sharp and volatile minds — that those skilled at this knack of unfolding and untying riddles are capable of finding in any kind of writing whatever they wish. But above all, the greatest room for play is given them by the obscure, ambiguous, and fantastical gibberish of prophetic jargon, where the authors deliver nothing of clear sense but shroud everything in riddles, so that posterity may interpret and apply them according to its own fancy.

The only philosopher who acknowledged a deity and still tried to root out divination altogether — as Cicero observes, and Montaigne with him.

## modern-en · laches · 12:1

Several very warlike nations have used a retreating and flying way of fighting as a singular advantage, and by doing so have made their backs more dangerous to their enemies than their faces. The Turks still keep something of this in their practice of arms. Socrates, in Plato, laughs at Laches, who had defined fortitude as standing firm in the ranks against the enemy. "What!" he says, "would it then be cowardice to overcome them by giving ground?" — urging at the same time the authority of Homer, who praises in Aeneas the science of flight. And when Laches, thinking better of it, admits the practice as it applies to the Scythians and, in general, to all cavalry, Socrates attacks him again with the example of the Lacedaemonian foot — a nation of all others the most stubborn in holding their ground — who, at the battle of Plataea, finding they could not break into the Persian phalanx, decided to scatter and retreat, so that the enemy, supposing they fled, should break up and disunite that great mass of men in pursuit; and by this stratagem they won the victory.

Who defined fortitude in Plato as standing firm in the ranks, and was laughed out of it by Socrates: would it be cowardice, then, to beat the enemy by giving ground? The same man who fled beside Socrates after the rout at Delium, and whose bearing in the retreat Alcibiades sets against his friend’s steady march. The older edition writes him Lachez there.

## modern-en · idanthyrses · 12:2

As for the Scythians, it is said that when Darius marched out to subdue them, he sent a herald to reproach their king with always retiring before him and avoiding battle. Idanthyrses — that was the king's name — answered that it was not for fear of him or any man living that he did so, but that it was the way of marching practised by his nation, who had neither tilled fields, nor cities, nor houses to defend, nor anything they need fear the enemy might profit by; but, if he had such a stomach to fight, let him just come to view their ancient burial places, and there he should have his fill.

## modern-en · guast · 12:3

Nevertheless, against cannon-fire, when a body of men is drawn up in front of a train of artillery — as the demands of war often require — it is unbecoming to leave one's post to avoid the danger, since because of its violence and swiftness we reckon it inevitable; and many a man, by ducking, stepping aside, and other such motions of fear, has been thoroughly laughed at by his companions. And yet, in the campaign the Emperor Charles V made into Provence against us, the Marquis del Guasto, going to reconnoitre the city of Arles and stepping out from behind the cover of a windmill under which he had made his approach, was spotted by the Seigneur de Bonneval and the Seneschal of Agenais, who were walking on the theatre aux arenes. They pointed him out to the Sieur de Villiers, commissary of the artillery, who pointed a culverin so admirably well and aimed it so exactly that, had the marquis not slipped aside when he saw the match put to it, it was reckoned certain the shot would have taken him full in the body. And in the same way, some years earlier, Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino and father of the queen-mother, laying siege to Mondolfo, a place in the territories of the Vicariate in Italy, saw the gunner put the match to a piece pointed straight at him. It was well for him that he ducked, for otherwise the shot, which only grazed the top of his head, would no doubt have hit him full in the chest. To tell the truth, I do not think these evasions are performed out of any judgment, for how can any man living judge of high or low aim on so sudden an occasion? It is much easier to believe that fortune favoured their apprehension, and that it might just as well, on another occasion, lead them to face the danger as to seek to avoid it. For my own part, I confess I cannot help starting when the rattle of a harquebus thunders in my ears suddenly, and in a place where I had not expected it — something I have observed in others too, braver fellows than I.

Who went to reconnoitre Arles from behind a windmill and was spotted; the culverin was so exactly levelled at him that only his seeing the fire given and slipping aside saved him.

## modern-en · margaret-of-navarre · 13:0

There is no subject so trivial that it does not deserve a place in this rhapsody. By our common rule of civility, it would be a marked insult to an equal, and much more to a superior, to fail to be at home when he has told you he will come to visit. Queen Margaret of Navarre adds, further, that it would be a rudeness in a gentleman to go out, as we so often do, to meet a man who is coming to see him, however high his condition may be; that it is more respectful and more civil to stay at home to receive him, if only to avoid missing him on the road, and that it is enough to receive him at the door and to attend on him there. For my part, anxious as I am to reduce the ceremonies of my house, I very often forget both these vain offices. If by chance someone is offended at this, I cannot help it; better to offend him once than to offend myself every day, for it would be a perpetual slavery. To what end do we avoid the servile attendance of courts, if we bring the same trouble back into our own private houses? It is also a common rule at all assemblies that the lesser sort should be on the place first, since it is more fitting to the better sort to make others wait and expect them.

Who held that a gentleman is rude to go out and meet a visitor, and that it is more civil to stay at home and receive him at the door.

## modern-en · montmorency · 14:1

The Constable Monsieur de Montmorency, having at the siege of Pavia been ordered to cross the Ticino and take up his quarters in the Faubourg St Antonio, was held up by a tower at the end of the bridge so stubborn as to endure a battery; for which he hanged every man he found inside. General of the army at Dreux, where he was racked through and through with the enemy’s artillery, his battalion routed and himself taken prisoner, while the Duc de Guise halted with the forces he commanded; and who at the siege of Pavia hanged every man in the tower that had held up his crossing of the Ticino, and later trussed up the governor and ensign of the Castle of Villano for the same reason — the custom Montaigne is explaining, that a place not tenable by the rules of war may be defended only at the defenders’ own risk.

## modern-en · vervins · 15:0

I once heard tell of a prince, and a great captain, who, when at his table the proceedings against Monsieur de Vervins were related to him — Vervins had been sentenced to death for surrendering Boulogne to the English — openly maintained that a soldier cannot justly be put to death for lack of courage. And, in truth, there is reason to make a great distinction between faults that merely proceed from weakness and those that are clearly the effects of treachery and malice. In the latter, we act against the rules of reason that nature has imprinted in us; whereas, in the former, it seems we might appeal to the same nature, which left us in such a state of imperfection and weakness of courage, in our own defence. So that many have thought we ought to be answerable only for what we commit against our conscience; and it is partly on this rule that those base their opinion who disapprove of capital or bloody punishments for heretics and unbelievers, and those also who hold that a judge is not accountable for having failed in his administration through mere ignorance.

Sentenced to death for surrendering Boulogne to the English — the case that prompted a great captain to maintain, at table, that no soldier can justly be put to death for want of courage.
