## modern-en · ammianus-marcellinus · 15:4

It also appears that the Roman laws once punished those with death who had run away; for Ammianus Marcellinus says that the Emperor Julian commanded ten of his soldiers, who had turned their backs in an encounter against the Parthians, to be first degraded, and afterwards put to death, in accordance, he says, with the ancient laws. And yet elsewhere, for the same kind of offence, he only condemned others to remain among the prisoners under the baggage ensign. The harsh punishment that the people of Rome inflicted on those who fled from the battle of Cannae, and on those who ran away with Cnaeus Fulvius at his defeat, did not extend to death. And yet I think there is a danger that disgrace may make such offenders desperate, and turn them not merely into half-hearted friends but into actual enemies.

The historian, who says the Emperor Julian had ten soldiers that turned their backs against the Parthians first degraded and then put to death, and who observes the manner of the Parthians’ arming so curiously because it was so different from the Roman. Not the Tullius Marcellinus of chapter 70.

Of recent memory, the Seigneur de Franget, lieutenant to the Maréchal de Châtillon's company, having by the Maréchal de Chabannes been put in charge of Fuenterrabia in place of Monsieur de Lude, and having surrendered it to the Spaniards, was for this condemned to be stripped of all nobility, and both he and his descendants declared base, taxable, and forever incapable of bearing arms — a severe sentence afterwards duly executed at Lyon. And since, all the gentlemen who were in Guise when the Count of Nassau entered it underwent the same punishment, as several others have done since for the like offence. For it often happens, on the contrary, that everyone would rather hold forth on someone else's province than on his own, thinking it so much extra reputation acquired — witness the jeer Archidamus put upon Periander, that "he had given up the glory of being an excellent physician for the reputation of a very bad poet." And just observe how lavish and full Caesar is when he wants to make us understand his inventions for building bridges and contriving engines of war, and how succinct and reserved by comparison when he speaks of the offices of his profession, his own valour, and military conduct. His deeds prove him a great captain well enough, and he knew this; but he also wanted to be thought an excellent engineer — a quality somewhat outside the field, and not one we should look for in him. The elder Dionysius was a very great captain, as his fortune required; but he took a great deal of trouble to gain a private reputation as a poet, and yet he was never cut out for one. A man of the legal profession, brought not long ago to see a study furnished with all sorts of books, on his own subject and on every other, took no interest at all in any of them, but fell rather rudely and magisterially to comment on a barricade set across the spiral staircase in front of the door of the study — a thing a hundred captains and common soldiers see every day without noticing or finding fault with.

The Spartan king who told Periander that he had given up the glory of being an excellent physician to gain the repute of a very bad poet — and who was a little surprised, Montaigne fancies, at Thucydides’s answer when he asked which was the better wrestler, Pericles or himself: that it was hard to affirm, for when he had thrown him Pericles always persuaded the spectators he had had no fall, and carried away the prize.

## modern-en · langey · 16:8

Which is why (something I would have lightly passed over in another writer) I lingered over and carefully considered one passage in the history written by Monsieur de Langey, a man of very great judgment in matters of that kind. After giving an account of the fine oration Charles V had made in the Consistory at Rome, in the presence of the Bishop of Macon and Monsieur du Velly, our ambassadors there, in which he had mixed in several injurious expressions to the dishonour of our nation — and, among the rest, "that if his captains and soldiers were not men of another stamp of fidelity, resolution, and skill in arms than those of the king, he would put a rope round his neck and immediately go to him to beg for mercy" (and the emperor seems really to have held this, or only a very slightly better, opinion of our military men, for he afterwards, twice or three times in his life, said the very same thing); as also, that he challenged the king to fight him in his shirt, with rapier and dagger, in a boat. The said Sieur de Langey, going on with his history, adds that the said ambassadors, sending a dispatch to the king on these matters, concealed the greater part, and in particular the last two passages. At which I could not but wonder, that it should be in an ambassador's power to suppress anything he ought to convey to his master, especially something of such importance as this, coming from the mouth of such a person and spoken in so great an assembly. And I should rather have thought it the servant's duty faithfully to lay the whole matter before him as it passed, so that the liberty of selecting, arranging, judging, and concluding should remain with him. For to conceal or disguise the truth out of fear that he may take it otherwise than he ought, and out of fear it may prompt him to some extreme resolution — and in the meantime to leave him in the dark about his own affairs — seems to me to belong rather to the man who is to give the law than to the one who is only to receive it; to the one in supreme command, and not to one who ought to regard himself as inferior, not only in authority but also in prudence and good counsel. I, for my part, would not be served so even in my own small affairs.

The historian of the French wars whose account of Charles V’s speech in the Consistory at Rome Montaigne dwells on, because the ambassadors who heard it sent home a despatch with the worst of it left out.

## modern-en · publius-crassus · 16:9

We so willingly slip the collar of command on any pretext, and are so ready to usurp dominion, every one of us so naturally aspires to liberty and power, that no advantage a superior gets from the wit or valour of those he employs ought to be as dear to him as a straightforward and sincere obedience. To obey by reason of one's own understanding rather than out of subjection is to corrupt the office of command. So it was that Publius Crassus, the man whom the Romans reckoned five times happy, when he was consul in Asia sent for a Greek engineer to bring him the larger of two ships' masts he had noticed at Athens, for use in some battery engine he meant to make. The engineer, presuming on his own skill and sufficiency in such matters, thought fit to do otherwise than directed, and brought the smaller one, which, by the rules of his art, was really more proper for the use in hand. But Crassus, though he listened to his reasons very patiently, would not, however well-grounded they were, take them as current pay, but had him soundly whipped for his pains, valuing the interest of discipline far more than the interest of the work in hand.

Whom the Romans reputed five times happy. Consul in Asia, he sent a Greek engineer for the greater of two ships’ masts, and had the man whipped for bringing the lesser — which was, by the rules of art, the fitter of the two. Montaigne sets discipline against the work in hand and then, at the end of the chapter, wonders whether Crassus had not invited the man’s judgment after all.

## modern-en · bourbon · 17:2

I am not naturalist enough (as they call it) to make out by what secret springs fear has its motion in us; but, that aside, it is a strange passion, and one that the physicians say there is no other that more quickly dethrones our judgment from its proper seat. So true is this that I myself have seen many people become frantic with fear, and even in those of the steadiest temper it is certain that during the fit it produces a terrible bewilderment and confusion. I leave aside the common run of people, to whom it represents one moment their great-grandfathers risen from their graves in their shrouds, and another moment werewolves, nightmares, and chimeras. But even among soldiers — a sort of men over whom fear, of all others, ought to have the least power — how often has it turned flocks of sheep into armed squadrons, reeds and bulrushes into pikes and lances, friends into enemies, and the white cross of France into the red cross of Spain! When Monsieur de Bourbon took Rome, an ensign on guard at Borgo San Pietro was seized with such fright at the first alarm that he threw himself out at a breach with his colours on his shoulder and ran straight toward the enemy, thinking he had retreated towards the inner defences of the city; and only with great trouble, when he saw Monsieur de Bourbon's men, who took it for a sally upon them, drawing up to receive him, did he at last come to himself and realise his mistake. Then facing about, he retreated at top speed back through the same breach by which he had come out, but only after he had first blindly advanced more than three hundred paces into the open field. It did not turn out so well with Captain Giulio's ensign at the time when St Paul was taken from us by the Count of Bures and Monsieur de Reu, for he, so amazed with fear that he flung himself, colours and all, out of a port-hole, was immediately cut to pieces by the enemy. And in the same siege there was a very memorable fear that so seized, contracted, and froze up the heart of a gentleman that he sank down, stone-dead, in the breach, without any manner of wound or hurt at all. The like madness sometimes pushes on a whole multitude: for in one of the encounters Germanicus had with the Germans, two great parties were so seized with fear that they ran two opposite ways, the one to the very place from which the other had fled. Sometimes fear adds wings to the heels, as in the first two cases; sometimes it nails them to the ground and fetters them from moving, as we read of the Emperor Theophilus, who in a battle he lost against the Agarenes was so astonished and stupefied that he had no power to fly —

Who took Rome — the sack in which an ensign on guard at Borgo San Pietro ran three hundred paces the wrong way in a fright, colours on his shoulder, and had to run back through the same breach.

## modern-en · manuel · 17:5

— until Manuel, one of the principal commanders of his army, having jogged and shaken him to bring him out of his trance, said to him: "Sir, if you will not follow me, I will kill you, for it is better that you should lose your life than, by being taken, lose your empire." But fear shows its utmost power when it drives us into a valiant despair, having first stripped us of all sense of duty and honour. In the first pitched battle the Romans lost against Hannibal, under the consul Sempronius, a body of ten thousand foot that had taken fright, seeing no other escape for their cowardice, threw themselves headlong on the great battalion of the enemy, and with marvellous force and fury charged through and through it, routing it with a very great slaughter of the Carthaginians — buying themselves an inglorious flight at the same price they might have gained a glorious victory.

One of Theophilus’s principal commanders, who told his stupefied emperor that it was better to lose his life than, by being taken, to lose his empire.

## modern-en · croesus · 18:3

Even children know the story of King Croesus on this point. Taken prisoner by Cyrus and condemned by him to die, on his way to execution he cried out, "O Solon, Solon!" When this was reported to Cyrus, who sent to ask what it meant, Croesus explained that he was now finding, to his cost, how true the lesson Solon had once given him had been — namely, "that, however fortune may smile upon them, men can never be called happy until they have been seen to pass over the last day of their lives," because of the uncertainty and mutability of human things, which on the smallest and most trivial occasions are liable to be entirely changed into the contrary condition. And so it was that Agesilaus answered someone saying what a happy young man the King of Persia was, to come so young to so mighty a kingdom: "Yes," he said, "but neither was Priam unhappy at his years." In a short time, kings of Macedon, successors of that great Alexander, became carpenters and scribes at Rome; a tyrant of Sicily a schoolmaster at Corinth; a conqueror of half the world and general of so many armies, a wretched suppliant to the rascally officers of a king of Egypt — so much did the prolongation of five or six months of life cost the great Pompey. And in our fathers' days, Ludovico Sforza, the tenth Duke of Milan, under whom all Italy had so long bowed, was seen to die a wretched prisoner at Loches, but not until he had lived ten years in captivity, which was the worst part of his fortune. The fairest of all queens, widow to the greatest king in Europe — did she not come to die at the hand of an executioner? Unworthy and barbarous cruelty. And a thousand other examples there are of the same kind. It seems that, just as storms and tempests have a malice against the proud and overtowering heights of our lofty buildings, there are also spirits above that are envious of the greatnesses here below:

The King of Lydia, taken by Cyrus and led out to execution crying “O Solon, Solon!” — because he had found what Solon told him true to his cost: that no man can be called happy until he has been seen to pass over the last day of his life. Marching his army through the waste lands near Sardis he met an infinite number of serpents, which his horses devoured with great appetite; Herodotus calls it a prodigy of ominous portent to his affairs.

This is why, at this last moment, all the other actions of our life are to be tested and sifted. It is the master-day; it is the day that is judge of all the rest. "It is the day," says one of the ancients, "that must be judge of all my preceding years." To death I refer the assaying of the fruit of all my studies; then we shall see whether my discourses came only from my mouth, or from my heart. I have seen many men by their dying give a good or a bad name to their whole life. Scipio, Pompey's father-in-law, in dying well, removed the ill opinion everyone had until then conceived of him. Epaminondas, asked which of three he most esteemed, Chabrias, Iphicrates, or himself, said: "You must first see us die before that question can be answered." And indeed it would be a great wrong to weigh him without the honour and grandeur of his end.

Pompey’s father-in-law, who by the manner of his dying removed the ill opinion everyone had held of him until then.

## modern-en · xenophilus · 19:5

Now, of all the benefits virtue confers on us, contempt of death is one of the greatest, because it is what fits human life with a soft and easy tranquillity, and gives us a pure and pleasant taste of living, without which all other pleasures would be extinguished. This is why all the rules centre and converge on this one article. And although they all likewise teach us, by common accord, to despise pain, poverty, and the other accidents human life is subject to, it is not with the same urgency — partly because those accidents are not so inevitable (the greater part of mankind pass their whole lives without ever knowing what poverty is, and some without sorrow or sickness, like Xenophilus the musician, who lived a hundred and six years in perfect and continual health); and partly because, at the worst, death can whenever we please cut short and put an end to all other inconveniences. ## modern-en · methuselah · 19:21

The Romans, finding that this poor syllable death sounded so harshly to their ears and seemed so ominous, found a way to soften and spin it out by a circumlocution. Instead of saying "So-and-so is dead," they said "So-and-so has lived," or "So-and-so has ceased to live" — for, provided there was any mention of life in the phrase, even past life, it carried some sound of consolation. From them we borrowed our expression, "The late Monsieur So-and-so." Perhaps, as the saying goes, the words we have lived are worth our money. I was born between eleven and twelve o'clock in the forenoon on the last day of February 1533, by our reckoning, which begins the year on the 1st of January; and it is now just fifteen days since I turned thirty-nine years old, complete. I expect to live, at least, as many more. In the meantime, it would be folly to trouble myself with the thought of a thing so far off. But what? Young and old die on the same terms; no one leaves life otherwise than as if he had just entered it. And no man is so old and decrepit that, having heard of Methuselah, he does not think he has another twenty good years to come. Fool that you are! Who has guaranteed you the term of your life? You depend on physicians' tales: rather consult facts and experience. By the common course of things, you have for some time been living by extraordinary favour; you have already outlived the ordinary span. To prove it, count up your acquaintances and see how many more have died before reaching your age than have made it; and of those who ennobled their lives by their fame, just keep a tally, and I will lay you a wager you will find more who died before than after thirty-five. It is both reasonable and pious to take Jesus Christ Himself for an example: He ended His life at thirty-three. The greatest man who was no more than a man, Alexander, died also at the same age. How many ways death has to surprise us!

Whose years are the reason, Montaigne says, that no man is so old and decrepit that he does not think he has twenty good ones left.

## modern-en · aeschylus · 19:24

To say nothing of fevers and pleurisies, who would ever have imagined that a Duke of Brittany would be crushed to death in a crowd, as that duke was at the entry of Pope Clement, my neighbour, into Lyons? Have you not seen one of our kings killed at a tilting match, and one of his ancestors die from being jostled by a hog? Aeschylus, warned of being killed by the fall of a house, took every possible precaution — and was knocked on the head by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle's talons in the air. Another man was choked by a grape-seed; an emperor was killed by the scratch of a comb while combing his hair. Aemilius Lepidus died by stumbling at his own threshold, and Aufidius by knocking against the door as he entered the council chamber. And between the very thighs of women: Cornelius Gallus the praetor; Tigillinus, captain of the watch at Rome; Ludovico, son of Guido di Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua; and (a worse example) Speusippus, a Platonic philosopher, and one of our Popes. Poor Judge Bebius granted a postponement in a case for eight days; but in the meantime he himself was condemned by death, and his own stay of life expired. While Caius Julius the physician was anointing the eyes of a patient, death closed his own. And if I may bring in an example of my own blood: a brother of mine, Captain St. Martin, a young man of twenty-three who had already given sufficient proof of his courage, was playing a match at tennis when he received a blow from a ball a little above his right ear. As it left no sign of wound or bruise, he took no notice and did not even sit down to rest; nevertheless he died within five or six hours of an apoplexy caused by that blow.

Who took care to avoid the house that was threatening to fall on him, and was killed by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle’s talons.

Aeschylus, warned of being killed by the fall of a house, took every possible precaution — and was knocked on the head by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle's talons in the air. Another man was choked by a grape-seed; an emperor was killed by the scratch of a comb while combing his hair. Aemilius Lepidus died by stumbling at his own threshold, and Aufidius by knocking against the door as he entered the council chamber. And between the very thighs of women: Cornelius Gallus the praetor; Tigillinus, captain of the watch at Rome; Ludovico, son of Guido di Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua; and (a worse example) Speusippus, a Platonic philosopher, and one of our Popes. Poor Judge Bebius granted a postponement in a case for eight days; but in the meantime he himself was condemned by death, and his own stay of life expired. While Caius Julius the physician was anointing the eyes of a patient, death closed his own. And if I may bring in an example of my own blood: a brother of mine, Captain St. Martin, a young man of twenty-three who had already given sufficient proof of his courage, was playing a match at tennis when he received a blow from a ball a little above his right ear. As it left no sign of wound or bruise, he took no notice and did not even sit down to rest; nevertheless he died within five or six hours of an apoplexy caused by that blow.

Montaigne’s brother, twenty-three years old and already proved in the field, who took a tennis ball a little above the right ear, felt no wound, did not even sit down — and died of an apoplexy five or six hours later.

## modern-en · thales · 19:122

"To what purpose should you try to draw back, if there is no way to evade it? You have seen plenty of examples of those who were well content to die, as thereby delivered from heavy miseries; but have you ever found any who were dissatisfied with dying? It must therefore be very foolish to condemn a thing you have not experienced either in your own person or in anyone else's. Why do you complain of me and of destiny? Do we do you any wrong? Is it for you to govern us, or for us to govern you? Though, perhaps, your years are not complete, yet your life is. A man of small stature is as much a man as a giant; neither men nor their lives are measured by the yard. Chiron refused to be immortal when he was told the conditions on which he was to enjoy it, by the god of time itself and its duration, his father Saturn. Just seriously consider how much more unbearable and painful an immortal life would be to man than the life I have already given him. If you had not death, you would eternally curse me for having deprived you of it. I have mixed a little bitterness with it, so that, seeing how convenient it is, you might not too greedily and indiscreetly seek to embrace it; and so that you might be so settled in this moderation as neither to be sick of life nor to have any antipathy for dying — which I have decreed you shall do once — I have tempered both of them between pleasure and pain. It was I that taught Thales, the most eminent of your sages, that to live and to die were indifferent, which made him, very wisely, answer the man who asked him why he did not die: 'Because,' he said, 'it is indifferent.' Water, earth, air, and fire, and the other parts of this creation of mine, are no more instruments of your life than they are of your death. Why do you fear your last day? It contributes no more to your dissolution than every one of the rest. The last step is not the cause of your weariness; it only declares it. Every day travels towards death; the last only arrives at it." These are the good lessons our mother Nature teaches.

The most eminent of the sages, whom Nature taught that living and dying were indifferent — which is why, asked why then he did not die, he answered: because it is indifferent.

## modern-en · simon-thomas · 20:2

I am one of those who feel the power of imagination most strongly. Everyone is jostled by it, but some are knocked flat by it. It makes a very piercing impression upon me, and I make it my business to dodge it, lacking the strength to resist. I could live by the help of cheerful, healthy company alone: the mere sight of another's pain materially pains me, and I often take over the sensations of another person. A perpetual cough in someone else tickles my own lungs and throat. I more unwillingly visit a sick person I love and owe duty to than one I am indifferent about. I take possession of the disease I am concerned with, and lodge it in myself. I am not at all surprised that fancy gives fevers and sometimes kills people who give it too much scope and are too willing to indulge it. Simon Thomas was a great physician of his day. I remember meeting him one day at Toulouse at the house of a rich old fellow troubled with weak lungs. Discussing the method of cure with the patient, the doctor told him that one helpful thing would be for him to give me reason to enjoy his company so much that I would come often to see him; by which means, fixing his eyes on my fresh complexion and his imagination on the sprightliness and vigour glowing in my youth, and filling all his senses with the flourishing age I was then in, his bodily state might perhaps be improved. But the doctor forgot to say that mine, at the same time, might be made worse. Gallus Vibius bent his mind so hard on finding out the essence and motions of madness that, in the end, he went out of his wits himself, and to such a degree that he could never afterwards recover his judgment, and might boast he had become a fool by too much wisdom. Some men, through fear, anticipate the hangman; and there was the man whose eyes, on being unbound to have his pardon read to him, were found stark dead upon the scaffold, by the stroke of imagination alone. We start, tremble, turn pale, and blush as we are variously moved by imagination; and lying in bed we feel our bodies stirred by its power to such a degree that we sometimes expire from it. And boiling youth, when fast asleep, grows so heated with fancy as in a dream to satisfy amorous desires:

A great physician of his time, who prescribed Montaigne’s company to a rich old man with weak lungs — that the sight of a fresh complexion and the imagination of a young man’s vigour might mend his habit of body. He forgot to add, Montaigne says, that it might make the young man’s worse.

## modern-en · cippus · 20:4

Though it is no new thing to see horns grown overnight on the forehead of one who had none when he went to bed, what happened to Cippus, King of Italy, is memorable: having one day been a delighted spectator at a bullfight, and having dreamed all night that he had horns on his head, he actually, by force of imagination, caused them to grow there. Passion gave to the son of Croesus the voice that nature had denied him. And Antiochus fell into a fever, inflamed by the beauty of Stratonice too deeply imprinted in his soul. Pliny claims to have seen Lucius Cossitius, who from a woman was turned into a man on her wedding day itself. Pontanus and others report a similar metamorphosis happening in our own time in Italy. And, through the vehement desire of himself and his mother:

Who watched a bullfight with delight, dreamed all night that he had horns on his head, and by the force of imagination grew them.

## modern-en · mary-germain · 20:6

I myself, passing through Vitry-le-François, saw a man whom the Bishop of Soissons had named Germain in confirmation, whom all the inhabitants of the place had known to be a girl until the age of twenty-two, called Mary. He was, at the time I was there, full of beard, old, and unmarried. He told us that by straining himself in a leap his male organs had come out; and the girls of the place have, to this day, a song warning each other not to take too great strides, for fear of being turned into men, as Mary Germain was. It is no wonder if this kind of accident happens often; for if imagination has any power in such matters, the desire is so continually and vigorously fixed on this subject that, in order not to relapse into the same thought and violence of longing, it would be better, once for all, to give these young girls the things they crave.

The man the Bishop of Soissons confirmed as Germain, whom the whole town had known as a girl called Mary until she was twenty-two. Montaigne saw him at Vitry le François, full of beard, old and unmarried; he said his male organs came out when he strained himself in a leap, and the girls of the place still have a song warning each other against taking too great strides.

## modern-en · dagobert · 20:7

Some attribute the scars of King Dagobert and of St. Francis to the force of imagination. It is said that by it bodies will sometimes be moved from their places; and Celsus tells us of a priest whose soul would be carried away into such an ecstasy that his body would for a long time remain without sense or breath. St. Augustine mentions another who, on hearing any lamentable or doleful cries, would immediately fall into a swoon and be so far out of himself that it was no use calling out, bawling in his ears, pinching or burning him until he voluntarily came to. Then he would say he had heard voices as it were far off, and had felt them pinching and burning him; and, to show that this was no obstinate dissimulation in defiance of his sense of feeling, it was clear that all the while he had neither pulse nor breath.

Whose scars, with St Francis’s, some attribute to the force of imagination.

## modern-en · jacques-pelletier · 20:10

A Count of a very great family, with whom I was very intimate, had married a fair lady who had previously been courted by a man present at the wedding. All his friends were in great fear — especially an old lady, a kinswoman of his, who was directing the ceremony and in whose house it was held — that the rival would play foul with sorcery. She told me her fear. I told her to leave it to me. I happened to have on me a flat plate of gold engraved with certain celestial figures, supposed to be good against sunstroke or headache when applied to the suture; to keep it firm, it was sewed to a ribbon to be tied under the chin — a piece of nonsense closely related to the one I am speaking of. Jacques Pelletier, who lived in my house, had presented it to me as a rare curiosity. I had a fancy to make some use of this trinket, and so privately told the Count that he might possibly run the same fortune other bridegrooms had run, especially since someone was in the house who would no doubt be glad to do him such a service. But let him go boldly to bed: I would do him the office of a friend, and, if needed, would not spare a miracle in my power, provided he would swear on his honour to keep it to himself; only, when they came to bring him his caudle, if matters had not gone well, to give me such-and-such a sign, and leave the rest to me. Now his ears had been so battered, and his mind so prepossessed with the endless chatter on the subject, that when the moment came, he did indeed find himself tied by the trouble of his imagination, and at the appointed time gave me the sign. Whereupon I whispered in his ear that he should get up, on the pretence of putting us out of the room, and in a jesting way pull my nightgown off my shoulders — we were of much the same height — throw it over his own, and keep it on him until he had carried out what I directed: which was that, when we had all gone out of the chamber, he should withdraw to make water, repeat three times such and such words and as often perform such and such actions; that each of the three times he should tie the ribbon I had put into his hand around his waist, and be sure to place the medal fastened to it, with the figures in a certain posture, exactly upon his loins; and that, having on the last of the three times tied the ribbon so tight that it could neither untie nor slip, he should confidently return to his business — and, by the way, not forget to spread my gown over the bed so that it would be sure to cover them both. These monkey-tricks are the main of the effect: our fancy is so easily seduced as to believe that such strange means must necessarily come from some abstruse science; their very emptiness gives them weight and reverence. And it is certain that my figures showed themselves to be more venereal than solar, more active than prohibitive. It was a sudden whim, mixed with a little curiosity, that made me do something so contrary to my nature: for I am an enemy to all subtle and counterfeit actions, and detest all kinds of trickery, though for sport and to someone's benefit; for though the action may not be vicious in itself, the manner is.

Who lived in Montaigne’s house and gave him the graven gold plate against sunstroke that Montaigne then used, with some private instructions and his own nightgown, to cure a bridegroom of an imagined impotence.

## modern-en · amasis · 20:11

Amasis, King of Egypt, having married Laodice, a very beautiful Greek virgin, although otherwise known for his abilities, found himself quite another man with his wife and could not by any means enjoy her; at which he was so enraged that he threatened to kill her, suspecting her of witchcraft. As is usual in matters of fancy, she put him onto devotion; and having made his vows to Venus, he found himself divinely restored the very first night after his offerings and sacrifices. Now women are to blame to greet us with that disdainful, coy, and angry face which extinguishes our vigour even as it kindles our desire — which made the daughter-in-law of Pythagoras say that "the woman who goes to bed with a man must put off her modesty with her petticoat, and put it back on with it." The soul of the assailant, agitated by many alarms at once, readily loses the power of performance; and once the imagination has played this trick on a man and shamed him (which it never does except at the first encounter, since men are then more ardent and eager, and at this first account a man gives of himself, he is much more afraid of failing), having made a bad start, he falls into such fever and vexation at the accident that it tends to remain with him on subsequent occasions.

Who married the beautiful Greek Laodice, found himself quite another man with her, threatened to kill her for a witch — and after vows to Venus was divinely restored the first night after his sacrifices.

The soul of the assailant, agitated by many alarms at once, readily loses the power of performance; and once the imagination has played this trick on a man and shamed him (which it never does except at the first encounter, since men are then more ardent and eager, and at this first account a man gives of himself, he is much more afraid of failing), having made a bad start, he falls into such fever and vexation at the accident that it tends to remain with him on subsequent occasions.

The Greek virgin Amasis married and at first could not enjoy.

## modern-en · vives · 20:13

The unruly freedom of this member is very remarkable — so importunately ungovernable in its swelling and impatience when we have no need of it, and so unseasonably disobedient when we stand most in need of it; so imperiously contending in authority with the will, and with such haughty obstinacy refusing all our solicitation, both of hand and mind. And yet, though his rebellion is so universally complained of, and proof drawn from it to condemn him, if he had retained me to plead his cause, I should perhaps bring the rest of his fellow members under suspicion of conspiring against him out of pure envy at the importance and pleasure peculiar to his employment, and of having, by collusion, armed the whole world against him by maliciously charging him alone with their common offence. For let anyone consider whether there is any one part of our bodies that does not often refuse to perform its office at the will's command, and that does not often exercise its function in defiance of her command. Every one of them has passions of its own, that rouse and waken, stupefy and benumb them, without our consent. How often do involuntary movements of the face betray our inward thoughts, and disclose our most private secrets to bystanders. The same cause that animates this member also, without our knowledge, animates the lungs, the pulse, and the heart, the sight of a pleasing object imperceptibly spreading a flame through all our parts with a feverish motion. Is it only these veins and muscles that swell and slacken without the consent not only of the will but even of our knowledge? We do not command our hairs to stand on end, nor our skin to shiver with fear or desire; the hands often go to parts we do not direct them to; the tongue will be tied and the voice frozen when we do not know how to help it. When we have nothing to eat and would willingly suppress it, the appetite does not on that account stop stirring up the parts that are subject to it, no more, no less, than the other appetite we were speaking of; and likewise unseasonably leaves us when it thinks fit. The vessels that serve to discharge the belly have their own dilations and compressions, without and beyond our concurrence, just as do those that serve to purge the kidneys; and what St. Augustine offers, to vindicate the prerogative of the will, of having seen a man who could on command release his rear as often as he pleased, Vives, his commentator, further reinforces with another example from his own day — of a man who could break wind in tune. But these cases do not prove any more pure obedience in that part; for is anything commonly more tumultuous or indiscreet? To which let me add that I myself knew a man so rude and ungovernable that for forty years together he made his master vent with one continuous, uninterrupted outburst, and it is likely will do so till he dies of it. And I could heartily wish I only knew by reading how often a man's belly, by holding back a single puff, brings him to the very door of an exceedingly painful death; and that the emperor who gave free leave to break wind anywhere had at the same time given us the power to do it. But for our will, on whose behalf we are prosecuting, with how much greater probability may we reproach her herself with mutiny and sedition, for her irregularity and disobedience? Does she always will what we would have her will? Does she not often will what we forbid her to will, and to our manifest harm? Does she suffer herself, any more than the rest, to be governed and directed by the conclusions of our reason? To conclude, I should move, in defence of the gentleman my client, that in this matter his cause being inseparably and indistinctly joined with an accomplice, he alone is called in question, and that by arguments and accusations which cannot be charged on the other — whose business it is sometimes inopportunely to invite, but never to refuse, and to invite, moreover, in a tacit and quiet manner; and therefore the malice and injustice of his accusers are most plainly apparent. It is the same with beasts: witness Jacob's sheep, and the hares and partridges that the snow turns white on the mountains. There was at my house, a little while ago, a cat seen watching a bird at the top of a tree: after they had for some time fixed their eyes on each other, the bird at last let herself fall, dead, into the cat's claws — either dazzled by the force of her own imagination, or drawn by some attractive power of the cat. Those addicted to the pleasures of the field have no doubt heard the story of the falconer who, having earnestly fixed his eyes on a kite in the air, laid a wager that he could bring her down by the sole power of his sight, and did so, as it was said — for the tales I borrow I lay upon the consciences of those from whom I have them. The reasonings are mine, and rest on the proofs of reason, not of experience; to which everyone is at liberty to add his own examples. Whoever has none, let him not refuse, given the number and variety of accidents, to believe that there are plenty of them; if I do not apply them well, let someone else do so for me. Likewise, in the subject I am treating — our manners and motions — testimonies and instances, however fabulous, serve as well as the true, provided they are possible; whether they really happened or not, at Rome or Paris, to John or Peter, they are still within the range of human capacity, which is enough for me. I see and make my advantage of it, in shadow as well as in substance; and among the various readings of history, I cull out the most rare and memorable to fit my own turn. There are authors whose sole aim and design is to give an account of things that have happened; mine, if I could reach it, would be to deliver what may happen. There is a just liberty in the schools, of supposing similitudes when they have none at hand. I do not, however, make any use of that privilege, and in this matter, by a religious scrupulousness, I surpass all historical authority. In the examples I bring in of what I have heard, read, done, or said, I have forbidden myself to dare to alter even the most trivial and indifferent circumstances; my conscience does not falsify a syllable; what my ignorance may do, I cannot say.

Whose sheep are Montaigne’s scriptural instance that a mother’s fancy marks what she carries.

## modern-en · isocrates · 22:25

Whoever would disengage himself from this violent prejudice of custom would find several things received with absolute and undoubting opinion that have no other support than the grizzled head and wrinkled face of ancient usage. But the mask once off, and things being referred to the decision of truth and reason, he will find his judgment, as it were, altogether overturned, and yet restored to a much surer footing. For example, I shall ask him what can be more strange than to see a people obliged to obey laws they never understood; bound in all their domestic affairs — marriages, gifts, wills, sales, and purchases — to rules they cannot possibly know, being neither written nor published in their own language, and of which they are forced to purchase both the interpretation and the use? Not according to the ingenious opinion of Isocrates, who counselled his king to make the trades and dealings of his subjects free, frank, and profitable to them, and their quarrels and disputes burdensome, weighed down with heavy charges and penalties — but, by a prodigious opinion, to make sale of reason itself, and treat laws as merchandise. I think myself indebted to fortune that, as our historians report, it was a Gascon gentleman, a countryman of mine, who first opposed Charlemagne when he tried to impose on us Latin and imperial laws.

The Athenian rhetorician, who counselled his king to make his subjects’ trade free and their lawsuits expensive, and who says that defect is nearer allied to moderation than excess.

## modern-en · thyestes · 22:24

Once, taking it on myself to justify something in use among us, accepted with absolute authority for many leagues round about, and not content, as men commonly do, to establish it merely by force of law and example but inquiring still further into its origin, I found the foundation so weak that I, whose business it was to confirm others, was very near being dissatisfied myself. It is by this same prescription that Plato sets out to cure the unnatural and preposterous loves of his time, treating it as a sovereign remedy — namely, that public opinion condemns them; that poets and all other kinds of writers tell horrible stories about them; a recipe by virtue of which the most beautiful daughters no more allure their fathers' lust, nor brothers of the finest shape and figure their sisters' desire; the very fables of Thyestes, Oedipus, and Macareus, with the harmony of their song, infusing this wholesome opinion and belief into the tender brains of children. Chastity is, in truth, a great and shining virtue, the usefulness of which is sufficiently known; but to treat it, and set it off in its true value, according to nature, is as hard as it is easy to do so according to custom, laws, and precepts. The fundamental and universal reasons are of very obscure and difficult research, and our masters either lightly pass over them, or, not daring even to touch them, throw themselves into the liberty and protection of custom, where they puff themselves up and triumph to their heart's content. Those who refuse to be drawn off from this original source commit a still greater error, and deliver themselves to wild opinions — witness Chrysippus, who, in so many of his writings, scattered the little account he made of incestuous unions, with however near a relation.

One of the three fables — with Oedipus and Macareus — by which, Montaigne says following Plato, the poets put a wholesome horror of incest into children’s heads.

## modern-en · thucydides · 22:33

Those who give the first shock to a state are almost naturally the first overwhelmed in its ruin. The fruits of public commotion are seldom enjoyed by the man who first set it going; he beats and disturbs the water for someone else's net. The unity and structure of this monarchy, of this grand edifice, having been ripped and torn in its old age by this thing called innovation, has since shown a rent and given sufficient admittance to such injuries. The royal majesty comes down with greater difficulty from the summit to the middle than it falls and tumbles headlong from the middle to the bottom. But if the inventors do the greater mischief, the imitators are more vicious — to follow examples whose horror and offence they have already felt and punished. And if there can be any honour in ill-doing, these last must yield to the others the glory of contriving and the courage of making the first attempt. All sorts of new disorders easily draw, from this primitive and ever-flowing fountain, examples and precedents to trouble and disrupt our government. We read in our very laws, made as a remedy for this first evil, the beginnings and pretexts of all sorts of wicked enterprises; and what Thucydides said of the civil wars of his time befalls us: that, in favour of public vices, they gave them new and more plausible names for their excuse, sweetening and disguising their true titles — which must be done, forsooth, to reform our conscience and belief:

The historian of the Peloponnesian war, cited for what happens to language in a civil war: the parties give the public vices new and more plausible names to excuse them. It is he who told Archidamus that when he had thrown Pericles the man always persuaded the spectators he had had no fall.

## modern-en · octavius · 22:54

since the ordinary discipline of a healthy state does not provide for these extraordinary accidents: it presupposes a body that holds itself up in its principal members and offices, and a common consent in its obedience and observance. A legitimate procedure is cold, heavy, and constrained, and not fit to make head against a headstrong and unbridled one. It is, to this day, cast in the dish of those two great men, Octavius and Cato, in the two civil wars of Sylla and Caesar, that they would rather suffer their country to undergo the last extremities than relieve their fellow-citizens at the expense of its laws, or be guilty of any innovation. For, in truth, in these last necessities, where there is no other remedy, it would perhaps be more prudent to stoop and yield a little, to receive the blow, than, by opposing without possibility of doing good, to give occasion to violence to trample all under foot; and better to make the laws do what they can, when they cannot do what they would. After this manner did the man who suspended them for twenty-four hours; and he who, for once, shifted a day in the calendar; and the other who, of the month of June, made a second of May. The Lacedaemonians themselves, so religious observers of the laws of their country, being constrained by one of their own edicts which expressly forbade them to choose the same man twice as admiral, and on the other hand, their affairs necessarily requiring that Lysander should again take that command upon him, they made one Aratus admiral — true enough, but with this addition, that Lysander went out as general of the navy. Whom Plutarch commends for knowing how to command not only according to the laws but over them, when the public necessity required it. Against Machanidas he let his own archers and slingers be chased and cut in pieces before his face rather than leave his post, and charged the enemy’s foot only once their horse had gone off in the pursuit — the case Montaigne sets beside the Duc de Guise’s at Dreux; and he is one of the captains who held that rich accoutrement inflames a soldier’s courage. The older edition misprints his name Philopcemen in that second place.

## modern-en · apollo · 22:42

according to what the oracle answered those of Delphi who, fearing to be invaded by the Persians in the Median war, asked Apollo how they should dispose of the holy treasure of his temple — whether they should hide it, or move it to some other place? He returned them the answer that they should remove nothing from there and only take care of themselves, for he was sufficient to look after what belonged to him.

The god of the Delphic oracle, who told the people of Delphos, afraid of the Persians, to stir nothing of his treasure and to look to themselves — he was sufficient to look after what was his.

## modern-en · jacques-amyot · 23:0

Jacques Amyot, grand almoner of France, one day told me a story that does great honour to one of our princes — and ours he was on several very good counts, though originally of foreign extraction. During our first commotions, at the siege of Rouen, this prince was warned by the queen-mother of a conspiracy against his life, with her letters naming the very man who was to carry it out: a gentleman of Anjou or Maine who normally frequented the prince's household. The prince did not breathe a syllable of this to anyone. The next day he went up to St Catherine's Mount, from which our battery was playing against the town (for the siege was still on), accompanied by the said lord almoner and another bishop. He saw the gentleman who had been pointed out to him, and sent for him at once. When the man came before him, already pale and trembling under the weight of his guilt, the prince said: "Monsieur So-and-so, you can guess what I have to say to you; your face gives it away. There's no point in disguising your scheme — I'm so well informed of your business that any attempt to conceal or deny it will only make things worse for you. You know perfectly well such-and-such details" (the most secret circumstances of the conspiracy), "so as you value your life, confess the whole truth of the plot." The poor man, seeing himself trapped and convicted (the whole business had been disclosed to the queen by one of the accomplices), didn't know what to do. He folded his hands, begged and pleaded for mercy, and threw himself at his prince's feet. The prince raised him up and went on: "Now, sir, tell me — have I ever offended you? Have I, out of private hatred or malice, wronged any kinsman or friend of yours? It's not even three weeks since I first laid eyes on you. What could possibly have driven you to attempt my death?" In a trembling voice the gentleman replied that it was no private grudge against him personally, but the general interest of his party; that certain people had urged him on, persuading him it would be a meritorious act, by any means available, to wipe out so great and so powerful an enemy of their religion. "Well," said the prince, "I'll show you how much more charitable my religion is than yours. Yours has counselled you to kill me, without hearing me speak, without my having given you any cause for offence; mine commands me to forgive you, even though by your own confession you stand convicted of a design to kill me without reason. Get out. Don't let me see you again. And if you're wise, choose more honest counsellors from now on for your schemes."

Grand almoner of France, who told Montaigne the story of the prince who forgave the gentleman sent to murder him at the siege of Rouen. The older edition spells him Amiot.

## modern-en · l-cinna · 23:1

The Emperor Augustus, while in Gaul, received reliable information of a conspiracy that L. Cinna was contriving against him. He resolved to make an example of the man, and to that end summoned his friends to meet in council the next morning. But the intervening night he spent in great inner agitation, considering that he was about to put to death a young man from an illustrious family, nephew to the great Pompey. The thought drove him into a series of passionate outbursts. "What then," he said, "am I to live in perpetual anxiety and alarm, and let my would-be assassin wander freely about? Will he go unpunished for having conspired against my life — a life I've defended through so many civil wars, so many battles by land and sea? After settling universal peace over the whole world, am I to pardon a man who's plotted not just to murder me but to slaughter me at sacrifice?" — for the plan was to kill him while he officiated. After a long silence he started up again, louder, raging at himself: "Why are you alive, if so many would benefit from your death? Will there be no end to your reprisals and cruelties? Is your life worth so much that so much harm must be done to preserve it?" His wife Livia, seeing him in this perplexity, said: "Will you take a woman's advice? Do as the physicians do — when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity has got you nowhere so far: Lepidus followed Salvidienus, Murena followed Lepidus, Caepio followed Murena, Egnatius followed Caepio. Try sweetness and clemency now. Cinna is convicted; pardon him. He'll never have the heart to harm you afterwards, and it'll add to your glory." Augustus was relieved to find an advocate of his own inclination. He thanked his wife, countermanded the summons to council, and ordered Cinna to be brought to him alone. When Cinna arrived, the room cleared and a chair set for him, Augustus said: "First, Cinna, I ask you to hear me out patiently. Don't interrupt — I'll give you time to answer afterwards. You know, Cinna, that I took you prisoner in the enemy's camp, where you were not merely an enemy by circumstance but an enemy by birth. I spared your life, restored all your goods, and finally set you up so comfortably by my generosity that the victors envied the defeated. The priestly office you petitioned me for, I granted you — after denying it to others whose fathers had always borne arms in my service. After all these favours, you've undertaken to kill me." Cinna cried out that he was very far from harbouring any such wicked thought. "You're not keeping your promise, Cinna," Augustus continued, "that you wouldn't interrupt me. Yes, you've undertaken to murder me, in such a place, on such a day, in such company, in such a manner." At those words, seeing Cinna struck dumb — not because of his promise but because his conscience had collapsed under the weight of the evidence — Augustus went on: "Now, to what end were you going to do it? To be emperor? Believe me, the Republic is in a sorry state if I'm the only man standing between you and the empire. You can't even defend your own household — only the other day you were beaten in a lawsuit by a mere freed slave's interest. Have you no means, no power anywhere except enough to take on Caesar? I'll step down from the throne if I'm the only obstacle to your hopes. Do you think the Paulli, the Fabii, the Cossii, the Servilii, and so many other noble Romans — noble not just in name but by the virtue that honours their nobility — would tolerate you?" After this, and a great deal more (he spoke for two long hours), he ended: "Now go, Cinna. Go. I give you the life I'd already given you once, when you were an enemy — and now I give it back to you again, traitor and parricide as you are. Let friendship begin between us from this moment, and let's see whether I have given, or you have received, your life with the better faith." And with that he left him. Some time later he advanced Cinna to the consulship, complaining that Cinna hadn't had the nerve to ask for it. He kept him afterwards as a very close friend, and was eventually made sole heir to his entire estate. Now — from the time of this episode, which befell Augustus in the fortieth year of his life, he never had another conspiracy or attempt made against him. He reaped the proper reward of his generous clemency. But things didn't go that way with our prince. His moderation and mercy did not protect him; he later fell into the net of a similar treason. So vain and futile a thing is human prudence; through all our projects, counsels, and precautions, Fortune will still be mistress of events.

Pompey’s nephew, of an illustrious family, who conspired to kill Augustus at sacrifice — and was told the whole plot back to his face, place, day and company, and then given his life a second time. He was made consul afterwards, was Augustus’s great friend, and left him his whole estate.

After this, and a great deal more (he spoke for two long hours), he ended: "Now go, Cinna. Go. I give you the life I'd already given you once, when you were an enemy — and now I give it back to you again, traitor and parricide as you are. Let friendship begin between us from this moment, and let's see whether I have given, or you have received, your life with the better faith." And with that he left him. Some time later he advanced Cinna to the consulship, complaining that Cinna hadn't had the nerve to ask for it. He kept him afterwards as a very close friend, and was eventually made sole heir to his entire estate. Now — from the time of this episode, which befell Augustus in the fortieth year of his life, he never had another conspiracy or attempt made against him. He reaped the proper reward of his generous clemency. But things didn't go that way with our prince. His moderation and mercy did not protect him; he later fell into the net of a similar treason. So vain and futile a thing is human prudence; through all our projects, counsels, and precautions, Fortune will still be mistress of events.

The last of the four houses in Augustus’s list.

## modern-en · dion · 23:7

You'll read in history of many who, fearing for their lives, took the course of meeting and pre-empting conspiracies by punishment and revenge; but I find very few who got any advantage from this — witness so many Roman emperors. Whoever finds himself in such danger ought not to expect much from his vigilance or his power. For how hard a thing it is to secure oneself from an enemy hiding behind the face of the most devoted friend, or to read the wills and inner thoughts of those in our personal service. It does little good to have a guard of foreigners around you and to be always fenced in by armed men: whoever despises his own life is master of yours. And besides, this continual suspicion, which makes a prince mistrustful of all the world, must of necessity be a strange torment to him. That's why Dion, when warned that Callippus was watching for an opportunity to take his life, never had the heart to inquire more closely into it. He said he'd rather die than live in that misery — having to stand continually on guard, not just against his enemies but against his friends too. Alexander demonstrated the same point even more vividly and more roundly in action when, having been warned by a letter from Parmenio that his most beloved physician Philip had been bought with Darius' money to poison him, he handed Philip the letter to read and at the same moment drank off the potion Philip had brought him. Wasn't this to express a resolution that if his friends meant to send him out of the world, he was willing to give them the opportunity? Alexander is the supreme model for daring acts; but I don't know whether there's another passage in his life that shows such firm courage as this, or so illustrious an image of the beauty and greatness of his mind.

Warned that Callippus was watching for a chance to kill him, he would not inquire any further into it: he had rather die than live having to stand guard against his friends as well as his enemies.

## modern-en · duke-of-athens · 23:19

A stranger, having publicly said he could teach Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, an infallible method for uncovering all the conspiracies his subjects could contrive against him, if Dionysius would pay him a good sum for his trouble, was sent for. Dionysius wanted to learn so necessary an art. The man answered that the only art he knew was this: Dionysius should give him a talent of silver and then boast that he'd received an unparalleled secret from him. Dionysius liked the trick, and accordingly had six hundred crowns counted out to him. It wasn't likely he'd give so large a sum to an unknown man except on account of some extraordinary disclosure, and the belief in this kept his enemies on edge. Princes, in fact, are wise to publicise the information they receive about plots against their lives, so as to convince people they have such good intelligence that nothing can be plotted against them without their getting wind of it instantly. The Duke of Athens did many foolish things in setting up his new tyranny over Florence, but one stood out above the rest: receiving the first intimation of a conspiracy the people were hatching against him from Matteo di Morozzo, one of the conspirators, he promptly put Morozzo to death — to suppress the rumour, so that no one would think any of his subjects disliked his government.

Who did a great many foolish things in setting up his tyranny over Florence, and this the most notable: told of the conspiracy by one of the conspirators, he put the informer to death at once, so that nobody should think the city disliked his government.

## modern-en · hercules · 24:7

And as for the philosophers — a sort of men remote from public affairs — they were also sometimes mocked, by the comic licence of their times, for opinions and manners that made them appear ridiculous to men of a different cast. Make them judges of a lawsuit, of human conduct? They're ready to take it on, and immediately begin to ask whether there's life, whether there's motion, whether man is anything other than an ox; what it is to act and to suffer; what kinds of animals law and justice are. Speak about the magistrates, or to one, and they do it with a rude, irreverent, indecent liberty. Let them hear a prince or a king praised, and they think no more of him than of a shepherd, a goatherd, or a herdsman — a lazy Corydon busy milking and shearing his herd, but more roughly and harshly than the herdsman himself. Do you regard a man as great for being lord of two thousand acres? They laugh at such a pitiful little patch, claiming the whole world for their own possession. Do you boast of your nobility, descended from seven rich successive ancestors? They look at you with contempt, as men who have no proper idea of nature's universal picture, and who fail to consider how many ancestors every one of us has had — rich, poor, kings, slaves, Greeks, and barbarians. Even if you were the fiftieth in descent from Hercules, they regard it as great vanity to set such a value on what is merely a gift of fortune. And so the common people scorned them in turn, as men ignorant of the most elementary and ordinary things, presumptuous and insolent.

From whom, the philosophers say, you might be the fiftieth descendant and still have nothing but a gift of fortune to boast of.

## modern-en · crates · 24:11

As for the philosophers — as I said — if they were great in knowledge, they were even greater in action. Take the geometer of Syracuse: when he was disturbed at his contemplation to apply his skill to the defence of his country, he immediately set in motion dreadful and prodigious engines that produced effects beyond all human expectation. Yet he himself disdained all his handiwork, thinking that in this he had played the mere mechanic and violated the dignity of his art, of which these performances were only trivial experiments and playthings. So whenever the philosophers have been put to the test of action, they've been seen to rise to such a pitch that it's clear their souls were marvellously elevated and enriched by their knowledge. But some of them, seeing the reins of government in the hands of incompetent men, kept clear of all political administration. Crates, when asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, answered: "Until our armies are no longer commanded by fools." Heraclitus resigned the royalty to his brother; and to the Ephesians, who reproached him for spending his time playing with children before the temple, he said: "Isn't it better to do this than to sit at the helm of affairs in your company?" Others have raised their imagination above the world and fortune, and looked on the tribunals of justice, even the thrones of kings, as paltry and contemptible. Empedocles refused the royalty the Agrigentines offered him. Thales was once arguing against the trouble men take to grow rich, and someone in the company answered that he was like the fox who complained of what he couldn't reach. He had a mind, for the joke's sake, to show the contrary. He gathered up all his wits for the occasion, applied them wholly to profit and gain, set up a trading operation, and in one year brought in such great wealth that the most experienced merchants couldn't, in a whole lifetime of effort, have heaped together so much. As for what Aristotle reports of those who called him, Anaxagoras, and others of their profession wise but not prudent — for not applying their study to more profitable things — I don't really swallow that verbal distinction; nor does it serve to excuse my pedants, for if you look at the low and needy circumstances they're content with, the more reasonable verdict is that they are neither wise nor prudent.

Asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, he answered: till our armies are no more commanded by fools. He is also named to place his brother Pasicles, the philosopher who laid his hand in the wrong place in petitioning a great man.

## modern-en · lucullus · 24:23

We take other men's knowledge and opinions on trust — which is an idle, superficial sort of learning. We must make it our own. We're like the man who, needing fire, went to a neighbour's house to fetch some and, finding a very good one there, sat down to warm himself without remembering to carry any back with him. What good does it do us to have a stomach full of meat if it isn't digested, isn't incorporated into us, doesn't nourish and sustain us? Can we imagine that Lucullus, whom letters alone (without any experience) made so great a captain, learned to be so in that perfunctory way? We let ourselves lean so heavily on another man's arm that we destroy our own strength. Do I want to fortify myself against the fear of death? It must be at Seneca's expense. Do I want to extract some consolation for myself or my friend? I borrow it from Cicero. I could have found it in myself if I'd been trained to make use of my own reason. I don't like this dependent, mendicant understanding; for though we can become learned by other men's learning, a man can only be wise by his own wisdom:

Whom letters alone, without any experience, made so great a captain — and who did not learn it, Montaigne says, in the perfunctory way we learn.

## modern-en · protagoras · 24:33

These pedants of ours, as Plato says of the Sophists their cousins, are of all men the ones who most pretend to be useful to humanity, and yet alone of all men they not only fail to improve what is committed to them — as a carpenter or mason would — but make their charges worse, and make us pay them for making them worse into the bargain. If the rule Protagoras proposed to his pupils were followed — that they should either pay his asking price or swear an oath in the temple as to how much they reckoned the benefit they'd received under his tuition was worth, and pay him accordingly — my pedagogues would find themselves badly stuck if they had to be judged by the affidavits of my experience. My Perigord dialect very neatly calls these pretenders to learning lettre-ferits — letter-stamped, as if letters had been hammered onto them with a mallet. And in truth, for the most part, they appear to be deprived even of common sense. The farmer and the cobbler go simply and honestly about their business, speaking only of what they know and understand; but these fellows, in order to make a show and gain a reputation, parade about their ridiculous knowledge that floats on the surface of the brain, constantly tangling themselves up in their own nonsense. They speak fine words sometimes, true enough — let someone wiser apply them. They're wonderfully well acquainted with Galen, but not at all with the patient's disease; they'll already have deafened you with a long row of laws, while understanding nothing of the case in hand; they have the theory of everything — let who will put it into practice.

The sophist who let his pupils either pay his demand or swear in the temple what they thought the teaching had been worth — a rule under which, Montaigne says, his own pedagogues would be sorely gravelled.

## modern-en · adrian-turnebus · 24:37

Whoever closely examines and thoroughly sifts this sort of people, with whom the world is so pestered, will find, as I have done, that for the most part they understand neither others nor themselves; that their memories are full enough, but their judgment totally empty — with a few exceptions, men whom nature has of itself formed into better shape. I noticed this, for example, in Adrian Turnebus, who, having never professed anything but pure learning, and in that, in my opinion, the greatest man we've seen in a thousand years, had nothing of the pedant in him except the wearing of his gown and a little outward fashion that could never be civilised into courtier ways — which in themselves are nothing. I hate our people who can less easily endure an ill-cut robe than an ill-shaped mind, and who measure a man by the leg he makes, by his behaviour, even by the very fashion of his boots, to judge what kind of man he is. Within Turnebus, there wasn't a more polished soul on earth. I have often deliberately put him onto subjects far from his profession, and found such a clear insight, such a quick apprehension, such a solid judgment, that you'd have thought he'd practised nothing else but arms, and been employed all his life in affairs of state. These are great and vigorous natures,

The one man of pure learning Montaigne exempts from the charge of pedantry, and in his opinion the greatest of the last thousand years: nothing of the pedant about him but the gown, and within, not a more polished soul upon earth. Montaigne says he put him on arguments far outside his profession and found him as quick as if he had spent his life in arms or affairs of state.

## modern-en · francis-brittany · 24:49

And this, perhaps, is the reason why neither we nor theology require much learning in women. Francis, Duke of Brittany, son of John V, when someone was talking with him about his marriage to Isabella, daughter of the King of Scotland, and added that she was modestly bred and without any learning, answered that he liked her the better for it, and that a woman was wise enough if she could tell her husband's shirt from his doublet. So it's no great wonder, as some make of it, that our ancestors held letters in no greater esteem, and that even today they're rarely found in the principal councils of princes. If the goal of acquiring wealth, which is the only thing we propose to ourselves through law, medicine, pedantry, and even divinity itself, didn't keep them in credit, you'd see them, no doubt, in as pitiful a condition as ever. And what loss would that be, if they teach us neither to think well nor to do well?

John V’s son, who was told that Isabella of Scotland was homely bred and without learning, and answered that he liked her the better: a woman is wise enough if she can tell her husband’s shirt from his doublet.

## modern-en · astyages · 24:57

It is a thing worth great consideration, that in the excellent — indeed, for its perfection, prodigious — civil regime laid down by Lycurgus, though so concerned for the education of children as the matter of greatest importance, even at the very seat of the Muses, he makes so little mention of learning, as if that high-spirited youth, disdaining all other subjection but that of virtue, ought to be supplied not with tutors to read them arts and sciences, but with masters who would only instruct them in valour, prudence, and justice — an example Plato followed in his Laws. Their method of discipline was to put questions to the boys about judgments on men and their actions; if the boys praised or condemned this or that person or deed, they had to give a reason for so doing, and by this means they sharpened their understanding and learned what was right. Astyages, in Xenophon, asks Cyrus to give an account of his last lesson, and the lesson went like this: "A big boy in our school, having a short little jacket, took by force a longer one from another boy who wasn't as tall as he was, and gave him his own in exchange. I, being appointed judge of the dispute, ruled that each should keep the coat he had, because each was now better fitted with the other's than with his own. Whereupon my master told me I'd done badly: I had only considered the fit of the garments, when I ought to have considered the justice of the thing, which required that nothing be forcibly taken from anyone that was rightfully his." And Cyrus adds that he was whipped for his pains — just as we are in our villages for forgetting the first aorist of ——.

Cyrus’s grandfather in Xenophon, who asked him for an account of his last lesson and got the story of the two cassocks and the whipping.

## modern-en · antipater · 24:61

They used to go, it's said, to the other cities of Greece to look for rhetoricians, painters, and musicians; but to Lacedaemon for legislators, magistrates, and generals. At Athens you learned to speak well; here, to do well. There, to disengage yourself from a sophistical argument and untangle the imposture of captious syllogisms; here, to evade the baits and lures of pleasure and, with a noble courage and resolution, to overcome the threats of fortune and death. Those people cudgelled their brains about words; these made it their business to inquire into things. There was an endless babbling of the tongue; here, a continual exercise of the soul. So it's no wonder, when Antipater demanded fifty boys from them as hostages, they answered — quite the opposite of what we would do — that they would rather give him twice as many grown men, so highly did they value the loss of their country's education. When Agesilaus pressed Xenophon to send his sons to Sparta to be brought up, he said: "Not to learn logic or rhetoric, but to be instructed in the noblest of all sciences — the science of obeying and commanding."

Who demanded fifty children of the Spartans for hostages and was told they would rather give him twice as many grown men, so much did they value the loss of their country’s education — and who, threatening them severely to bring them to a certain demand, was answered that if he threatened them with more than death they would die the more willingly.

## modern-en · tamerlane · 24:63

Examples have shown us that in military affairs, and all others of that active sort, the study of the sciences softens and saps men's courage rather than strengthening and exciting it. The most powerful empire in the world today is that of the Turks — a people equally trained in the esteem of arms and the contempt of letters. I find Rome was more warlike before she grew so learned. The most warlike nations now in existence are the most rude and ignorant: the Scythians, the Parthians, Tamerlane — proof enough. When the Goths overran Greece, the only thing that preserved the libraries from the fire was that someone convinced them to leave this kind of furniture untouched for the enemy, as the surest way to divert them from arms and fix them in a lazy, sedentary life. When our King Charles VIII found himself master of the kingdom of Naples and a good part of Tuscany almost without striking a blow, the nobles around him put this unexpected ease of conquest down to this: the princes and nobles of Italy were more concerned to make themselves clever and learned than vigorous and warlike.

One of Montaigne’s proofs that the most warlike nations are the most rude and ignorant, and the man who overthrew Bajazet in the furious battle after which Bajazet nearly escaped on an Arabian mare.

## modern-en · danaides · 25:2

I never seriously settled down to read any book of solid learning except Plutarch and Seneca; and there, like the Danaids, I'm forever filling and forever leaking; something of it drips onto this paper, but little or nothing stays with me. History is my particular game where reading is concerned, or else poetry, for which I have a particular fondness and esteem. For as Cleanthes said, just as the voice, forced through the narrow throat of a trumpet, comes out sharper and more forceful, so a sentence pressed within the harmony of verse seems to me to dart out more briskly upon the understanding, and strikes my ear and apprehension with a smarter and more pleasing effect. As for the natural parts I have, of which this is the test, I find them bowing under the burden. My fancy and judgment only grope in the dark, tripping and stumbling on the way; and when I've gone as far as I can, I'm in no way satisfied. I still see a new and greater extent of land before me, with a troubled and imperfect sight, wrapped up in clouds I can't penetrate. And as I take it upon myself to write indifferently about whatever comes into my head, using nothing but my own natural means, if I happen to meet, in some good author (as often happens), the same topics I've attempted to write upon — as just now, in Plutarch's "Of the Force of Imagination" — to see myself so weak, so faint, so heavy and flat, in comparison with those better writers, I both pity and despise myself. Yet I take some pleasure in this, that my opinions often have the honour and good fortune to coincide with theirs, that I'm travelling in the same path, though at a very great distance, and can say, "Ah, that is so." I'm further satisfied to find I have one quality that not everyone is blessed with: the ability to see the vast difference between them and me. And in spite of all that, I let my own inventions, low and feeble as they are, run on in their course, without mending or papering over the defects this comparison has laid bare to my view. To be honest, a man needs a strong back to keep pace with such people. The indiscreet scribblers of our times, who among their laborious nothings insert whole sections and pages from ancient authors, hoping by that means to lend lustre to their own writings, do quite the opposite; for the infinite contrast between the ornaments and their own composition makes their own work look so sallow and deformed that they lose much more than they gain.

Who eternally fill and whose vessels eternally run out — Montaigne’s figure for his own reading of Plutarch and Seneca. The modern edition spells them Danaids.
