The philosophers Chrysippus and Epicurus were of two entirely opposite tempers in this: the first not only mixed passages and sayings from other authors into his books, but entire pieces — in one, the whole Medea of Euripides — which gave Apollodorus occasion to say that if a man picked out of his writings everything that was not his, he'd be left with blank paper. ## modern-en · capilupus · 25:4

The other day I happened to come across this piece of luck. I was reading a French book where, after long wandering through a great many words so dull, so insipid, so void of wit or common sense that they were really only French words, after a long and tedious slog I came at last to a passage that was lofty, rich, and lifted to the very clouds. Had I found either a gentle slope or a gradual ascent up to it, there'd have been some excuse; but it was so sheer a precipice, so wholly cut off from the rest of the work, that by the first six words I found myself flying off into another world, and from there saw the vale I had climbed out of as so deep and low that I've never had the heart to descend into it again. If I set out one of my discourses with such rich spoils, it would too clearly expose the imperfection of my own writing. To rebuke in others the fault I'm guilty of myself seems to me no more unreasonable than condemning (as I often do) in myself the faults of others; they should be reproved everywhere and given no sanctuary. I know perfectly well how brazenly I try, at every turn, to equal myself to my thefts, to make my style march hand in hand with them, not without an audacious hope of deceiving my reader's eye. But it's as much by the benefit of my application that I hope to do it as by my invention or any force of my own. Besides, I don't pretend to fight the whole body of these champions, nor hand to hand with any single one of them; it's only by skirmishes and light feints that I engage them. I don't grapple with them — I only try their strength, and never push so far as I pretend. If I could hold them in play, I'd be a brave fellow indeed, for I only attack them where they are most sinewy and strong. To cover yourself (as I've seen some do) with another man's armour, so that even your fingertips don't show; to carry on a project (as anyone with a touch of the scholar can do on an ordinary subject) under old inventions patched up here and there with your own scraps, and then to try to conceal the theft and pass it off as your own — that's first an injustice and meanness of spirit in those who do it; since they have nothing of their own fit to win them a reputation, they try to do it by foisting on the world things that aren't theirs at all in their own name. And then it's a ridiculous folly to content yourself with the ignorant approval of the common sort by such a pitiful trick, at the same time degrading yourself in the eyes of men of understanding, who turn up their noses at all that borrowed plaster, even though their praise alone is worth having. For my own part, there's nothing I'd less willingly do; nor have I said so much about others except to get a better chance to explain myself. Nor do I aim, in this, at the composers of centos who openly declare themselves such — of which I've known several very ingenious in my time, particularly one writing under the name of Capilupus, besides the ancients. These are really men of wit, and they make it clear they are, both in that way and in others — as for example Lipsius, in that learned and laborious tissue of his Politics.

A composer of centos Montaigne knew of, and one of the writers he exempts from the charge of stitching other men’s work into their own under their own name — because such men declare themselves for what they are.

## modern-en · cimon · 25:7

Now, madam, if I had any competence on this subject, I couldn't employ it better than by offering my best instructions to the little man who threatens you shortly with a happy birth — for you are too generous to begin otherwise than with a male. Having had so great a hand in arranging your marriage, I have a particular interest in the greatness and prosperity of whatever issue comes from it; besides which, your long possession of my service obliges me to wish honour and advantage to everything that concerns you. But in truth, all I understand about this is that the greatest and most important difficulty of human knowledge is the education of children. For as in agriculture the husbandry preceding planting, and the planting itself, is straightforward and well known, but once what is planted comes alive there's a great deal more to be done, more art, more care, more difficulty in cultivating and bringing it to perfection — so it is with men. It's no hard matter to get children; but once they're born, the trouble, anxiety, and care of training, instructing, and bringing them up begins. The signs of their inclinations at that tender age are so obscure, and the promises so uncertain and deceptive, that it's very hard to build any solid judgment or conjecture on them. Look at Cimon, for instance, and Themistocles, and a thousand others, who much disappointed the expectations people had of them. Cubs of bears and puppies readily reveal their natural disposition; but men, as soon as they grow up, settling into certain habits, taking on certain opinions, conforming to particular laws and customs, easily change — or at least disguise — their true and real character. And yet it's hard to force the bent of nature. So, for not having chosen the right course, we often take great pains and waste a good part of our time training up children for things they are by nature totally unfit for. In this difficulty, all the same, I'm clearly of the opinion that they ought to be brought up in the best and most useful studies, without taking too much notice of, or being too superstitious about, the slight prognostics they give of themselves in their tender years — to which Plato, in his Republic, gives, it seems to me, too much weight.

With Themistocles, one of the thousand men who very much deceived the expectation others had of them — Montaigne’s warning against reading a child’s promise too early. It is he who besieged Boges in Eion and offered him a safe return into Asia with all his wealth.

## modern-en · candale · 25:8

Madam, science is a great ornament and a thing of marvellous use, especially for persons raised to the rank of fortune you are. In truth, in people of mean and low condition it can't perform its true office; for its natural inclination is to assist in the conduct of war, in the government of peoples, in negotiating the leagues and friendships of princes and foreign nations, rather than in framing a syllogism in logic, pleading a case in law, or prescribing a dose of pills in medicine. So, madam, since I'm sure you won't omit so necessary a feature in the education of your children — you yourself having tasted its sweetness, being of a learned line (we still have the writings of the ancient Counts of Foix, from whom your husband and yourself are both descended; and Monsieur de Candale, your uncle, daily obliges the world with more, which will extend the reputation of this quality in your family for many ages to come) — I'll take this occasion to share with you one particular fancy of my own, contrary to the common method, which is all I can contribute to your service in this matter.

Diane de Foix’s uncle, who every day obliges the world with writings of his own.

## modern-en · arcesilaus · 25:11

It's the custom of teachers to be eternally booming into their pupil's ears, as if pouring through a funnel, while the pupil's only business is to repeat what they've said. I want a tutor to correct this error, and right from the start, according to the capacity he has to deal with, to put it to the test — letting his pupil taste things himself, and discover and choose for himself, sometimes opening the way for him, sometimes leaving him to open it on his own. That is, I don't want the tutor alone to invent and speak; he should also hear his pupil speak in turn. Socrates, and after him Arcesilaus, first made their pupils speak, and then they spoke to them.

Who, like Socrates before him, made his scholars speak first and then spoke to them — and whom pure wine despatched as it did Stilpo, though in his case not by design. The older edition prints him Arcesilas in the Apology.

Quoted for the line Montaigne makes his pupil’s rule: I love to doubt as well as to know.

## modern-en · epicharmus · 25:25

Let him at least know that he knows. He'll need to drink in their knowledge, but not be poisoned by their precepts; and no matter if he forgets where he got his learning, provided he knows how to apply it to his own use. Truth and reason are common to everyone, and belong no more to the one who spoke them first than to the one who speaks them after; it's no more according to Plato than according to me, since both he and I equally see and understand them. Bees cull their various sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but afterwards they themselves make the honey, which is all and purely their own — no more thyme and marjoram. In the same way, the boy will transform and shuffle together the fragments he borrows from others, to compile a work absolutely his own — that is, his judgment. His instruction, labour, and study aim at nothing else but to form that. He's not obliged to disclose where he got the materials that helped him, but only to show what he himself has done with them. Men who live by pillage and borrowing display their purchases and their buildings to every passer-by; they don't broadcast how they got the money. We don't see a lawyer's fees and perquisites; we see the alliances he uses to fortify himself and his family, and the titles and honours he's secured. No man advertises his income, or at least how it comes in, but everyone publishes his acquisitions. The advantages of our study are to become better and wiser. As Epicharmus says, it's the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that improves everything, that orders everything, that acts, rules, and reigns; all the other faculties are blind, and deaf, and without soul. And we certainly render it timid and servile by not allowing it the liberty to do anything of itself. Who ever asked his pupil what he thought of grammar and rhetoric, or of such-and-such a sentence of Cicero? Our masters stick them, fully feathered, into our memories, where they're set up like oracles, the letters and syllables themselves treated as the substance of the thing. To know by rote is not to know; it just means to retain what one has entrusted to memory. What a man truly knows and understands he disposes of freely, without reference to the author he got it from or fumbling through the pages of his book. A merely bookish learning is a poor, paltry kind of learning; it may serve for decoration, but it provides no foundation for any structure to be built on it — according to Plato, who says that constancy, faith, and sincerity are the true philosophy, and the other sciences, directed to other ends, are only counterfeit paint. I could wish that Paluel or Pompey, those two famous dancers of my time, could have taught us to cut capers just by watching them, without our stirring from our seats — as these men pretend to inform the understanding without ever setting it to work. Or that we could learn to ride, handle a pike, play the lute, or sing without the trouble of practice, as these try to teach us to judge and speak well without exercising us in judging or speaking. Now in the start of our studies, and in their progress, whatever presents itself to us is book enough: a roguish trick of a page, a stupid mistake of a servant, a joke at the table — all are fresh subjects.

Who said it is the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that orders and rules everything, and that all the other faculties are blind and deaf and without soul.

## modern-en · marcellus · 25:51

In this conversation with men, I mean also, and chiefly, those who only live in the records of history: by reading those books, he'll converse with the great and heroic souls of the best ages. It's an idle, vain study for those who treat it negligently; but for those who do it with care and observation, it's a study of incalculable value — and the only study, as Plato reports, that the Lacedaemonians reserved for themselves. What profit will he not reap, as to the business of men, by reading Plutarch's Lives! But let my governor remember what end his instructions are mainly directed at, and not so much impress on his pupil's memory the date of Carthage's fall as the manners of Hannibal and Scipio, nor so much where Marcellus died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there. Let him not teach him so much the narrative parts of history as how to judge them. The reading of history, in my opinion, is something we apply ourselves to with the most varying degrees of attention. I have read a hundred things in Livy that another has not, or not noticed at least; and Plutarch has read a hundred things there that I never could find, or perhaps that the author never wrote. To some it's merely a grammar exercise; to others the very anatomy of philosophy, by which the most abstruse parts of our human nature are reached. There are in Plutarch many long discourses very worth reading and observing carefully — he is, in my view, of all writers the greatest master in that kind of writing — but there are a thousand others he has only touched and glanced at, where he only points his finger to show us which way we may go if we will, and contents himself with sometimes giving us one brisk hit on the trickiest point of the question, from which we must grope out the rest for ourselves. Take, for example, his saying that the inhabitants of Asia came to be vassals of one man because they couldn't pronounce one syllable, which is "No." That saying perhaps gave La Boétie the matter and occasion to write his "Voluntary Servitude." Just to see him pick out a slight action in a man's life, or a mere word that hardly seems to amount even to that, is itself a whole discourse. It's to our prejudice that men of understanding should so immoderately affect brevity; no doubt their reputation is the better for it, but in the meantime we are the worse for it. Plutarch had rather we should applaud his judgment than commend his knowledge; he had rather leave us with an appetite to read more than glutted with what we've read already. He knew very well that one may say too much even on the best subjects, and that Alexandridas justly reproached someone who made very good but too long speeches to the Ephori, saying: "O stranger! you speak the things you should speak, but not as you should speak them." Those who have lean, spare bodies stuff themselves out with clothes; so those who are short on substance try to make up for it with words.

Whose death, Montaigne says, the pupil should be taught to judge rather than to locate: not so much where he died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there.

## modern-en · theodorus-gaza · 1:6

And, directly contrary to my first examples, the bravest of all men, the one most famous for clemency to those he overcame — Alexander — after great difficulty stormed the city of Gaza. Entering, he found Betis, its commander, of whose valour during the siege he had had striking and repeated proof, standing alone, abandoned by his soldiers, his armour hacked to pieces, drenched in blood and wounds, and still fighting in a crowd of Macedonians striking him from every side. Alexander, nettled at so dear-bought a victory — he had two fresh wounds of his own — said to him: 'You shall not die as you intend, Betis. You shall suffer every torment that can be inflicted on a captive.' To which Betis answered only with a fierce and disdainful look. 'What,' said Alexander, watching his haughty, obstinate silence, 'is he too stiff to bend a knee? Too proud to utter one suppliant word? Then I will conquer this silence. If I cannot force a word from his mouth, I will at least extract a groan from his heart.' And turning his anger into fury, he ordered Betis's heels bored through and had him dragged alive, mangled and torn apart, at the back of a cart. Was it that the height of courage was so natural and familiar to this conqueror that, since he could not admire it, he respected it less? Or that he held valour to be so peculiarly his own that his pride could not, without envy, endure it in another? Or that the natural impetuosity of his fury was simply incapable of opposition? Surely, had it been capable of moderation, the sack and ruin of Thebes would have moderated it: to see so many valiant men, lost and without further defence, slaughtered before his eyes — above six thousand put to the sword, of whom not one was seen to flee or heard to cry for quarter, but every one running here and there to seek out the victorious enemy and provoke them to give him an honourable end. Not one was seen who, however weakened by wounds, did not in his last gasp still try to take revenge, and with all the weapons of a brave despair to sweeten his own death in the death of an enemy. Yet their valour drew no pity, and the length of one day was not enough to satisfy the conqueror's thirst for revenge. The slaughter went on to the last drop of blood that could be shed, and stopped only when it met none but unarmed people — old men, women, and children — thirty thousand of whom were carried away as slaves.

The grammarian whose method Montaigne sets against his own: precepts so intricate and harsh, and words so vain and lean, that there is no hold to be taken of them.

## modern-en · demetrius-grammarian · 25:70

It's a thousand pities that matters should be at such a pass in this age of ours, that philosophy, even with men of understanding, is looked on as a vain and fantastic name, a thing of no use or value, either in opinion or in effect — of which I think those quibbles and petty sophistries that block the entrance to it are the cause. People are much to blame for representing philosophy to children as a thing of such difficult access, with such a frowning, grim, and formidable aspect. Who has disguised her like this, with that false, pale, ghostly countenance? There's nothing more airy, more cheerful, more frolicsome — I had almost said, more wanton. She preaches nothing but feasting and merriment; a melancholy, anxious look shows she doesn't live there. Demetrius the grammarian, finding a knot of philosophers sitting and chatting together in the temple at Delphi, said to them: "Either I'm much mistaken, or, by your cheerful and pleasant faces, you're not engaged in any very deep discussion." To which one of them, Heracleon the Megarean, replied: "It's for those who are puzzling whether the future tense of such-and-such a verb is spelt with a double A, or hunting after the derivation of the comparatives and superlatives, to knit their brows while talking of their science; but philosophical discourse always cheers and gladdens those who pursue it, and never makes them sad or downcast."

Who found a knot of philosophers chatting in the temple at Delphos and told them that by their cheerful faces they could not be engaged in very deep discourse.

## modern-en · flora · 25:90

For the rest, this method of education should be carried on with a stern sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants, who, instead of tempting and luring children into letters by apt and gentle means, present nothing in fact but rods and ferules, horror and cruelty. Away with this violence! Away with this compulsion! Nothing, I'm convinced, more dulls and degenerates a well-born nature. If you would have him fear shame and chastisement, don't harden him to them. Inure him to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers he ought to despise; wean him from all effeminacy and delicacy in clothes and lodging, eating and drinking; accustom him to everything, so he may not be a Sir Paris, a carpet-knight, but a sinewy, hardy, vigorous young man. From childhood to my present age I've been of this opinion, and I'm still of it. But among other things, the strict regime of most of our colleges has always displeased me; they could perhaps have erred less harmfully on the indulgent side. It's a real house of correction for imprisoned youth. They're made debauched by being punished before they've done anything to deserve it. Just walk in when they're at their lessons and you'll hear nothing but the cries of boys being beaten and the thunder of pedagogues drunk with fury. A pretty way that, to lure these tender and timorous souls to love their books — with a furious face and a rod in hand! A cursed and pernicious method! Besides what Quintilian has very well observed, that this imperious authority is often followed by very dangerous consequences, and particularly our way of chastising. How much more decent would it be to see their classrooms strewn with green leaves and fine flowers than with the bloody stumps of birch and willow! If it were left to me, I'd paint the school with pictures of joy and gladness, Flora and the Graces, as the philosopher Speusippus did his. Where their profit is, let them also have their pleasure. The food that's proper and wholesome for children should be sweetened with sugar, and what's dangerous to them embittered with gall. It's marvellous to see how careful Plato is in his Laws about the gaiety and diversions of the youth of his city, and how much and how often he expatiates on the races, sports, songs, leaps, and dances — of which, he says, antiquity gave the ordering and patronage specifically to the gods themselves, to Apollo, Minerva, and the Muses. He goes on at length and is very particular in giving countless precepts for exercises; but as for the lettered sciences, he says very little, and only seems to recommend poetry on account of music.

With the Graces, one of the figures Speusippus painted his school with — and which Montaigne would paint a school with instead of birch and willow. Not the courtesan of 72:14 and 97:38, whose name she was taking until the census of the unkeyed table names ran over chapter 72.

## modern-en · demophoon-steward · 25:91

All singularity in our manners and conditions is to be avoided, as inconsistent with civil society. Who wouldn't be astonished at so strange a constitution as that of Demophoön, steward to Alexander the Great, who sweated in the shade and shivered in the sun? I've seen people who fled the smell of a ripe apple more swiftly than from the shot of a harquebus; others afraid of a mouse; others who threw up at the sight of cream; others ready to faint at the making of a feather bed; Germanicus could endure neither the sight nor the crowing of a cock. I won't deny there may, perhaps, be some hidden cause and natural aversion in these cases; but in my opinion a man could overcome it, if he took it in time. Precept has worked so effectively on me, though not without some effort, I confess, that, beer excepted, my appetite accommodates itself indifferently to all sorts of food. Young bodies are supple; one should therefore at that age bend and shape them to all fashions and customs. And provided one can keep the appetite and the will within their due limits, let a young man, in God's name, be made fit for all nations and all companies, even for debauchery and excess if need be — that is, where he does it in compliance with the customs of the place. Let him be able to do anything, but love to do nothing but what is good. The philosophers themselves don't justify Callisthenes for forfeiting his master Alexander's favour by refusing to pledge him a cup of wine. Let him laugh, play, drink, even wench with his prince. Indeed I'd have him, even in his debauches, outdo the rest of the company, and excel his companions in ability and stamina — and that he may not stop doing it for want of power or knowledge how, but only for want of will.

Going one day to Orleans, I met on the plain this side of Clery two pedants travelling toward Bordeaux, about fifty paces apart; and a good way behind them, I noticed a troop of horse, with a gentleman at their head who was the late Monsieur le Comte de la Rochefoucauld. One of my men asked the leading master of arts who that gentleman was that came after him. He, not having seen the train that followed, and thinking his companion was meant, answered pleasantly, "He's not a gentleman; he's a grammarian; and I am a logician." Now we, who, on the contrary, do not pretend to be breeding a grammarian or a logician but a gentleman, let us leave them to abuse their leisure; our business lies elsewhere. Let our pupil only be well furnished with things, and words will follow fast enough; he'll pull them after him if they don't come voluntarily. I've heard people make excuses that they can't express themselves, pretending to have their minds full of a great many fine things which, for lack of eloquence, they can't bring out. It's a mere pretext, nothing else. Do you want to know what I think of it? I think they're nothing but shadows of some imperfect images and conceptions they don't know what to make of, and consequently can't bring out. They don't yet understand themselves what they're trying to say, and if you just watch how they haggle and stammer on the verge of delivery, you'll soon conclude that their labour is not in giving birth but in conception — that they're still licking their formless embryo. For my part I hold, and Socrates lays it down, that whoever has a sprightly and clear conception in his mind will express it well enough in one language or another, and, if he's mute, by signs.

He knows nothing of ablative, conjunctive, substantive, or grammar — no more than his footman, or a fishwife on the Petit Pont — and yet they'll give you a bellyful of talk if you'll listen, and perhaps stumble as little in their language as the best masters of art in France. All this fine paint is easily rubbed off by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth; these flourishes only serve to amuse the common sort, who can't take in more solid and nourishing diet, as Aper very evidently shows in Tacitus. The ambassadors of Samos, having prepared a long and elegant oration, came to Cleomenes, king of Sparta, to incite him to war against the tyrant Polycrates. After listening to their speech with great gravity and patience, he gave them this answer: "As for the exordium, I don't remember it, nor consequently the middle of your speech; and as to the conclusion, I won't do what you ask." A very neat answer, I think, and a pack of learned orators very sweetly stuck. And what about the other man? The Athenians were to choose one of two architects for a very great building they had designed. The first, a pert affected fellow, offered his services in a long premeditated discourse on the subject of the work, and by his eloquence won the votes of the people. But the other said only three words: "Athenians, what this man says, I will do." When Cicero was in the heat and flow of an eloquent harangue, many were struck with admiration; but Cato only laughed, saying, "We have a comical consul." Let it come before or after, a good sentence, or something well said, is always in season; if it doesn't fit well with what went before, nor cohere much with what follows, it's good in itself. I'm not one of those who think that good rhyme makes a good poem. Let a man make short long and long short if he likes — it's no great matter; if there's invention, and if the wit and judgment have done their work, I'll say, "There's a good poet, but a poor rhymer."

Who demonstrates in Tacitus how easily the fine decoration of painted speech is effaced by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth.

## modern-en · nicolas-grouchy · 25:144

No doubt Greek and Latin are very great ornaments, and of very great use; but we buy them too dear. I'll set out one way, tried on my own person, by which they can be had cheaper, and anyone who wants to may make use of it. My late father, having made the most precise inquiries any man could make among men of the greatest learning and judgment for an exact method of education, was warned by them of the inconvenience then in use, and made to believe that the tedious time we spent learning the tongues of men who had them for nothing was the sole cause we couldn't reach the greatness of soul and perfection of knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans. I don't, however, believe that to be the only cause. So it was, that my father's expedient was this: in my infancy, before I began to speak, he committed me to the care of a German, who later died a famous physician in France, totally ignorant of our language and very fluent and a great critic in Latin. This man, whom he had fetched out of his own country and engaged with a great salary for this one purpose, had me continually with him. He had two others of lesser learning joined to him, to attend me and relieve him; they spoke to me in no language but Latin. As to the rest of the household, it was an inviolable rule that neither my father, nor my mother, nor any valet or chambermaid spoke anything in my presence but the few Latin words each had learned to gabble with me. It's not to be imagined what an advantage this proved for the whole family: my father and mother by this means learned enough Latin to understand it perfectly and to speak it well enough for any necessary use; so did those of the servants who were most often with me. In short, we Latined it at such a rate that it overflowed to all the neighbouring villages, where there still remain, established by custom, several Latin names of artisans and their tools. As for myself, I was over six years old before I understood any more French or Perigord dialect than Arabic; and without art, books, grammar, precept, whipping, or the cost of a tear, I had by that age learned to speak Latin as pure as my master's, since I had no means of mixing it with anything else. If, for example, they were to give me a theme in the college fashion, they gave it to the others in French, but to me they had to give it in bad Latin, to turn it into good. And Nicolas Grouchy, who wrote a book De Comitiis Romanorum; Guillaume Guérente, who wrote a commentary on Aristotle; George Buchanan, that great Scottish poet; and Marc-Antoine Muret (whom France and Italy have both acknowledged as the best orator of his time), my domestic tutors, all of them often told me that I had in my infancy that language so fluent and ready that they were afraid to enter into conversation with me. Buchanan in particular, whom I later saw in attendance on the late Mareschal de Brissac, then told me he was about to write a treatise on education, the example for which he intended to take from mine — for he was then tutor to that Comte de Brissac who afterwards proved so brave and valiant a gentleman.

No doubt Greek and Latin are very great ornaments, and of very great use; but we buy them too dear. I'll set out one way, tried on my own person, by which they can be had cheaper, and anyone who wants to may make use of it. My late father, having made the most precise inquiries any man could make among men of the greatest learning and judgment for an exact method of education, was warned by them of the inconvenience then in use, and made to believe that the tedious time we spent learning the tongues of men who had them for nothing was the sole cause we couldn't reach the greatness of soul and perfection of knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans. I don't, however, believe that to be the only cause. So it was, that my father's expedient was this: in my infancy, before I began to speak, he committed me to the care of a German, who later died a famous physician in France, totally ignorant of our language and very fluent and a great critic in Latin. This man, whom he had fetched out of his own country and engaged with a great salary for this one purpose, had me continually with him. He had two others of lesser learning joined to him, to attend me and relieve him; they spoke to me in no language but Latin. As to the rest of the household, it was an inviolable rule that neither my father, nor my mother, nor any valet or chambermaid spoke anything in my presence but the few Latin words each had learned to gabble with me. It's not to be imagined what an advantage this proved for the whole family: my father and mother by this means learned enough Latin to understand it perfectly and to speak it well enough for any necessary use; so did those of the servants who were most often with me. In short, we Latined it at such a rate that it overflowed to all the neighbouring villages, where there still remain, established by custom, several Latin names of artisans and their tools. As for myself, I was over six years old before I understood any more French or Perigord dialect than Arabic; and without art, books, grammar, precept, whipping, or the cost of a tear, I had by that age learned to speak Latin as pure as my master's, since I had no means of mixing it with anything else. If, for example, they were to give me a theme in the college fashion, they gave it to the others in French, but to me they had to give it in bad Latin, to turn it into good. And Nicolas Grouchy, who wrote a book De Comitiis Romanorum; Guillaume Guérente, who wrote a commentary on Aristotle; George Buchanan, that great Scottish poet; and Marc-Antoine Muret (whom France and Italy have both acknowledged as the best orator of his time), my domestic tutors, all of them often told me that I had in my infancy that language so fluent and ready that they were afraid to enter into conversation with me. Buchanan in particular, whom I later saw in attendance on the late Mareschal de Brissac, then told me he was about to write a treatise on education, the example for which he intended to take from mine — for he was then tutor to that Comte de Brissac who afterwards proved so brave and valiant a gentleman.

Who wrote a comment upon Aristotle, another of those tutors, and one of the three whose Latin tragedies Montaigne acted in at the College of Guienne. The modern edition spells him Guérente.

## modern-en · counts-of-foix · 25:8

Madam, science is a great ornament and a thing of marvellous use, especially for persons raised to the rank of fortune you are. In truth, in people of mean and low condition it can't perform its true office; for its natural inclination is to assist in the conduct of war, in the government of peoples, in negotiating the leagues and friendships of princes and foreign nations, rather than in framing a syllogism in logic, pleading a case in law, or prescribing a dose of pills in medicine. So, madam, since I'm sure you won't omit so necessary a feature in the education of your children — you yourself having tasted its sweetness, being of a learned line (we still have the writings of the ancient Counts of Foix, from whom your husband and yourself are both descended; and Monsieur de Candale, your uncle, daily obliges the world with more, which will extend the reputation of this quality in your family for many ages to come) — I'll take this occasion to share with you one particular fancy of my own, contrary to the common method, which is all I can contribute to your service in this matter.

The house Diane de Foix and her husband are both descended from, and whose writings Montaigne cites as evidence that learning runs in the family.

## modern-en · the-graces · 25:90

For the rest, this method of education should be carried on with a stern sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants, who, instead of tempting and luring children into letters by apt and gentle means, present nothing in fact but rods and ferules, horror and cruelty. Away with this violence! Away with this compulsion! Nothing, I'm convinced, more dulls and degenerates a well-born nature. If you would have him fear shame and chastisement, don't harden him to them. Inure him to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers he ought to despise; wean him from all effeminacy and delicacy in clothes and lodging, eating and drinking; accustom him to everything, so he may not be a Sir Paris, a carpet-knight, but a sinewy, hardy, vigorous young man. From childhood to my present age I've been of this opinion, and I'm still of it. But among other things, the strict regime of most of our colleges has always displeased me; they could perhaps have erred less harmfully on the indulgent side. It's a real house of correction for imprisoned youth. They're made debauched by being punished before they've done anything to deserve it. Just walk in when they're at their lessons and you'll hear nothing but the cries of boys being beaten and the thunder of pedagogues drunk with fury. A pretty way that, to lure these tender and timorous souls to love their books — with a furious face and a rod in hand! A cursed and pernicious method! Besides what Quintilian has very well observed, that this imperious authority is often followed by very dangerous consequences, and particularly our way of chastising. How much more decent would it be to see their classrooms strewn with green leaves and fine flowers than with the bloody stumps of birch and willow! If it were left to me, I'd paint the school with pictures of joy and gladness, Flora and the Graces, as the philosopher Speusippus did his. Where their profit is, let them also have their pleasure. The food that's proper and wholesome for children should be sweetened with sugar, and what's dangerous to them embittered with gall. It's marvellous to see how careful Plato is in his Laws about the gaiety and diversions of the youth of his city, and how much and how often he expatiates on the races, sports, songs, leaps, and dances — of which, he says, antiquity gave the ordering and patronage specifically to the gods themselves, to Apollo, Minerva, and the Muses. He goes on at length and is very particular in giving countless precepts for exercises; but as for the lettered sciences, he says very little, and only seems to recommend poetry on account of music.

With Flora, the figures Speusippus painted his school with.

## modern-en · plautus · 25:146

The first taste I had for books came to me from the pleasure of reading the fables of Ovid's Metamorphoses; for at about seven or eight I gave up all other diversions to read them, both because this was my native language, the easiest book I was acquainted with, and because of the subject, the most suited to my age. As for Lancelot of the Lake, Amadis of Gaul, Huon of Bordeaux, and such farragoes, by which children are most delighted, I had never so much as heard their names — nor do I yet know what they contain; so strict was the discipline I was raised in. But this was enough to make me neglect the other lessons prescribed me; and there I was infinitely lucky to have to do with an understanding tutor, who knew very well how to discreetly turn a blind eye to this and other little truancies of the same nature. By this means I ran through Virgil's Aeneid, then Terence, then Plautus, then some Italian comedies, lured by the sweetness of the subject; whereas if he had been so foolish as to break me off this diversion, I really believe I'd have brought away from college nothing but a hatred of books, as almost all our young gentlemen do. But he managed the business very tactfully, seeming to take no notice, and allowing me only such time as I could steal from my regular studies — which whetted my appetite to devour those books. For the chief things my father expected from those to whom he'd entrusted my education were affability and good humour; and to tell the truth, my manners had no vice but sloth and want of mettle. The fear wasn't that I'd do ill, but that I'd do nothing; no one predicted I'd be wicked, only useless; they foresaw idleness, not malice; and it's turned out accordingly. The complaints I hear of myself are these: "He's idle, cold in the offices of friendship and family, and in public matters too detached, too disdainful." But the most pointed of them don't say, "Why has he taken such-and-such? Why hasn't he paid so-and-so?" but, "Why doesn't he part with anything? Why doesn't he give?" And I'd take it as a favour if men would expect no greater works of supererogation from me than these. But they're unjust to demand from me what I don't owe, far more rigorously than they require from others what they do owe. In condemning me to that, they spoil the gratification of the act and deprive me of the gratitude that would be my due for it; whereas the active doing of good ought to have greater value coming from my hands, since I've never been on the receiving end at all. I can dispose all the more freely of my fortune the more it is mine, and of myself the more I am my own. And yet, if I were good at making my own case, I might quite easily turn aside these reproaches and let some people understand they aren't so much offended that I don't do enough, as that I'm able to do a great deal more than I do.

The Latin comic poet, one of the books the boy Montaigne ran through by stealth after Ovid and Terence, allured by the sweetness of the subject.

## modern-en · andreas-goveanus · 25:150

— I played the chief parts in the Latin tragedies of Buchanan, Guérente, and Muret, that were performed in our College of Guienne with great dignity. Now Andreas Goveanus, our principal, in this part of his charge as in all the others, was without comparison the best of his employment in France; and I was looked on as one of the best actors. It's an exercise I don't disapprove of in young people of quality; and I've since seen our princes, after the example of some of the ancients, in person handsomely and commendably perform these exercises; it was even permitted to persons of quality to make a profession of it in Greece.

Principal of the College of Guienne, and without comparison the best man in that employment in France.

## modern-en · chilo · 26:17

It is the novelty, more than the size, of things that tempts us to inquire into their causes. We ought to judge nature's infinite power with more reverence, and with a fuller acknowledgment of our own ignorance and weakness. How many unlikely things are testified to by people worthy of belief? Even if we cannot bring ourselves to accept them outright, we should at least suspend judgment, for to condemn them as impossible is, by a rash presumption, to claim that we know the outer limits of what is possible. If we properly understood the difference between the impossible and the unusual — and between what runs against the order of nature and what runs against common opinion — we would obey Chilo's rule of "Ne quid nimis": neither believe too quickly nor too slowly.

Who enjoined the rule Ne quid nimis — nothing too much — and who said: love him as if you were one day to hate him, and hate him as if you were one day to love him.

## modern-en · froissart · 26:18

When we read in Froissart that the Comte de Foix in Béarn knew, the day after, of the defeat of John, King of Castile, at Aljubarrota — and by what means he tells us he knew — we may be allowed a smile; the same for what our annals report about Pope Honorius performing the public obsequies of King Philip Augustus at Rome on the very day he died at Mantes, and ordering the like throughout Italy. These witnesses are perhaps not authoritative enough to bind us. But what about Plutarch, who, besides several examples drawn from antiquity, tells us that he himself knows for certain that under Domitian the news of Antony's defeat in Germany was published at Rome — many days' travel away — and spread through the whole world on the same day as the battle? And what about Caesar's opinion that the report often outruns the event itself? Shall we say that these careful men let themselves be taken in by the common run, because they were less clear-sighted than we are? Is there anything more delicate, more lucid, more lively than Pliny's judgment when he chooses to put it to work? Anything less affected? Leaving aside his learning, of which I make less account — in which of these qualities do any of us match him? And yet there is hardly a young schoolboy who does not catch him in untruth and pretend to set him right about the workings of nature. When we read in Bouchet the miracles wrought by the relics of St. Hilary, away with them: his standing is not enough to take from us the right to contradict him. But to condemn all such stories wholesale, out of hand, strikes me as a singular impudence. The great St. Augustine testifies that he saw a blind child recover sight at the relics of St. Gervasius and St. Protasius at Milan; a woman at Carthage cured of cancer by the sign of the cross made over her by a newly baptised woman; his close friend Hesperius driving the spirits out of his haunted house with a little earth from Our Lord's sepulchre, which earth, carried into the church, suddenly cured a paralytic; and a woman in a procession who, having touched St. Stephen's shrine with a nosegay and then rubbed her eyes with it, recovered her sight after years of blindness — among other miracles he claims to have seen with his own eyes. How do we excuse him, and the two holy bishops Aurelius and Maximinus, both of whom he names as witnesses? Are they ignorant, simple, credulous? Or malicious impostors? Is any man alive impudent enough to think himself the equal of these men in virtue, piety, learning, judgment, or any sort of perfection?

In whom Montaigne finds the Comte de Foix knowing in Bearn, the day after it happened, the defeat of John of Castile.

Bishop of Poictiers and the famous enemy of the Arian heresy, whose relics Bouchet records the miracles of. Hearing in Syria that his only daughter Abra was being sought in marriage, he wrote telling her to put worldly pleasures aside for a greater husband — and then prayed without ceasing that God would take her out of the world, which soon happened, to his singular joy. His wife, hearing how it had been done, begged the same for herself and got it.

## modern-en · laelius · 27:26

When Laelius, in the presence of the Roman consuls, who, after sentencing Tiberius Gracchus, were prosecuting all who had had any familiarity with him, came to ask Caius Blosius, who had been Gracchus's chief friend, how much he would have done for him, and Blosius answered, "All things" — "What! all things?" said Laelius. "And what if he had ordered you to set fire to our temples?" — "He would never have ordered me that," Blosius replied. "But what if he had?" said Laelius. "I would have obeyed him," said the other. If he was as perfect a friend to Gracchus as the histories report, there was still no need to offend the consuls by so bold a confession; he might have kept his confidence in Gracchus's disposition to himself. But those who attack his answer as seditious miss the point, and do not see — as was the case — that Blosius had Gracchus's will in his pocket, both by the power of a friend and by his thorough knowledge of the man. They were more friends than citizens, more friends to each other than either enemies or friends to their country, more friends than they were friends to ambition or innovation. Having absolutely given themselves up to one another, each held the reins of the other's inclination absolutely; and if we suppose all this guided by virtue and conducted by reason — which it could not have been without — Blosius's answer was what it ought to be. If any of their actions had gone off the handle, they were not (by my measure of friendship) friends to one another, nor even to themselves. As for the rest, that answer sounds no worse than my own would, if someone asked me, "If your will should order you to kill your daughter, would you do it?" — and I answered yes. This expresses no agreement to such an act, since I have no suspicion of my own will, and as little of such a friend's. No eloquence in the world could dispossess me of my certainty about my friend's intentions and resolutions. There is not a single action of his, with whatever face it might wear, that I could not at first glance trace back to its true motive. Our souls were drawn so closely together, had regarded each other with such ardent affection and laid open the very bottom of our hearts to each other with the same affection, that I not only knew his as well as my own — in any concern of mine I would have trusted my interest more willingly with him than with myself.

Who asked Caius Blosius, in front of the Roman consuls prosecuting everyone who had been familiar with Tiberius Gracchus, how much he would have done for him — and got the answer: all things. Many at Rome thought and would usually say that the greatest of Scipio’s acts were in part due to him, his constant practice being to advance and support Scipio’s grandeur and renown without any care of his own; and with Fabricius he is one of the two ancients whose countenance and behaviour Montaigne says our people would think barbarous.

## modern-en · suidas · 30:24

As for the rest, they live in a country that is very pleasant and temperate, so that, as my witnesses tell me, it is rare to hear of anyone falling ill, and they assure me they have never seen any of the natives palsied, bleary-eyed, toothless, or bent with age. The country lies along the seashore, fenced on the inland side by great high mountains, with a stretch of about a hundred leagues between. They have plenty of fish and meat, none of which look like ours, and they eat them with no cookery beyond plain boiling, roasting, and grilling. The first man to ride in there on a horse, though in earlier voyages he had become acquainted and familiar with them, frightened them so badly with his centaur appearance that they killed him with their arrows before they could make out who he was. Their houses are very long, big enough to hold two or three hundred people, made of the bark of tall trees, one end stuck in the ground and the trees leaning on each other at the top to support one another, like some of our barns, where the roof comes right down to the ground and serves as side walls too. They have wood so hard that they cut with it and make their swords from it, and grills from it to grill their meat. Their beds are of cotton, slung from the roof like our sailors' hammocks, every man with his own — for the wives sleep apart from their husbands. They rise with the sun, and as soon as they are up, eat for the whole day, since they have no further meals. They do not drink at meals — as Suidas reports of certain other peoples of the East who never drank with their food — but drink very often during the rest of the day, and sometimes to a rousing pitch. Their drink is made of a certain root and is the colour of our claret, and they only ever drink it lukewarm. It keeps no more than two or three days; it has a slightly sharp, brisk taste, is not at all heady, but very kind to the stomach; laxative to strangers but a pleasant beverage to those used to it. Instead of bread they use a certain white compound, like coriander seeds; I have tasted it — the flavour is sweet and a little bland. The whole day is spent in dancing. The young men go off to hunt wild beasts with bows and arrows; meanwhile some of the women are busy heating their drink, which is their chief occupation. One of their old men, in the morning before they begin to eat, preaches to the whole household, walking from one end of the house to the other and repeating the same sentence over and over until he has completed the round — for their houses are at least a hundred yards long. Valour against their enemies and love toward their wives are the two heads of his sermon, never failing to remind them, in closing, that it is their wives who give them their drink warm and well-seasoned. The shape of their beds, ropes, swords, the wooden bracelets they tie around their wrists when they go to fight, and the great canes hollowed out at one end, by whose sound they keep the cadence of their dances, are to be seen in several places, and among them at my house. They shave themselves all over, and much more neatly than we do, with no razor but one of wood or stone. They believe in the immortality of the soul, and that those who have deserved well of the gods are lodged in that part of heaven where the sun rises, and the damned in the west.

The Greek lexicographer, cited for what he reports of some people of the East who drink only outside their meals.

## modern-en · achilles · 27:19

Nor will the very picture the Academy paints of it, as I read them, contradict me when I say this: the first frenzy that the son of Venus put into the heart of the lover at the sight of the bloom of a budding youth — to which they allowed all the brazen, passionate efforts that an immoderate ardour can produce — was founded simply on outward beauty, the false image of physical generation. It could not be founded on the soul, which was still hidden, only just beginning to emerge, and not yet ripe enough to bloom. If this frenzy seized a base spirit, the means by which it pressed its suit were rich presents, favours toward promotion, and such trumpery, all of which the Academy entirely rejects. If it seized a more generous soul, the courtship was correspondingly noble: philosophical instruction, exhortations to revere religion, to obey the laws, to die for one's country, examples of valour, prudence, and justice — the lover working to make himself acceptable through the grace and beauty of his soul, his body's beauty being long past — hoping, by this companionship of minds, to set up a firmer and more lasting contract. When such a courtship reached its goal in due season (for what they did not require in the lover, namely patience and discretion in pursuit, they strictly required in the beloved, since he had to judge of an inward beauty hard to know and hidden), then there arose in the beloved the desire for a spiritual conception by means of a spiritual beauty. This was the main thing; the bodily was incidental and secondary — the reverse of the lover's case. For this reason they preferred the beloved, maintaining that the gods preferred him too, and they greatly blame the poet Aeschylus for having, in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus, given the lover's part to Achilles, who was in the first beardless flower of his youth and the handsomest of the Greeks. After this general union, with the sovereign and worthiest part presiding, governing, and doing its proper offices, great advantages followed, they say, for both private and public life — it made up the strength and power of the countries where it prevailed, and the chief security of liberty and justice. The healthy loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton are their examples. Hence they called it sacred and divine, and held that nothing was hostile to it except the violence of tyrants and the baseness of the common people. Finally, all that can be said in favour of the Academy is that this was a love which ended in friendship — which fits well enough with the Stoic definition of love:

To whom Aeschylus gave the lover’s part in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus — for which the Academy very much blames him, Achilles being in the first and beardless flower of his adolescence and the handsomest of all the Greeks.

## modern-en · eudamidas · 27:28

If, in the friendship I am speaking of, one could give to the other, the receiver of the favour would be the one putting his friend in his debt. Each of them, contending above all to be useful to the other, the one who provides the opportunity is the generous one — giving his friend the satisfaction of doing for him the thing he most desires to do. When the philosopher Diogenes was short of money, he used to say that he was reclaiming it from his friends, not asking for it. To show how this works in practice, let me give you an ancient and singular example. Eudamidas, a Corinthian, had two friends: Charixenus the Sicyonian and Areteus the Corinthian. Coming to die poor, while his two friends were rich, he made his will in this fashion: "I bequeath to Areteus the keeping of my mother, to provide for her in her old age; and to Charixenus I bequeath the task of marrying my daughter, and giving her as good a dowry as he is able; and should one of these die first, I substitute the survivor in his place." The first to see the will laughed at it, but the legatees, when they heard, accepted it with very great content. One of them, Charixenus, died five days later; the whole charge now falling on Areteus, he took care of the old woman with great affection, and out of the five talents he had to his name he gave two and a half as dowry for his own only daughter, and two and a half as dowry for Eudamidas's daughter, and held both weddings on the same day.

A Corinthian who died poor with two rich friends, and left his mother’s maintenance to Areteus and his daughter’s marriage to Charixenus — a will everyone laughed at and the legatees accepted with content. Montaigne says the force of friendship shows more in leaving them the chance of the benefit than in their discharging it.

## modern-en · callicles · 29:7

The archer who shoots over the mark misses just as much as one who shoots short; and it is equally hard on my sight to look up at a great light and to look down into a dark abyss. Callicles in Plato says that the furthest reaches of philosophy are harmful, and advises against diving into it beyond the point where it pays off. Taken moderately, he says, it is pleasant and useful, but pushed too far it leaves a man brutish and vicious, scornful of religion and the common laws, an enemy to civil society and to all human pleasures, useless for any public office, unable to help others or even himself, and a ready target for every kind of insult and injury. He is right. In its excess, philosophy enslaves our natural freedom, and through some impertinent subtlety it leads us off the fair, beaten path that nature has marked out for us.

Who says in Plato that the extremity of philosophy is hurtful, and that taken beyond the limits of profit it renders a man brutish, a contemner of religion and the laws, and unfit for any public administration. Montaigne says he says true.

## modern-en · thomas-aquinas · 29:8

The love we feel for our wives is entirely lawful, and yet theology thinks it right to keep it in check. I recall reading somewhere in St. Thomas Aquinas a condemnation of marriages within the forbidden degrees, with this among his reasons: there is some danger that the friendship a man feels for such a woman will become immoderate; for if the conjugal affection is full and perfect between them, as it ought to be, and is then further loaded with the affection of kinship, there is no doubt the husband will be carried beyond the bounds of reason.

Who condemns marriage within the forbidden degrees partly for fear the friendship should be immoderate: a conjugal affection surcharged with the affection of kindred will carry a husband beyond the bounds of reason.

## modern-en · zenobia · 29:11

Marriage is a solemn, religious tie, and so the pleasure we draw from it should be a sober and serious delight, mixed with a certain gravity — a discreet, conscientious sort of pleasure. And since its chief end is generation, some have questioned whether, when men are out of hope of children — too old, or when the wife is already pregnant — it is lawful to embrace our wives. It is homicide, according to Plato. Certain nations — the Mohammedan among others — abhor any union with women who are pregnant; others, with women who are in their courses. Zenobia would let her husband in only for a single encounter, after which she sent him off to manage his own appetites for the whole period of her conception, and only after that would receive him again — a brave and generous example of conjugal continence. It was, no doubt, from some lascivious poet, himself in great straits for a little of this sport, that Plato borrowed the story that Jupiter was once so hot for his wife that, not having the patience to wait for the couch, he threw her down on the floor, where the violence of pleasure made him forget the great and important decisions he had just taken with the other gods in their heavenly council, and made him boast that he had had as good a time of it as when, unknown to her parents, he first took her maidenhead.

Who would admit her husband for one encounter only and then left him to himself for the whole time of her conception — a brave and generous example, Montaigne says, of conjugal continence.

## modern-en · aelius-verus · 29:12

The kings of Persia used to invite their wives to the start of their feasts; but once the wine had really begun to work, and they meant to give pleasure its head, they sent them back to their private quarters, so that they would not have to take part in their immoderate lust, sending in other women in their stead, with whom they were not bound by the same decorum. Not all pleasures and all forms of gratification fit all persons. Epaminondas had put a young man in prison for certain debaucheries; when Pelopidas pleaded that, at his request, the young man might be released, Epaminondas refused; but he granted it at once, at the first word, to a wench of his who made the same plea — saying that this was a favour fit for one such as she, but not for a general. Sophocles, joint praetor with Pericles, happened to see a fine boy go by and exclaimed, "What a charming boy!" "That might do very well," answered Pericles, "for someone other than a praetor, who must keep not only his hands but his eyes chaste." The emperor Aelius Verus answered his wife, who reproached him with his love of other women, that he did it on a conscientious account, since marriage was a name of honour and dignity, not of wanton and lascivious desire; and our church history preserves with great reverence the memory of a woman who left her husband because she would not yield to his indecent and inordinate desires. ## modern-en · gallio · 29:16

Human wisdom misuses its talent as much when it sets to work cutting down the number and sweetness of the pleasures that are naturally our due, as it uses it well when it artfully dresses up and disguises the ills of life to soften the feel of them. Had I been in charge, I would have taken another, more natural course — one which, to tell the truth, is both convenient and holy, and which perhaps I could have set within bounds. But our spiritual and bodily physicians, as if by mutual agreement, can find no other way to cure the body's and the soul's infirmities than by misery and pain. To this end, vigils, fasts, hair-shirts, distant and solitary banishments, perpetual imprisonments, scourges, and other afflictions have been introduced — but on the understanding that they will sting, that they will be real afflictions; not turn out as they did with one Gallio, who, having been exiled to Lesbos, was soon reported back in Rome to be living merry as the day is long, and that what had been laid on him as a penance had turned to his pleasure. The Senate then thought fit to recall him home to his wife and family, and confine him to his own house, in order to suit the punishment to his actual feelings. To the man whom fasting makes more healthful and more lively, and to the man whose palate prefers fish to flesh, the prescription of these would have no curative effect — any more than drugs swallowed with appetite and pleasure cure the patient. The bitterness of the potion and the patient's aversion are necessary for the cure to work. The nature that would eat rhubarb like buttered turnips would frustrate the use and virtue of it; it must be something to trouble and disturb the stomach, that must purge and cure it. And here the common rule — that contraries cure — fails, for in this one case ill is cured by ill.

Exiled to Lesbos and found to be living there as merry as the day was long, so that the Senate recalled him and confined him to his own house with his wife and family — to fit the punishment to his feeling.

When King Pyrrhus invaded Italy, after surveying the order of the army the Romans had sent out to meet him, he said: "I do not know what kind of barbarians these may be" — for so the Greeks called all other nations — "but the disposition of this army that I see before me has nothing barbarous in it." ## modern-en · arsac · 30:10

It seems that in this great body of the earth there are two sorts of motion, as in our own — one natural and the other feverish. When I think of the impression our river, the Dordogne, has made in my time on its right bank, how in twenty years it has gained so much ground and undermined the foundations of so many houses, I take it for an unusual agitation; for if it had always run that way, or were to do so in future, the look of the world would be wholly changed. But rivers alter their course, beating now against one bank, now the other, and sometimes keeping quietly to their channel. I am not speaking of sudden floods, the causes of which everyone understands. In Médoc, by the seashore, my brother, Sieur d'Arsac, sees an estate he owned there buried under the sands that the sea throws up before it; the tops of some houses are still to be seen, and his rents and lands have been turned into pitiful, barren scrub. The people of the place say that of late years the sea has been driving so hard against them that they have lost more than four leagues of land. These sands are her outriders, and we can now see great mounds of moving sand marching half a league ahead of her, taking the land as they go.

Montaigne’s brother, who watches an estate of his in Medoc being buried under the sand the sea drives before it, the tops of some houses still showing and his rents turned to barren pasture.

## modern-en · leonidas · 30:37

— he who gives up nothing of his self-possession in the face of imminent death, who dying still throws his enemy a fierce and disdainful look, is overcome not by us but by fortune; he is killed, not conquered. The most valiant are sometimes the most unfortunate. There are defeats more triumphant than victories. Those four sister victories — the fairest the sun ever looked on, of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale, and Sicily — never dared to set their united glory against the single glory of the rout of King Leonidas and his men at the pass of Thermopylae. Who ever ran with a more glorious purpose, a higher ambition, toward winning a battle than Captain Iscolas did toward the certain loss of one? Who could have come up with a more subtle device to secure his own safety than he found to assure his own destruction? He was sent to defend a certain pass of the Peloponnese against the Arcadians; finding it utterly impossible, given the lie of the ground and the imbalance of forces, and seeing that all who faced the enemy must inevitably be left dead on the spot, yet judging it unworthy of his own virtue and magnanimity, and of the Lacedaemonian name, to fail in any part of his duty, he chose a middle course between those two extremes. He saved the youngest and fittest of his men for the service and defence of their country and sent them back; with the rest, whose loss would be of less moment, he resolved to hold the pass and, by their deaths, make the enemy pay as dearly as possible for getting through. And so it fell out: surrounded on all sides by the Arcadians, he and his men, after killing a great many of the enemy, were cut to pieces. Is there a single trophy dedicated to the conquerors that was not far more due to those who lost? The part of true conquering lies in the encounter, not in the coming out the other side; the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.

Whose discomfiture at the pass of Thermopylae, Montaigne says, outweighs the four sister victories of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale and Sicily put together.

## modern-en · sarah · 30:39

The men there have several wives, and the more wives the higher their reputation for valour. And it is one very remarkable feature of their marriages that the same jealousy our wives use to keep us from the friendship and intimacy of other women, theirs use to further their husbands' desires and to procure them many partners. Above all things concerned for their husbands' honour, they make it their chief care to seek out and bring in as many companions as they can, since this is held to be evidence of their husband's worth. Most of our ladies will cry out that this is monstrous; in truth, it is not so, but a truly matrimonial virtue of the highest order. In the Bible, Sarah, with Leah and Rachel, the two wives of Jacob, gave the most beautiful of their handmaids to their husbands; Livia, in her own interest, indulged Augustus's passions for other women; and the wife of King Deiotarus, Stratonice, not only gave up a beautiful young maid in her service to her husband's embraces, but carefully brought up the children he had by her and helped them on to the succession of their father's crown.

Who with Leah and Rachel gave the most beautiful of her handmaids to her husband — Montaigne’s scriptural parallel to the cannibal wives who seek out companions for their husbands.

## modern-en · charles-ix · 30:43

Three of these people, not foreseeing how dear a knowledge of the corruptions of this part of the world would one day cost their happiness and peace of mind — nor that their dealings with us are leading, as I take them to be, straight to their ruin (poor wretches, to let themselves be taken in by the desire for novelty, leaving the serenity of their own sky to come so far to gape at ours!) — were at Rouen when the late King Charles IX was there. The king himself talked with them a good while; they were shown our fashions, our pomp, the shape of a great city. Afterwards someone asked their opinion, wanting to know what among all the things they had seen they thought most worth admiring. To which they answered three things — of which I have forgotten the third, and am sorry for it, but two I still remember. They said, first, that they thought it very strange that so many tall men, bearded, strong, well-armed, who stood about the king (probably they meant the Swiss Guard), should submit to obeying a child, and not rather pick out one of their own number to command. Secondly (they have a way of speaking in their language by which they call men the halves of one another) they had noticed that there were among us men full and crammed with every sort of good, while their other halves were begging at their doors, lean and half-starved with hunger and poverty; and they thought it strange that these needy halves were able to bear such inequality and injustice, and did not take the others by the throat or set fire to their houses.

At Rouen when three of the cannibals were brought there, and who talked with them a good while. They said it was strange that so many tall bearded armed men should submit to obey a child.

## modern-en · don-john-of-austria · 31:4

Among one Indian nation there is a praiseworthy custom: when anything goes against them in some encounter or battle, they publicly ask pardon of the sun, who is their god, as though they had done some unjust act, always crediting their good or bad fortune to divine justice and submitting their own judgment and reason to it. It is enough for a Christian to believe that all things come from God, to receive them with acknowledgment of his divine and unsearchable wisdom, and so to accept them gratefully with whatever face they may wear. But I do not approve of the common practice of trying to confirm and support our religion by the success of our enterprises. Our belief has foundation enough without needing to be authorised by events. The people, accustomed to such plausible arguments, well-suited to their taste, are likely, when those arguments fail, to stagger in their faith too. So in this war we are now engaged in on account of religion, those who had the upper hand at the affair of Rochelabeille made loud boasts of it as an infallible approval of their cause, and then, when they had to excuse their misfortunes at Moncontour and Jarnac by calling them fatherly scourges and corrections — "because the people were not yet wholly at their mercy" — they show plainly enough what it is to draw two sorts of grist out of the same sack, and to blow hot and cold with the same mouth. It would be better to ground the common people in the solid, real foundations of truth. There was a fine naval battle won a few months ago under the command of Don John of Austria against the Turks; but it has also pleased God at other times to let us see victories just as great at our own expense. In short, it is a hard thing to reduce divine matters to our scales without losing a great deal of the weight in the spillage. And anyone who would try to give a reason why Arius and his Pope Leo, the principal heads of the Arian heresy, both died, at different times, of such similar and strange deaths (for, called away from disputation by a griping in the bowels, they both suddenly gave up the ghost on the privy), and would aggravate this divine vengeance by the circumstances of the place, might as well throw in the death of Heliogabalus, who was also killed in a privy. And Irenaeus, indeed, came to a similar end. God, pleased to show us that the good have something else to hope for, and the wicked something else to fear, than the fortunes or misfortunes of this world, manages and applies them according to his own hidden will and pleasure, and deprives us of the means of foolishly making a profit of them. So those people delude themselves who try to dive into these mysteries by the strength of human reason. They never strike one blow without taking two in return — of which St. Augustine makes a great proof against his opponents. It is a contest decided more by strength of memory than by force of reason. We must content ourselves with the light the sun is pleased to communicate to us by his rays; and whoever lifts up his eyes to take in more, let him not think it strange if, for the reward of his presumption, he loses his sight.

Under whose command the fine naval battle against the Turks was won a few months before Montaigne wrote — a victory he will not let anyone use as proof of a cause, since God has let us see as great ones at our own expense.

So in this war we are now engaged in on account of religion, those who had the upper hand at the affair of Rochelabeille made loud boasts of it as an infallible approval of their cause, and then, when they had to excuse their misfortunes at Moncontour and Jarnac by calling them fatherly scourges and corrections — "because the people were not yet wholly at their mercy" — they show plainly enough what it is to draw two sorts of grist out of the same sack, and to blow hot and cold with the same mouth. It would be better to ground the common people in the solid, real foundations of truth. There was a fine naval battle won a few months ago under the command of Don John of Austria against the Turks; but it has also pleased God at other times to let us see victories just as great at our own expense. In short, it is a hard thing to reduce divine matters to our scales without losing a great deal of the weight in the spillage. And anyone who would try to give a reason why Arius and his Pope Leo, the principal heads of the Arian heresy, both died, at different times, of such similar and strange deaths (for, called away from disputation by a griping in the bowels, they both suddenly gave up the ghost on the privy), and would aggravate this divine vengeance by the circumstances of the place, might as well throw in the death of Heliogabalus, who was also killed in a privy. And Irenaeus, indeed, came to a similar end. God, pleased to show us that the good have something else to hope for, and the wicked something else to fear, than the fortunes or misfortunes of this world, manages and applies them according to his own hidden will and pleasure, and deprives us of the means of foolishly making a profit of them. So those people delude themselves who try to dive into these mysteries by the strength of human reason. They never strike one blow without taking two in return — of which St. Augustine makes a great proof against his opponents. It is a contest decided more by strength of memory than by force of reason. We must content ourselves with the light the sun is pleased to communicate to us by his rays; and whoever lifts up his eyes to take in more, let him not think it strange if, for the reward of his presumption, he loses his sight.

Also slain in a house of office — which Montaigne adds to show how little such coincidences prove.

But to push contempt of death so far as to use it for clearing our minds of honours, riches, dignities, and the other gifts we call goods of fortune — as if reason alone were not enough to persuade us to give them up without this added injunction — I had never seen it commanded or practised until I came across this passage of Seneca. He was advising Lucilius, a man of great power and authority close to the emperor, to give up his lavish and pleasure-seeking way of life and retire to some quiet, solitary, philosophical existence. When Lucilius raised difficulties, Seneca said: "My opinion is that either you leave that life of yours, or life itself. I would advise the gentler way: untie, rather than break, the knot you have rashly tied. But if it cannot be untied otherwise, then break it cleanly. No man is so cowardly that he would not rather fall once than be always falling." I would have expected such counsel from Stoic severity, but it is stranger coming, as it does, from Epicurus, who writes the same thing on a similar occasion to Idomeneus. And I think I have noticed something like it — though with Christian moderation — among our own people.

The man of power about the emperor whom Seneca advises either to leave that life of his or life itself: better once to fall than to be always falling.
