## modern-en · abra · 32:3

St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, that famous enemy of the Arian heresy, was in Syria when word reached him that Abra, his only daughter, whom he had left at home under her mother's care, was being sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country — a virtuous, well-brought-up girl, beautiful, rich, and in the flower of her youth. He wrote back to her (as the record shows) that she should remove her affection from all the pleasures and advantages being offered, since on his travels he had found a far greater and worthier match for her: a husband of much greater power and magnificence, who would clothe her in robes and jewels of inestimable value. His aim was to wean her from the appetite for worldly delights and to join her wholly to God. And since the nearest and surest route to that, as he saw it, was his daughter's death, he never stopped praying and pleading with the Almighty to please call her out of this world and take her to himself. And it came to pass: soon after his return she died, at which he showed a singular joy. This seems to outdo the others, since he turns to this method from the start where they only resort to it secondarily, and it was on his own only daughter. But I will not leave out the rest of the story, even though it suits my purpose. St. Hilary's wife, learning from him how their daughter's death had been brought about by his deliberate prayer, and how much happier she was to be removed from this world than to have remained in it, conceived so vivid a sense of eternal and heavenly bliss that she begged her husband with utmost insistence to do the same for her. And God, at their joint request, soon called her too — a death embraced with singular and mutual contentment.

St Hilary’s only daughter, left at home under her mother’s eye, sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country, and prayed out of the world by her father.

Sometimes she seems to play with us in the very nick of an affair. Monsieur d'Estrees, then ensign to Monsieur de Vendome, and Monsieur de Licques, lieutenant in the Duc d'Ascot's company, were both rivals for the sister of the Sieur de Fougueselles, though on opposite sides — as often happens between frontier neighbours. ## modern-en · constantine-founder · 33:7

Doesn't she seem to play the artist here? Constantine, son of Helena, founded the empire of Constantinople, and many ages later, Constantine, son of Helen, brought it to its end. Sometimes she likes to mimic our miracles. We are told that when King Clovis was besieging Angoulême, the walls fell down on their own by divine favour; and Bouchet has it from some author that when King Robert was laying siege to a city and had slipped away from the siege to keep the feast of St. Aignan at Orleans, the walls of the besieged city collapsed in sudden ruin, without any assault, while he was at his devotions in a certain part of the Mass. But she did just the opposite in our Milan wars: Captain Rense was besieging Arona for us and had dug a mine under a great stretch of the wall; when the mine was sprung, the wall lifted off its foundations — and then dropped back down, whole and entire, exactly on its base, so that the besieged took no harm at all from the attempt.

Who founded the empire of Constantinople.

Sometimes she plays the physician. Jason of Pheres, given up by the doctors because of an abscess in his chest, decided to rid himself of his pain at least by death, and threw himself recklessly into the thick of the enemy in a battle. He was so luckily wounded clean through the body that the abscess burst and he was completely cured. Did she not also outdo the painter Protogenes at his own art? He had finished a picture of a dog, panting and out of breath, well rendered in every other part but he could not get the foam and slaver coming from its mouth quite right. Furious with his work, he snatched up his sponge, which had soaked up various colours from cleaning his brushes, and hurled it at the picture meaning to ruin it. Fortune guided the sponge to land just at the dog's mouth, where it produced what all his skill could not. Does she not sometimes direct our plans and correct them? Isabel, Queen of England, sailing from Zealand back into her own kingdom with an army to support her son against her husband, would have been lost had she landed at the port she meant to, where the enemy lay in wait; but fortune, against her wishes, drove her into another harbour where she landed safely. And that man of old who, throwing a stone at a dog, hit and killed his mother-in-law — was he not right to declare:

Given over by the physicians for an imposthume in his breast, he threw himself into the thickest of the enemy to be rid of the pain by death at least — and was so fortunately wounded through the body that the imposthume broke and he was cured.

## modern-en · icetes · 33:10

Icetes had hired two soldiers to kill Timoleon at Adrana in Sicily. They picked their moment while he was at a sacrifice and pushed into the crowd. As they were signalling to each other that the time had come, a third man stepped in and felled one of them with a sword stroke across the head, leaving him dead on the spot, and ran off. The other, thinking himself discovered and as good as dead, fled to the altar and begged for mercy, promising to confess the whole plot. As he was doing so, laying out the full conspiracy, the third man — the one who had run — was caught and dragged through the crowd as a murderer, hauled before Timoleon and the chief men of the assembly. There he cried for pardon, pleading that he had justly killed his father's murderer. He proved it on the spot through reliable witnesses whom good fortune had conveniently provided — that his father had indeed been killed in the city of Leontini by the very man on whom he had now taken revenge. He was at once awarded ten Attic minae for having had the good fortune, by setting out to avenge his father's death, to preserve the life of the common father of Sicily. Fortune, truly, in her workings exceeds all the rules of human prudence.

Who contracted with two soldiers to kill Timoleon at Adrana in Sicily.

Swords drawn, they rushed full tilt at one another, and fortune so guided the points that they each inflicted an equally mortal wound — while granting their brave friendship just enough strength left to draw out the bloody swords and embrace one another in their dying. They held each other so closely and so warmly that the executioner cut off both their heads at once, leaving the bodies still locked together in that noble bond, their wounds joined mouth to mouth, lovingly sucking in each other's last blood and life.

I have heard — to the great shame of the age we live in — that two of the most learned men of our day died so poor they had hardly bread to put in their mouths: Lilius Gregorius Giraldus in Italy and Sebastianus Castalio in Germany. so were we; but, like people who put out the day's light by burning artificial light, we have, with borrowed forms and fashions, destroyed our own. King Agesilaus, into a decrepit old age, wore the same clothes in winter that he wore in summer. ## modern-en · stilpo · 38:26

When Stilpo had escaped the burning of his town, where he lost his wife, his children, and his goods, Demetrius Poliorcetes, seeing him appear undisturbed amid such a ruin of his country, asked him whether he had suffered no loss. Stilpo answered, No; and that, thank God, nothing of his had been lost. This was also what the philosopher Antisthenes meant when he said wryly that "a man should furnish himself with such things as would float, and that could escape the storm with their owner." And indeed a wise man never loses anything if he has himself. When the city of Nola was destroyed by the barbarians, Paulinus, who was bishop of the place, having lost everything he had and being himself a prisoner, prayed like this: "O Lord, keep me from feeling this loss; for you know that they have not yet touched anything of what is truly mine." The riches that made him rich and the goods that made him good were still intact. This is what it is to choose treasures that can defend themselves from plunder and violence, and to hide them in a place no one can enter and that can only be betrayed by ourselves. Wives, children, goods are to be had, and especially health, by those who can get them; but we are not to set our hearts on them so far that our happiness depends on them. We must reserve a back-shop, wholly our own and entirely free, in which to set up our true liberty, our chief solitude and retreat. There we are mostly to keep our own company, and so privately that no foreign acquaintance or commerce is admitted; there to laugh and to talk as if without wife, children, goods, retinue, or attendance — so that when it falls out that we must lose any or all of them, it will be no new thing for us to be without them. We have a mind pliable enough in itself to be company; it has what is needed to attack and defend, to receive and to give. Let us not, then, fear that we shall languish in this solitude under a dreary emptiness.

Who escaped the burning of his town having lost wife, children and goods, and told Demetrius Poliorcetes that he had received no loss, since fortune had nothing of his — and who, oppressed with age, is said to have purposely hastened his end by drinking pure wine.

## modern-en · antisthenes · 38:3

the contagion is very dangerous in a crowd. A man must either imitate the vicious or hate them — both dangerous, either to resemble them because they are many or to hate many because they are different from us. Merchants who go to sea are right to be careful that those they sail with are not dissolute blasphemers or otherwise vicious; they regard such company as unlucky. That is why Bias said, with a smile, to those who, caught in a dangerous storm with him, were calling on the gods: "Hush, speak softly, so they may not know you are here in my company." And, more telling still, Albuquerque, viceroy in the Indies for King Emmanuel of Portugal, in an extreme peril of shipwreck, took a young boy upon his shoulders for this sole reason: that in the shared danger the boy's innocence might serve to recommend him to the divine favour and bring them safe to shore. It isn't that a wise man cannot live contented anywhere and be alone even in the middle of a palace crowd; but if it is left to his choice, the schoolman will tell you he should flee the very sight of the crowd. He will put up with it if he must; but if it is up to him, he will choose to be alone. He cannot think himself sufficiently free of vice if he still has to contend with it in other men. Charondas punished as evildoers those convicted of keeping bad company. There is nothing so unsociable and so sociable as man — the one through his vice, the other through his nature. And Antisthenes, in my view, did not give a good enough answer when someone reproached him for frequenting bad company by saying that doctors live well enough among the sick — for if doctors contribute to the patients' health, they cannot help, through contagion, constant exposure to disease, and familiarity with it, impairing their own.

The Cynic, who thought it a poor sort of commendation that Ismenias played excellently well on the flute.

The riches that made him rich and the goods that made him good were still intact. This is what it is to choose treasures that can defend themselves from plunder and violence, and to hide them in a place no one can enter and that can only be betrayed by ourselves. Wives, children, goods are to be had, and especially health, by those who can get them; but we are not to set our hearts on them so far that our happiness depends on them. We must reserve a back-shop, wholly our own and entirely free, in which to set up our true liberty, our chief solitude and retreat. There we are mostly to keep our own company, and so privately that no foreign acquaintance or commerce is admitted; there to laugh and to talk as if without wife, children, goods, retinue, or attendance — so that when it falls out that we must lose any or all of them, it will be no new thing for us to be without them. We have a mind pliable enough in itself to be company; it has what is needed to attack and defend, to receive and to give. Let us not, then, fear that we shall languish in this solitude under a dreary emptiness.

Bishop of Nola, who when the barbarians ruined the city lost everything he had and was taken prisoner, and prayed only to be kept from feeling the loss — they had touched nothing that was his.

On the subject of letters, I will add this to what has been said: it is a kind of writing in which my friends think I can do something; and I am willing to confess that I would have preferred to publish my whimsies in that form than in any other, had I had someone to write to. But I lacked the kind of settled correspondence I once had — one that would draw me to it, raise my fancy, and sustain me. As for trafficking with the wind, as some others have done, and forging imaginary names to address letters to, on a serious subject — I could only ever do this in a dream, being a sworn enemy of every kind of falsification. I should have been more diligent and more confident if I had had a judicious and indulgent friend to address, rather than exposing myself like this to the various judgments of a whole public; and I am much mistaken if I would not have done better that way. I have naturally a humorous and familiar style; but it is a style of my own, not fit for public business — like the language I speak, too compact, irregular, abrupt, idiosyncratic. As for letters of ceremony that have no substance beyond a polite weaving of courteous words, I am hopelessly at a loss; I have neither faculty nor taste for those tedious offerings of service and affection; I believe little of them from others, and I would not forgive myself for saying to others more than I myself believe. This is, no doubt, very far from current practice; for there has never been so abject and servile a prostitution of offers: life, soul, devotion, adoration, vassal, slave, and I can't tell what else — all such expressions so commonly and indifferently bandied about by everyone to everyone, that when they want to declare a greater and more respectful inclination on more deserving occasions, they have nothing left to express it with. I have a deep loathing of any whiff of flattery, which is why I naturally drop into a shy, rough, blunt way of speaking which, to those who do not know me, may seem to smack a little of disdain. I honour most those to whom I show the least honour, and where my soul moves with the greatest cheerfulness I easily forget the ceremonies of look and gesture, and offer myself faintly and bluntly to those to whom I am most devoted — they should, I think, read it in my heart; and the wording of what I say only injures the love I have inwardly conceived. As for welcoming, taking leave, giving thanks, accosting, offering one's services, and all those verbal formalities that the ceremonious laws of our modern civility prescribe, I know no one as stupidly unfurnished with such language as myself; and I have never been employed in writing letters of favour or recommendation without the man for whom they were written thinking my intervention cold and inadequate. The Italians are great printers of letters; I believe I have at least a hundred separate volumes of them, of which Annibale Caro's seem to me the best. If all the paper I have scribbled to the ladies, back when my hand was really prompted by passion, were still in existence, perhaps one might find a page worthy to be passed on to our young men in love, who are bewildered by that fury. I always write my letters at top speed — so headlong that, though I write quite illegibly, I would rather do it myself than employ another, since I can find no one able to keep up with me; and I never copy any out again. I have got the great ones who know me used to enduring my blots and crossings out, and to paper without fold or margin. The letters that cost me the most pains are the worst; when I begin dragging it along by the ears, it's a sign that I am not really in it. I throw myself in without forethought or design; the first word starts the second, and so on to the end of the chapter. The letters of this age consist more in fine edges and prefaces than in matter. Just as I would rather write two letters than fold and seal one (and always give that job to someone else), so, when the real business of my letter is finished, I would gladly hand it on to another to add those long harangues, offers, and prayers we put at the bottom — and I would be glad if some new custom would relieve us of that trouble; likewise of heading them with a long string of qualities and titles, which, for fear of mistakes, I have often left out altogether, especially to men of the long robe and of finance. There are so many new offices, such a shuffling and arranging of titles of honour, that it is hard to get them right; and yet, since they are so dearly bought, they cannot be altered or omitted without giving offence. I find it equally in bad taste to clutter the fronts and inscriptions of the books we send to the press with the like.

Whose printed letters Montaigne thinks the best of the hundred volumes of them he owns.

## modern-en · john-of-portugal · 40:8

When the kings of Castile banished the Jews from their lands, John, King of Portugal, in return for eight crowns a head, sold them refuge in his own kingdom for a limited period, on condition that when the period expired they were to leave, and he would furnish ships to transport them to Africa. The day came, and they were given to understand that any who remained in the kingdom afterwards would become slaves; the vessels provided were poorly equipped; and those who embarked were treated brutally and shamefully by the crews, who, among other indignities, kept them crisscrossing at sea — now forward, now back — until they had used up all their provisions and were forced to buy more from the sailors at extortionate prices for so long that they were not set on shore until they had been stripped to their very shirts. When news of this inhuman treatment reached those who had remained behind, the greater part of them resolved to accept slavery; some made a show of converting. Emmanuel, John's successor, on coming to the throne first set them at liberty, then changed his mind and ordered them out of the country, assigning three ports for their departure. He hoped, says Bishop Osorius — no contemptible Latin historian of these recent times — that since the favour of liberty he had granted them had failed to convert them to Christianity, the difficulty of trusting themselves to the mercy of the sailors and of abandoning a country in which they were now settled and had grown rich, in order to expose themselves in strange and unknown regions, would at last do it. But, finding himself mistaken in this expectation, and that they were all resolved on the voyage, he cut off two of the three ports he had promised them, so that the length and discomfort of the passage might reduce some to compliance — or that he might, by squeezing them all into one place, more conveniently carry out what he had designed: which was to seize every child under fourteen from the arms of their fathers and mothers, transporting them out of sight and contact, into a place where they could be instructed and brought up in our religion. He says this produced a most horrid spectacle. The natural affection between parents and children, and beyond that their zeal for their ancient belief, fighting against this violent decree, fathers and mothers were commonly seen killing themselves; and, by a still more terrible example, throwing their own young children into wells and pits out of love and compassion, to escape the severity of the law. As for the rest, when the appointed time expired, for lack of means to transport them they fell back into slavery. Some also turned Christian, but on whose faith — and on that of their descendants, even today, a hundred years on — few Portuguese yet feel they can rely; though custom and length of time are far more powerful counsellors in such changes than any other constraint. In the town of Castelnaudari, fifty heretic Albigensians let themselves be burned alive in a single fire rather than renounce their views.

Who sold the Jews banished from Castile a retreat in his dominions for eight crowns a head and a fixed term, and after the term made slaves of those who stayed.

What, moreover, about pain — which Aristippus, Hieronymus, and most of the sages have reputed the worst of all evils; and which even those who have denied it in words have admitted in their conduct? Posidonius, racked with a sharp and painful disease, was visited by Pompey, who apologised for having come at such a bad moment to hear him discourse on philosophy. ## modern-en · foulke-of-anjou · 40:52

William, our last Duke of Guienne, the father of that Eleanor who carried the duchy into the houses of France and England, wore continuously for the last ten or twelve years of his life a suit of armour under a religious habit, by way of penance. Foulke, Count of Anjou, went all the way to Jerusalem to have himself whipped there by two of his servants, with a rope around his neck, before the sepulchre of our Lord. But don't we still, every Good Friday in various places, see great numbers of men and women beating and whipping themselves until they tear and cut the flesh to the very bone? I have often seen it, and without any trick to it; and it was said that there were some among them (they go disguised) who for money undertook by this means to bear the religious penance of others, by a contempt of pain all the greater because the incentives of devotion are more powerful than those of greed. Q. Maximus buried his son when he was consul, M. Cato his when praetor-elect, and L. Paulus both of his within a few days of each other, all of them with a countenance that showed no kind of grief. I once said jokingly of a certain man that he had cheated divine justice; for the violent death of three of his grown children was sent to him on a single day, as a severe scourge, presumably; and so far from being afflicted by it, he took it for a particular grace and favour of heaven. I do not go in for these monstrous humours, although I lost two or three children at nurse, if not without grief at least without complaint, and there is hardly an accident that cuts closer to the quick. I see many other grounds of sorrow that, if they happened to me, I would barely feel; and I have despised some, when they have come on me, to which the world has given so terrible a figure that I would blush to boast of my equanimity.

## modern-en · dionysius-the-younger · 40:75

My second condition of life was to have money of my own; I managed things so that I soon laid up a considerable sum out of a modest fortune, on the principle that what one really owns is what one sets aside out of one's ordinary spending, and that one cannot absolutely rely on revenue one only hopes to receive, however clear the hope may be. "For what," I said, "if I should be caught short by some accident?" And after such empty and vicious imaginings, I would very wisely, by this hoarding, provide against all eventualities; and could, moreover, answer those who objected that the number of these was too vast that, if I couldn't lay up for all, I could at least do it for some, and for many. Yet this was not done without a great deal of solicitude and anxiety. I kept it very close, and though I dare to talk so boldly about myself, I never spoke truly of my money — but falsely, as others do, who being rich pretend to be poor, and being poor pretend to be rich, dispensing their consciences from ever telling sincerely what they have: a ridiculous and shameful prudence. Was I going on a journey? It seemed to me I was never well enough provided; and the more I loaded myself with money, the more I loaded myself with fear — one moment about the danger of the roads, the next about the loyalty of the man in charge of my baggage; of whom, like some others I know, I was never sufficiently sure unless I kept him constantly in view. If I happened to leave my cash-box behind, oh, what strange suspicions and anxieties I fell into, and, what was worse, without daring to share them with anybody. My mind was eternally taken up with such things; so that, all in all, there is more trouble in keeping money than in earning it. And even if I didn't really do all I say, or wasn't really as ridiculously anxious about my money as I've made out, it still cost me something at least to restrain myself from being so. I drew little or no advantage from what I had, and my expenses seemed no less to me for having more to spend; for, as Bion said, hairy men are as angry as bald men at being plucked. Once you are used to it and have set your heart on your hoard, it is no longer at your service: you can't bring yourself to break into it. It's like a building you fancy must inevitably collapse to ruin if you so much as stir a single pebble; necessity must take you by the throat before you will bring yourself to touch it. I would sooner have pawned anything I owned, or sold a horse, and with much less reluctance, than have made the slightest breach in that beloved purse I had so carefully laid by. But the danger is that a man cannot easily set certain limits to this desire (they are hard to find for things one takes to be good), and to hold this good husbandry short of degenerating into miserliness. People are forever intent on adding to the heap, and increasing the stock from sum to sum, until at last they vilely deprive themselves of the enjoyment of their own goods, and put everything in reserve without making any use of it at all. By this rule the richest people in the world are those set to guard the walls and gates of a wealthy city. All money-men, I conclude, are misers. Plato sets out the corporal or human goods in this order: health, beauty, strength, riches; and riches, he says, are not blind, but very clear-sighted, when illuminated by prudence. Dionysius the Younger did a very fine thing on this subject; he was informed that one of his Syracusans had hidden a treasure in the ground, and sent word for him to bring it. The man brought it, secretly keeping back only a small part for himself, with which he went off to another city, where, having been cured of his appetite for hoarding, he began to live in a more liberal style. When Dionysius heard of it, he had the rest of the treasure returned to him, saying that since the man had learned to use it, he was very willing to give it back.

Dionysius the son, who heard that a Syracusan had hidden a treasure, sent for it, and afterwards gave it back when he found the man had learned to live without it.

## modern-en · catulus-luctatius · 41:7

And yet we have some examples of just that. Catulus Luctatius in the Cimbrian war, having done all he could to make his fleeing soldiers turn and face the enemy, finally fled with them himself, faking the coward, so that his men would look as though they were following their captain rather than running from the enemy — sacrificing his own reputation in order to cover the shame of others. When Charles V came into Provence in 1537, it is said that Antonio de Leva, seeing the emperor firmly resolved on the expedition and believing it would do him great honour, nevertheless very stiffly opposed it in council, so that the entire glory of the resolution would be attributed to his master, and it could be said his own wisdom and foresight were such that, against everyone else's opinion, he had brought about so great an enterprise — which was to do him honour at his own expense. The Thracian ambassadors, coming to console Archileonida, the mother of Brasidas, on the death of her son, and praising him to the point of saying he had left no equal behind him, she rejected this private and particular praise to attribute it to the public: "Don't tell me that," she said. "I know the city of Sparta has many citizens both greater and of greater worth than he." In the battle of Crécy, the Prince of Wales, then very young, had been given command of the vanguard; the brunt of the battle happened to fall in that part of the field, which led the lords with him, finding themselves overmatched, to send to King Edward to come up to their relief. He asked how his son was, and being told he was alive and on horseback: "Then I'd do him wrong," said the king, "to go and rob him of the honour of winning this battle he has sustained so long and so bravely. Whatever risk he runs, the honour shall be entirely his own." And accordingly he would neither come up himself nor send help, knowing that if he went, it would be said all would have been lost without his rescue, and the honour of the victory would be wholly given to him.

Many at Rome thought, and often said, that the greatest of Scipio's deeds were in part due to Laelius, whose constant practice it was always to advance and uphold Scipio's grandeur and renown without any care for his own. And Theopompus, king of Sparta, said to a man who told him the republic couldn't fail because he himself knew so well how to command: "It's rather," he replied, "because the people know so well how to obey." Just as women who succeeded to peerages had, despite their sex, the privilege of attending and voting in trials within the jurisdiction of the peers, so the ecclesiastical peers, despite their profession, were obliged to attend our kings in their wars, not just with their friends and servants but in person. The Bishop of Beauvais did so when he was with Philip Augustus at the battle of Bouvines, where he played a notable part in the action; but he didn't think it fitting for him to share in the fruit and glory of that violent and bloody trade. He took several of the enemy that day with his own hand and turned them over to the first gentleman he met, leaving it to him either to kill them or to accept their surrender, referring the whole execution to that other hand. He did this with the Earl of Salisbury, William, whom he handed over to Messire Jehan de Nesle. By a similar subtlety of conscience to the one I have just mentioned, he would kill but not wound, and so always fought with a mace. And a certain person of my own time, being reproached by the king for having laid hands on a priest, flatly and positively denied any such thing — meaning he had cudgelled and kicked him.

## modern-en · alfonso-of-the-asses · 42:57

But let us go back to Hiero, who further complains of the inconveniences he found in his royalty: he could not look around and travel the world freely, being a kind of prisoner within the bounds and limits of his own dominion; and in everything he did he was forever surrounded by a pressing crowd. And indeed, when I see our kings sitting alone at table, surrounded by so many people chattering around them and so many strangers staring at them, as they always are, I have often been moved more to pity than to envy their condition. King Alfonso used to say that in this respect asses were better off than kings, since their masters let them feed at their own ease and pleasure — a favour that kings cannot get from their servants. And it has never occurred to me that it could be of any great benefit to the life of a man of sense to have twenty people gabbling around him while he is on the privy; or that the services of a man worth ten thousand livres a year, or who has taken Casale or defended Siena, should be either more comfortable or more acceptable to him than those of a good groom of the chamber who knows his job. The advantages of sovereignty are in a manner only imaginary; every degree of fortune has in it some image of principality. Caesar calls all the lords of France, who hold their lands in free franchise, roitelets or petty kings; and in truth, the title of "sire" excepted, they go pretty far toward kingship. Just look in the provinces remote from court — Brittany, for example — and notice the train, the vassals, the officers, the employments, the service, the ceremony, and the state of a lord who lives retired from court in his own house, among his own tenants and servants; and observe besides the flight of his imagination: there is nothing more royal; he hears talk of his master once a year, as of a king of Persia, with no further acknowledgment of him than through some remote kinship his secretary keeps track of in some register. And, to tell the truth, our laws are easy enough — so easy that a French gentleman scarcely feels the weight of sovereignty pressing on his shoulders more than twice in his life. Real and effective subjection only touches those among us who voluntarily put their necks under the yoke, and who aim at wealth and honours through such services: for a man who loves his own fireside, and can manage his household without falling out with his neighbours or getting tangled up in lawsuits, is as free as the Doge of Venice.

Who used to say that in this asses were in a better condition than kings, their masters permitting them to feed at their own ease and pleasure, a favour that kings cannot obtain of their servants. The Essays do not identify him with the King Alfonso who instituted the Order of the Band.

## modern-en · henry-ii-france · 43:0

The way our laws try to regulate idle and wasteful spending on food and clothing seems to me quite the opposite of what they intend. The right way would be to breed a contempt in men for silks and gold as vain, frivolous, and useless; whereas we, in fact, enhance their honour and price tag, which is hardly the way to put people off them. To pass a law that nobody but princes can eat turbot, or wear velvet and gold lace, and to forbid these things to ordinary people — what is that but to bring them into greater esteem, and set everyone all the more on edge to eat and wear them? Let kings leave off these emblems of grandeur; they have plenty of others. Such excesses are more excusable in anyone else than in a prince. We can learn from the example of several nations better ways to mark out social rank (which I do think is necessary in a state) without nourishing this kind of corruption and obvious nuisance. It is strange how quickly and easily custom in these indifferent things establishes itself and becomes authority. We had hardly been wearing plain cloth a year, in keeping with the court's mourning for Henry II, before silks had already fallen into such contempt with everyone that a man dressed in silk was automatically taken for a tradesman; silks were split between the doctors and surgeons, and although almost everyone else went about in the same kind of dress, there was nevertheless, in one thing or another, sufficient distinction of social rank. How suddenly do greasy chamois and linen doublets become the fashion in our armies, while all neatness and richness of dress fall into contempt? Let kings just take the lead and begin to give up this expense, and within a month the thing will be done throughout the kingdom, without edict or ordinance; we shall all follow. It ought rather to be proclaimed, on the contrary, that nobody should wear scarlet or goldsmith's work but courtesans and acrobats.

The King of France for whose mourning the court wore cloth a year, so that silk fell into such contempt that a man so clad was concluded a citizen; whom Montaigne himself saw unable for his heart to hit on a Gascon gentleman’s name, and obliged to call one of the queen’s maids of honour by the general name of her race because her own was so hard to pronounce; and whom Monsieur de Carnavalet served. Not the Henry II of England whose son kept the feast of the hundred and ten Williams.

## modern-en · otho · 44:0

Reason directs that we should always go the same way, but not always at the same pace. And though a wise man ought not to give such free rein to human passions as to let them deviate from the right path, he may, without prejudice to his duty, leave it to them to hurry or to slow his speed, and not fix himself like a motionless and unfeeling Colossus. If virtue itself could put on flesh and blood, I believe the pulse would beat faster going on to an assault than going on to dinner: that is, there is a necessity that she should warm up and be stirred on this occasion. I have noticed, as something extraordinary, certain great men who in the highest enterprises and most important affairs have kept themselves in such a settled and serene calm as not to disturb their sleep. Alexander the Great, on the day fixed for that furious battle between him and Darius, slept so deeply and so long in the morning that Parmenio was forced to come into his chamber and, standing by his bedside, call him by name several times — the hour to go and fight compelling him to do so. The Emperor Otho, having resolved to kill himself that night, after settling his domestic affairs, dividing his money among his servants, and putting a good edge on a sword he had chosen for the purpose, and now waiting only to be sure that all his friends had got safely away, fell into so sound a sleep that the gentlemen of his chamber heard him snore. The death of this emperor has in it circumstances paralleling that of the great Cato, and particularly this just-mentioned one: for Cato, ready to dispatch himself, holding his hand only in expectation of the return of a messenger he had sent to bring word whether the senators he had sent away had got clear of the port of Utica, fell into so sound a sleep that those in the next room heard him snore; and when the man he had sent to the port had woken him to tell him that stormy weather had prevented the senators from putting to sea, he sent off another messenger, and composing himself again in bed, settled to sleep, and slept until the return of the last messenger brought him certain news that they were gone. We may further compare him with Alexander in the great and dangerous storm that threatened him through the sedition of the tribune Metellus, who, attempting to publish a decree to call Pompey with his army into the city at the time of Catiline's conspiracy, was opposed only — and stoutly — by Cato, so that very sharp language and bitter threats passed between them in the senate on the matter. But it was the next day, in the forenoon, that the controversy was to be decided, where Metellus, besides the favour of the people and of Caesar — at that time of Pompey's faction — was to appear accompanied by a rabble of slaves and gladiators; and Cato fortified only with his own courage and constancy; so that his relatives, household, and many of his virtuous friends were in great fear for him, to the point that some passed the whole night without sleep, eating, or drinking, for the danger they saw him in; his wife and sisters did nothing but weep and torment themselves in his house. He, on the contrary, comforted everyone, and after supping in his usual way, went to bed and slept soundly till morning, when one of his fellow tribunes roused him to go to the encounter. The knowledge we have of the greatness of this man's courage from the rest of his life may surely warrant us in judging that his composure came from a soul so far raised above such accidents that he disdained to let them take any more hold on his imagination than any ordinary incident.

Who, resolved to kill himself that night, settled his domestic affairs, divided his money among his servants, set a good edge on the sword he had chosen, waited only to be satisfied that his friends had got away safe, and then fell into so sound a sleep that the gentlemen of his chamber heard him snore. Vitellius’s insults to his soldiers afterwards did what their own captains could not, and made them fall upon the man who had offered them.

## modern-en · sextus-pompeius · 44:1

In the naval engagement that Augustus won against Sextus Pompeius in Sicily, just as the battle was about to begin, he was so fast asleep that his friends had to wake him to give the signal for the fight: this was what gave Mark Antony occasion afterwards to reproach him that he hadn't the courage so much as to look on the order of his own squadrons with open eyes, and hadn't dared to show himself to the soldiers until Agrippa had brought him news of the victory won. But as for young Marius, who did much worse (on the day of his last battle against Sulla, after he had drawn up his army and given the word and signal for battle, he lay down under the shade of a tree to rest himself, and fell so soundly asleep that the rout and flight of his men could barely wake him, having seen nothing of the fight), he is said to have been at that time so utterly worn out with labour and lack of sleep that nature could hold out no longer. Now, on what has been said, the physicians may decide whether sleep is so necessary that our lives depend on it; for we read that King Perseus of Macedon, being a prisoner at Rome, was killed by being kept from sleep; but Pliny gives examples of people who have lived long without it. Herodotus speaks of nations where the men sleep and wake by half-years; and those who write the life of the sage Epimenides assert that he slept fifty-seven years on end.

Whom Augustus beat in the naval engagement in Sicily that Augustus slept through, until his friends woke him to give the signal of battle.

## modern-en · machanidas · 45:1

Our battle of Dreux is striking for several extraordinary incidents — though those who have little affection for M. de Guise, and care little for his reputation, are eager to blame him. They say his halt, his delay with the forces under his command while the Constable, who was general of the army, was being raked through and through by the enemy's artillery, his battalion routed, himself taken prisoner — is inexcusable. He would have done much better, they argue, to risk a flank charge than to wait for the chance to fall on the enemy's rear, and so suffer such a heavy and consequential loss. But quite apart from what the outcome later showed, anyone who weighs the case without passion or prejudice will readily admit that the aim of a captain — and indeed of every private soldier — should be the overall victory, and that no particular incident, however close to his own interest, should pull him from that pursuit. Philopoemen, in an encounter with Machanidas, had sent out a strong party of his archers and slingers to open the skirmish. They were routed and hotly pursued by the enemy, who, riding their luck and chasing the rout, swept past the battalion where Philopoemen was stationed. His own men were straining to attack, but he refused to leave his post or to expose himself to relieve them. He let his archers be cut down before his eyes, and then, when he saw the enemy foot left unprotected by their cavalry, charged in. Even though they were Lacedaemonians, he caught them at the very moment when, thinking the victory secured, they were beginning to break their ranks. He destroyed them with ease and then set off in pursuit of Machanidas. The case is very like Monsieur de Guise's.

Whom Philopoemen fought, and who let his own horse run off in pursuit past the battalion where Philopoemen stood: Philopoemen suffered his archers and slingers to be chased and cut in pieces before his face rather than leave his post, then charged the enemy’s foot when the horse had left it unprotected, and afterwards put himself in pursuit of Machanidas.

It is as amusing to sort the tables by the guests' names as it was for the Emperor Geta to sort the courses of his meal by the first letters of the dishes themselves — so that everything starting with B was served together: brawn, beef, bream, bustards, becca-ficos, and so on. Another item: there is a saying that it is good to have a good name, meaning credit and a good reputation. But beyond that, it is genuinely useful to have a well-sounding name — easy to pronounce, easy to remember — because kings and other great people will then more easily recognise us and more reluctantly forget us. Even among our own servants, we tend to call and employ the ones whose names come most readily to the tongue. I myself saw Henry II, when for the life of him he could not call up the name of a gentleman from our country of Gascony, fall back on calling one of the queen's maids of honour by the general name of her family because her own name was so hard to pronounce or remember. ## modern-en · du-guesclin · 46:9

But this thought drags me, against my will, onto another topic. Let us look a little closer at — and, for God's sake, examine — the foundation on which we build this glory and reputation for which the world is turned upside down. What do we mean by this renown we hunt after with such effort? In the end it is Peter or William who carries it, takes it as his own, and whom it alone concerns. What a brave faculty hope is — in a mortal subject, and in a moment, it thinks nothing of laying hold of infinity, immensity, eternity, and of stocking its master's poverty, at will, with anything he can imagine or desire! Nature has given us this passion as a pretty toy to play with. And this Peter or William — what is it, when all is said and done? A sound, or three or four strokes of the pen, so easy to vary that I would love to know to whom the glory of so many victories should be assigned: Guesquin? Glesquin? Gueaquin? And yet there is more at stake here than in Lucian, where Sigma sues Tau in court; for —

The famous constable, to whom belong so many sieges, battles, wounds, imprisonments and services done to the crown of France — and whose name Montaigne spells three ways over, to ask which of the letters is to be rewarded for them.

## modern-en · nicholas-denisot · 46:12

the chase here is very much in earnest: which of these letters is to be rewarded for so many sieges, battles, wounds, imprisonments, and services rendered to the crown of France by this famous constable? Nicholas Denisot never bothered himself with anything beyond the letters of his name, whose order he scrambled to build up by anagram the Count d'Alsinois, on whom he handsomely settled the glory of his own poetry and painting. The historian Suetonius was satisfied with just the sense of his name, and dropped his father's surname Lenis to leave Tranquillus as heir to his reputation. Who would believe that Captain Bayard has no honour but what he derives from the deeds of Peter Terrail; or that Antonio Iscalin should sit and watch himself robbed, to his face, of the honour of so many sea voyages and commands by sea and land under the names of Captain Paulin and the Baron de la Garde? Second, these strokes of the pen are common to thousands of people. How many in each family share the same name and surname? And how many more in different families, ages, and countries? History tells us of three Socrateses, five Platos, eight Aristotles, seven Xenophons, twenty Demetrii, twenty Theodores — and we can guess how many more she never met. What is to stop my stable-boy from calling himself Pompey the Great? But when all is done, what virtue, what authority, what secret machinery is there that pins onto my dead stable-boy, or onto the other Pompey whose head was cut off in Egypt, this glorious renown and these so honoured flourishes of the pen, to their advantage?

Who altered the whole contexture of the letters of his own name to build up the Count d’Alsinois by anagram, and then handsomely endowed that figure with the glory of his poetry and his painting.

## modern-en · monsieur-de-foix · 47:8

But why might one not also argue the opposite — that it is the mark of a hasty and insatiable spirit not to know how to bound and restrain its appetite; that to exceed the measure God has set on his favours is to abuse them; and that to fling yourself back into danger after a victory is to put yourself a second time at the mercy of fortune; that one of the great pieces of discretion in war is not to drive an enemy to despair? Sulla and Marius, in the Social War, after defeating the Marsians, saw a reserve body still coming on, goaded by despair like maddened beasts, and judged it not wise to take their charge. Had Monsieur de Foix's ardour not carried him so furiously after the remains of the victory at Ravenna, he would not have darkened it with his own death. And the fresh memory of his example saved Monsieur d'Anguien from the same misfortune at the battle of Serisoles. It is dangerous to press a man for whom you have left no way out except his weapons, for necessity teaches violent decisions:

Whose ardour transported him so furiously in pursuit of the remains of the victory of Ravenna that he obscured it by his own death.

## modern-en · sertorius · 47:14

In the same way, if one had to decide whether soldiers should be lavishly and sumptuously dressed or armed only as the immediate task requires, the argument for the first might run as follows — and Sertorius, Philopoemen, Brutus, Caesar, and others held this view: that fine attire inflames a soldier's courage and is a spur to him; and that it also makes him fight more stubbornly, since his arms are in effect his estate and his whole inheritance to defend. This is why, says Xenophon, the men of Asia carried their wives and concubines, with their best jewels and richest possessions, with them to the wars. But the arguments would line up just as readily on the other side: that a general ought to reduce, not enlarge, his men's anxiety about saving themselves; that fine equipment makes them doubly afraid to risk their persons, and serves as a double temptation to the enemy to fight more resolutely where such booty and rich spoils are to be had. The thing was famously observed in earlier times as a powerful incentive to the Romans against the Samnites. Antiochus, showing Hannibal the army he had raised — marvellously splendid and rich in every kind of equipage — asked him whether the Romans would be satisfied with that army. "Satisfied?" replied Hannibal. "Yes, no doubt — however great their greed." Lycurgus not only forbade his soldiers all manner of finery in their gear but also forbade them to strip the enemies they defeated, because he wanted, as he said, poverty and frugality to shine alongside the rest of the battle.

One of the captains of the opinion that a soldier richly and sumptuously accoutred is the more inflamed with courage and the more obstinate in fight, having his arms, which are in a manner his whole inheritance, to defend.

## modern-en · vitellius · 47:15

At sieges and on other occasions where we come up close to the enemy, we readily let our men taunt, abuse, and revile him with every kind of injurious language. There is some colour of reason in this: it is no small thing to strip them of all hope of mercy or terms by reminding them that no quarter is to be expected from an enemy they have provoked so far, and that no remedy is left except victory. And yet Vitellius found himself fooled by this approach. He had to deal with Otho's soldiers, who were weaker in valour, long unused to war and softened by the pleasures of Rome. He stung them at last with so much abuse — reproaching them with cowardice and with regret for the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind in the city — that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation could have produced, and made them fall upon him with a fury their own captains had been unable to rouse in them. And indeed, when the injuries cut to the quick, it can easily happen that the man who was going reluctantly to fight on his prince's behalf will pitch in with another kind of spirit when the quarrel becomes his own.

Who so nettled Otho’s soldiers with injurious language, reproaching them with cowardice and with the mistresses and entertainments they had left behind at Rome, that he inspired them with a resolution no exhortation had had the power to give them, and made them fall upon himself.

## modern-en · levinus · 47:16

Considering how important it is to keep the general of an army alive, and that the enemy's whole aim is directed straight at the head on which all the rest depend, the course taken by so many great captains — changing their dress and disguising themselves just before engaging — seems past dispute. And yet the inconvenience a man runs into by doing so is no less than the one he thinks to avoid. The captain, hidden from the recognition of his own men, no longer has the courage his presence and example would have inspired in them; not seeing the familiar marks and ensigns of their leader, they soon conclude that either he is dead or, despairing of the business, has gone off to look after himself. And experience shows both methods have succeeded and failed. What happened to Pyrrhus in the battle he fought against the Consul Levinus in Italy will serve to illustrate both points. By hiding himself in Megacles's armour and giving Megacles his own, he undoubtedly saved his life — but by that very means he came very close to the other disaster of losing the battle. Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus loved to be recognisable in a fight by rich equipment and armour of a particular gleam and colour. Agis, Agesilaus, and that great Gilippus, on the contrary, used to fight without any display, with no imperial escort or distinguishing marks.

The consul against whom Pyrrhus fought in Italy on the day the king shrouded his person in Megacles’s armour.

And yet the inconvenience a man runs into by doing so is no less than the one he thinks to avoid. The captain, hidden from the recognition of his own men, no longer has the courage his presence and example would have inspired in them; not seeing the familiar marks and ensigns of their leader, they soon conclude that either he is dead or, despairing of the business, has gone off to look after himself. By hiding himself in Megacles's armour and giving Megacles his own, he undoubtedly saved his life — but by that very means he came very close to the other disaster of losing the battle. Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus loved to be recognisable in a fight by rich equipment and armour of a particular gleam and colour. Agis, Agesilaus, and that great Gilippus, on the contrary, used to fight without any display, with no imperial escort or distinguishing marks.

## modern-en · clearchus · 47:17

Among the other faults laid to Pompey's charge at Pharsalia, he is reproached for keeping his army standing still to receive the enemy's charge — "because by doing so" (I will here lift Plutarch's own words, which are better than mine) "he deprived himself of the violent impact that running adds to the first shock of arms, and he prevented that crash of the combatants into one another that usually gives them greater impetuosity and fury, especially when they rush in with full force, their courage rising with the shouts and the run. He chilled the soldiers' ardour, as it were, and made it more reserved." That is what Plutarch says. But if Caesar had come off worse, why might not someone else have argued the reverse — that the strongest and steadiest fighting stance is one in which a man is planted firm, without motion; that those who hold steady on the march, closing up and reserving their strength for the moment of action, have a great advantage over men who are disordered, who have already spent half their breath running headlong into the charge. Besides, an army is a body made up of so many individual members that it is impossible for it to move at that pace without breaking the order of battle, and without the leading men being engaged before their comrades can come up to help them. In that unnatural battle between the two Persian brothers, the Lacedaemonian Clearchus, who commanded the Greeks on Cyrus's side, led them on softly and without haste toward the charge, but when they were within fifty paces he hurled them on at full speed, hoping in so short a run to keep order and save their wind and at the same time to give weight and impetus both to their persons and to their missile weapons. Others have settled the question for their own armies this way: if your enemy comes at you full tilt, stand firm to receive him; if he stands still to receive you, charge him full tilt.

## modern-en · fabricius-luscinus · 49:0

I would gladly forgive our people for taking no pattern or rule of perfection but their own particular manners and customs — for it is a common vice, not just of the common run but of nearly all men, to walk in the beaten road their ancestors trod before them. I am content that, when they see a Fabricius or a Laelius, they think his face and bearing barbarous, since he is neither dressed nor groomed in our manner. But what I find fault with is their singular thoughtlessness in letting themselves be so blinded and bullied by the authority of present fashion that they change their opinions every month, if custom requires it, and revise their judgments on questions that touch them personally. When they wore the busk of their doublets up to their breasts, they stiffly insisted that was its proper place; a few years later, when it had slipped down between the thighs, they could laugh at the old fashion as uncomfortable and unbearable. The fashion now in use leads them to condemn both of the other two with such firm conviction and such universal consent that you would think a kind of madness had crept in among them, blinding their understanding to this strange degree. Now, given that our turnover of fashions is so prompt and abrupt that all the tailors in the world cannot dream up enough new whim-whams to feed our vanity, it must often happen that the discarded styles come back in again, and then drop into the same contempt; and that the same judgment, in fifteen or twenty years, will pass through half a dozen not only different but contradictory opinions, with an unbelievable lightness and inconstancy. Not one of us is so discerning as not to be taken in by this contradiction and, both in external and internal sight, blinded without realising it.

The nickname "the Trembling" by which they called Sancho XII, king of Navarre, tells us that valour will set the limbs trembling just as fear does. Those who were arming that king — or whoever else, on a like occasion, was apt to fall into the same agitation — tried to settle him down by playing down the danger he was about to face. "You don't understand me," he said, "for if my flesh could know the danger my courage will straight away carry it into, it would sink to the ground." Stupidity and wisdom meet at the same midpoint of feeling and resolution in the bearing of life's accidents: the wise master and triumph over ill, the others never know it; the latter, you might say, sit on this side of the accidents, the former go beyond them, having weighed and considered their character, measured and judged them for what they are, and then, by force of a vigorous soul, leapt out of their reach; they look down on them and trample them underfoot, having a solid and well-fortified soul against which the darts of fortune, when they come to strike, must necessarily rebound and blunt themselves, meeting a body in which they can make no impression. The ordinary middling sort of men are lodged between these two extremes, made up of those who notice their evils, feel them, and are not able to bear them. Infancy and decrepitude meet in the weakness of the brain; avarice and prodigality meet in the same thirst and desire to get.

## modern-en · theodosius · 56:13

One of our Greek historians justly criticises the age he lived in, because the secrets of the Christian religion were scattered into the hands of every mechanic to expound and argue over as he saw fit, and says we ought to be much ashamed — we who by God's special favour enjoy the pure mysteries of piety — to let them be profaned by the ignorant rabble; considering that the pagans expressly forbade Socrates, Plato, and the other sages to inquire into or even so much as mention the things entrusted to the priests of Delphi. He says further that the factions of princes on theological subjects are armed not with zeal but with fury; that zeal springs from divine wisdom and justice and governs itself with prudence and moderation, but degenerates into hatred and envy, producing tares and nettles instead of grain and wine, when it is driven by human passions. And it was well said by another, who, advising the Emperor Theodosius, told him that disputes did not so much rock the schisms of the Church to sleep as rouse and animate heresies; that therefore all contentions and dialectical disputes were to be avoided, and men were to acquiesce wholly in the formulas of faith laid down by the ancients. And the Emperor Andronicus, having overheard some great men at high words with Lapodius in his palace about a point of ours of great importance, gave them so sharp a check as to threaten to have them thrown into the river if they did not stop. The very women and children nowadays presume to lecture the oldest and most experienced men on the ecclesiastical laws; whereas the first of those of Plato forbids them even to inquire into the civil laws, which were to stand in place of divine ordinances; and, allowing the old men to confer among themselves or with the magistrate about such things, he adds — provided it not be in the presence of the young or of profane persons.

The emperor whom an adviser told that disputation did not rock the schisms of the Church asleep but roused and animated heresies, and that men should acquiesce in the formulas of faith the ancients had established.

We fluctuate between various inclinations; we will nothing freely, nothing absolutely, nothing constantly. In any man who had set down clear laws and rules in his head for his own conduct, we would notice a steadiness of manner, an order, a sure relation of one thing and action to another, shining through his whole life. Empedocles observed this very disparity in the people of Agrigentum: they gave themselves up to pleasure as if every day were their last and built as if they were going to live forever. The judgment is not hard to make, as is very evident in the younger Cato; whoever has found one step in him will be led to all the rest — it is a harmony of perfectly tuned notes that cannot jar. With us it is quite the opposite: every particular action requires a particular judgment. The surest course to steer by, in my opinion, would be to take our measure from the nearest related circumstances, without engaging in a longer inquiry or drawing any larger conclusion. I was told, during the civil disorders of our poor kingdom, that a girl, near where I was then staying, had thrown herself out of a window to avoid being forced by a common soldier billeted in the house. She was not killed by the fall, and so, repeating her attempt, she would have cut her own throat had she not been stopped. Still, having wounded herself enough to look in real danger, she freely confessed that the soldier had so far only pestered her with courtship, urgent solicitation, and gifts, but that she was afraid he would in the end resort to violence — all of which she delivered with such a look and accent, soaked moreover in her own blood (the highest testimony of her virtue), that she seemed another Lucretia. Yet I have since been well assured that, both before and after, she was not such a difficult piece. And, as the innkeeper says in Ariosto, however handsome a man and worthy a gentleman you may be, do not conclude too much about your mistress's inviolable chastity just because you were turned away — for all you know, she may have a better stomach for your muleteer.

But as the grounds for suspicion grew daily, until at last it became plain fact, the poor woman was driven to have it proclaimed in her parish church that whoever had done the deed and would freely confess could not only be forgiven but, if he liked, married. Whereupon a young fellow who served her as a labourer, encouraged by the proclamation, declared that one holiday he had found her — having taken too much of the bottle — so fast asleep by the fireplace and in so indecent a posture that he could conveniently do his business without waking her. ## modern-en · anaxarchus · 59:51

— when Anaxarchus, on the order of Nicocreon, tyrant of Cyprus, was placed in a stone mortar and pounded with iron mauls, never stopped saying, "Strike, batter, break — it is not Anaxarchus, it is only his sheath you pound and crush"; when we hear our martyrs cry out to the tyrant from the middle of the flame, "This side is roasted enough — fall to and eat, it is well done; now set to work on the other"; when we hear the child in Josephus, torn piecemeal with pincers, defy Antiochus and cry out in a steady, assured voice, "Tyrant, you waste your effort — I am still at ease. Where is the pain? Where are the torments with which you so threatened me? Is this all you can do? My constancy torments you more than your cruelty does me. Pitiful coward, you weaken and I grow stronger; make me complain, make me bend, make me yield if you can; encourage your guards, cheer up your executioners — see, see, they faint and can do no more; arm them, goad them, spur them on" — one must confess that there is some frenzy, some fury, however holy, possessing those souls at such a moment. When we come to these Stoical sallies — "I had rather be mad than voluptuous," says Antisthenes; when Sextius tells us he had rather be fettered by affliction than by pleasure; when Epicurus presumes to play with his gout, and, refusing health and ease, defies all torments, despising the lesser pains as beneath his contest, hungering and calling out for others sharper, more violent, and more worthy of him —

Who, put into a stone mortar by command of Nicocreon and laid upon with mauls of iron, did not cease to say: strike, batter, break — it is not Anaxarchus, it is but his sheath that you pound and bray so.

## modern-en · damidas · 60:3

When Philip had forcibly entered the Peloponnese and someone said to Damidas that the Lacedaemonians stood likely to suffer greatly if they did not in time reconcile themselves to his favour, "Why, you wretched fellow," he replied, "what can they suffer who do not fear to die?" Agis, too, was asked how a man might live free. "Why," he said, "by despising death." These, and a thousand other sayings to the same effect, plainly mean more than patiently awaiting the stroke of death when it comes — for there are several accidents of life worse to suffer than death itself. Witness the Lacedaemonian boy captured by Antigonus and sold as a slave who, when his master ordered him to some base task, said, "You shall see whom you have bought — it would be a shame for me to serve, when liberty is within my reach," and so saying, threw himself from the top of the house. When Antipater severely threatened the Lacedaemonians, the better to bring them to grant a demand of his, they replied, "If you threaten us with worse than death, we shall die more willingly"; and to Philip, who had written that he would frustrate all their undertakings, "What, will you also stop us from dying?" This is the meaning of the saying that the wise man lives as long as he ought, not as long as he can; and that the most obliging present nature has given us, and which removes all colour for complaining of our condition, is that she has placed the keys of life in our own keeping. She has provided only one door into life, but a hundred thousand ways out. We may be cramped for earth to live on, but earth enough to die on can never be wanting, as Boiocalus answered the Romans. Why complain of this world? It does not detain you; your own cowardice is the cause if you live in pain. There needs no more to die than to will to die:

To whom someone said that the Lacedaemonians were likely to suffer much if they did not reconcile themselves to Philip in time: why, you pitiful fellow, he replied, what can they suffer who do not fear to die?

## modern-en · therykion · 60:35

Among those of the first of these two opinions, there has been great debate as to what occasions are sufficient to justify deliberate self-murder, which they call "a reasonable exit." For though they say that men must sometimes die for trivial causes, since those that detain us in life are of no great weight either, yet there must be some limit. There are fantastic and senseless impulses that have driven not only individual men but whole nations to destroy themselves, of which I have given examples elsewhere. We also read of the Milesian virgins, who by a mad compact hanged themselves one after another until the magistrate took order in it, decreeing that the bodies of any found so hanged should be drawn naked through the city by the same halter. When Therykion tried to persuade Cleomenes to dispatch himself because of the ill posture of his affairs and, having missed a more honourable death in the lost battle, to accept this second-best one rather than give the conquerors leisure to inflict on him either a shameful death or a degrading life, Cleomenes, with a courage truly Stoic and Lacedaemonian, rejected his advice as unmanly and base: "That," he said, "is a remedy that will never be unavailable, but one a man should not resort to while an inch of hope remains." He told him that it was sometimes constancy and valour to live; that he wanted even his death to be of use to his country, and would make of it an act of honour and virtue. Therykion, nevertheless, thought himself in the right and did his own business; and Cleomenes did the same afterwards, but only after he had first tried out the utmost malice of fortune. Not all the troubles in the world are weighty enough to make a man die to dodge them; and besides, there are so many sudden and unexpected changes in human affairs that it is hard to judge rightly when we are at the end of our hope:

Who tried to persuade Cleomenes to despatch himself after the battle he had lost, rather than give the conquerors leisure to make him undergo an ignominious death or an infamous life — and, his counsel being rejected as unmanly and mean, went and did his own business.

## modern-en · democritus-aetolian · 60:45

Seneca says only those which keep on disturbing the functions of the soul for a long time. And there have been some who, to avoid a worse death, have chosen one of their own liking. Democritus, general of the Aetolians, brought as a prisoner to Rome, found a way to escape by night; but, hotly pursued by his keepers, he fell on his own sword and died rather than let himself be retaken. Antinous and Theodotus, when their city of Epirus was reduced by the Romans to the last extremity, advised the people to kill themselves universally. The people preferring to give themselves up to the enemy, the two chiefs went to seek the death they wanted, rushing furiously upon the enemy with intent to strike home but not to ward off any blow. When the Island of Gozzo was taken some years ago by the Turks, a Sicilian who had two beautiful marriageable daughters killed them both with his own hand, along with their mother who ran in to save them; that done, he sallied out of the house with a crossbow and arquebus, killed with two shots the two Turks nearest his door, and drawing his sword charged furiously among the rest, where he was quickly surrounded and cut to pieces — by that means delivering his family and himself from slavery and dishonour. The Jewish women, after circumcising their children, threw them and themselves down a precipice to escape the cruelty of Antigonus. I have been told of a man of rank in one of our prisons whose friends, hearing that he would certainly be condemned, suborned a priest to tell him — to spare him the disgrace of such a death — that the only means of his deliverance was to commend himself to such-and-such a saint under such-and-such vows, and to fast eight days together without taking any nourishment, whatever weakness or faintness he might feel. He followed their advice, and so destroyed himself before he was aware, not suspecting death or any danger in the experiment. Scribonia, advising her nephew Libo to kill himself rather than wait for the stroke of justice, told him that to keep his life only to put it after into the hands of those who within three or four days would haul him to execution was to do other people's business, and that to keep his blood for them to gratify their malice was to serve his enemies.

General of the AEtolians, brought prisoner to Rome, who escaped by night and, closely pursued by his keepers, fell upon his own sword rather than be retaken. Not the philosopher of Abdera.

I have been told of a man of rank in one of our prisons whose friends, hearing that he would certainly be condemned, suborned a priest to tell him — to spare him the disgrace of such a death — that the only means of his deliverance was to commend himself to such-and-such a saint under such-and-such vows, and to fast eight days together without taking any nourishment, whatever weakness or faintness he might feel. He followed their advice, and so destroyed himself before he was aware, not suspecting death or any danger in the experiment. Scribonia, advising her nephew Libo to kill himself rather than wait for the stroke of justice, told him that to keep his life only to put it after into the hands of those who within three or four days would haul him to execution was to do other people's business, and that to keep his blood for them to gratify their malice was to serve his enemies.

The other of the two chiefs of Epirus who did that.

## modern-en · nicanor · 60:46

We read in the Bible that Nicanor, the persecutor of the law of God, having sent his soldiers to seize the good old man Razis — surnamed, for his virtue, the father of the Jews — the good man, seeing no other remedy, his gates burned down and the enemies ready to take him, chose to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of his wicked adversaries and let himself be cruelly butchered by them, contrary to the honour of his rank. He stabbed himself with his own sword, but in haste the blow had not gone home; so he ran and threw himself headlong from the top of a wall on the men below. They moved apart and made room, and he landed straight on his head. Yet, feeling still in himself some remains of life, he renewed his courage, sprang up on his feet all bloody and wounded, and making his way through the crowd to a steep rock, drew out his bowels through one of his wounds and, tearing and pulling them apart with both hands, threw them among his pursuers, all the while calling on divine vengeance for their cruelty and injustice.

The persecutor of the law of God who sent his soldiers to seize Razis.

## modern-en · lucius-aruntius · 60:50

History is everywhere full of people who, by a thousand routes, have exchanged a painful and tedious life for death. Lucius Aruntius killed himself, he said, to flee both the future and the past. Granius Silvanus and Statius Proximus, after being pardoned by Nero, killed themselves — either disdaining to live by the favour of so wicked a man, or so as not to be troubled at some other time to seek a second pardon, given the readiness of his nature to suspect and credit accusations against worthy men. Spargapises, son of Queen Tomyris, taken prisoner of war by Cyrus, used the first favour Cyrus showed him — ordering him untied — to kill himself, claiming no other benefit of liberty than to be revenged upon himself for the disgrace of having been captured. Boges, governor of Eion for King Xerxes, besieged by the Athenian army under Cimon, refused the terms offered (a safe return into Asia with all his wealth), unable to bear surviving the loss of a post his master had given him to keep. So, after defending the city to the last extremity, when nothing was left to eat, he first threw all the gold and everything else the enemy could plunder into the river Strymon, then ordered a great pyre lit and the throats cut of all the women, children, concubines, and servants, whose bodies he threw into the fire, and at last leaped into it himself.

Who killed himself to fly, he said, both the future and the past.
