## modern-en · ninachetuen · 60:51

Ninachetuen, an Indian lord, at the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to strip him, with no clear cause, of his command in Malacca, in order to transfer it to the King of Campar, took this resolution: he had a scaffold built, longer than broad, supported by columns royally hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers and abundant perfumes; and when all was ready, he came out into the street in a robe of cloth of gold studded with jewels of great value, and mounted the steps to the scaffold, at one corner of which he had a pyre of aromatic wood lit. Everyone ran to see what these unusual preparations were for; whereupon Ninachetuen, with a manly but indignant air, set out how much he had served the Portuguese nation, and with how unspotted fidelity he had behaved in his charge; that, having so often, sword in hand, shown for others that honour was much dearer to him than life, he was not to abandon care for it on his own behalf; that, since fortune denied him any way of resisting the affront prepared for him, his courage at least required him to free himself from the feeling of it, and not to become a tale told by the people or a triumph to men less deserving than himself. Having said this, he leaped into the fire.

An Indian lord who, hearing the first whisper that the Portuguese Viceroy meant to take his command in Malacca from him without apparent cause and give it to the King of Campar, built a scaffold hung with tapestry and strewn with flowers, came out in cloth of gold set with jewels, set out from it how much he had obliged the Portuguese nation and with how unspotted a fidelity, said that fortune denying him all means of opposing the affront his courage at least enjoined him to free himself from the sense of it, and leapt into the fire he had lighted at one corner.

## modern-en · sextilia · 60:52

Sextilia, wife of Scaurus, and Paxaea, wife of Labeo, to encourage their husbands to escape the dangers pressing upon them — in which they had no share but conjugal affection — voluntarily sacrificed their own lives to serve them in this extreme necessity for company and example. What they did for their husbands, Cocceius Nerva did for his country, with less utility though with equal devotion: this great lawyer, flourishing in health, wealth, reputation, and favour with the emperor, had no other reason to kill himself but the bare pity of the miserable state of the Roman Republic. Nothing can be added to the beauty of the death of the wife of Fulvius, a familiar favourite of Augustus. Augustus, having discovered that he had divulged an important secret entrusted to him, received him very coldly one morning when he came to court and looked grimly at him. Fulvius returned home in despair and told his wife sorrowfully that, having fallen into this misfortune, he was resolved to kill himself; to which she answered roundly, "It is only right that you should, since after so often experiencing the looseness of my tongue you would not take warning. But let me kill myself first" — and without saying more she ran herself through the body with a sword. Vibius Virrius, despairing of the safety of his city, besieged by the Romans, and of their mercy, in the last debate of his city's senate, after many arguments to the same end, concluded that the noblest way to escape fortune was by their own hands. He told them the enemy would have them in honour, and Hannibal would feel how many faithful friends he had abandoned, and invited those who approved his advice to come to a good supper he had ready at home, where, after they had eaten well, they would all drink together of what he had prepared — "a drink," he said, "that will deliver our bodies from torments, our souls from insult, and our eyes and ears from feeling the many hateful evils the conquered suffer from cruel and implacable conquerors." He said he had arranged for proper persons to throw their bodies on a funeral pyre before his door as soon as they were dead. Many approved this high resolution, but few imitated it. Twenty-seven senators followed him, who, after having tried to drown the thought of this fatal decision in wine, ended the feast with the deadly mess; and embracing one another, after lamenting together their country's misfortune, some withdrew home to their own houses, others stayed to be burned with Vibius on his funeral pyre. All were so long in dying — the vapour of the wine having clogged the veins and so deferred the effect of the poison — that some of them came within an hour of seeing the enemy inside the walls of Capua, which was taken the next morning, and of undergoing the miseries they had at so dear a rate tried to avoid. Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Wife of Scaurus, who with Paxaea voluntarily sacrificed her own life to encourage her husband to avoid the dangers pressing upon him, in which she had no other share than conjugal affection.

Jubellius Taurea, another citizen of the same place, when the Consul Fulvius was returning from the shameful butchery of two hundred and twenty-five senators, called him back fiercely by name and, having stopped him, said, "Give the word that someone may dispatch me too, after the slaughter of so many others, so that you may boast of having killed a much braver man than yourself." Fulvius, dismissing him as a madman, and also having received letters from Rome censuring the inhumanity of his execution that tied his hands, Jubellius went on: "Since my country has been taken, my friends are dead, and I have with my own hands killed my wife and children to spare them the desolation of this ruin, and I am denied to die the death of my fellow citizens, let me borrow from virtue vengeance on this hated life" — and drawing a short sword he had hidden on him, he ran it through his own breast, falling backward and dying at the consul's feet.

Wife of Labeo, who did the same for him.

## modern-en · cleombrotus · 60:57

But men sometimes covet death out of hope of a greater good. "I desire," says St. Paul, "to be with Christ," and "who shall rid me of these bands?" Cleombrotus of Ambracia, after reading Plato's Phaedo, conceived so great a desire for the life to come that, without any other occasion, he threw himself into the sea. By which it appears how improperly we call this voluntary dissolution despair — to which the eagerness of hope often inclines us, and sometimes a calm and tempered desire arising from a mature and deliberate judgment. Jacques du Chastel, bishop of Soissons, on St. Louis's foreign expedition, seeing the king and whole army about to return to France, leaving the cause of religion unfinished, took the resolve to go straight to Paradise instead. So, having taken a solemn farewell of his friends, he charged alone, in the sight of everyone, into the enemy's army, where he was at once cut to pieces. In a certain kingdom of the newly discovered world, on a day of solemn procession when the idol they worship is drawn in public on a chariot of marvellous size, besides the many seen cutting off pieces of their flesh to offer to it, there are others who throw themselves down in its path, to be crushed and broken to pieces under the heavy wheels, to obtain after death the veneration of sanctity — which is duly paid them. The death of the bishop, sword in hand, has more magnanimity in it and less sensation, since the heat of battle takes away part of the latter.

Who, having read Plato’s Phaedo, entered into so great a desire of the life to come that without any other occasion he threw himself into the sea — which is why Montaigne says we call this voluntary dissolution despair improperly, the eagerness of hope often inclining us to it.

## modern-en · boutieres · 61:3

In our fathers' time, Monsieur de Boutières nearly lost Turin by having, while in good company at supper, put off reading information sent to him of the treason plotted against that city, which he commanded. And this same Plutarch has informed me that Julius Caesar would have saved himself if, on his way to the Senate the day he was assassinated by the conspirators, he had read a note handed to him on the way. He also tells the story of Archias, the tyrant of Thebes, who, the night before the design Pelopidas had plotted to kill him and restore his country to liberty was executed, was sent a full written account of the whole conspiracy by another Archias, an Athenian; and this packet having been delivered to him while he sat at supper, he put off opening it, saying — what afterwards became a proverb in Greece — "Business tomorrow."

Who had like to have lost Turin from delaying, while engaged in good company at supper, to read the information sent him of the treason plotted against the city he commanded. The modern edition spells him Boutières.

He also tells the story of Archias, the tyrant of Thebes, who, the night before the design Pelopidas had plotted to kill him and restore his country to liberty was executed, was sent a full written account of the whole conspiracy by another Archias, an Athenian; and this packet having been delivered to him while he sat at supper, he put off opening it, saying — what afterwards became a proverb in Greece — "Business tomorrow."

The Athenian who sent him that warning.

## modern-en · la-brousse · 62:0

The Sieur de la Brousse, my brother, and I, travelling one day together during the time of our civil wars, met a gentleman of good standing. He was of the opposite party, though I did not know it, for he pretended otherwise. The trouble in this kind of war is that the cards are so shuffled — your enemy not distinguished from yourself by any obvious mark of language or dress, having been raised under the same laws, climate, and manners — that it is very hard to avoid confusion and disorder. This made me afraid of meeting any of our own troops in a place where I was not known, that I might not be in fear to tell my name, and perhaps worse — as had happened to me before, when by such a mistake I lost both men and horses, including an Italian gentleman, my page, whom I had bred with the greatest care and affection, in whom a youth of great promise was wretchedly extinguished. But the gentleman my brother and I met had so desperate, half-dead a fear of meeting any horsemen or passing by any of the towns that held for the King, that I at last realised it was the alarm of conscience. The poor man felt as if through his visor and the crosses on his cassock one might have seen into his bosom and read the most secret intentions of his heart — so wonderful is the power of conscience. It makes us betray, accuse, and fight against ourselves, and for want of other witnesses, give evidence against ourselves:

Montaigne’s brother, travelling with him one day during the civil wars when they met the gentleman whose half-dead fear at every passing horse Montaigne at last discovered to be alarms of conscience.

## modern-en · bessus · 62:3

This story is in every child's mouth: Bessus the Paeonian, reproached for wantonly pulling down a nest of young sparrows and killing them, replied that he had reason to do so, since those little birds never ceased falsely accusing him of the murder of his father. The parricide had until then been concealed and unknown, but the avenging fury of conscience caused it to be revealed by the very man who was to suffer for it. Hesiod corrects Plato's saying that punishment closely follows sin: it is, he says, born at the same moment as the sin. Whoever expects punishment already suffers it, and whoever has deserved it expects it. Wickedness contrives torments against itself:

The Paeonian, reproached for pulling down a nest of young sparrows and killing them, who replied that he had reason, seeing those little birds never ceased falsely to accuse him of the murder of his father — and so gave up a parricide that had till then been unknown.

## modern-en · petilius · 62:18

There are a thousand examples of this; but three of one and the same person will be enough. Scipio, being accused one day before the people of Rome of crimes of a very high nature, instead of excusing himself or flattering his judges, said, "It will be a fine thing for you to sit in judgment on a head by whose means you have the power to judge all the world." Another time, to a string of impeachments brought against him by a tribune of the people, instead of making his defence he said, "Let us go, citizens — let us go and give thanks to the gods for the victory they gave me over the Carthaginians on this day," and walking off ahead toward the temple, he had presently the whole assembly, and his accuser himself, following at his heels. And when Petilius, put up to it by Cato, demanded an account of the money that had passed through his hands in the province of Antioch, Scipio, coming into the senate for that purpose, produced from under his robe a book in which, he told them, was an exact account of his receipts and disbursements; but when he was asked to hand it over to the prothonotary for examination, he refused, saying he would not do himself so great a disgrace, and in the presence of the whole senate tore the book in pieces with his own hands. I do not believe that the most calloused conscience could have counterfeited so great an assurance. He had naturally too high a spirit and was used to too high a fortune, says Titus Livius, to know how to be guilty, and to lower himself to the meanness of defending his innocence. The putting of men to the rack is a dangerous invention, and seems to be more a trial of patience than of truth. Both the man who has the fortitude to endure it conceals the truth, and the man who has not — for why should pain sooner make me confess what is, than force me to say what is not? And on the other hand, if the man who is not guilty of what he is accused of has the courage to undergo those torments, why should not the guilty man have the same, when so fair a reward as life is in his sights? I believe the basis of this invention comes from considering the force of conscience: for in the guilty man it seems to assist the rack in making him confess his fault and shake his resolution; and in the innocent it fortifies him against the torture. But, all said, it is in plain truth a trial full of uncertainty and danger. What would not a man say, what would not a man do, to avoid such unbearable torments?

Whom Cato set on to demand an account of the money that had passed through Scipio’s hands in the province of Antioch.

## modern-en · julius-canus · 63:4

Julius Canus, a noble Roman of rare constancy and virtue, had been condemned to death by that worthless creature Caligula. Among the many remarkable proofs he gave of his resolve, just as he was about to receive the executioner's stroke, a philosopher friend of his asked him: "Well, Canus, where is your soul now? What is she doing? What are you thinking of?" — "I was thinking," he answered, "of how to hold myself ready, with my faculties settled and fixed, to see whether in this short, quick instant of death I could catch the motion of the soul as she leaves the body, and whether she feels anything in the parting; so that, if I could, I might come back afterwards and report it to my friends." This man philosophises not just up to death but in death itself. What an extraordinary self-possession, what bravery of mind, to want his own death to be a lesson to him, and to have the leisure to think of other matters in such a moment:

A noble Roman condemned to die by Caligula who, going to the stroke, was asked by a philosopher friend what his soul was doing, and answered that he was keeping his mind settled and fixed to try whether in that short and quick instant he could perceive the motion of the soul as she parted from the body — and come back, if he could, to tell his friends of it.

## modern-en · hortensius · 63:41

This is, instead of blowing the child's nose, cutting it off altogether. I think the cure is worse than the disease. But granting that it must be sheer presumption to entertain people with talk about oneself, still, pursuing my general design, I cannot refrain from an action that publishes this weakness of mine, nor conceal a fault which I not only practise but profess. To speak my mind freely, however, I think that the habit of condemning wine because some people get drunk on it is itself to be condemned; we can only abuse what is good in itself, and I believe that this rule only has the popular vice in view. These are bridles for calves, with which neither the saints — whom we hear speaking so freely about themselves — nor the philosophers, nor the theologians let themselves be curbed; and neither will I, who am as little of the one as the other. If they do not write of themselves expressly, at least when the occasion calls for it they do not hesitate to step out into the open. What does Socrates discourse on more than himself? To what does he more often direct and steer the conversation of his disciples, than to speak of themselves — not of the lesson in their book, but of the substance and motion of their souls? We confess ourselves religiously to God and our confessor; and to our neighbours, in front of everyone. But some will answer that there we say nothing but accusations against ourselves. Why then, we are saying everything; for our very virtue itself is faulty and porous. My trade and my art is to live; anyone who forbids me to speak according to my own sense, experience, and practice might as well order an architect to speak of building not from his own knowledge but from his neighbour's, by someone else's knowledge and not his own. If it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues, why does Cicero not prefer the eloquence of Hortensius, and Hortensius that of Cicero? Perhaps they mean that I should give testimony of myself by works and effects, not just by words. What I mostly paint is my thoughts, a subject without shape and incapable of producing visible results; it is all I can do to give it body in this airy form of the voice. The wisest and most devout men have lived in great care to avoid any showy effects. Effects would speak more of fortune than of me; they show their own face, not mine, and only uncertainly, by inference; they are samples of one particular virtue. I expose myself entire. It is a body in which, at a single view, the veins, muscles, and tendons all appear, each in its place — here the effects of a cold, there of a beating heart, very tentatively. I do not write my deeds; I write myself and my essence.

The orator whose eloquence Montaigne asks why Cicero does not prefer to his own, if it is vainglory for a man to publish his own virtues — and why Hortensius does not prefer Cicero’s.

## modern-en · madame-destissac · 65:0

To Madame d'Estissac.

The dedicatee of the chapter on the affection of fathers to their children, and a widow young enough that everyone who knows at what age her husband left her, and the offers made to her, can see how well she has employed her widowhood.

## modern-en · monsieur-destissac-husband · 65:2

Now, madam, having to draw my own portrait to the life, I would have left out an important feature if I had not also represented the honour I have always had for you and your merits — which I have deliberately chosen to put at the start of this chapter, because, among the many other fine qualities you possess, the tender love you have shown your children stands very high. Whoever knows at what age Monsieur d'Estissac, your husband, left you a widow; the great and honourable matches that have since been offered to you, as many as to any lady of your rank in France; the constancy and steadiness with which, for so many years, you have borne so many sharp difficulties, the burden and conduct of business that has hounded you in every corner of the kingdom, and is not yet tired of harassing you; and the happy result you have given to all of it, by your own prudence or good fortune — anyone who knows all that will easily agree with me that we have no more vivid example of maternal devotion in our times than yours. I thank God, madam, that it has been so well placed; for the great hopes that Monsieur d'Estissac your son gives of himself are firm enough that when he comes of age you will harvest from him all the obedience and gratitude of a very good man. But since, on account of his tender years, he has not been able to take in those services of the highest value which he has received from you in such number, I want, if these papers should one day come into his hands when I no longer have mouth or speech to tell him myself, that he should receive from me a true account of what is being more effectively shown to him by its effects already: namely, that there is no gentleman in France more indebted to a mother's care, and that he cannot, in the future, give better or more certain proof of his own worth and virtue than by acknowledging you for the excellent mother that you are.

Her husband, who left her a widow young.

## modern-en · muley-hassam · 65:17

Muley Hassan, king of Tunis, the one whom the Emperor Charles V restored to his kingdom, reproached the memory of his father Mahomet with his frequenting of women, calling him loose, effeminate, and a begetter of children. The Greek histories tell us that Iccus the Tarentine, Chryso, Astyllus, Diopompos, and others, to keep their bodies in shape for the Olympic games and similar exercises, denied themselves during that training all dealings with Venus. In a certain country of the Spanish Indies men were not allowed to marry until after forty, yet the girls were given over at ten. It is not time for a gentleman of thirty to give place to his son of twenty; he is himself in a position to serve both in war and in the court of his prince; he needs all his resources; and yet, no doubt, he ought to surrender a share — but not so great a share as to forget himself for others. For such a man, the answer fathers usually have at the ready — "I will not take off my clothes before I go to bed" — serves well enough.

King of Tunis, whom the Emperor Charles restored, and Montaigne’s instance in that chapter. The modern edition spells him Hassan.

## modern-en · minos · 65:39

Now, considering this simple reason for loving our children — that we have begotten them, and so call them our second selves — it strikes me that there is another kind of offspring that comes from us no less deserving of recognition. For what we engender by the soul, the children of our understanding, of our courage, and of our abilities, springs from nobler parts than those of the body, and is much more our own; in this generation we are both father and mother. These cost us a great deal more and bring us more honour, if there is anything of good in them. As for our other children, their value is far more theirs than ours; the share we have in them is very little. But of these the whole beauty, all the grace and value, is ours, and they also represent us more vividly than the others. Plato adds that these are immortal children, who immortalise and deify their fathers, like Lycurgus, Solon, and Minos. Now, since history is full of examples of the common affection of fathers for their children, it does not seem inappropriate to bring in a few examples of this other kind. Heliodorus, that good bishop of Trikka, chose rather to lose the dignity, the income, and the devotion of so venerable a prelacy than to lose his daughter — a daughter who survives to this day, very graceful and shapely, but perhaps a little too carefully and wantonly dressed up, and too amorous for a clergyman's daughter. There was in Rome a certain Labienus, a man of great worth and authority and, among other qualities, excellent in every branch of literature, who was, I take it, the son of that great Labienus, the chief of Caesar's captains in the Gallic wars, who, afterwards taking Pompey's side, so valiantly held out his cause until he was beaten by Caesar in Spain. This Labienus I am now speaking of had several enemies, envious of his good qualities; and, very likely, the courtiers and favourites of the emperors of his time, who were highly offended at his independence and at the paternal spirit, hostile to tyranny, which he still kept up — with which we may suppose he had tinged his books and writings. His adversaries prosecuted several pieces he had published before the magistrates in Rome, and managed to have them condemned to the fire. It was on him that this new form of punishment was begun, which was later carried on against others at Rome: to punish writings and studies themselves with death. There would not be cruelty and material enough for cruelty, if we did not mix into it things that nature has exempted from all feeling and suffering, such as reputation and the products of the mind — if we did not extend bodily punishment to the teachings and monuments of the Muses. Now, Labienus could not endure this loss, nor outlive his so dear offspring, and so had himself conveyed and shut up alive in the tomb of his ancestors, where he managed to kill and bury himself at the same stroke. It is hard to show a more violent fatherly affection than this. Cassius Severus, a man of great eloquence and his very intimate friend, on seeing the books burned, cried out that by the same sentence they ought to condemn him to the fire as well, since he carried in his memory everything they contained. The same thing happened to Cremutius Cordus, who, being accused of having praised Brutus and Cassius in his books — that filthy, slavish, and corrupt Senate, worthy of a worse master than Tiberius, condemned his writings to the flames. He was willing to keep them company, and killed himself by starvation. The good Lucan, condemned by that scoundrel Nero, at the last gasp of his life, when most of his blood had already run out through the veins of his arms, which he had had his physician open to make him die, and when the cold had taken hold of his extremities and was creeping up towards his vitals, the last thing he had in his memory was some verses of his Pharsalia, which he recited, dying with them on his lips. What was this, but a tender and fatherly farewell to his children, in imitation of the goodbyes and embraces with which we part from ours when we come to die — and an effect of that natural inclination which suggests to our memory, in this last extremity, those things which were dearest to us during the time of our life?

With Lycurgus and Solon, one of the lawgivers whom Plato says their immortal children — the issue of the understanding rather than of the body — immortalise and deify.

There would not be cruelty and material enough for cruelty, if we did not mix into it things that nature has exempted from all feeling and suffering, such as reputation and the products of the mind — if we did not extend bodily punishment to the teachings and monuments of the Muses. Now, Labienus could not endure this loss, nor outlive his so dear offspring, and so had himself conveyed and shut up alive in the tomb of his ancestors, where he managed to kill and bury himself at the same stroke. It is hard to show a more violent fatherly affection than this. Cassius Severus, a man of great eloquence and his very intimate friend, on seeing the books burned, cried out that by the same sentence they ought to condemn him to the fire as well, since he carried in his memory everything they contained. The same thing happened to Cremutius Cordus, who, being accused of having praised Brutus and Cassius in his books — that filthy, slavish, and corrupt Senate, worthy of a worse master than Tiberius, condemned his writings to the flames. He was willing to keep them company, and killed himself by starvation. The good Lucan, condemned by that scoundrel Nero, at the last gasp of his life, when most of his blood had already run out through the veins of his arms, which he had had his physician open to make him die, and when the cold had taken hold of his extremities and was creeping up towards his vitals, the last thing he had in his memory was some verses of his Pharsalia, which he recited, dying with them on his lips. ## modern-en · phidias · 65:40

Can we believe that Epicurus — who, as he says himself, dying of the unbearable pain of the stone, had all his consolation in the beauty of the doctrine he was leaving behind him — could have received the same satisfaction from many children, however well-conditioned and brought up, if he had had them, as he did from the production of so many rich writings? Or that, had it been his choice to leave behind him a deformed and dull child or a foolish and ridiculous book, he, or any other man of his understanding, would not rather have chosen to run the first misfortune than the other? It might, perhaps, have been an impiety in Saint Augustine, if, on the one hand, it had been proposed to him to bury his writings, from which religion has received such great fruit, or, on the other, to bury his children (had he had them), if he had not rather chosen to bury his children. And I do not know whether I would not much rather have begotten one perfectly beautiful book through association with the Muses than by lying with my wife. What I give to this, such as it is, I give absolutely and irrevocably, as men do to their bodily children. That little I have done for it is no longer at my own disposal; it may know things that have gone from me, and may hold from me what I have not kept; and which, as from a stranger, I should have to borrow back from it, if I needed it. If I am wiser than my book, it is richer than I. There are few men addicted to poetry who would not be much prouder to be the father of the Aeneid than of the handsomest youth in Rome, and who would not bear the loss of the one much better than the loss of the other. For according to Aristotle, the poet, of all artists, is the fondest of his work. It is hard to believe that Epaminondas, who boasted that, in lieu of any posterity, he was leaving behind two daughters who would one day do their father honour (meaning the two victories he won over the Spartans), would have willingly consented to exchange these for the most beautiful creatures in all Greece; or that Alexander or Caesar ever wished to be deprived of the greatness of their glorious deeds in war, for the convenience of children and heirs, however perfect and accomplished. Indeed, I greatly doubt whether Phidias, or any other excellent sculptor, would be as anxious about the preservation and continuance of his natural children as he would be about a rare statue, which he had brought to perfection by long labour and study according to his art. And as for those furious and disordered passions which have sometimes inflamed fathers towards their own daughters, or mothers towards their own sons, the like is also found in this other kind of parenthood: witness what is told of Pygmalion, who, having made the statue of a woman of singular beauty, fell so passionately in love with this work of his that the gods, in favour of his passion, breathed life into it.

The sculptor. Montaigne makes a great question whether he, or any other excellent sculptor, would be so solicitous of the preservation of his natural children as of a supremely beautiful statue finished with long study and care.

## modern-en · johannes-secundus · 67:5

Among books that are simply pleasant, of the moderns, Boccaccio's Decameron, Rabelais, and the Basia of Johannes Secundus (if those can be classed under that heading) are worth reading for amusement. As for the Amadis and that kind of stuff, they did not have enough credit to arrest even my childhood. And I will say further, whether boldly or rashly, that this old, heavy soul of mine is no longer tickled by Ariosto, no, not even by the worthy Ovid; his facility and inventions, which once ravished me, are now no longer to my taste, and I can hardly have the patience to read him. I speak my opinion freely about everything, even about things that perhaps exceed my capacity and that I do not consider in any way under my jurisdiction. Accordingly, the judgment I deliver is meant to show the measure of my own sight, not of the things I am so bold as to criticise. When I find myself put off by Plato's Axiochus, as by a work — with all due respect to such an author — without force, my judgment does not believe itself: it is not so arrogant as to set itself against the authority of so many other famous judgments of antiquity, which it considers its tutors and masters, and with whom it is rather content to err. In such a case, it condemns itself either to stop at the outer bark, being unable to penetrate to the heart, or to consider the work by some false light. It is content with only sparing itself trouble and confusion; as to its own weakness, it frankly acknowledges and confesses it. It thinks it gives a just interpretation to the appearances presented to it by its own conceptions, but they are weak and imperfect. Most of Aesop's fables have several senses and meanings, of which the mythologists chose some one that fits the fable; but for the most part, this is only the first face that presents itself, and a superficial one; there still remain others, more vivid, essential, and profound, into which they have not been able to penetrate. And so it is with me.

Whose Basia, with the Decameron and Rabelais, Montaigne reckons among the books worth reading for amusement — if, he adds, they may be ranged under that title.

## modern-en · cicero-the-younger · 67:21

But since the matter preached and the preacher are different things, I would as gladly see Brutus in Plutarch as in a book of his own. I would rather be certainly informed of the conversation he had in his tent with some particular friends of his the night before a battle, than of the harangue he made to his army the next day; and of what he did in his study and chamber, than of what he did in the public square and in the senate. As to Cicero, I am of the common opinion that, learning aside, he had no great natural excellence. He was a good citizen, of an affable nature, as all fat, heavy men such as he was usually are; but given to ease, and had in truth a mighty share of vanity and ambition. Nor do I know how to excuse him for thinking his poetry fit to be published; it is no great fault to make bad verses, but it is a fault not to be able to judge how unworthy his verses were of the glory of his name. As for his eloquence, that is wholly beyond comparison, and I believe it will never be equalled. The younger Cicero, who resembled his father in nothing but the name, was once commanding in Asia, and had several strangers at his table, with Cestius seated at the lower end, as people often intrude at the open tables of the great. Cicero asked one of his people who that man was, who promptly told him the name; but he, as one whose thoughts were taken up with something else and who had forgotten the answer given him, asked the same question three or four times over. The fellow, to deliver himself from so many answers and to make him remember the man by some particular detail, said, "It is that Cestius, of whom you were told that he makes no great account of your father's eloquence in comparison with his own." At which Cicero, suddenly stung, ordered poor Cestius to be seized at once, and had him very well whipped in his own presence — a very discourteous host! Yet even among those who, all things considered, have reputed his eloquence incomparable, there have been some who have not hesitated to note some faults in it: as that great Brutus, his friend, for example, who said it was a broken and feeble eloquence, fractam et elumbem. The orators nearest to the age in which he lived also reproached him for the care he took with a certain long cadence in his periods, and particularly noticed his repeated use of the words esse videatur. For my part, I prefer a shorter style, that comes off more roundly. He does sometimes shuffle his parts more briskly together, but very seldom. I have myself noted this one passage:

Who resembled his father in nothing but the name. Commanding in Asia, he had Cestius at the lower end of his table, was told who the man was, and had him whipped on the spot — a proceeding, Montaigne notes, of a host and a judge at once.

## modern-en · asinius-pollio · 67:28

For the most part, and especially in these recent ages, people are picked out for this work from among the common sort on the sole consideration of well-speaking, as if we were to learn grammar from them; and the men so chosen have fair reason — being hired for nothing else, and pretending to nothing but babble — not to be very concerned with anything but that, so that, with a fine jingle of words, they prepare for us a pretty piece of reports they pick up in the streets. The only good histories are those written by men who held command in the affairs they write about, or who took part in conducting them, or at least had the conduct of others of the same kind. Such are almost all the Greek and Roman histories: for, several eyewitnesses having written on the same subject, in a time when grandeur and learning commonly met in the same person, if any error has crept in it must of necessity be a very slight one, and on a very doubtful incident. What can one expect from a physician writing of war, or from a mere scholar treating of the designs of princes? If we wanted to note how scrupulous the Romans were in this matter, only one example would be needed: Asinius Pollio found in the histories of Caesar himself something misreported — a mistake caused either by Caesar's inability to have his eye in every part of his army at once, having credited certain individuals who had given him an inaccurate account, or by his not having had a sufficiently exact account from his lieutenants of what they had done in his absence. From this we may see how delicate the search for truth is, when one cannot trust the report of a battle from the knowledge of the man who commanded there, nor from the soldiers who were engaged in it, unless, after the method of a judicial enquiry, the witnesses are confronted and objections weighed on each least detail of every incident. In good earnest, the knowledge we have of our own affairs is much more obscure; but this has been sufficiently dealt with by Bodin, and according to my own view. To support a little the weakness of my memory (which is so extreme that more than once I have happened to pick up books again as new and unseen, that I had carefully read a few years before and scribbled over with my notes), I have lately adopted the custom of noting at the end of every book (that is, of those I never intend to read again) the time when I finished it and the judgment I had formed of it, so that this might at least represent to me the character and general idea I had conceived of the author in reading it; and I will copy out some of those notes here.

Who found mistakes in Caesar’s own histories, into which Caesar had fallen either because he could not have his eye in all parts of his army at once, or because he trusted the particular reports of others.

He has sufficiently handled the question Montaigne leaves aside at 67:28, and Montaigne agrees with his sentiment there.

## modern-en · eginhard · 67:31

On the Memoirs of Monsieur du Bellay I have this: "It is always pleasant to read things written by those who have experienced how they should be conducted; but it cannot be denied that there is a manifest falling-off in these two lords from the freedom and liberty of writing that shine in the earlier historians — such as the Sieur de Joinville, the familiar companion of St Louis; Eginhard, chancellor to Charlemagne; and, more recently, Philippe de Commines. What we have here is rather an apology for King Francis, against the Emperor Charles V, than history. I will not believe that they falsified anything as to matter of fact; but they make a common practice of twisting the judgment of events, often against reason, to our advantage, and of leaving out whatever is ticklish to handle in their master's life — witness the affairs of Messieurs de Montmorency and de Biron, which are omitted here; even the very name of Madame d'Étampes is not to be found. Secret actions a historian may keep quiet; but to pass over in silence what all the world knows, and things that have drawn after them public and momentous consequences, is an inexcusable defect. In short, whoever wants a thorough knowledge of King Francis and the events of his reign, let him seek it elsewhere, if my advice prevails. The only profit one can reap from these Memoirs is in the particular accounts of the battles and other exploits of war in which these gentlemen were personally engaged; in some words and private actions of the princes of their time; and in the treaties and negotiations carried out by the Seigneur de Langey, where there are things everywhere worth knowing, and discourses above the common strain."

Chancellor to Charlemagne, and with the Sire de Joinville and Philip de Commines one of the elder historians in whom the freedom and liberty of writing shines — by comparison with which Montaigne finds a manifest decadence in the two lords of his own subject.

I will not believe that they falsified anything as to matter of fact; but they make a common practice of twisting the judgment of events, often against reason, to our advantage, and of leaving out whatever is ticklish to handle in their master's life — witness the affairs of Messieurs de Montmorency and de Biron, which are omitted here; even the very name of Madame d'Étampes is not to be found. Secret actions a historian may keep quiet; but to pass over in silence what all the world knows, and things that have drawn after them public and momentous consequences, is an inexcusable defect. In short, whoever wants a thorough knowledge of King Francis and the events of his reign, let him seek it elsewhere, if my advice prevails. The only profit one can reap from these Memoirs is in the particular accounts of the battles and other exploits of war in which these gentlemen were personally engaged; in some words and private actions of the princes of their time; and in the treaties and negotiations carried out by the Seigneur de Langey, where there are things everywhere worth knowing, and discourses above the common strain."

Whose proceedings, with Monsieur de Montmorency’s, are among the things Montaigne complains are omitted from the memoirs he is discussing — as are actions that did not succeed, and speeches and countenances the writer durst not report.

This is one of the reasons why Epaminondas, who belonged to yet a third sect, refused the riches fortune offered him by very lawful means — because, he said, he had to contend with poverty; in which extreme he kept himself to the last. Socrates put himself, I think, to a still harder test, keeping for his exercise a confounded scolding wife — a sparring partner with sharp blades. Metellus, alone of all the Roman senators, having attempted, by the power of virtue, to withstand the violence of Saturninus, tribune of the people at Rome, who was bent on passing an unjust law in favour of the commons — and, by so doing, having incurred the capital penalties Saturninus had set against the dissenters — addressed those who, in this extremity, were leading him to execution with words to this effect: that it was too easy and too base to do ill; and that to do well where there was no danger was a common thing; but that to do well where there was danger was the proper office of a man of virtue. Metellus's words show very clearly what I want to make out: that virtue refuses ease for a companion; that the easy, smooth, downhill way along which the regular steps of a sweet disposition are conducted is not the way of true virtue; she demands a rough and stormy passage. She wants either outward difficulties to wrestle with — like Metellus's, by means of which fortune delights to interrupt the speed of her career — or inward difficulties, brought on by the disordered appetites and imperfections of our condition to disturb her.

Who alone of all the Roman senators attempted, by the power of virtue, to withstand the violence of Saturninus — and who, told that to do ill was easy and to do well where there was no danger common, answered that to do well where there was danger was the proper office of a man of virtue. Montaigne makes his the type of the exotic difficulty that virtue seeks out.

## modern-en · raimond-sebond · 69:0

Learning is, indeed, a very great and very substantial accomplishment, and those who despise it betray their own lack of understanding well enough. But I do not prize it at the inflated rate some others do — as Herillus the philosopher did, for one, who placed the sovereign good in it and maintained that "it alone can make us wise and contented," which I do not believe. No more do I believe what others have said: that learning is the mother of all virtue, and all vice proceeds from ignorance — which, if true, would require a very long explanation. My house has long been open to men of knowledge, and is well known to them. For my father, who governed it for fifty years and more, fired by the new ardour with which Francis the First embraced letters and brought them into esteem, hunted after the acquaintance of learned men with great diligence and expense, receiving them into his house as persons sacred and touched with some particular inspiration of divine wisdom. He collected their sayings and sentences as so many oracles, with all the more reverence and religious devotion as he was the less able to judge of them, for he had no learning, any more than his predecessors. For my part I love such men, but I do not adore them. Among others, Peter Bunel, a man of great reputation for knowledge in his time, having spent some days at Montaigne in my father's company along with others of his sort, presented him at his departure with a book entitled _Theologia naturalis; sive Liber Creaturarum, magistri Raimondi de Sebonde._ Since Italian and Spanish were familiar to my father, and this book was written in a kind of jargon — Spanish with Latin endings — he hoped that with a little help he might be able to understand it, and so he recommended it as a very useful book, and one suited to the time in which he gave it to him. That was when Luther's new doctrines were beginning to come into vogue, and in many places to shake our ancient belief — wherein he was very well advised, foreseeing wisely, by his own reason, that the beginning of this disorder would easily slide into an abominable atheism. For the common people, lacking the faculty of judging things for themselves, allow themselves to be carried away by chance and appearance. Once they have been emboldened to despise and challenge opinions they had previously held in extreme reverence — those on which their salvation depends — and once some articles of their religion have been brought into doubt and dispute, they soon throw all the other parts of their belief into the same uncertainty. They had no other authority or foundation than the ones they have already disturbed, and they shake off every impression they had received from the authority of the laws or the reverence of ancient custom as if it were a tyrannical yoke:

The Spaniard, practising physic at Toulouse two hundred years before, whose Theologia naturalis Peter Bunel gave Montaigne’s father and Montaigne translated at his father’s command. He undertakes to establish every article of the Christian religion against the atheists by human and natural reason, and Montaigne, who thinks nobody has done better on that subject, gives the whole chapter to answering the two objections made to him. The older edition prints his name Sehond once, and the Latin title has him as Raimondi de Sebonde.

## modern-en · orpheus · 69:15

There is no hostility so remarkable as the Christian. Our zeal performs wonders when it seconds our inclinations to hatred, cruelty, ambition, avarice, slander, and rebellion; but when it moves against the grain, towards kindness, gentleness, and temperance — unless by some miracle a rare and virtuous disposition prompts us — we don't stir hand or foot. Our religion is meant to root out vices; instead it shields, nourishes, and incites them. We must not mock God. If we believed in him — I do not say by faith, but with a simple belief; that is to say (and I say it to our great shame), if we believed in him and recognized him as we do any other story, or as we would one of our companions — we should love him above all other things for the infinite goodness and beauty that shines in him. At the very least he would go equal in our affection with riches, pleasure, glory, and our friends. The best of us is not so afraid to outrage him as he is afraid to injure his neighbour, his kinsman, or his master. Is there any understanding so weak that, having on one side the object of one of our vicious pleasures and on the other (in equal knowledge and persuasion) the prospect of immortal glory, would trade the first for the second? And yet we often renounce it out of mere contempt: for what lust tempts us to blaspheme, if not, perhaps, the very desire to give offence? The philosopher Antisthenes, as he was being initiated into the mysteries of Orpheus, when the priest told him "that those who professed themselves of that religion were certain to receive perfect and eternal felicity after death," answered, "If you believe that, why don't you die yourself?" Diogenes, more bluntly in his usual manner and farther from our purpose, said to a priest who similarly preached to him to take up his religion in order to obtain the happiness of the other world, "What! you'd have me believe that Agesilaus and Epaminondas, who were so great, will be miserable, while you, who are nothing but a calf and can do nothing to the point, will be happy because you are a priest?" If we received these great promises of eternal blessedness with the same reverence and respect as we do a philosophical discourse, we should not hold death in such horror:

In whose mysteries Antisthenes was being initiated when the priest told him that those who professed that religion were certain of perfect and eternal felicity after death, and was asked why, believing it, he did not die himself.

## modern-en · apollonius-tyanaus · 69:40

Presumption is our natural and original disease. The most wretched and frail of all creatures is man, and also the proudest. He feels and sees himself lodged here in the dirt and filth of the world, nailed and riveted to the worst, deadest part of the universe, in the lowest storey of the house, the most remote from the heavenly arch, with animals of the worst condition of the three; and yet, in his imagination, he places himself above the circle of the moon and brings the heavens under his feet. By the same vanity of imagination he equals himself to God, attributes divine qualities to himself, withdraws and separates himself from the crowd of other creatures, parcels out the portions of the animals (his fellows and companions), and distributes to them portions of faculty and force as he himself thinks fit. How does he know, by the strength of his understanding, the secret and inner motions of animals? From what comparison between them and us does he conclude the stupidity he attributes to them? When I play with my cat, who knows whether I am not more her sport than she is mine? We mutually entertain each other with our play. If I have my hour to begin or to refuse, she has hers too. Plato, in his picture of the golden age under Saturn, lists among the chief advantages a man then had his communication with the beasts, from whom, asking and learning, he knew the true qualities and differences of them all, and by this acquired a very perfect intelligence and prudence, and led his life more happily than we can do. Do we need any better proof to condemn human impudence in the matter of beasts? This great author was of the opinion that nature, in the bodily form she gave them, had for the most part only had regard to the use of the prognostics derived from them in his time. The defect that hinders communication between them and us — why may it not be on our side as well as on theirs? It is still to be determined where the fault lies that we do not understand each other — for we understand them no more than they understand us; and by the same reasoning they may think us beasts as we think them. It is no great wonder if we do not understand them, when we do not understand a Basque or a Troglodyte. And yet some have boasted that they understood them — Apollonius of Tyana, Melampus, Tiresias, Thales, and others. And seeing, as cosmographers report, that there are nations who have a dog for their king, they must necessarily be able to interpret his voice and motions. We must observe the parity between us, have some tolerable understanding of their meaning, and let beasts have some of ours — about the same. They caress us, threaten us, and beg of us, and we do the same to them.

With Melampus, Tiresias and Thales, one of those who have boasted that they understood the speech of beasts.

Why should we say that only man, by knowledge built up through art and meditation, can distinguish things useful to his being and proper for the cure of his diseases from those which are not — that only he can know the virtues of rhubarb and polypody? When we see the goats of Candia, when wounded with an arrow, choose dittany out of a million of plants for their cure; the tortoise, when she has eaten a viper, immediately go out to look for origanum to purge herself; the dragon to rub and clear his eyes with fennel; the storks to give themselves enemas of seawater; the elephants to draw the darts and javelins thrown at them in battle not only out of their own bodies, and out of the bodies of their companions, but even out of the bodies of their masters (witness the elephant of King Porus whom Alexander defeated), and to do so with such dexterity that we ourselves could not do it with so little pain to the patient — why do we not say that this too is knowledge and reason? To allege, to their disparagement, that it is by the sole instruction and dictate of nature that they know all this is not to take away from them the dignity of knowledge and reason, but with greater force to attribute it to them than to us, for the honour of so infallible a mistress. Chrysippus, though in other respects as scornful a judge of the condition of animals as any other philosopher whatsoever, considering the movements of a dog who comes to a place where three roads meet — whether hunting for his lost master, or in pursuit of some game that flies before him — sniffing first one of the ways, then another, and after having made sure of two without finding the trace of what he seeks, dashing into the third without examination, was forced to confess that this reasoning was in the dog: "I have traced my master to this place; he must of necessity have gone one of these three ways; he is not gone this way nor that, he must then infallibly be gone this other." And assuring himself by this conclusion, he makes no use of his nose in the third way, nor ever lays it to the ground, but lets himself be carried on by the force of reason. This piece of pure logic — this use of propositions divided and joined, this proper enumeration of parts — is it not every bit as good that the dog should know all this of himself as from Trapezuntius?

Whose elephant, Montaigne’s instance among the beasts that physic themselves, drew the darts and javelins out of its own body and out of its master’s. Alexander defeated him.

I must not omit what Plutarch says he saw of a dog at Rome, with the Emperor Vespasian the father, at the theatre of Marcellus. This dog was the assistant of a player who was performing a farce of several parts and characters, in which the dog had his part. Among other things, he had to pretend, for some time, to be dead from a certain drug he was supposed to have eaten. After he had swallowed a piece of bread that passed for the drug, he began after a while to tremble and stagger, as if taken giddy; at last, stretching himself out stiff as if dead, he suffered himself to be drawn and dragged from place to place, as was his role; and afterwards, when he sensed that it was time, he began first to stir gently, as if waking out of a profound sleep, and lifting up his head looked about him in such a way that astonished all the spectators.

The emperor in whose company at the theatre of Marcellus Plutarch says he saw the dog that counterfeited death.

## modern-en · arrian · 69:82

More understanding is required in the teaching of others than in being taught. Now, setting aside what Democritus held and proved — that most of the arts we have were taught us by other animals (weaving and sewing by the spider; building by the swallow; music by the swan and nightingale; and the making of medicines by various animals) — Aristotle is of opinion that nightingales teach their young to sing, and spend much time and care doing so; whence it happens that those we bring up in cages, and which have not had time to learn from their parents, lack much of the grace of their singing. We may judge by this that they improve by discipline and study; and even among the wild, it is not the case that all alike — each has learned to do better or worse, according to his capacity. And they are so jealous of each other while learning that they compete with rivalry, and with such a vigorous competition that sometimes the loser falls dead on the spot, the breath failing sooner than the voice. The younger ones ruminate pensively and begin to mutter some broken notes; the pupil listens to the master's lesson, and gives the best account he is able; they fall silent by turns; one hears faults corrected, and may observe certain rebukes from the teacher. "I once saw," says Arrian, "an elephant with a cymbal hung at each leg, and another fastened to his trunk, at the sound of which all the others danced round about him, rising and bending at certain cadences as they were guided by the instrument; and it was delightful to hear this harmony." In the spectacles of Rome elephants were commonly seen taught to move and dance to the sound of the voice, in dances with several changes and cadences very hard to learn. And some have been known to be so intent on their lesson as to practise it privately by themselves, so as not to be scolded or beaten by their masters.

Who reports the elephant with a cymbal hung at each leg and another on his trunk, at whose sound the others danced round about him, rising and bending at certain cadences.

## modern-en · juba · 69:84

I will not leave out this other example of a dog, also from Plutarch (I am muddling all order, but I do not aim at arrangement here any more than anywhere else throughout my book). Plutarch says he saw it aboard a ship. This dog, being puzzled how to get the oil at the bottom of a jar, which he could not reach with his tongue because of the narrow mouth of the vessel, went and fetched stones and dropped them into the jar until he made the oil rise high enough for him to reach it. What is this but the effect of a very subtle capacity? It is said the ravens of Barbary do the same when the water they would drink is too low. This action is somewhat akin to what Juba, a king of their nation, reports of elephants: that when, by the cunning of the hunter, one of them is trapped in certain deep pits prepared for them and covered over with brush to deceive them, all the rest bring in great diligence many stones and logs of wood to raise the bottom so he may get out. But this animal in several other effects approaches so close to human capacity that, if I were to recount all that experience has shown of them, I should easily get granted what I usually maintain: that there is more difference between this man and that than between this beast and this man. The keeper of an elephant in a private house in Syria robbed him at every meal of half his ration. One day his master came to feed him himself, and poured the full measure of barley that he had ordered for his allowance into his manger; the elephant, casting an angry look at the keeper, separated the one half from the other with his trunk and pushed it aside, declaring in this way the wrong done him. And another elephant, whose keeper mixed stones in with his corn to make up the measure, went to the pot where the keeper was boiling meat for his own dinner and filled it with ashes. These are particular cases. But what all the world has seen, and all the world knows, is that in all the armies of the Levant one of the greatest forces consisted in elephants, with which they did, without comparison, far greater execution than we do now with our artillery — which roughly takes their place on a day of battle (as may easily be supposed by those well read in ancient history);

A king of their nation, who relates of the elephants that they pull the darts out of one another.

## modern-en · androdus · 69:133

"One day," he says, "in Rome, they entertained the people with a show of fighting between several strange beasts, and principally of lions of an unusual size. There was one among the rest who, by his furious bearing, by the strength and largeness of his limbs, and by his loud and dreadful roaring, attracted the eyes of all the spectators. Among the slaves presented to the people in this combat of beasts there was one Androdus, of Dacia, belonging to a Roman lord of consular dignity. This lion, having seen him at a distance, first made a sudden stop, as if in a wondering posture, and then softly approached nearer in a gentle and peaceable manner, as though to renew acquaintance with him. This being done, and now sure of what he sought for, he began to wag his tail, as dogs do when they fawn on their masters, and to kiss and lick the hands and thighs of the poor wretch, who was beside himself and almost dead with fear. Androdus, brought a little to himself by this kindness of the lion, having taken heart enough to look at him and recognize him, it was a singular pleasure to see the joy and caresses that passed between them. At which, the people breaking into loud acclamations of joy, the emperor had the slave called to him, to learn the cause of so strange an event; and Androdus told him a new and a very strange story: 'My master,' he said, 'being proconsul in Africa, I was forced, by his severity and cruel usage, being daily beaten, to steal from him and run away; and, to hide myself safely from a person of such great authority in the province, I thought it best to flee to the solitudes, sands, and uninhabitable parts of that country, resolving that if I could no longer find means to support life, I would somehow kill myself. The sun being excessively hot at noon, and the heat intolerable, I came upon a private and almost inaccessible cave, and went into it. Soon after, this lion came in to me, with one foot wounded and bloody, complaining and groaning with the pain he endured. At his coming I was extremely afraid; but he, having spotted me hiding in the corner of his den, came gently up to me, holding out and showing me his wounded foot, as if he were asking my assistance in his distress. I then drew out a great splinter he had got there, and growing a little more familiar with him, squeezing the wound, I thrust out the matter, dirt, and gravel that had got into it, and wiped and cleansed it as best I could. He, finding himself somewhat better, and much eased of his pain, lay down to rest, and presently fell asleep with his foot in my hand. From that time forward, he and I lived together in this cave three whole years on the same diet; for of the beasts he killed hunting he always brought me the best pieces, which I roasted in the sun for want of fire, and so ate. At last, weary of this wild and brutish life, while the lion was one day gone out to hunt for our ordinary provision, I left the cave, and on the third day after was taken by the soldiers, who brought me from Africa to this city, to my master, who at once condemned me to die and to be exposed thus to the wild beasts. Now, from what I see, this lion was also taken soon after, and is now seeking to repay me for the kindness and cure he received at my hands.' This is the story Androdus told the emperor, who also passed it from hand to hand to the people; whereupon, at the general request, he was absolved from his sentence and set at liberty, and the lion was, by order of the people, presented to him. We afterwards saw," says Apion, "Androdus leading this lion, in nothing but a small leash, from tavern to tavern at Rome, and receiving whatever money everyone gave him, the lion being so gentle as to allow himself to be covered with the flowers the people threw upon him; everyone he met saying, 'There goes the lion who entertained the man; there goes the man who cured the lion.'"

The runaway slave who drew a thorn from a lion’s foot in an African cave and lived with the beast three years on the game it brought him; and who, condemned long afterwards to the beasts at Rome, was recognised by that same lion and spared, and afterwards led him about the taverns on a small leash while the people threw flowers on him.

## modern-en · dionysius-heracleotes · 69:182

But we must trample under foot this foolish vanity, and briskly and boldly shake the ridiculous foundation on which these false opinions are founded. As long as man shall believe he has any means and power of himself, he will never acknowledge what he owes to his Maker; his eggs shall always be chickens, as the saying is; we must therefore strip him to his shirt. Let us see some notable examples of the effects of his philosophy. Posidonius, tormented by a disease so painful that it made him writhe his arms and gnash his teeth, thought he had sufficiently scorned the pain by crying out against it: "Do thy worst — I will not confess that thou art an evil." He felt the pain as much as my footman, but he made a bravado of bridling his tongue, at least, and keeping it within the laws of his sect: _Re succumbere non oportebat, verbis gloriantem._ ["It did not become him, who spoke so big, to confess his frailty when he came to the test."] Arcesilaus, ill of the gout, when Carneades who had come to see him went away troubled at his condition, was called back, and showing him his feet and breast, said, "There is nothing comes from there to here." This has a slightly better grace, for he feels himself in pain and would be free of it, but his heart, nevertheless, is not conquered nor subdued by it. The other stands more obstinately to his point, but, I fear, more verbally than really. And Dionysius Heracleotes, afflicted with a vehement smarting in his eyes, was reduced to give up these Stoic resolutions. But even if knowledge should, in effect, do what they say, and could blunt the point and dull the edge of the misfortunes that attend us, what does she do, more than what ignorance does more purely and evidently? The philosopher Pyrrho, being at sea in great danger because of a mighty storm, offered nothing for imitation to those with him in that extremity but a hog they had on board that was fearless and unconcerned at the tempest. Philosophy, when she has said all she can, refers us at last to the example of a gladiator, wrestler, or muleteer, in which sort of people we commonly observe much less apprehension of death, much less sense of pain and other inconveniences, and more endurance, than knowledge ever furnished to anyone who was not born and bred to hardship. What makes us cut into the tender limbs of an infant, or of a horse, more easily than into our own — but ignorance only? How many has the mere force of imagination made sick? We often see men cause themselves to be let blood, purged, and physicked to cure them of diseases they only feel in opinion. When real infirmities fail us, knowledge lends us hers: that colour, that complexion portends some catarrhous defluxion; this hot season threatens us with a fever; this break in the life-line of your left hand gives you notice of some near and dangerous indisposition; and at last she roundly attacks health itself, saying, "This sprightliness and vigour of youth cannot continue in this state; some blood must be taken and the heat abated, lest it turn against yourself." Compare the life of a man subjected to such imaginings with that of a labourer who lets himself be led by his natural appetite, measuring things only by the present sense, without knowledge and without forecast, who feels no pain or sickness but when he is really ill — whereas the other has the stone in his soul before he has it in his bladder, as if it were not time enough to suffer the evil when it shall come, but he must anticipate it by fancy, and run to meet it.

Who, afflicted with a vehement smarting in his eyes, was reduced to quit his Stoical resolutions.

for that tickling and stinging which is in certain pleasures, and that seem to lift us above simple health and passiveness — that active, moving, and (I don't know how) itching and biting pleasure — even that very pleasure itself aims at nothing but insensibility as its mark. As life becomes more pleasant through simplicity, it also becomes more innocent and better, as I was saying just now. ## modern-en · velleius · 69:230

Finally, if I were to examine whether it is in man's power to find what he seeks, and whether the long search in which he has busied himself for so many ages has enriched him with any new strength or any solid truth — I believe he will confess, if he speaks his conscience, that all he has gained by so long an inquiry is to have learned to recognize his own weakness. We have only, through long study, confirmed and verified the natural ignorance we were in before. The same thing has happened to truly wise men that happens to the ears of corn: they shoot up and hold their heads high while empty, but once full and swollen with grain in maturity they begin to droop and bow. So men, having tried and sounded all things, and having found in that mass of knowledge and that store of so many various things nothing solid, nothing firm — nothing but vanity — have given up their presumption and acknowledged their natural condition. It is what Velleius reproaches Cotta and Cicero with, "that they had learned of Philo that they had learned nothing." Pherecydes, one of the seven sages, writing to Thales on his deathbed, said: "I have given orders to my people, after my burial, to bring my writings to you. If they please you and the other sages, publish them; if not, suppress them. They contain no certainty that I myself am satisfied with. Nor do I pretend to know the truth or to attain to it. I open things rather than discover them." The wisest man that ever lived, asked what he knew, answered, "He knew this — that he knew nothing." Thereby he verified what has been said: that the greatest part of what we know is the least of what we do not know; that even what we think we know is only a piece, and a very small piece, of our ignorance. We know things in dreams, says Plato, and are ignorant of them in truth. _Omnes pene veteres nihil cognosci, nihil percipi, nihil sciri posse dixerunt; angustos sensus, imbecilles animos, brevia curricula vitae._ "Almost all the ancients declared that nothing could be known, perceived, or understood; that the senses are too limited, men's minds too weak, the course of life too short." And of Cicero himself, who owed his learning everything he was worth, Valerius says: "He began to lose his taste for letters in his old age; and even at his studies he was very independent of any one party, following what he thought probable now in one sect, now in another, forever wavering under the doubts of the Academy." _Dicendum est, sed ita ut nihil affirment, quaeram omnia, dubitans plerumque, et mihi diffidens._ "I must speak, but in such a way as to affirm nothing; I inquire into everything, but mostly in doubt, and distrusting myself."

Who reproaches Cotta and Cicero with having learned of Philo that they had learned nothing.

For the rest, the very share we allow the beasts of nature's bounty, even by our own admission, is very much to their advantage. We attribute to ourselves imaginary and fantastic goods, future and absent goods, for which human capacity cannot answer by herself; or goods we falsely attribute to ourselves by the licence of opinion, like reason, knowledge, and honour — and leave to them as their portion essential, durable, and palpable goods: peace, repose, security, innocence, and health; health, I say, the fairest and richest present that nature can make us. Insomuch that philosophy, even the Stoic, is bold enough to say that Heraclitus and Pherecides, had they been able to trade their wisdom for health, and to have rid themselves — the one of his dropsy, the other of the lousy disease that tormented him — would have done well. By which they set a higher value on wisdom, comparing and putting it in the balance with health, than they do in this other proposition, which is also theirs: that if Circe had presented Ulysses with two potions, the one to make a fool become a wise man, the other to make a wise man become a fool, Ulysses ought rather to have chosen the latter than consent to the one by which Circe changed his human form into that of a beast; and they say that wisdom itself would have spoken to him in these terms: "Forsake me, let me alone, rather than lodge me under the body and figure of an ass." What! shall the philosophers, then, abandon this great and divine wisdom for this bodily and earthly covering? Then it is no longer by reason, by discourse, and by the soul that we excel the beasts; it is by our beauty, our fair complexion, and the fine symmetry of our parts, for which we must give up our intelligence, our prudence, and all the rest. Well, I accept this open and frank confession; certainly they knew that those things on which we set so much value are no other than vain fancy. If beasts had all the virtue, knowledge, wisdom, and Stoic perfection, they would still be beasts, and would not be comparable to man — miserable, wicked, mad man. For in short, whatever is not as we are is nothing worth; and God, in order to procure himself some esteem among us, must put himself into that shape, as we shall show shortly. By which it appears that it is not on any true ground of reason, but by a foolish pride and vain opinion, that we prefer ourselves to other animals and separate ourselves from their society and condition.

One of the seven sages, who wrote to Thales on his death-bed to have his books given to his friends, and to be buried if they approved them; and, on Cicero’s testimony, the first to introduce the immortality of the soul, in the time of King Tullus. The older edition calls him Syrius where the modern says of Syros — the epithet, not another man, though the sentence is broken across the paragraph boundary at 69:468 and reads like one.

## modern-en · clitomachus · 69:235

Whoever goes searching for anything must come to one of these conclusions: that he has found it, that it cannot be found, or that he is still searching. All philosophy divides into these three branches; its design is to seek out truth, knowledge, and certainty. The Peripatetics, Epicureans, Stoics, and others have thought they had found it. They established the sciences we have, and treated them as certain knowledge. Clitomachus, Carneades, and the Academics have despaired in their search, and concluded that truth could not be grasped by our understanding. The result with them is weakness and human ignorance. This sect has had the most numerous and noblest followers. Pyrrho and the other skeptics or epechists — whose dogmas many of the ancients trace back to Homer, the seven sages, Archilochus, and Euripides, with Zeno, Democritus, and Xenophanes added to the list — say they are still inquiring after truth. They conclude that the others, who think they have found it, are infinitely deceived; and that the second group, who decide that human reason cannot attain to it, are guilty of too daring a vanity, for to set up a measure of our power to know and judge the difficulty of things is itself a great and extreme knowledge, of which they doubt man is capable:

Who with Carneades and the Academics despaired in the search for truth, and concluded that it could not be conceived by our understandings.
