Thales, who first inquired into this kind of matter, believed God to be a Spirit that made all things of water. Anaximander, that the gods were always dying and coming back into life, and that there were an infinite number of worlds. Anaximenes, that the air was God, procreate and immense, always in motion. Anaxagoras was the first of the opinion that the description and arrangement of all things was directed by the power and reason of an infinite spirit. Alcmaeon assigned divinity to the sun, moon, stars, and the soul. Pythagoras made God a spirit spread through the nature of all things, from which our souls are drawn. Parmenides, a circle surrounding the heavens, holding the world up by the heat of light. Empedocles pronounced the four elements, of which all things are composed, to be gods. Protagoras had nothing to say whether they were or were not, or what they were. Democritus thought at one time that the images and their circulations were gods; at another, the nature that throws off those images; and then, our science and intelligence. Plato divides his belief into several opinions: in his _Timaeus_, he says that the Father of the World cannot be named; in his _Laws_, that men should not inquire into his being; and elsewhere, in the very same books, he makes the world, the heavens, the stars, the earth, and our souls into gods, accepting moreover those received by ancient institution in every republic.

Who held that the gods were always dying and entering into life again; and, with Hesiod, that the soul was a thing composed of earth and water.

## modern-en · parmenides · 69:249

So it is with most of this third sort of authors, as the ancients have noted in the writings of Anaxagoras, Democritus, Parmenides, Xenophanes, and others. Their way of writing is doubtful both in substance and design, inquiring rather than teaching, even when they mix some dogmatic stretches into the style. Don't we see the same thing in Seneca and Plutarch? How many contradictions are to be found in them if a man pries narrowly! So many that the reconciling lawyers ought first to reconcile each of them with himself. Plato seems to have affected this method of philosophizing in dialogues, so that he might with greater decency, through several mouths, deliver the diversity and variety of his own fancies. It is just as well to treat things variously as conformably — and better, that is to say more fully and to greater profit. Take an example from ourselves: judgments are the highest point of all dogmatic and definitive speech; and yet those _arrêts_ our parliaments deliver to the people, even the most exemplary, the ones most fit to nourish in them the reverence due that dignity — owing chiefly to the competence of the persons involved — draw their beauty not so much from the conclusion (with judges, an everyday matter) as from the heat and dispute of the various and contrary arguments that the matter of law and equity allows. And the broadest field for reproach that some philosophers have against others is drawn from the diversities and contradictions in which every one of them is caught up — either on purpose, to show the wavering of the human mind on every subject, or unwittingly compelled by the slipperiness and incomprehensibility of all matter. Which is the sense of the maxim: "In a slippery and sliding place let us suspend our belief." For, as Euripides says,

Who made God a circle surrounding the heaven and supporting the world by the ardour of light; and who, alone of all the philosophers before Heraclitus, would not allow things to have motion.

## modern-en · theophrastus · 69:268

Xenophon reports a similar perplexity in Socrates's teaching: at one point men are not to inquire into the form of God, then a moment later he makes him hold that the sun is God, and the soul God; that there is only one God, and then that there are many. Speusippus, Plato's nephew, makes God a certain power that governs all things, and says he has a soul. Aristotle says at one time it is the spirit, at another the world; at one time he gives the world another master, at another he makes God the heat of heaven. Xenocrates makes eight: five named among the planets; a sixth composed of all the fixed stars as so many members; the seventh and eighth, the sun and moon. Heraclides Ponticus does nothing but float between opinions, finally stripping God of sense and making him shift from one form to another, until in the end he calls him heaven and earth. Theophrastus wanders in the same indecision among his fancies, attributing the superintendence of the world now to understanding, now to heaven, now to the stars. Strato says it is nature, having the power of generation, increase, and diminution, without form or sentience. Zeno says it is the law of nature, commanding good and forbidding evil — which law is an animal; and he sets aside the customary gods, Jupiter, Juno, Vesta. Diogenes of Apollonia, that it is air. Xenophanes makes God round, seeing and hearing, not breathing, and having nothing in common with human nature. Aristo thinks the form of God incomprehensible, strips him of sense, and does not know whether he is an animal or something else. Cleanthes at one time supposes it to be reason, at another the world, at another the soul of nature, at another the supreme heat rolling and surrounding all. Perseus, Zeno's disciple, was of the opinion that men have given the title of god to those who have been useful and added some notable advantage to human life — even to useful things themselves. Chrysippus made a confused heap of all the preceding theories, and counted, among a thousand forms of gods he invents, men who have been deified. Diagoras and Theodorus flatly denied that there were any gods at all. Epicurus makes the gods shining, transparent, and air-permeable, lodged as between two forts, between two worlds, safe from blows, clothed in human shape and with members like ours — members that serve them no purpose:

Who says the ears are the most dangerous instruments about us for receiving violent impressions, and who attributes to Nicetas of Syracuse the opinion that it is the earth that moves.

## modern-en · isis · 69:277

The Egyptians, with an impudent prudence, forbade on pain of hanging that anyone should say their gods, Serapis and Isis, had formerly been men; yet no one was ignorant they had been. Their effigies, represented with a finger to the mouth, signified (says Varro) the mysterious order to their priests to conceal their mortal origin, since revealing it would by necessary consequence cancel all the veneration paid to them. Since man so much desired to equal himself to God, he would have done better, says Cicero, to draw those divine conditions to himself, and bring them down here below, than to send his corruption and misery up on high. But, to take it as it stands, he has done both, with equal vanity of opinion.

With Serapis, one of the gods the Egyptians forbade anyone, on pain of hanging, to say had formerly been men.

## modern-en · tiberius-sempronius · 69:300

Man cannot be anything but what he is, nor imagine anything beyond the reach of his capacity. "It is greater presumption," says Plutarch, "in mere men to attempt to speak and discourse of the gods and demi-gods, than in a man utterly ignorant of music to deliver an opinion on singing, or in a man who has never seen a camp to dispute about arms and warfare, presuming by some slight conjecture to understand the effects of an art he is wholly a stranger to." Antiquity, I believe, thought to pay a compliment to the divine grandeur, and to add something to it, by likening it to man — investing it with man's faculties, decking it out with his ugly humours and most shameful necessities; offering it our food to eat, presenting it with our dances, mummeries, and farces to amuse it, our clothes to cover it, our houses to live in; coaxing it with the scent of incense and the sound of music, with festoons and nosegays; and to suit it to our vicious passions, flattering its justice with inhuman vengeance, and with the ruin and dissipation of the things it created and preserves. So Tiberius Sempronius burnt the rich spoils and arms he had taken from the enemy in Sardinia, as a sacrifice to Vulcan; Paulus Aemilius did the same with the spoils of Macedonia, to Mars and Minerva; Alexander, on reaching the Indian Ocean, threw several great vessels of gold into the sea in honour of Thetis; and loaded her altars too with the slaughter not only of innocent beasts, but of men, as several nations, ours included, were commonly used to do. I believe there is no nation under the sun that has not done the same:

Who burnt the rich spoils and arms he had gained from the enemy in Sardinia as a sacrifice to Vulcan, Montaigne’s first instance of flattering divine justice with the ruin of the things it made.

## modern-en · zamolxis · 69:303

The Getae held themselves immortal, and considered their death nothing but a journey to their god Zamolxis. Every five years they dispatched one of their number to him, to beg whatever necessities they needed. This envoy was chosen by lot. The manner of dispatching him, after he had been instructed by word of mouth what he was to deliver, was this: three of those present held up javelins, on which the rest threw his body with all their force. If he were wounded in some mortal part and died on the spot, it was taken as a sure sign of divine favour; if he escaped, he was viewed as a wicked, accursed wretch, and another was sent in his place after the same manner. Amestris, mother of Xerxes, when she had grown old, had fourteen young men of the best families of Persia buried alive at once, according to the religion of the country, to gratify some underworld deity. Even today the idols of Temixtitan are cemented with the blood of small children, and the gods take delight in no sacrifice but these pure and infant souls — a justice thirsty for innocent blood:

The god of the Getae, who hold themselves immortal and their death nothing but a journey to him; and, at 73:90, the legislator of the Scythians, who gave out his laws under the name of Vesta. The older edition spells him Xamolxis there.

## modern-en · paulina · 69:345

_Profecto non Deum, quem cogitare non possunt, sed semetipsos pro illo cogitantes, non illum, sed seipsos, non illi, sed sibi comparant._ "Certainly they do not imagine God, whom they cannot imagine; they imagine themselves in his place; they do not compare him, but themselves — not to him, but to themselves." In natural things, effects only partly relate to their causes. What is this to the purpose? His condition is above the order of nature, too elevated, too remote, and too mighty, to allow itself to be bound and fettered by our conclusions. It is not through ourselves that we arrive there; our ways are too low. We are no nearer heaven on top of Mount Cenis than at the bottom of the sea; measure the distance with your astrolabe. They drag God down even to the carnal knowledge of women, so many times, and so many generations. Paulina, the wife of Saturninus, a matron of great reputation at Rome, thinking she lay with the god Serapis, found herself in the arms of a lover of hers, through the pandering of the priests of his temple. Varro, the most subtle and learned of all the Latin authors, in his book on theology, writes that the sexton of Hercules's temple, throwing dice with one hand for himself and with the other for Hercules, played him for a supper and a wench; if he won, at the expense of the offerings; if he lost, at his own. The sexton lost and paid for the supper and the wench. Her name was Laurentina; she saw by night this god in her arms, who furthermore told her that the first man she met the next day should give her a heavenly reward; which turned out to be Taruncius, a rich young man, who took her home to his house, and in time left her his heiress. She, in her turn, thinking to do something pleasing to the god, left the people of Rome as her heirs; and so divine honours were paid to her. As if it were not enough that Plato was originally descended from the gods by a double line, and that he had Neptune as the common father of his race — it was confidently believed at Athens that Aristo, wanting to enjoy the fair Perictione, could not, and was warned by the god Apollo in a dream to leave her unpolluted and untouched until she should first have given birth. These were the father and mother of Plato. How many ridiculous stories there are of like cuckoldings, committed by the gods against poor mortal men! And how many husbands wrongly slandered in favour of the children! In the Mahometan religion, the people's belief furnishes plenty of Merlins — that is, fatherless children, spiritual, divinely conceived in the wombs of virgins, who carry names that signify as much in their language.

## modern-en · nausiphanes · 69:327

Furthermore, how many things are there in our own experience that contradict the fine rules we have cut out for and laid down to nature? And yet we undertake to draw God himself within them! How many things do we call miraculous and contrary to nature? Every nation and every man does this in proportion to his own ignorance. How many occult properties and quintessences do we daily discover? For us to go "according to nature" is no more than to go "according to our understanding," so far as it can follow and so far as we can see into it; everything beyond that is, forsooth, monstrous and irregular. By that account, all things will be monstrous to the wisest and most understanding men — for human reason has persuaded them that there is no kind of ground or foundation, not so much as to be assured that snow is white, and Anaxagoras held it to be black; whether there is anything, or nothing; whether there is knowledge or ignorance, which Metrodorus of Chios denied man could determine; or whether we live, as Euripides doubts whether the life we live is life, or whether what we call death is not life: [--Greek--] and not without some appearance. For why do we derive the title of being from this instant, which is but a flash in the infinite course of an eternal night, and so short an interruption of our perpetual and natural condition — death possessing all the before and after this moment, and also a good part of the moment itself? Others swear there is no motion at all, like the followers of Melissus, and that nothing stirs. For if there is but one, neither can the spherical motion be of any use to him, nor motion from one place to another, as Plato proves; "that there is neither generation nor corruption in nature." Protagoras says there is nothing in nature but doubt; that a man may equally dispute of all things, even of this — whether a man can equally dispute of all things. Nausiphanes, that of things that seem to be, none is more than it is not; that there is nothing certain but uncertainty. Parmenides, that of what seems, there is not one thing in general; that there is but one thing. Zeno, that one same is not, and that there is nothing; if there were one thing, it would either be in another or in itself; if in another, they are two; if in itself, they are also two — the comprehending and the comprehended. By these doctrines the nature of things is no other than a shadow, either false or empty.

Who held that of things which seem to be, nothing is more than it is not.

## modern-en · erasistratus · 69:412

The Stoics, around and within the heart. Erasistratus, adjoining the membrane of the epicranium. Empedocles, in the blood — as also Moses, which was why he forbade the eating of the blood of beasts, because the soul is seated there. Galen thought every part of the body had its own soul. Strato has placed it between the eyebrows. _Qua facie quidem sit animus, aut ubi habitet, ne quaerendum quidem est:_ "What shape the soul is of, or where it lives, is not even to be asked," says Cicero. I very willingly deliver this author to you in his own words; for why should I alter eloquence itself? Besides, it would be a poor prize to steal the matter of his inventions; they are neither very frequent nor of any great weight, and are sufficiently known. But the reason Chrysippus argues that it is around the heart, as do all the rest of that sect, ought not to be omitted: "It is," he says, "because when we mean to affirm anything we lay our hand upon our breast; and when we pronounce ἐγώ, which means I, we let the lower jaw drop toward the stomach." This passage ought not to pass without a remark on the vanity of so great a man; for besides that these considerations are infinitely slight in themselves, the last is only a proof to the Greeks that they have their souls lodged in that part. No human judgment is so sprightly and watchful that it does not sometimes nod. Why are we afraid to say so? Aristotle, an excrement drawn from the nourishment of the blood, the last to be distributed throughout our limbs. Others, that it is blood, concocted and digested by the heat of the genitals — which they argue from the fact that in excessive exertion a man passes pure blood; here there seems to be more likelihood, if one could draw any appearance out of so infinite a confusion. Now to get this seed to do its work, how many contrary opinions do they put forward? Aristotle and Democritus are of the opinion that women have no sperm, and that what they shed is only a sweat distilled by heat and pleasure and movement, which contributes nothing to generation. Galen, on the contrary, and his followers, believe that without the meeting of seeds there can be no generation. Here are the physicians, the philosophers, the lawyers, and the divines, all by the ears with our wives over the dispute: "How long do women carry their fruit?" And I, for my part, on the example of myself, side with those who maintain that a woman goes eleven months with child. The world is built on this experience. There is no woman so commonplace that she cannot give her opinion on all these controversies; and still we cannot agree.

I make use of this public conviction." Now the weakness of human arguments on this subject is particularly manifest in the fabulous details they have added on as consequences of this opinion, to work out what sort of condition this immortality of ours might be. Pythagoras himself said he remembered having been Aethalides, then Euphorbus, then Hermotimus, and finally had passed from Pyrrhus into Pythagoras, with a memory of himself going back two hundred and six years. Man cannot be anything but what he is, nor imagine anything beyond the reach of his capacity. Antiquity, I believe, thought to pay a compliment to the divine grandeur, and to add something to it, by likening it to man — investing it with man's faculties, decking it out with his ugly humours and most shameful necessities; offering it our food to eat, presenting it with our dances, mummeries, and farces to amuse it, our clothes to cover it, our houses to live in; coaxing it with the scent of incense and the sound of music, with festoons and nosegays; and to suit it to our vicious passions, flattering its justice with inhuman vengeance, and with the ruin and dissipation of the things it created and preserves. So Tiberius Sempronius burnt the rich spoils and arms he had taken from the enemy in Sardinia, as a sacrifice to Vulcan; Paulus Aemilius did the same with the spoils of Macedonia, to Mars and Minerva; Alexander, on reaching the Indian Ocean, threw several great vessels of gold into the sea in honour of Thetis; and loaded her altars too with the slaughter not only of innocent beasts, but of men, as several nations, ours included, were commonly used to do. ## modern-en · tethys · 69:656

We have no communication with being, because all human nature is always in the middle, between being born and dying, giving only an obscure appearance and shadow, a weak and uncertain opinion of itself. And if perhaps you fix your thought on trying to apprehend your own being, it will be like grasping water — for the harder you clench your hand to squeeze and hold what is by its own nature flowing, the more you lose of what you would grasp and hold. So, since all things are subject to pass from one change to another, reason — which looks there for a real substance — finds itself deceived, unable to lay hold of anything that subsists and remains; for everything is either entering into being and has not yet arrived there, or is beginning to die before it is born. Plato said that bodies never had any existence, only birth — conceiving that Homer had made Ocean and Tethys father and mother of the gods, to show us that all things are in perpetual fluctuation, motion, and variation; the opinion, as he says, of all the philosophers before his time, except Parmenides alone, who would not allow things to have motion, and on whose power he sets a great value. Pythagoras held that all matter was flowing and unstable; the Stoics, that there is no present time, and that what we call so is nothing but the juncture and meeting of the future and the past; Heraclitus, that no man ever entered twice into the same river; Epicharmus, that he who borrowed money an hour ago no longer owes it now; and that he who was invited last night to come to dinner today comes nevertheless uninvited, since they are no longer the same men, but have become others; and that no mortal substance could be found twice in the same condition — for by the suddenness and quickness of the change, it disperses one moment and reunites the next; it comes and goes in such a way that what begins to be born never arrives at the perfection of being, since that birth is never finished and never stops, as being at an end, but is always shifting and changing from one seed to another. As human seed is first made, in the mother's womb, into a formless embryo; then delivered as a suckling infant; then becomes a boy, then a youth, then a man, and finally a decrepit old man — so that each successive age and generation is always destroying and spoiling the one before:

Whom Homer made, with the Ocean, father and mother of the gods — Plato’s evidence, in Montaigne’s report of him, that bodies never had any existence but only birth, and that all things are in perpetual fluctuation, motion and variation. The older edition prints her as Thetis, which is the sea-goddess’s name and not hers.

How many occult properties and quintessences do we daily discover? For us to go "according to nature" is no more than to go "according to our understanding," so far as it can follow and so far as we can see into it; everything beyond that is, forsooth, monstrous and irregular. By that account, all things will be monstrous to the wisest and most understanding men — for human reason has persuaded them that there is no kind of ground or foundation, not so much as to be assured that snow is white, and Anaxagoras held it to be black; whether there is anything, or nothing; whether there is knowledge or ignorance, which Metrodorus of Chios denied man could determine; or whether we live, as Euripides doubts whether the life we live is life, or whether what we call death is not life: [--Greek--] and not without some appearance. For why do we derive the title of being from this instant, which is but a flash in the infinite course of an eternal night, and so short an interruption of our perpetual and natural condition — death possessing all the before and after this moment, and also a good part of the moment itself? Others swear there is no motion at all, like the followers of Melissus, and that nothing stirs. For if there is but one, neither can the spherical motion be of any use to him, nor motion from one place to another, as Plato proves; "that there is neither generation nor corruption in nature." Protagoras says there is nothing in nature but doubt; that a man may equally dispute of all things, even of this — whether a man can equally dispute of all things. Nausiphanes, that of things that seem to be, none is more than it is not; that there is nothing certain but uncertainty. Zeno, that one same is not, and that there is nothing; if there were one thing, it would either be in another or in itself; if in another, they are two; if in itself, they are also two — the comprehending and the comprehended. By these doctrines the nature of things is no other than a shadow, either false or empty.

Xenophon reports a similar perplexity in Socrates's teaching: at one point men are not to inquire into the form of God, then a moment later he makes him hold that the sun is God, and the soul God; that there is only one God, and then that there are many. But if Numa attempted to model his people's devotion on this plan — to tie them to a purely mental religion, with no fixed object and no material mixture — he undertook a useless thing. The human mind could never bear up, floating in such an infinity of formless thoughts. Some definite image must be presented to it after its own model. The divine majesty has, in a sense, allowed himself to be circumscribed in bodily limits for our benefit. His supernatural and heavenly sacraments wear the signs of our earthly condition; his worship goes by perceptible offices and words — for it is man who believes and prays. Inside him are other gods — the sea, the earth, the stars — who entertain one another with a harmonious perpetual agitation, a divine dance, sometimes meeting, sometimes drawing apart; concealing and revealing themselves; changing their order, now in front, now behind. Heraclitus was positive that the world was made of fire, and was destined by fate one day to be set ablaze and consumed, and then renewed again. And Apuleius says of men: _Sigillatim mortales, cunctim perpetui._ "In particular they are mortal; taken altogether, eternal." Alexander wrote to his mother an account drawn by an Egyptian priest from their monuments, testifying to the infinite antiquity of that nation and embracing the birth and progress of other countries. Cicero and Diodorus say that in their time the Chaldaeans kept a register of four hundred thousand years and more. Aristotle, Pliny, and others say that Zoroaster flourished six thousand years before Plato's time. Plato says the people of the city of Sais have written records going back eight thousand years, and that the city of Athens was built a thousand years before Sais. Epicurus, that at the same time things are here in the posture we see them, they are the same and arranged in the same way in several other worlds — which he would have asserted with even greater assurance had he seen the resemblance and concordance of the newly discovered world of the West Indies with ours, present and past, in so many odd particulars.

Legislator of the Bactrians and Persians, who gave his laws the authority of the God Oromazis as Numa gave his the patronage of Egeria; and whom Aristotle, Pliny and others say flourished six thousand years before Plato’s time.

## modern-en · lucius-domitius · 70:28

In the civil wars of Caesar, Lucius Domitius, captured in the Abruzzi, having poisoned himself, afterwards repented. In our own time it has happened that a certain person, resolved to die, did not strike deep enough at the first thrust — the sensibility of the flesh resisting his arm — and gave himself two or three more wounds, but could never bring himself to push it home. While Plautius Silvanus was on trial, Urgulania, his grandmother, sent him a dagger with which, being unable to kill himself, he had his servants cut his veins. Albucilla, in Tiberius's time, having, to kill himself, struck with too much tenderness, gave his adversaries the opportunity to imprison and put him to death in their own way. And that great leader Demosthenes, after his rout in Sicily, did the same; and C. Fimbria, having struck himself too feebly, begged his servant to finish him off. On the contrary, Ostorius, who could not use his own arm, disdained to employ his servant's for anything but to hold the dagger straight and firm, while he, bringing his throat to it, ran himself through. It is, in truth, a morsel to be swallowed without chewing, unless one is thoroughly resolved. And yet the emperor Hadrian made his physician mark and circle on his breast the mortal place where he was to stab the man to whom he had given orders to kill him. For this reason it was that Caesar, when asked what death he thought most desirable, answered, "The least premeditated and the shortest." If Caesar dared say it, it is no cowardice in me to believe it. "A short death," says Pliny, "is the sovereign good fortune of human life." People do not much care to recognise it. No one can be said to be resolute for death who fears to face it and cannot meet it with his eyes open. Those whom we see, in their criminal punishments, running to their death, hastening and pressing for their execution, do not do so out of resolution, but because they will not give themselves leisure to consider it; it is not being dead that troubles them, but dying:

Taken in the Abruzzi in Caesar’s civil wars, who poisoned himself upon it and afterwards repented.

## modern-en · pomponius-atticus · 70:33

That Pomponius Atticus, to whom Cicero writes so often, being sick, had Agrippa, his son-in-law, and two or three more of his friends called to him and told them that, having found all the means tried for his recovery to be in vain, and that all he did to prolong his life prolonged and increased his pain, he was resolved to put an end to both; he asked them to approve of his determination, or at least not to waste their labour in trying to dissuade him. Now, having chosen to destroy himself by abstinence, his disease was thereby cured; the remedy he had taken to kill himself restored him to health. His physicians and friends, rejoicing at so happy an outcome and coming to congratulate him, found themselves very much deceived — it being impossible for them to make him alter his purpose. He told them that since he must one day die, and was now so far along the road, he would save himself the labour of beginning again another time. This man, having considered death at leisure, was not only not discouraged at its approach, but actively sought it; for being content that he had entered the combat, he made it a point of bravery to see the end of it. It is far beyond not fearing death to taste and relish it.

Cicero’s correspondent, who being sick called Agrippa his son-in-law and two or three friends to tell them that since every means practised for his recovery was in vain, and all he did to prolong his life prolonged his pain, he had resolved to put an end to both. Having chosen abstinence as the means, he was cured by it — and refused to alter his purpose, saying that as he must one day die, and was now so far on his way, he would save himself the labour of beginning another time.

## modern-en · tullius-marcellinus · 70:35

Tullius Marcellinus, a young Roman, having a mind to anticipate the hour of his fate, to be rid of a disease that troubled him more than he was willing to endure (though his physicians had assured him of a certain — if not immediate — cure), called a council of his friends to deliberate about it. Of these, some — out of unmanliness — gave him the counsel they would have taken themselves; others, out of flattery, gave him the counsel they thought he would most like; but a Stoic said this to him: "Do not concern yourself, Marcellinus, as if you were deliberating about a matter of importance; it is no great matter to live — your servants and the beasts live; but it is a great thing to die handsomely, wisely, and firmly. Just think how long you have been doing the same things: eat, drink, sleep; drink, sleep, eat. We endlessly wheel in the same circle. Not only intolerable accidents, but even satiety of living, can incline a man to want to die." Marcellinus did not need a man to advise, but a man to help. His servants were afraid to meddle in the business; but this philosopher made them understand that domestics fall under suspicion even when it is in doubt whether the master's death was voluntary or not, and that it would be as bad an example to hinder him as to kill him, for —

A young man of Rome who had a mind to anticipate the hour of his destiny, to be rid of a disease that troubled him more than he was willing to endure, though his physicians assured him of a certain cure. He called a council of friends; some advised out of unmanliness, some out of flattery, and a Stoic told him it was no great matter to live, since his servants and his beasts lived, but a great thing to die handsomely, wisely and firmly. He divided a sum of money among his servants, forsook all nourishment, and on the third day, having caused himself to be sprinkled with warm water, fainted by degrees and not without some kind of pleasure, as he declared himself.

## modern-en · sextus-peduceus · 73:18

If this were true, men need only be virtuous in public; we would have no further reason to keep the operations of the soul — the true seat of virtue — regular and in order, except insofar as they come to the knowledge of others. Is it then a matter only of slyly and circumspectly doing wrong? "If you knew," says Carneades, "of a serpent lurking in a place where, with no warning, someone is about to sit down, by whose death you stood to gain, you do wrong if you do not warn him of the danger; and so much the more because the act would be known to no one but you." If we do not take the rule of right-doing from ourselves, if impunity passes with us for justice, to how many kinds of wickedness will we abandon ourselves every day? I do not find what Sextus Peduceus did — faithfully returning the treasure that C. Plotius had committed to his sole secrecy and trust (a thing I have often done myself) — so very commendable; I should have thought doing otherwise an execrable baseness. And I think it useful in our day to recall the example of P. Sextilius Rufus, whom Cicero accuses of having entered upon an inheritance against his conscience, though not against the law — indeed by the law's own determination; and of M. Crassus and Hortensius, who, because of their authority and power, were called in by a stranger to share in a forged will (so that he could secure his own part), and were content not to have a hand in the forgery while not refusing to take their share. Safe enough, if they could shelter themselves from accusations, witnesses, and the law's notice:

Who faithfully restored the treasure C. Plotius had committed to his sole secrecy and trust — which Montaigne says he does not find so commendable, having often done it himself, as he would think it an execrable baseness to have done otherwise.

It was perhaps for this reason that Timon, mocking him, called him the great manufacturer of miracles. Since men, by their inadequacy, cannot pay themselves enough in real coin, let counterfeit be added on top. It is a method all legislators have used; there is no government that does not have some mixture either of ceremonial pomp or of false belief, serving as a curb to keep the people in their duty. That is why most of them have fabulous origins, enriched with supernatural mysteries — and why bastard religions have gained credit and been countenanced by men of understanding. It is why Numa and Sertorius, to give their men a better opinion of them, fed them this foolery: one claimed that the nymph Egeria, the other that his white hind, brought him all his counsels from the gods. And every government has a god at the head of it — the others falsely, that one truly, which Moses set over the Jews at their departure out of Egypt. On the Memoirs of Monsieur du Bellay I have this: "It is always pleasant to read things written by those who have experienced how they should be conducted; but it cannot be denied that there is a manifest falling-off in these two lords from the freedom and liberty of writing that shine in the earlier historians — such as the Sieur de Joinville, the familiar companion of St Louis; Eginhard, chancellor to Charlemagne; and, more recently, Philippe de Commines. What we have here is rather an apology for King Francis, against the Emperor Charles V, than history. I will not believe that they falsified anything as to matter of fact; but they make a common practice of twisting the judgment of events, often against reason, to our advantage, and of leaving out whatever is ticklish to handle in their master's life — witness the affairs of Messieurs de Montmorency and de Biron, which are omitted here; even the very name of Madame d'Étampes is not to be found. Secret actions a historian may keep quiet; but to pass over in silence what all the world knows, and things that have drawn after them public and momentous consequences, is an inexcusable defect. In short, whoever wants a thorough knowledge of King Francis and the events of his reign, let him seek it elsewhere, if my advice prevails. The only profit one can reap from these Memoirs is in the particular accounts of the battles and other exploits of war in which these gentlemen were personally engaged; in some words and private actions of the princes of their time; and in the treaties and negotiations carried out by the Seigneur de Langey, where there are things everywhere worth knowing, and discourses above the common strain."

St Louis’s familiar companion, and with Eginhard and Philip de Commines one of the elder historians Montaigne trusts. ## modern-en · xenocrates · 69:268

Xenophon reports a similar perplexity in Socrates's teaching: at one point men are not to inquire into the form of God, then a moment later he makes him hold that the sun is God, and the soul God; that there is only one God, and then that there are many. Speusippus, Plato's nephew, makes God a certain power that governs all things, and says he has a soul. Aristotle says at one time it is the spirit, at another the world; at one time he gives the world another master, at another he makes God the heat of heaven. Xenocrates makes eight: five named among the planets; a sixth composed of all the fixed stars as so many members; the seventh and eighth, the sun and moon. Heraclides Ponticus does nothing but float between opinions, finally stripping God of sense and making him shift from one form to another, until in the end he calls him heaven and earth. Theophrastus wanders in the same indecision among his fancies, attributing the superintendence of the world now to understanding, now to heaven, now to the stars. Strato says it is nature, having the power of generation, increase, and diminution, without form or sentience. Zeno says it is the law of nature, commanding good and forbidding evil — which law is an animal; and he sets aside the customary gods, Jupiter, Juno, Vesta. Diogenes of Apollonia, that it is air. Xenophanes makes God round, seeing and hearing, not breathing, and having nothing in common with human nature. Aristo thinks the form of God incomprehensible, strips him of sense, and does not know whether he is an animal or something else. Cleanthes at one time supposes it to be reason, at another the world, at another the soul of nature, at another the supreme heat rolling and surrounding all. Perseus, Zeno's disciple, was of the opinion that men have given the title of god to those who have been useful and added some notable advantage to human life — even to useful things themselves. Chrysippus made a confused heap of all the preceding theories, and counted, among a thousand forms of gods he invents, men who have been deified. Diagoras and Theodorus flatly denied that there were any gods at all. Epicurus makes the gods shining, transparent, and air-permeable, lodged as between two forts, between two worlds, safe from blows, clothed in human shape and with members like ours — members that serve them no purpose:

Plato’s successor at the Academy, who makes eight gods — five named among the planets, a sixth composed of all the fixed stars as of so many members, the seventh and eighth the sun and moon — and who with the Egyptians makes the soul a mobile number; and whose lecture, walked into by chance, reformed the debauched Polemon on the spot. The older edition prints him Zenocrates in the Apology, on the same misprint as Zenophanes for Xenophanes.

I remember, then, that from my infancy I was observed to carry myself in a way, I don't know quite how, that smacked of pride and arrogance. Let me say by the way that it is not unreasonable to suppose we have qualities and inclinations so much our own, so deeply rooted in us, that we have no way of feeling and recognising them; and that the body keeps a certain bent from such natural inclinations without our knowledge or consent. It was an affectation of a piece with his beauty that made Alexander carry his head on one side, and made Alcibiades lisp; Julius Caesar scratched his head with one finger, which is the trick of a man full of worrying thoughts; and Cicero, as I recall, used to wrinkle his nose, the sign of a man given to mocking. Such tics may take hold in us without our noticing. There are other, artificial ones I won't get into — bows and salutations, by which men acquire (often undeservedly) the reputation of being humble and courteous; one can be humble out of pride. I am prodigal enough with my hat, especially in summer, and never receive a salute without returning it, from people of any rank, unless they are in my own service. I should make it a request to some princes I know that they be more sparing of that ceremony, and bestow it where it is more due, for being so indiscriminately conferred on everyone, it is thrown away to no purpose; if it is given without respect of persons, it loses its effect. Among irregular forms of bearing, let us not forget that haughty one of the Emperor Constantius, who always in public held his head upright and stiff, without bending or turning to either side, not even to look at those who saluted him from one side; planting his body in a rigid, motionless posture, not letting it yield to the motion of his coach, not daring even to spit, blow his nose, or wipe his face in front of others. I don't know whether the gestures observed in me belonged to this first category, or whether I really had some hidden tendency to this vice, as may well have been the case; I cannot be held accountable for the motions of the body. But as to the motions of the soul, I must confess here what I think of the matter.

Who always in public held his head upright and stiff, without bending or turning to either side, not so much as to look on those who saluted him — Montaigne’s instance of a haughty irregularity of deportment. Also Julian the Apostate’s predecessor, against whose party Julian was severe at the beginning of his reign.

## modern-en · amafanius · 74:26

They abandon me throughout; all I write is rough, polish and beauty are lacking; I cannot set things off to advantage; my handling adds nothing to the material — so my material had better be forceful, very full, and have a lustre of its own. If I pick subjects that are popular and lively, it is to follow my own bent, since I do not affect a solemn, ceremonious wisdom as the world does, and to keep myself more sprightly — not my style more loose, which would rather have things grave and severe (at least if I may call "style" what is in fact an unformed and irregular way of speaking, a popular jargon, a procedure without definition, division, or conclusion, perplexed like that of Amafanius and Rabirius). I can neither please, nor delight, nor even tickle my readers; the best story in the world is spoiled by my handling and goes flat. I can only speak in rough earnest, and am entirely lacking that easy facility I observe in many of my acquaintances, of entertaining the first comer and keeping a whole company going, or holding a prince's ear with all kinds of talk without tiring themselves out. They never lack matter, thanks to the gift and grace they have of seizing on the first thing that comes up and adjusting it to the humour and capacity of the people they are with. Princes are not much fond of solid discourse, and I am not fond of telling stories. The first and easiest reasons, which are usually those best received, I do not know how to deploy: I am a bad orator for the common sort. I tend to say on every topic the extremest thing I know. Cicero thinks that in treatises of philosophy the opening is the hardest part; if that is true, I am wise to stick to the conclusion. And yet one ought to know how to tune the string to every note, and the highest is the one least often touched. There is at least as much skill in raising up an empty subject as in carrying a weighty one. A man must sometimes handle things superficially, sometimes push them home. I know perfectly well that most people stay at this lower level because they cannot conceive of things otherwise than through this outer bark; but I also know that the greatest masters — Xenophon and Plato — are often seen stooping to this low and popular manner of speaking and treating of things, but holding it up with graces that never fail them.

With Rabirius, the pattern of the inform and irregular way of speaking Montaigne owns to: a popular jargon, proceeding without definition, division or conclusion.

My library, which is a fine one as village libraries go, is in a corner of my house. If anything comes into my head that I want to look up or write down, I am afraid I shall forget it just walking across the courtyard, and have to commit it to someone else's memory. If, in speaking, I venture the least bit from my subject, I am infallibly lost — which is why I keep myself strictly on the point in discourse. I am forced to call the men who serve me either by the names of their offices or their birthplace, for names are very hard for me to remember. I can tell, perhaps, that there are three syllables, that it has a harsh sound, that it begins or ends with a particular letter; but that is all. And if I lived long, I do not doubt I should forget my own name, as some others have done. Messala Corvinus was two years without any trace of memory, and the same is said of Georgius Trapezuntius. The most remarkable men, as I have judged from outward appearance (for to judge them according to my own method, I should have to penetrate a great deal deeper), for soldiers and military leadership, were the Duc de Guise, who died at Orléans, and the late Marshal Strozzi; and for men of great ability and uncommon virtue, Olivier and de l'Hospital, Chancellors of France. Poetry, in my opinion, has also flourished in this age of ours; we have plenty of very good craftsmen at the trade — D'Aurat, Beza, Buchanan, L'Hospital, Mondoré, Turnèbe. As to the French poets, I believe they have raised their art to the highest point it can ever reach; and in those parts of it where Ronsard and Du Bellay excel, I find them little inferior to ancient perfection. Adrien Turnèbe knew more, and knew what he did know better, than any man of his time, or long before him. The lives of the late Duke of Alva and of our Constable de Montmorency were both great and noble, and had many rare resemblances of fortune. But the beauty and glory of the death of the latter, in sight of Paris and of his king, in their service, against his nearest relations, at the head of an army victorious by his conduct, and by a sudden stroke, in such extreme old age — it deserves, I think, to be recorded among the most remarkable events of our time. As also the steady goodness, sweetness of manners, and conscientious ease of Monsieur de la Noue, in so great an injustice of armed parties (the true school of treason, inhumanity, and robbery) — where he always kept up the reputation of a great and experienced captain.

## modern-en · metellus-macedonicus · 74:91

By that standard I would have been great and rare, just as I find myself today small and common by the standard of certain past ages, when, if no other better qualities went along with them, it was ordinary and common to see a man moderate in his vengeance, gentle in resenting injuries, religious of his word, neither double nor pliant, not adjusting his faith to others' wishes or the turn of the times. I would rather see all affairs go to wreck and ruin than break my faith to save them. As for this new virtue of feigning and dissimulation, now in such credit, I mortally hate it; and of all vices I find none that shows so much baseness and meanness of spirit. It is a cowardly and servile humour to hide and disguise oneself under a mask, and not to dare to show oneself as one is. By this our servants are trained up in treachery: brought up to say what is not true, they make no conscience of a lie. A noble heart should not belie its own thoughts; it should let itself be seen within; all there is good, or at least human. Aristotle reckons it the office of magnanimity to love and hate openly, professedly; to judge and speak with all freedom; and not to value the approval or disapproval of others against the truth. Apollonius said that lying was for slaves, and truth-speaking for free men: it is the chief and fundamental part of virtue; we must love it for itself. The man who speaks truth because he is bound to, and because it serves him, and who is not afraid to lie when it matters to nobody, is not sufficiently true. My soul naturally abhors lying, and hates the very thought of it. I feel an inward shame and a sharp remorse if a lie ever escapes me — as it sometimes does, when I am surprised by occasions that give me no time to prepare. A man should not always tell everything, for that would be folly; but what a man says should be what he thinks, otherwise it is knavery. I do not understand what advantage men think they get from constant counterfeiting and dissimulating, if not never to be believed even when they speak the truth. It may pass with people once or twice; but to make a profession of concealing one's thought, and to brag, as some of our princes have done, that they would burn their shirts if they knew their true intentions (a saying of the old Metellus of Macedon), or that those who do not know how to dissemble do not know how to rule — that is to warn everyone who has dealings with them that everything they say is nothing but lying and deceit:

Author of the saying some of our princes have bragged of since: that they would burn their shirts if they knew their true intentions. The older edition prints him Metellius.

## modern-en · soliman · 74:95

Those of our time who, in formulating the duty of a prince, have considered only the good of his affairs and have preferred that to the care of his faith and conscience, might have something to say to a prince whose affairs fortune had so placed that he could establish them forever by once breaking his word; but it does not work that way: they often buy in the same market; they make more than one peace and enter into more than one treaty in their lives. Gain tempts the first breach of faith, and almost always presents itself, as in all other bad acts — sacrileges, murders, rebellions, treasons — being undertaken for some kind of advantage. But this first gain has infinite ill consequences, throwing the prince out of all correspondence and negotiation by this example of infidelity. Soliman, of the Ottoman race — a race not very particular about keeping their words or compacts — when, in my infancy, he landed his army at Otranto, hearing that Mercurino de' Gattinara and the inhabitants of Castro were being held prisoner after having surrendered the place contrary to the articles of their capitulation, sent orders that they should be released, saying that, since he had other great enterprises in hand in those parts, the disloyalty, though it carried a show of present utility, would in future bring on him a disrepute and distrust of infinite prejudice.

Of the Ottoman race, a race not very solicitous of keeping their words or compacts — and yet, being told that Mercurino de’ Gattinara and the inhabitants of Castro were held prisoner against the articles of their capitulation, he took it ill. Also the Soliman who said that victories obtained without the master are never complete. The modern edition writes him Suleiman.

## modern-en · ulpian · 74:149

But how it comes about I do not know, and yet it is certainly so: there is as much vanity and weakness of judgment in those who profess the greatest abilities, who take on learned callings and bookish employments, as in any other kind of men. Either because more is required and expected of them, and common defects are not excusable in them, or because the opinion they have of their own learning makes them bolder to expose and lay themselves too open, by which they lose and betray themselves. As a craftsman more clearly shows his lack of skill in a rich material he is working with, if he disgraces the work by bad handling and contrary to the rules required, than in some material of less value; and people are more displeased by a disproportion in a statue of gold than in one of plaster. So do these men when they advance things that in themselves and in their place would be good — but they use them without discrimination, honouring the memories at the expense of their understandings, and making themselves ridiculous by honouring Cicero, Galen, Ulpian, and St Jerome all in the same way.

One of the four names Montaigne says the pedants honour alike, at the expense of their own understandings — with Cicero, Galen and St Jerome.

## modern-en · marshal-strozzi · 74:157

The most remarkable men, as I have judged from outward appearance (for to judge them according to my own method, I should have to penetrate a great deal deeper), for soldiers and military leadership, were the Duc de Guise, who died at Orléans, and the late Marshal Strozzi; and for men of great ability and uncommon virtue, Olivier and de l'Hospital, Chancellors of France. Poetry, in my opinion, has also flourished in this age of ours; we have plenty of very good craftsmen at the trade — D'Aurat, Beza, Buchanan, L'Hospital, Mondoré, Turnèbe. As to the French poets, I believe they have raised their art to the highest point it can ever reach; and in those parts of it where Ronsard and Du Bellay excel, I find them little inferior to ancient perfection. Adrien Turnèbe knew more, and knew what he did know better, than any man of his time, or long before him. The lives of the late Duke of Alva and of our Constable de Montmorency were both great and noble, and had many rare resemblances of fortune. But the beauty and glory of the death of the latter, in sight of Paris and of his king, in their service, against his nearest relations, at the head of an army victorious by his conduct, and by a sudden stroke, in such extreme old age — it deserves, I think, to be recorded among the most remarkable events of our time. As also the steady goodness, sweetness of manners, and conscientious ease of Monsieur de la Noue, in so great an injustice of armed parties (the true school of treason, inhumanity, and robbery) — where he always kept up the reputation of a great and experienced captain.

With the Duc de Guise who died at Orleans, the most remarkable man Montaigne judged by outward appearance for soldiership and military conduct.

## modern-en · salvianus · 75:16

imprint themselves better on paper than on flesh. What if I listen a little more attentively than usual to books, watching whether I can pilfer anything that might adorn or support my own? I have not in the least studied to make a book; but I have in some way studied because I had made it — if it is studying to scratch and pinch now one author and then another, either by the head or by the foot, not with any intention of forming opinions from them, but to assist, support, and fortify those I have already embraced. But whom shall we believe in the report he makes of himself, in so corrupt an age — considering that there are so few, if any, whom we can believe when speaking of others, where there is less interest in lying? The first thing done in the corruption of manners is the banishing of truth; for, as Pindar says, to be true is the beginning of a great virtue, and the first article that Plato requires in the governor of his Republic. The truth of these days is not what really is, but what every man persuades another man to believe; just as we give the name of money not only to genuine coin, but to false coin too, if it will pass. Our nation has long been reproached with this vice; for Salvianus of Marseilles, who lived in the time of the Emperor Valentinian, says that lying and perjury are with the French not a vice but a way of speaking. Anyone wishing to push this testimony further might say that today it is a virtue with them; men form and fashion themselves to it as to an exercise of honour, for dissimulation is one of the most notable qualities of this age.

Of Marseilles, who lived in the time of the Emperor Valentinian, and says that lying and forswearing themselves is with the French not a vice but a way of speaking.

## modern-en · emperor-tacitus · 76:1

It is certain that in those first times, when our religion began to gain authority with the laws, zeal armed many against all kinds of pagan books, by which the learned suffered an excessive great loss — a disorder that I think did more damage to letters than all the flames of the barbarians. Cornelius Tacitus is very good testimony to this: for although the Emperor Tacitus, his kinsman, had by express order furnished all the libraries in the world with it, nevertheless one entire copy could not escape the searching examination of those who wanted to abolish it for the sake of only five or six idle clauses contrary to our belief.

Cornelius Tacitus’s kinsman, who by express order furnished all the libraries in the world with the history — and not one entire copy escaped those who wanted it abolished for five or six idle clauses contrary to our belief. Not the historian.

## modern-en · maris · 76:5

We have two good historians who were eye-witnesses of his actions. One of them, Marcellinus, in several places of his history sharply reproves an edict of his that forbade all Christian rhetoricians and grammarians to keep school or to teach, and says he wishes that act of his had been buried in silence: it is probable that if he had done anything more severe against us, he, fond as he was of our party, would not have passed it over in silence. He was indeed sharp against us, but not a cruel enemy; for our own people tell this story of him: that one day, walking through the city of Chalcedon, Maris, bishop of the place, was bold enough to tell him that he was impious and an enemy to Christ — at which, they say, he was moved only to reply, "Go, poor wretch, and lament the loss of your eyes"; to which the bishop replied, "I thank Jesus Christ for taking away my sight, that I may not see your impudent face" — affecting in that, they say, a philosophical patience. But this action of his bears no comparison with the cruelty he is said to have practised on us. "He was," says Eutropius, my other witness, "an enemy to Christianity, but without putting his hand to blood." And to return to his justice, there is nothing he can be accused of in that, except the severity he exercised in the beginning of his reign against those who had followed the party of Constantius, his predecessor. As for his sobriety, he always lived a soldier's life, and observed a diet and routine like one who is preparing and steeling himself for the austerities of war. His vigilance was such that he divided the night into three or four parts, the least of which was given to sleep; the rest was spent either in visiting the state of his army and guards in person, or in study; for among other rare qualities he was very excellent in every kind of learning. It is said of Alexander the Great that in bed, for fear lest sleep should divert him from his thoughts and studies, he always had a basin set beside his bed, and held out one hand with a ball of copper in it, so that, as he started to fall asleep and his fingers let go, the ball falling into the basin would wake him. But the other had his soul so bent upon what he had a mind to do, and was so little troubled by fumes thanks to his unusual abstinence, that he had no need of any such invention. As to his military experience, he was excellent in all the qualities of a great captain, as he was likely to be, having spent almost all his life in a continual exercise of war, and most of that time with us in France against the Germans and Franks: we hardly read of any man who saw more dangers, or who gave more frequent proofs of his personal valour.

Bishop of Chalcedon, in the story Montaigne’s own people tell of Julian the Apostate.

## modern-en · bajazet-ii · 78:1

Anyone who wants to argue that it is better for a prince to conduct his wars through others rather than in his own person will easily find examples from fortune of lieutenants who have brought great enterprises to a happy end, and others whose master's presence did more harm than good. But no virtuous and valiant prince can stomach so dishonourable a counsel. Under the pretext of preserving his head for the happiness of his kingdom, like the statue of a saint, they degrade him and pronounce him incapable of the office he holds, which is military through and through. I know one prince who would rather be beaten than sleep while another fights for him, and who never hears without a touch of jealousy of any brave deed done by his own officers in his absence. And Suleiman I said, with very good reason in my view, that victories obtained without the master are never complete. He might have said more — that the master should blush with shame to claim any share of the honour, having contributed nothing to the work but his voice and his thought. Not even those, considering that in such work the only direction and command that earn honour are the ones given on the spot, in the heat of action. No pilot does his job standing still. The princes of the Ottoman house, the foremost in the world for military fortune, have warmly embraced this view, and Bajazet II, along with his son, who broke with it and spent their time on learning and other retired pursuits, struck heavy blows against their empire. Murad III, who now reigns, is following their example and beginning to feel the same effect. Was it not Edward III of England who said this of our Charles V: "There has never been a king who put on his armour so seldom, and yet never a king who gave me so much trouble." He had reason to find it strange, as an effect of chance more than reason. And let those who want to count the kings of Castile and Portugal among the warlike and magnanimous conquerors look for someone other than me to agree — because, from twelve hundred leagues away in their idle quarters, by the conduct of their captains, they made themselves masters of both Indies, of which it remains to be seen whether they would even have had the courage to go and enjoy them in person.

Who with his son swerved from the Ottoman opinion that a prince should lead his own wars, spending their time in science and other retired employments, and gave great blows to their empire. Not the Bajazet of the snow tempest at 48:53.

Moulay Mohammed, king of Fez, who recently defeated Sebastian, king of Portugal, in the battle so famous for the death of three kings and the passing of that great kingdom to the crown of Castile, was extremely sick when the Portuguese entered his territory in arms. From that day on he grew steadily worse, drawing nearer to his end and foreseeing it. Yet no man ever used his remaining strength more vigorously and bravely than he did on that occasion. He felt too weak to undergo the pomp and ceremony of entering his camp, which in their fashion is magnificent, and so resigned that honour to his brother — but this was all of the general's role that he gave up. Everything else of any real use or necessity he carried out with exactness and glory, in his own person, his body stretched on a couch but his judgment and courage upright and firm to his last breath, and in a sense beyond it. He could have worn out his enemy, who had imprudently advanced into his territory, without striking a blow; and it was a very unfortunate circumstance that, for want of a little life or anyone to substitute in the conduct of the war and the affairs of a troubled state, he was driven to seek a doubtful and bloody victory when he already had a surer, better one in hand. Even so, he managed his lingering illness wonderfully, using it to wear out the enemy and to draw them far from the help of their fleet and the ports they held on the African coast, right up to the last day of his life, which he deliberately reserved for this great battle. He arranged his battalions in a circle, surrounding the Portuguese army on every side, and this circle closing in and drawing tight not only hindered the Portuguese in the fight — which was sharp enough thanks to the valour of the young invading king, since they had to present a front in every direction — but also blocked any flight after the defeat, so that, finding every exit held and shut by the enemy, they were forced to bunch up together again:

There is a remarkable relation and correspondence in the universal government of the works of nature, which makes it quite clear that it is neither accidental nor run by several masters. The diseases and conditions of our bodies show up in much the same way in states and governments: kingdoms and republics are founded, flourish, and decay with age as we do. We are subject to a build-up of humours, useless and dangerous — whether of the good ones (for even those the physicians fear; and since we have nothing stable in us, they say that an over-brisk and vigorous state of health must be reduced by art, lest our nature, unable to rest in any fixed condition and having nowhere higher to climb to improve itself, make too sudden and disorderly a retreat — which is why they prescribe purges and bleeding for wrestlers, to take down that overflowing health), or else of bad humours, which is the usual cause of sickness. States are very often sick from the same kind of repletion, and various sorts of purging have commonly been applied. Sometimes a great mass of families is sent out to clear the country, seeking new homes elsewhere and encroaching on others. In this way our ancient Franks came from the deepest part of Germany to seize Gaul and drive out its first inhabitants; in this way the infinite flood of men who came into Italy under Brennus and others was put together; in this way the Goths and Vandals, and also the people who now hold Greece, left their native country to go settle elsewhere with more room. There are scarcely two or three small corners of the world that have not felt the effects of such migrations. The Romans set up their colonies by this means: seeing their city grow immensely populous, they relieved it of the more superfluous people and sent them to inhabit and cultivate lands they had conquered. Sometimes too they kept wars going on purpose against some of their enemies, not only to keep their own men in action, for fear that idleness, the mother of corruption, might bring some worse trouble on them:

Under whose conduct, with others, that infinite deluge of men came into Italy — one of Montaigne’s instances of a state purging its own repletion by sending its excess abroad.

Before the principles Aristotle introduced were in repute, other principles satisfied human reason, as these do us now. What patent do these people have, what particular privilege, that the career of our invention should stop at them, and that the possession of our whole future belief should belong to them? They are no more exempt from being thrust out of doors than their predecessors were. When anyone presses me with a new argument, I ought to think that what I cannot answer, another can. To believe every likely thing that one cannot refute is great simplicity; by that means the entire common run — and we are all common — would have their belief as turnable as a weathercock. Their souls, being so easy to impose on, and offering no resistance, must perforce go on receiving impression after impression, the last each time wiping out the footprints of the one before. He who feels himself weak ought to answer, as is the practice, that he must speak with his counsel, or refer himself to wiser men, from whom he received his instruction. How long has medicine been practised in the world? I dare say he will easily prove this, but I do not think it would be wisdom to risk my life testing his own experience. We are not to believe everyone, the precept says, because everyone can say all things. A man of this profession of novelties and physical reforms told me not long since that all the ancients were notoriously mistaken about the nature and motion of the winds, which he would clearly demonstrate to me if I would give him a hearing. After I had patiently listened to his arguments, which all had every appearance of truth: "Then," I asked, "did those who sailed by Theophrastus go westward when they had their prow toward the east? Did they go sideways or backward?" "That's chance," he answered, "but it remains that they were mistaken." I replied that I would rather follow effects than reason. Now these things often clash with each other; and I have been told that in geometry — which claims to have reached the highest point of certainty of any science — there are inescapable demonstrations that overturn the truth of all experience. Jacques Pelletier told me in my own house that he had found two lines stretching toward each other to meet, which he affirmed could nevertheless never meet, even extended to infinity. And the Pyrrhonians make no other use of their arguments and their reason than to ruin the appearance of experience; and it is a wonder how far the suppleness of our reason has followed them in this attempt to contest the evidence of effects. For they affirm that we do not move, that we do not speak, and that there is neither weight nor heat, with the same force of argument with which we affirm the most likely things. ## modern-en · lyciscus · 84:7

Everyone can see that there is more bravery and disdain in subduing an enemy than in cutting his throat, in making him yield than in putting him to the sword; besides which, the appetite for revenge is more satisfied and pleased when its only aim is to make itself felt. That is why we do not fall on a beast or a stone when they hurt us, because they are incapable of being aware of our revenge; and to kill a man is to save him from the injury and offence we mean to do him. As Bias cried out to a wicked fellow, "I know that sooner or later you will have your reward, but I am afraid I will not be there to see it"; and pitied the Orchomenians because the penitence of Lyciscus for the treason committed against them came at a time when no one remained alive of those who had been hurt by the offence and whom the pleasure of this penitence might have reached. Revenge is to be pitied when the person on whom it is exercised is robbed of any means of suffering under it; for, as the avenger means to look on and enjoy the pleasure of his revenge, so the person he takes revenge on must be a spectator too, in order to be afflicted and to repent. "He will be sorry for it," we say — and because we have given him a pistol shot through the head, do we imagine he will be sorry? On the contrary, if we look closely, we will see that he pulls a face at us as he falls, and is so far from regret that he does not even reproach us; and we do him the kindest service in life, which is to make him die without feeling it, and quickly. We then have to hide and dodge the officers of justice who hunt us, while he is at rest. Killing is good for preventing an offence to come, not for avenging one that is already past, and is more an act of fear than of bravery, of precaution than of courage, of defence than of attack. It is plain that by killing we lose both the true end of revenge and the care of our reputation; we are afraid that, if he lives, he will do us another injury as great as the first. It is not out of animosity toward him but out of concern for yourself that you get rid of him.

Whose penitence for the treason committed against the Orchomenians came at a season when no one remained alive of those the offence had touched — which is why Montaigne pities them.
