## modern-en · mattecoulom · 84:15

I have a domestic interest in this discussion, for my brother, the Sieur de Matecoulom, was at Rome asked by a gentleman he hardly knew, and who was the defendant challenged by another, to be his second; in this duel he found himself paired with a gentleman much better known to him. (I would dearly like an explanation of these rules of honour that so often crash against, and confound, those of reason.) Having dispatched his man and seeing the two principals still on their feet and unhurt, he ran in to disengage his friend. What less could he have done? Should he have stood still, and, if luck had so ordered it, watched the man he had come to defend killed in front of him? What he had done so far did not help the case; the quarrel was still undecided. The courtesy that you can and certainly ought to show your enemy, when you have brought him to a bad pass and have a great advantage over him, I do not see how you can show it when another man's interest is involved, when you are only there as an assistant and the quarrel is not yours; he could be neither just nor courteous at the cost of the man he was there to serve. For this he was released from the prisons of Italy at the prompt and solemn request of our king. Indiscreet nation! We are not satisfied with letting the world know our vices and follies by report alone; we must go to foreign countries to show in person what fools we are. Put three Frenchmen in the deserts of Libya, and they will not live a month together without fighting; so that you would think this travel was deliberately designed to give foreigners the pleasure of our tragedies — and, for the most part, to such as rejoice and laugh at our miseries. We go to Italy to learn fencing, and practise the art at the cost of our lives before we have learned it; though by the rule of discipline we should put theory before practice. We give ourselves away as beginners:

Montaigne’s brother, asked at Rome by a gentleman he hardly knew to be his second in a duel — which Montaigne says he would not have him do again, and which gave him a domestic interest in the question. The modern edition writes him Matecoulon.

## modern-en · duke-of-orleans · 84:14

for in danger any kind of company is naturally consoling. Originally, third persons were called in only to prevent disorder and foul play, and to be witnesses to the outcome of the combat; but now things have gone so far that the witnesses themselves join in. Whoever is invited cannot decently stand by as an idle spectator, on pain of being suspected either of want of affection or of want of courage. Quite apart from the injustice and unworthiness of such a thing — of bringing in another man's strength and valour to defend your honour — I see it as a disadvantage to a brave man who relies on himself alone, to mix his fortune with that of a second. Every man runs danger enough on his own account without taking on the risks of someone else, and has enough to do to trust to his own valour for the defence of his life, without putting something so precious into a third man's hands. For unless it has been expressly agreed in advance to the contrary, it becomes a four-way combat, and if your second is killed, you have two on your hands, with good reason; and as for calling it foul play, it is so, yes — as it is foul play, when fully armed, to attack a man who has only the hilt of a broken sword in his hand, or, while clear and untouched, to attack one who is grievously wounded; but if these are advantages you have gained in the course of fighting, you may use them without reproach. The disparity and inequality are weighed and reckoned only from the condition of the combatants at the start; as for the rest, you must take your chance. Even if alone you had three enemies on you at once, your two companions being killed, you have no more wrong done to you than I would do in a battle by running through a man I saw engaged with one of our own, in just the same kind of advantage. The nature of group fighting is such that, where there is troop against troop — as when our Duke of Orleans challenged Henry, king of England, a hundred against a hundred; three hundred against as many, as the Argives against the Lacedaemonians; three against three, as the Horatii against the Curiatii — the multitude on each side is treated as one single man; the risk is mingled and mixed whenever there is company.

Who challenged the king of England, a hundred against a hundred — Montaigne’s instance that where there is troop against troop the multitude on either side is considered but as one single man. The Essays give him no more than the title.

## modern-en · publius-rutilius-consul · 84:21

Archery contests, tilting, and barriers — mock versions of warlike fighting — were the exercises of our forefathers. This other exercise is less noble in proportion as it serves only a private end; it teaches us to destroy one another against law and justice, and it always produces very bad effects. It is far more worthy and becoming to train ourselves in things that strengthen rather than weaken our state, things that aim at public safety and common glory. The consul Publius Rutilius was the first to teach his soldiers to handle their arms with skill and to join art with valour — not for the purposes of private quarrel, but for war and the contests of the people of Rome, a popular and civic defence. And besides the example of Caesar, who ordered his men to aim chiefly at the faces of Pompey's soldiers in the battle of Pharsalia, a thousand other commanders have thought to invent new forms of weapons and new ways of striking and defending, as the occasion required.

The first who taught the soldiers to handle their arms with skill, and joined art with valour — not for private quarrels but for the wars of the people of Rome. Not the Rutilius of the Itinerarium at 72:43, nor the Rutilius of Tacitus’s Agricola at 74:7.

## modern-en · amycus · 84:22

But just as Philopoemen condemned wrestling, in which he excelled, because the preparations involved in it differed from those that belong to military discipline, to which alone he held that men of honour should give themselves wholly, so it seems to me that this technique to which we accustom our limbs, these twists and motions young men are taught in this new school, are not only useless but actually contrary and harmful to the practice of fighting in battle. Our people also commonly use particular weapons specially designed for the duel, and I have seen it disapproved when a gentleman challenged to fight with rapier and dagger turned up in the equipment of a man-at-arms, or when another took his cloak instead of his dagger. It is worth noting that Laches in Plato, speaking of learning to fence in our manner, says he never knew any great soldier come out of that school, especially among the masters; and indeed, as for them, our own experience says the same. As for the rest, we may at least conclude that they are qualities with no relation or correspondence to each other; and in the education of the children of his republic, Plato bans the art of boxing, introduced by Amycus and Epeius, and that of wrestling, by Antaeus and Cercyon, because they have another end than fitting young men for the service of war, and contribute nothing to it. But I see I have somewhat wandered from my theme.

With Epeius, the introducer of the art of boxing, which Plato interdicts in the education of the children of his government because it has another end than to render youth fit for the service of war.

## modern-en · mauricius · 84:23

The Emperor Mauricius, warned by dreams and various omens that a certain Phocas, an obscure soldier, would kill him, asked his son-in-law Philip who this Phocas was, what his nature, qualities, and manners were like; and as soon as Philip, among other things, told him the man was cowardly and timid, the emperor immediately concluded that he was a murderer and cruel. What is it that makes tyrants so bloody? Only the anxiety for their own safety, and that their faint hearts can find them no other means of securing themselves than by wiping out those who might hurt them, even down to women, for fear of a scratch:

Warned by dreams and prognostics that an obscure soldier called Phocas should kill him, and told by his son-in-law Philip that the man was pusillanimous and fearful — whereupon he concluded at once that he was therefore murderous and cruel.

## modern-en · herodicus · 84:28

Among others condemned by Philip had been one Herodicus, prince of Thessaly; after him, Philip had had both his sons-in-law put to death, each leaving a young son behind. Theoxena and Archo were their two widows. Theoxena, though much courted to do so, could not be persuaded to remarry. Archo married Poris, the leading man among the Aenians, and had a great many children by him, whom, when she died, she left at a very tender age. Theoxena, moved by maternal affection for her nephews so as to have them under her own eyes and in her own care, married Poris. Then suddenly came the king's edict. This brave-spirited mother, suspecting Philip's cruelty and afraid of what the soldiers would do to these charming and tender children, was bold enough to declare that she would rather kill them with her own hands than hand them over. Poris, startled by this protest, promised to spirit them away and take them to Athens, to put them in the care of some faithful friends of his. They took advantage of an annual festival held at Aenia in honour of Aeneas, and went there. After appearing by day at the public ceremonies and the banquet, they slipped at night into a vessel set ready for the purpose, to escape by sea. The wind was contrary, and finding themselves in the morning in sight of the land they had left overnight, and being pursued by the port guards, Poris saw what was happening and did all he could to make the sailors strain to outrun the pursuers. But Theoxena, frantic with love and revenge, in keeping with her earlier resolution, prepared weapons and poison and laid them out in front of the children. "Come, my children," she said, "death is now the only means of your defence and freedom, and shall give the gods an opportunity to exercise their holy justice. These sharp swords and these full cups will open you the way to it; take courage, fear nothing. And you, my son, who are the eldest, take this steel in your hand, that you may die the more bravely." The children, with so powerful a counsellor on one side and the enemy at their throats on the other, all snatched eagerly at whatever was nearest to hand and, half dead, were thrown into the sea. Theoxena, proud of having so gloriously provided for the safety of her children, clasped her arms with great affection round her husband's neck. "Let us, my friend," she said, "follow these boys, and share the same tomb." And so, embraced, they threw themselves headlong into the sea, so that the ship was carried back without its owners into the harbour.

Prince of Thessaly, condemned by Philip, whose two sons were killed after him and whose two widows were Theoxena and Archo.

## modern-en · chalcondylas · 84:31

Chalcondylas, a writer of good credit, in the records he has left of things that happened in his own time and near at hand, tells us, as the most excessive of torments, of one the Emperor Mohammed often practised: cutting men in two across the diaphragm with a single stroke of a scimitar, so that they died two deaths at once. Both parts, he says, were seen to twitch and struggle for a long time after, in very great torment. I do not think there was much suffering in that movement: the torments that look most dreadful are not always the worst to endure, and I find that those other historians report of him to have been done to the Epirot lords are more horrible and cruel, where they were sentenced to be flayed alive piecemeal, in such a malicious way that they remained fifteen days in that misery.

A writer of good credit, in whose records of things that happened near him Montaigne finds the Emperor Mohammed’s way of cutting men in the middle by the diaphragm with one blow of a scimitar, so that they died two deaths at once.

Chief commander of the peasants of Poland, who committed so many mischiefs under the title of the Crusade; defeated and taken by the Vayvode of Transylvania, he was three days bound naked on the rack, and at the end of it made his beloved brother Lucat drink his blood while he looked on, and twenty of his most favoured captains feed upon him.

A young Turkish lord, having performed a notable exploit in his own person within sight of both armies, that of Murad and that of Hunyadi, on the point of joining battle, was asked by Murad what, in such tender and inexperienced years (for this was his first taste of arms), had inspired him with so brave a courage. He replied that his chief tutor in valour had been a hare. "For one day," he said, "out hunting, I came on a hare in her form, and although I had a brace of excellent greyhounds with me, I thought it would be surest to use my bow, since she sat very fair. I shot at her, and shot all forty arrows that I had in my quiver, not only without hurting her, but without even startling her from her form. At last I slipped my dogs after her, but to no more purpose than the shooting had been. From which I understood that she had been kept safe by her destiny, and that neither arrows nor swords can wound without the leave of fate, which we can neither hasten nor put off." This story may serve, in passing, to show how flexible our reason is to all sorts of images.

Whose army stood ready to join battle with Amurath’s when the young Turkish lord made his first sally into arms. The modern edition writes him Hunyadi.

## modern-en · caelius-orator · 88:15

Piso, otherwise a man of very eminent virtue, being angered against a soldier of his because, returning alone from foraging, he could give him no account of where he had left a comrade, took it for granted that he had killed him, and immediately condemned him to death. He had just been put on the gallows when, behold, the wandering comrade arrived — at which the whole army was delighted, and after many embraces between the two friends, the executioner brought the one and the other into Piso's presence, everyone there believing it would be a great pleasure to him too; but it turned out quite otherwise, for through shame and spite, his fury, which had not yet cooled, redoubled, and by a subtlety his passion suddenly suggested to him, he made three guilty men out of having found one innocent and had them all put to death — the first soldier, because sentence had been passed on him; the second, who had lost his way, because he was the cause of his comrade's death; and the executioner, for not having obeyed the order given to him. Anyone who has had to deal with peevish and obstinate women may have experienced what a rage it puts them in to oppose silence and coolness to their fury, and that one disdains to feed their anger. The orator Caelius was wonderfully short-tempered by nature, and to one who supped in his company, a man of gentle and mild conversation, who, so as not to provoke him, approved of and agreed with everything he said, Caelius, unable to bear that his bad mood should waste itself like this without food, said: "For the love of the gods, deny me something, so that we may be two." Women, in the same way, are angry only that others may be angry back, in imitation of the laws of love. Phocion, to a man who interrupted his speech with insulting and very abusive words, made no other reply than silence, giving him full leave and time to vent his spleen; which when he had accordingly done, and the storm had blown over, Phocion went on with his speech where he had left off, without any mention of the interruption. No reply can sting a man like that kind of contempt.

The orator, wonderfully choleric by nature, to whom a supper companion of a soft and gentle conversation contradicted nothing for fear of angering him — until Caelius cried out, contradict me in something, that we may be two. The older edition prints him Celius.

## modern-en · labienus-general · 89:10

There is in this same passage another charge against Plutarch I cannot stomach, where Bodin says that Plutarch sincerely paralleled Romans with Romans and Greeks with Greeks, but not Romans with Greeks: witness, he says, Demosthenes and Cicero, Cato and Aristides, Sulla and Lysander, Marcellus and Pelopidas, Pompey and Agesilaus — and that he favoured the Greeks by giving them such unequal partners. This is really to attack what is best in Plutarch and most worth praising; for in his Parallels (which is the most admirable part of all his work, and the one with which, I think, he was himself most pleased) the fidelity and sincerity of his judgments equal their depth and weight. He is a philosopher who teaches us virtue. Let us see whether we can defend him from this charge of falsity and bias. All I can imagine giving rise to the censure is the great and shining glamour of the Roman names we have in our minds: it does not seem likely to us that Demosthenes could rival the glory of a consul, proconsul, and praetor of that great Republic. But if you consider the truth of the thing, and the men in themselves — which is Plutarch's chief aim — and weigh their characters, their natures, and their parts rather than their fortunes, I think (contrary to Bodin) that Cicero and the elder Cato fall far short of the men they are compared with. For Bodin's purpose I would sooner have picked the younger Cato paired with Phocion: in that couple there would have been a more plausible inequality, in the Roman's favour. As for Marcellus, Sulla, and Pompey, I see well enough that their war-exploits are greater and more full of pomp and glory than those of the Greeks Plutarch matches them with; but the bravest and most virtuous actions, in war as elsewhere, are not always the most renowned. I often see the names of captains darkened by the brilliance of others of less merit — witness Labienus, Ventidius, Telesinus, and a few more. And to take it that way: if I had to complain on the Greek side, could I not say that Camillus was much less comparable to Themistocles, the Gracchi to Agis and Cleomenes, and Numa to Lycurgus? But it is folly to judge in one glance things that have so many faces. When Plutarch compares them, he does not for all that make them equal — and who could more learnedly and honestly have marked their distinctions? Does he set the victories, the feats of arms, the strength of the armies Pompey commanded, and his triumphs against those of Agesilaus? "I do not believe," he says, "that Xenophon himself, were he alive, with full leave to write whatever he pleased in Agesilaus' favour, would dare put them in the comparison." Does he speak of paralleling Lysander to Sulla? "There is," he says, "no comparison, either in the number of victories or in the risks of battles, for Lysander only won two naval battles." This is not to belittle the Romans: simply by naming them alongside the Greeks he can have done them no harm, whatever the gap between them — and Plutarch does not set them flatly opposite each other. There is no overall verdict; he only compares the pieces and circumstances one by one and gives each a separate judgment. So if anyone wants to convict him of partiality he ought to point to one of those particular judgments, or to say in general that he was wrong to match a given Greek with a given Roman when there were others better suited to pair him with.

One of the captains whose names Montaigne says are obscured by the splendour of other names of less desert, with Ventidius and Telesinus. Not the orator of 65:39 nor his father.

Epicharis, having tired out and glutted the cruelty of Nero's torturers — having endured their fire, their beating, their racks for a whole day without one syllable of confession about the conspiracy — was brought back to the rack the next day with her limbs almost torn to pieces. Who tired and glutted the cruelty of Nero’s satellites a whole day together — their fire, their beating, their racks — without one syllable of confession of her conspiracy, and the next day strangled herself with her own girdle: which makes Montaigne presume she had purposely lent her life to the trial of her fortitude the day before, to mock the tyrant.

## modern-en · lais · 90:2

Xenocrates went at the matter more harshly. His disciples, to test his continence, slipped Lais — that beautiful and famous courtesan — naked into his bed, armed only with her beauty, her wanton charms, and her love-philtres. Finding that, in spite of his reason and his philosophical rules, his unruly flesh was starting to mutiny, he had those members of his that had consented to the rebellion burned. By contrast, the passions that live entirely in the soul — ambition, greed, and the rest — give reason much more trouble, because she has to deal with them by her own means alone; nor are those appetites capable of satiety. They sharpen and grow with indulgence.

The beautiful and famous courtesan whom Xenocrates’s disciples slipped naked into his bed to try his continency, and whose beauty so far mutinied his unruly flesh that he gelded the members that had lent themselves to the revolt.

## modern-en · cleopatra · 90:3

Julius Caesar's example alone is enough to show the difference between these appetites. No man was ever more given to amorous pleasures than he was: one proof is the peculiar care he took of his body, going so far as to use the most lascivious means then in fashion — having all the hairs of his body plucked off, and rubbing himself all over with perfumes with the most painstaking attention. And he was a handsome man in himself: fair-skinned, tall, lively, full-faced, with quick hazel eyes — at least if we can trust Suetonius; the statues of him in Rome do not fully answer that description on every point. Apart from his wives, of whom he changed four — and leaving aside the affair of his youth with Nicomedes, king of Bithynia — he had the maidenhead of the famous Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, as the little Caesarion she bore him bears witness. He also courted Eunoe, queen of Mauretania, and in Rome Postumia, the wife of Servius Sulpicius; Lollia, the wife of Gabinius; Tertulla, the wife of Crassus; and even Mucia, wife of the great Pompey — which, the Roman historians say, was the reason Pompey divorced her, though Plutarch confesses he could not tell for certain. The two Curios, father and son, later reproached Pompey, when he married Caesar's daughter, with having made himself son-in-law to a man who had cuckolded him, and whom he used to call Aegisthus. Besides all these, he kept Servilia, Cato's sister and the mother of Marcus Brutus — from which, most people believe, came his great affection for Brutus, who had been born at a time when it was likely he was his son. So I think I have reason to take him for a man extremely given to debauchery, and of a very amorous constitution. But his other passion, ambition — by which he was infinitely struck — rose up to challenge the first, and that one was promptly forced to give way.

Queen of Egypt, whose maidenhead Caesar had — witness the little Caesario she bore him.

## modern-en · ladislaus · 90:5

What is reported of Ladislaus, king of Naples, as a counter-example is very striking. A great captain, brave and ambitious, he set up as the chief end of his ambition the pursuit of his pleasure and the enjoyment of some rare and excellent beauty. His death sealed the rest. By a long and grinding siege he had reduced Florence to such distress that the citizens were forced to negotiate surrender. He agreed to let them be, provided they handed over to him a beautiful girl he had heard of in their city. They had to give in — averting public ruin by a private wrong. She was the daughter of a famous physician of his day. Finding himself caught in so foul a necessity, he resolved on a desperate stroke. While everyone was helping to deck out his daughter, adorning her with ornaments and jewels to make her more agreeable to her new lover, he gave her a richly embroidered handkerchief, exquisitely perfumed — an item ladies there never go without — to use at the first encounter. This handkerchief, poisoned with all his skill, was rubbed between their warm flesh and open pores, and so suddenly let the poison in that their warm sweat at once turned cold and they died in each other's arms.

King of Naples, who having reduced Florence by a close and tedious siege was content to raise it for a beautiful maid, took her — and found in her bed a writing which her father had given her to keep her honour, to say she was diseased.

## modern-en · caius-calvus · 90:7

To return to his clemency. We have many striking examples from the time of his rule, when everything was in his hands. Caius Memmius had written some very sharp speeches against him, which he had answered just as sharply; yet he soon afterwards used his interest to make Memmius consul. Caius Calvus, who had composed several stinging epigrams against him, employed many of his friends to mediate a reconciliation; Caesar voluntarily resolved to write to him first. And our good Catullus, who had so roughly handled him under the name of Mamurra, came to apologise, and Caesar had him sit at his table that very same day. Having received word of some who were speaking ill of him, he did no more than declare in a public oration that he had been informed. He feared his enemies still less than he hated them. When certain conspiracies and plots against his life were uncovered to him, he was content to publish by proclamation that they were known to him, without prosecuting the conspirators further.

Who had composed several injurious epigrams against Caesar, and whom Caesar voluntarily persuaded himself to write to first, when Calvus employed friends to mediate a reconciliation.

## modern-en · caius-oppius · 90:6

But back to Caesar. His pleasures never stole a single minute from him, nor a single step away from any occasion that might serve his advancement. This passion held such sovereignty over the rest, and possessed his soul with such absolute authority, that it steered him as it pleased. In truth, it troubles me, when I consider the greatness of this man and the wonderful gifts he had: learned to such a degree in every kind of knowledge that there is hardly a science he did not write on; so great an orator that many have preferred his eloquence to Cicero's — and he, I think, did not believe himself Cicero's inferior in that, since he wrote his two anti-Catos to counterbalance the eloquence Cicero had spent on his own Cato. And was there ever a soul so vigilant, so active, so patient under labour as his? No doubt it was adorned with many rare seeds of virtue, lively, natural, and not put on. He was strikingly sober. So far from being delicate in his diet that Oppius relates how one day at table, when medicated oil had been set before him instead of ordinary oil in some sauce, he ate heartily of it rather than embarrass his host. Another time he had his baker whipped for serving him bread finer than the rest of the company's. Cato himself used to say of him that he was the first sober man who ever set out to ruin his country. As for Cato calling him a drunkard one day, it happened like this: both were in the Senate when Catiline's conspiracy was being debated, with Caesar himself under suspicion, and someone came in and handed him a sealed letter. Cato, taking it for some communication from the conspirators, demanded it be put into his hands; Caesar was forced to comply, to avoid further suspicion. It turned out to be a love-letter Servilia, Cato's sister, had written him. Cato, having read it, threw it back at him, saying, "There, drunkard." That was rather a word of disdain and anger than a real reproach for the vice — as we often abuse those who annoy us with the first insulting word that comes to mouth, however inapt to the person we are angry with. To which one may add that the vice Cato charged him with is wonderfully near the one he had just caught Caesar in; for Bacchus and Venus, as the proverb says, are very willing partners. But to my taste, Venus is far livelier company when she is paired with sobriety. Examples of his sweetness and clemency to those who had offended him are countless — leaving aside those from the civil wars, which (as his own writings show plainly enough) he practised partly to flatter his enemies and make them less afraid of his coming dominion and victory. But I must also say that even if these examples are not proof of natural sweetness, they at least demonstrate an astonishing self-confidence and largeness of spirit in him. He often released whole armies of his enemies, after defeating them, without ransom, not even deigning to bind them by oath either to favour him or simply to take up arms against him no more. Three or four times he took some of Pompey's officers prisoner, and as often set them at liberty. Pompey declared all those his enemies who did not follow him to war; Caesar declared all those his friends who sat still and did not actually take up arms against him. To the officers of his who deserted to the other side, he sent on, moreover, their arms, horses, and equipage. The cities he had taken by force he left at full liberty to follow whichever side they pleased, imposing no garrison on them but the memory of his gentleness and clemency. On the day of his great battle at Pharsalia he gave strict and explicit orders that, unless absolutely forced, no one should lay a hand on the citizens of Rome. These were, in my view, very risky ways of proceeding, and it is no wonder that those in our own civil wars who fight, as he did, against the ancient state of their country do not follow his example. They are extraordinary means, suited only to Caesar's fortune and to his astonishing foresight in handling affairs. When I think of the incomparable greatness of his soul, I forgive victory for not being able to disentangle itself from him, even in so unjust and wicked a cause.

Caesar’s companion on a journey, who finding himself ill was left the only lodging there was, Caesar lying all night on the hard ground in the open air; and who relates how Caesar, having medicated instead of common oil set before him in a sauce, ate heartily of it that he might not put his entertainer out of countenance. The bare Oppius at 49:27 is a name and not this man.

## modern-en · vercingetorix · 91:26

When he undertook that furious siege of Alesia, where there were eighty thousand men in garrison, with all Gaul up in arms to raise the siege and a relieving army on foot of one hundred and nine thousand horse and two hundred and forty thousand foot — what boldness and what high confidence it took in him not to give up the attempt but to resolve to face both these enormous difficulties, which he nevertheless overcame; and, after winning that great battle against the army outside, he soon reduced those inside to his mercy. The same thing happened to Lucullus at the siege of Tigranocerta against King Tigranes, but the enemy's quality there was not the same, given the softness of the men Lucullus was dealing with. I will set down here two rare and extraordinary incidents from this siege of Alesia. The first: the Gauls, having mustered their forces against Caesar and made a general review of them, resolved in their council of war to dismiss a good part of that huge multitude, so as not to fall into confusion. This example of fearing to be too many is new; but, properly considered, it stands to reason that the body of an army should be of moderate size and kept within certain bounds, both because of the difficulty of provisioning them and the difficulty of governing them and keeping them in order. At the very least, it is very easy to show by example that monstrously large armies have rarely accomplished anything of substance. As Cyrus says in Xenophon, "It is not the number of men, but the number of good men, that wins the advantage"; the rest only get in the way. And Bayezid based his decision to fight Tamerlane, against the opinion of all his captains, mainly on this — that his enemies' uncountable numbers gave him sure hope of confusion in their ranks. Scanderbeg, a very good and expert judge in such matters, used to say that ten or twelve thousand reliable fighting men were enough for a good leader to keep himself in order in every kind of military situation. The other thing I want to record, which seems contrary to the custom and rules of war, is that Vercingetorix, who was made general of all the parts of the revolted Gaul, went and shut himself up in Alesia. The man who commands a whole country ought never to shut himself up except in such extremity that the only place he has left is in danger, and that his only remaining hope is in the defence of that city; otherwise he should keep himself at liberty, so that he can take general measures for every part of his command.

Made general of all the parts of the revolted Gaul, and who — against both the custom and the rules of war, Montaigne says — went and shut himself up in Alexia with fourscore thousand men.

showed us a similar example in our civil wars; the Frenchmen in his army put up money out of their own purses to pay the foreigners who served with him. A soldier called Scaeva, who held one of the passes, invincibly maintained his position with one eye gone, one shoulder and one thigh shot through, and his shield struck in two hundred and thirty places. Granius Petronius was taken by Scipio in Africa: Scipio, having put the rest to death, sent him word that he gave him his life, since he was a man of quality and a quaestor. There are countless examples of their loyalty, but what was done by those besieged in Salona — a city that held out for Caesar against Pompey — must not be forgotten, for the rarity of what happened there. Marcus Octavius was holding them tightly besieged. Inside, they had been reduced to the extreme need of everything: to make up for the lack of men, with most either killed or wounded, they had freed all their slaves; to make ropes for their war-engines they had had to cut off all the women's hair; on top of all this they were starving, and yet they were resolved never to surrender. After the siege had dragged on long enough that Octavius had grown careless and slack in pressing his enterprise, they picked a day about noon, placed the women and children on the walls for show, and sallied out against the besiegers with such fury that they routed the first, second, and third bodies of troops, and then the fourth, and the rest; they beat them clean out of their trenches and chased them right down to their ships. Octavius himself was forced to flee to Dyrrachium, where Pompey lay. I do not at this moment remember another example where the besieged completely defeated the besieger and won the field, or where a sortie produced a pure and total victory.

Who kept Salona close besieged for Pompey, and grew so negligent by the length of it that the besieged sallied at noon and routed his whole camp.

## modern-en · lucius-cassius · 91:25

But where necessary occasion required, no man ever risked his person more than Caesar did. So much so that, for my part, I seem to read in many of his exploits a settled resolution to throw himself away rather than face the shame of being beaten. In his great battle with the people of Tournai, he charged right up to the head of the enemy without his shield, just as he saw the van of his own army beginning to give ground — and the same thing happened to him several other times. Hearing his people were besieged, he passed through the enemy's army in disguise to encourage them with his presence. Having crossed over to Dyrrachium with very slight forces, and seeing the rest of his army, which he had left to Antony's command, slow to follow him, he set out alone to recross the sea in a tremendous storm, and slipped away in secret to fetch the rest of his troops, with the ports on the other side held by Pompey and the whole sea in his enemy's possession. As for what he accomplished by sheer force of hand, there are many exploits in which the risk goes beyond all the rules of war. With what small means did he undertake to subdue the kingdom of Egypt, and afterwards to attack the forces of Scipio and Juba, ten times greater than his own? These men had I-don't-know-what more-than-human confidence in their fortune; and he used to say that in great undertakings men must embark, not deliberate. After the battle of Pharsalia, when he had sent his army on ahead into Asia and was crossing the Hellespont in a single vessel, he met Lucius Cassius at sea with ten tall warships — and had the courage not only to wait for him but to sail up to him and summon him to surrender, which he did.

Whom Caesar met at sea with ten tall men-of-war while passing the Hellespont in one single vessel — and had the courage not only to stay his coming but to sail up to him and summon him to yield, which he did.

## modern-en · arria · 92:9

Arria, the wife of Caecina Paetus, a man of consular rank, was the mother of another Arria, the wife of Thrasea Paetus — the same Thrasea whose virtue was so celebrated in Nero's time — and through this son-in-law she was the grandmother of Fannia (the resemblance of these men's and women's names, and of their fortunes, has led to several confusions). This first Arria, when her husband Caecina Paetus had been captured by some of the Emperor Claudius' men after the defeat of Scribonianus — whose party he had embraced in the war — begged those who were to carry him prisoner to Rome to take her along on their ship, where she would be much less expense and trouble to them than the many attendants they would otherwise have to maintain to wait on her husband, and that she alone would undertake to look after him in his room, his kitchen, and every other office. They refused. So she put herself into a fisherman's boat she hired on the spot, and in that way followed him from Illyria. After her arrival at Rome, Junia, the widow of Scribonianus, one day, on the strength of their similar fortunes, came up to her in the Emperor's presence; Arria pushed her off roughly with these words: "I," she said, "speak to you, or listen to anything you have to say! — to you, in whose lap Scribonianus was killed, and you are still alive?" These words, with several other signs, made her friends realise she would certainly take her own life, unable to endure her husband's misfortune. And Thrasea, her son-in-law, begging her not to throw herself away, and saying to her, "What — if I should suffer the same fate as Caecina, would you want your daughter, my wife, to do the same?" — "Would I?" she replied. "Yes, yes, I would: if she had lived as long, and in as good understanding with you, as I have lived with my husband." These answers made them all the more careful of her, and more watchful in their eye on her. One day, when she said to those guarding her, "You take all this trouble for nothing; you may indeed make me die a worse death, but to keep me from dying is not in your power" — she suddenly leapt from a chair where she had been sitting and with all her strength dashed her head against the wall, by which blow she was knocked flat in a faint and badly wounded. After they had with great difficulty brought her back to herself, she said, "I told you that if you denied me some easy way of dying, I would find another, however painful." The conclusion of so admirable a virtue was this. Her husband Paetus, not having resolution enough of his own to despatch himself as the emperor's cruelty had ordered him to, one day, after she had used all the reasons and exhortations she thought most likely to persuade him, she snatched the dagger he wore at his side, held it ready in her hand to clinch her admonitions, and saying "Do this, Paetus," in the same instant gave herself a mortal stab in the breast, then drew it out of the wound and presented it to him, ending her life with this noble, generous, and immortal saying — "Paete, non dolet" — having time to pronounce no more than those three never-to-be-forgotten words: "Paetus, it does not hurt."

The wife of Caecina Paetus, who followed her husband from Sclavonia in a hired fisher-boat when they would not take her into the ship; who told Junia, the widow of Scribonianus, that she would not hear a word from the woman in whose lap Scribonianus was slain and who was yet alive; and who, her husband wanting resolution to despatch himself as the emperor had enjoined, snatched the poniard from his side, stabbed herself, drew it out and presented it to him with the three words nobody forgets: Paetus, it does not hurt.

## modern-en · pompeia-paulina · 92:13

Pompeia Paulina, a young and very noble Roman lady, had married Seneca in his extreme old age. Nero, his fine pupil, sent his guards to him to deliver the death-sentence, which was carried out in this fashion: when the Roman emperors of those days had condemned a man of rank, they sent word by their officers to him to choose his manner of death, and to carry it out within such or such a time-limit, which was set, depending on the degree of their anger, either shorter or longer, so as to give him time to put his affairs in order — or sometimes to deny him even that, by the shortness of the period. If the condemned man seemed unwilling to obey the order, they had men ready to carry it out either by cutting the veins of his arms and legs, or by forcing him to swallow a dose of poison. But men of honour would not submit to that necessity, but called in their own doctors and surgeons for the job. Seneca, with a calm and steady face, heard their charge and at once called for paper to make his will. When the captain refused him this, he turned to his friends and said, "Since I am not allowed to leave you any other token of the debt I owe you, I leave you at least the best thing I have, namely the image of my life and conduct, which I beg you to keep in memory of me — and by doing so you will earn the glory of sincere and real friends." Then, one moment soothing with gentle words the grief he saw in them, the next raising his voice to rebuke them: "What," he said, "has become of all our fine philosophical maxims? What of all the provisions we have laid in for so many years against the strokes of fortune? Is Nero's cruelty unknown to us? What could we expect of one who has murdered his mother and his brother, but that he should put to death the tutor who brought him up?" After those general words, he turned to his wife and embraced her tightly in his arms, as, her heart and strength failing her, she was ready to sink down with grief; and he begged her, for his sake, to bear this stroke with a little more patience, telling her that the hour had come in which he was to show, not by argument and discourse but in action, the fruit he had reaped from his studies, and that he genuinely embraced his death, not only without grief but with joy. "And so, my dearest," he said, "do not dishonour it with your tears, lest it look as if you loved yourself more than my reputation. Restrain your grief, and console yourself in what you have known of me and of my actions, leading the rest of your life in the same virtuous way you have done up to now." Paulina, having recovered her spirits a little, and warmed the greatness of her courage with a most generous affection, replied: "No, Seneca, I am not a woman to let you go alone in such a moment. I will not have you think that the virtuous examples of your life have not taught me how to die; and when could I ever do it better, or more fittingly, or more as I would wish, than with you? So be sure: I will go along with you." Then Seneca, taking this noble and generous resolution of his wife in good part, and willing also to free himself from the fear of leaving her exposed to his enemies' cruelty after his death, said, "Paulina, I have instructed you in what would serve you for a happy life; but you, I see, are more set on the honour of dying. Truly, I will not grudge it to you. The steadiness and resolve in our common end are the same; but the beauty and glory of your part are much greater." That said, the surgeons at the same moment opened the veins of both their arms; but as Seneca's, more shrunken with age and abstinence, let his blood flow too slowly, he further ordered them to open the veins of his thighs. And so that the torments he was suffering might not pierce his wife's heart, and also to spare himself the affliction of seeing her in so sad a state, after a very affectionate farewell he begged her to allow them to carry her into her own room, which they did. But all these incisions still being not enough to make him die, he ordered Statius Annaeus, his physician, to give him a draught of poison, which had not much better effect — because of the weakness and coldness of his limbs it could not reach his heart. So they were forced to add a very hot bath; and then, feeling his end approach, while he still had breath he kept up admirable discourse on the subject of his present condition, which his secretaries took down as long as they could hear him; and his last words long remained in great honour and esteem among men, and it is a great loss to us that they have not come down to our day. Then, feeling the last pangs of death, with the bloody water of the bath he bathed his head and said, "This water I dedicate to Jupiter the Deliverer." Nero, hearing of all this at once, and fearing that the death of Paulina — who was one of the best-born ladies of Rome, and against whom he had no particular grudge — would turn into a reproach against him, sent orders in all haste to bind up her wounds. Her attendants did so without her knowledge, since she was already half dead and quite past all sensation. So although she lived against her own design, she lived very honourably, in a way befitting her own virtue, and her pale complexion afterwards bore continual witness to how much life had run out of her veins.

## modern-en · panaetius · 69:239

Take the most eminent side, the one with the greatest reputation: it will never be so sure that you won't have to attack and contend with hundreds upon hundreds of adversaries to defend it. Isn't it better to stay out of this uproar? You are allowed to embrace Aristotle's opinions on the immortality of the soul with as much zeal as you would defend your honour and life, and to call Plato a liar on that point — and is it forbidden to doubt him? If Panaetius may maintain his opinion about augury, dreams, oracles, and prophecies, of which the Stoics had no doubt at all, why may a wise man not do the same in everything he dared to do in those matters he had learned from his masters, established by the common consent of the school he professes and belongs to? If it is a child that judges, he doesn't know what it is; if a wise man, he is prepossessed. They have reserved themselves a marvellous advantage in battle, having relieved themselves of the trouble of defence. If you strike them, they don't mind, as long as they strike too; they turn everything to their own use. If they win, your argument is lame; if you win, theirs is; if they fall short, they verify ignorance; if you fall short, you do. If they prove that nothing is known, well and good; if they cannot prove it, well and good too: _Ut quum in eadem re paria contrariis in partibus momenta inveniuntur, facilius ab utraque parte assertio sustineatur_: "That when equal weights are found on opposite sides of the same matter, judgment may be more easily suspended on both." And they reckon they can show why a thing is false more easily than why it is true; what is not, more easily than what is; what they do not believe, more easily than what they do. Their way of speaking is: "I assert nothing; it is no more so than otherwise, or than neither one nor the other; I don't understand it. Appearances are everywhere equal; the law of speaking for or against is the same. Nothing seems true that cannot seem false." Their sacramental word is — that is to say, "I stand, I stir not." That is the refrain of their song, and other refrains of the same stuff. The effect is a pure, entire, perfect, and absolute suspension of judgment. They use their reason to inquire and debate, but not to fix and determine. Whoever can imagine a perpetual confession of ignorance — a judgment with no bias, no leaning, no inclination, on any occasion whatever — conceives a true idea of Pyrrhonism. I express this fancy as well as I can, because many find it hard to conceive, and the authors themselves represent it somewhat variously and obscurely.

Who called Plato the Homer of the philosophers, and left nothing unsaid in doing it.

## modern-en · pope-pius-ii · 93:16

It is against the order of nature that he should have made the most excellent thing that can be made; for the ordinary birth of things is imperfect — they grow and gather strength by growing — whereas he made the infancy of poetry and of several other sciences mature, perfect, and complete at the outset. For that reason he can be called the first and last of poets, in keeping with the fine testimony antiquity has left of him: "as there was no one before him whom he could imitate, so there has been no one since who could imitate him." His words, according to Aristotle, are the only words that have motion and action, the only substantial words. Alexander the Great, having found a rich casket among Darius' spoils, ordered it be set aside to keep his Homer in, saying that Homer was the best and most faithful counsellor he had in his military affairs. For the same reason Cleomenes, son of Anaxandridas, said that Homer was the poet of the Spartans, as being an excellent master of the discipline of war. There is also this singular tribute to him in Plutarch's judgment: that he is the only author in the world who never glutted or sickened his readers, always presenting himself as something new, and always flourishing in some fresh grace. That naughty Alcibiades, asking one who pretended to learning for a book of Homer, gave him a box on the ear because he had none — which he thought as scandalous as we should if we found one of our priests without a breviary. Xenophanes complained one day to Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, that he was so poor he could not afford to keep two servants. "What!" Hiero replied. "Homer, who was much poorer than you, keeps more than ten thousand, though he is dead." What did Panaetius leave unsaid when he called Plato the Homer of the philosophers? Besides, what glory can be compared to his? Nothing is more constantly on men's lips than his name and works; nothing is so well known and accepted as Troy, Helen, and the war fought over her — when perhaps there never was such a thing. Our children are still called by names he invented more than three thousand years ago; who does not know Hector and Achilles? Not only certain particular families but most nations also trace their origins to his inventions. Mehmed II, emperor of the Turks, writing to our Pope Pius II, said, "I am astonished the Italians take up arms against me, considering we share a common descent from the Trojans, and it is just as much my business as theirs to revenge the blood of Hector on the Greeks, whom they side with against me." Is it not a noble farce, in which kings, republics, and emperors have played their parts for so many ages, with the vast universe for a stage? Seven Greek cities contended for the honour of being his birthplace — so much honour even his obscurity helped him to:

To whom Mohammed the second wrote that he was astonished the Italians should appear against him, seeing they had their common descent from the Trojans and it concerned him as much as them to revenge the blood of Hector upon the Greeks.

Nothing is more constantly on men's lips than his name and works; nothing is so well known and accepted as Troy, Helen, and the war fought over her — when perhaps there never was such a thing. Our children are still called by names he invented more than three thousand years ago; who does not know Hector and Achilles? Not only certain particular families but most nations also trace their origins to his inventions. Mehmed II, emperor of the Turks, writing to our Pope Pius II, said, "I am astonished the Italians take up arms against me, considering we share a common descent from the Trojans, and it is just as much my business as theirs to revenge the blood of Hector on the Greeks, whom they side with against me." Is it not a noble farce, in which kings, republics, and emperors have played their parts for so many ages, with the vast universe for a stage? Seven Greek cities contended for the honour of being his birthplace — so much honour even his obscurity helped him to:

Whose blood Mohammed the second claimed a common descent from the Trojans entitled him to revenge upon the Greeks. The Hector of 69:282 is in Ovid’s Latin and the Hector of 74:18 is the title of a play.

that greatness, by which at the age of thirty-three he had passed victorious through the whole habitable earth and, in half a life, reached the very limit of what human nature can achieve — so that you cannot imagine what his proper span and the continued growth of his courage and fortune would have been, had he reached due maturity of age, without imagining something more than human. Consider the many royal lines he made spring from his soldiers, leaving the world, at his death, divided among four successors — simple captains in his army — whose posterity so long held and maintained that vast inheritance. Consider so many excellent virtues he was master of: justice, temperance, generosity, truth in his word, love towards his own people, humanity towards those he overcame. His character, in general, seems incapable of any sort of reproach — though some particular and exceptional actions of his may fall under censure. But it is impossible to carry off such great things as he did within the strict rules of justice; such men are to be judged in the gross, by the main end of their actions. The destruction of Thebes and Persepolis, the murder of Menander and of Hephaestion's physician, the massacre of so many Persian prisoners at one time, of a body of Indian soldiers (not without breaking his word), and of the Cossaeans down to the children themselves, are indeed lapses not easily excused. As for Cleitus, the fault was more than redeemed; and that action, as much as any other, displays the goodness of his nature, a nature most exquisitely formed for good. It was ingeniously said of him that he had his virtues from nature and his vices from fortune. As for his being a little given to bragging, a little too impatient of hearing himself ill spoken of, and as for those mangers, weapons, and bits he had scattered about in India — all those little vanities, it seems to me, can well be allowed to his youth and to the prodigious good fortune that attended him. And anyone who will set against them his many military virtues — his diligence, foresight, patience, discipline, subtlety, magnanimity, resolution, and good luck (in which, even without Hannibal's testimony, he stood first among men) — the admirable beauty and symmetry of his person, miraculous to the point of seeming a miracle, his stately bearing and awesome look, in a face so young, ruddy, and radiant:

This bundling together of so many varied pieces is done in such a way that I never set pen to paper except when I have too much idle time, and never anywhere but at home; so that it is put together amid endless interruptions and intervals, since occasions sometimes keep me away for months at a stretch. As for the rest, I never correct my first thoughts by any second ones; I may perhaps alter a word here and there, but only to vary the phrasing, not to undo my original meaning. I want to set down the progress of my moods, and let everyone see each piece as it came from the forge. I wish I had begun sooner, so I could have taken better notice of the course of my own changes. A servant of mine, whom I employed to copy out my drafts, thought he had hit on a prize by stealing several pieces from me — the ones he liked best; but it is my consolation that he will be no greater a gainer than I shall be a loser by the theft. I am seven or eight years older since I began, nor has it been without some new acquisition: in that time, by the bounty of age, I have made the acquaintance of the kidney stone. Long converse with the years does not pass off without some such inconvenience. I would have been glad if, out of all the infirmities old age has on offer for long-lived men, it had picked one more welcome to me, for it could not possibly have laid on me a disease I have dreaded so deeply from infancy onward; of all the misfortunes of old age, this is the one I have always feared most. I have often thought to myself that I was going on too long, and that in so long a voyage I was bound to run myself onto some rock or other. I noticed, and have often enough said so, that it was time to depart, and that life should be cut off at the sound and living part — by the surgeon's rule for amputations; and that nature charges very stiff interest from whoever does not pay back the principal at the proper time. And yet I was so far from ready that, in the eighteen months or so I have now been in this uncomfortable condition, I have so accustomed myself to it as to be content to live on with it; and I have found ways to comfort myself, and to hope. So much are men enslaved to their wretched existence that there is no condition so miserable they will not accept it, so long as they may live. Hear Maecenas:

I expose myself in my plainspoken opinion, and in the manner most my own: a tender negotiator, a novice, who would rather fail in the affair than fail himself. I have a free and open way that easily insinuates itself and earns belief with whoever I am dealing with, on the very first meeting. My free way of speaking has also easily cleared me of any suspicion of dissembling, by sheer vehemence — leaving nothing unsaid however hard or bitter (so that I could not have said worse behind their backs), and carrying along with it a plain show of simplicity and indifference. ## modern-en · philippides · 95:24

I say nothing to one party that I cannot, if need be, say to the other with a small change of tone; and I report nothing but things either indifferent, or already known, or of common consequence. I cannot allow myself, on any consideration, to tell them a lie. What is entrusted to my secrecy I religiously conceal; but I take on as few such trusts as I can. The secrets of princes are a troublesome burden to anyone with no stake in them. I am very willing to bargain that they trust me with little but rely confidently on what I tell them. I have always known more than I wanted to. One open way of speaking draws out another, and pulls out confidences, like wine and love. Philippides, in my opinion, answered King Lysimachus very well: asked what part of his estate he would like as a gift, he said, "Whatever you wish, so long as it is none of your secrets." I see that everyone is displeased if the bottom of the business he is employed in is hidden from him, or if there is any reservation in the matter; for my part, I am happy to know no more of the business than what they want me to handle, and I have no desire that my knowledge should exceed or fall short of what I have to say. If I must serve as an instrument of deceit, let it be at least with a clear conscience. I will not be considered so devoted or so loyal a servant as to be fit to betray anyone: someone who is unfaithful to himself may be excusably so to his master. But these are princes who don't accept men by halves and despise limited and conditional services: I can't help it; I tell them frankly how far I can go. For I should be a slave to nothing but reason, and I can hardly submit even to that. And they are to blame too for demanding from a free man the same subjection and obligation to their service as they get from someone they have made or bought, or whose fortune particularly and explicitly depends on theirs. The laws have delivered me from a great anxiety; they have chosen a side for me and given me a master; every other allegiance or obligation must be subordinate to that one, and cut off from it. Yet this is not to say that if my affection should incline me otherwise, my hand would at once obey it; the will and desire are a law to themselves, but actions must be commissioned by public appointment.

It is a precise life that keeps itself in good order in private. Anyone can play a part and look like an honest man on the stage; but within, in his own bosom, where everyone may do as he likes and where everything is hidden — to be regular there, that's the point. The next degree is to be regular in his house, in his daily actions, for which we are accountable to no one and where there is no study or artifice. So Bias, setting forth the excellent state of a private family, says: "such a one as the master is within, by his own virtue and temper, that he is abroad, for fear of the laws and people's reports." And it was a worthy saying of Julius Drusus, to the masons who offered him, for three thousand crowns, to fix his house so that his neighbours could no longer have the same view into it as before: "I will give you," he said, "six thousand to make it so that everybody can see into every room." It is recorded as honourable of Agesilaus that on his journeys he always took up his lodgings in temples, so that the people and the gods themselves could pry into his most private actions. Some men have been a wonder to the world in whom neither wife nor servant ever saw anything remarkable; few men have been admired by their own household; no one was ever a prophet, not just in his own house, but in his own country either — so the experience of histories tells us. It is the same in trifling things; even in this low example one may see the image of a greater one. In my country of Gascony they consider it a curiosity to see me in print: the further from home I am read, the better I am thought of. I have to pay printers in Guienne; elsewhere they pay me. It is on this principle that those build who hide themselves while present and living, in order to gain a name when they are dead and absent. I would rather have a great deal less in hand; I expose myself to the world on no other account than my present share, and when I leave the world I quit the rest. See this functionary whom the people escort in state, with awe and applause, right to his door; he sheds the pageant with his robe, and falls so much the lower the higher he had been exalted: within himself, all is in tumult and disorder. And even if all were well-ordered there, it will take a lively and well-chosen judgment to detect it in these low and private actions; to which one may add that order is a dull, sombre virtue. To storm a breach, conduct an embassy, govern a people — these are actions of renown; to scold, laugh, sell, pay, love, hate, and gently and justly converse with one's own family and with oneself; not to relax, not to give oneself the lie — these are rarer and harder, and less noticed. By which means, retired lives, whatever may be said to the contrary, perform duties as great as or greater than the others; and private men, says Aristotle, serve virtue more painfully and worthily than men in office. We prepare ourselves for grand occasions more out of vanity than conscience. The shortest way to glory would be to do for conscience what we do for glory. Alexander's virtue strikes me as having much less vigour on his great stage than that of Socrates in his low and obscure employment. I can easily imagine Socrates in Alexander's place; but Alexander in Socrates' — I cannot. Ask the one what he can do, he will answer, "Subdue the world"; ask the other the same question, he will say, "Live human life according to its natural condition" — a much more general, weighty, and legitimate science than the other.

Who answered the masons offering, for three thousand crowns, to put his house where his neighbours could no longer overlook it: I will give you six thousand, and make it so that everybody may see into every room of it.

## modern-en · james-of-naples · 97:40

These two engagements are accidental and depend on others; the one is troublesome by its rarity, the other withers with age, so that they could never have been sufficient for the business of my life. That of books, which is the third, is far more certain, and far more our own. It yields the other advantages to the first two, but has the constancy and ease of its service as its own share. It goes step by step with me my whole course, and everywhere it stands by me; it comforts me in old age and in solitude; it eases me of the troublesome burden of idleness, and delivers me at any hour from company I dislike; it blunts the point of griefs, if they are not extreme and have not got total possession of my soul. To divert myself from a troublesome fancy, I have only to run to my books; they at once fix me on them and chase the other out of my thoughts; and they don't mutiny at seeing that I have recourse to them only for want of other, more real, natural, and lively comforts; they always receive me with the same kindness. He may well walk on foot, they say, who leads his horse in his hand; and our James, King of Naples and Sicily, who, handsome, young, and healthy, had himself carried about on a barrow, stretched out on a pitiful mattress, in a poor robe of grey cloth and a cap of the same, yet attended by a royal train, litters, led horses of all sorts, gentlemen and officers — even he represented thereby a tender and unsteady authority: "The sick man has no cause to complain who has his cure in his sleeve." In the experience and practice of this maxim, which is a very true one, lies all the benefit I get from books. In fact, I make no more use of them, so to speak, than those who know them not. I enjoy them as misers do their money, in knowing that I may enjoy them whenever I please; my mind is satisfied with this right of possession. I never travel without books, in peace or in war; and yet sometimes I pass several days, even months, without looking at them. I'll read by and by, I say to myself, or tomorrow, or whenever I please; and meanwhile time slips away without inconvenience. For it is unimaginable how much I please myself and rest content in this thought, that I have them by me to divert myself with whenever I am so disposed, and in remembering what a refreshment they are to my life. It is the best provision I have yet found for this human journey, and I very much pity men of understanding who lack it. I more readily accept any other kind of diversion, however slight, because this one can never fail me.

## modern-en · hempricourt · 98:4

I may, perhaps, have glanced elsewhere at some kind of public diversion. And the practice of military diversion, which Pericles used in the Peloponnesian war, and a thousand others in other places — to draw the enemy's forces out of their own country — is too common in history to need mention. It was an ingenious device by which Monseigneur d'Hempricourt saved both himself and others in the city of Liège, into which the Duke of Burgundy, who was besieging it, had made him enter to carry out the articles of their promised surrender. The people, assembled by night to deliberate on it, began to mutiny against the agreement, and several of them resolved to fall upon the commissioners, whom they had in their power. He, sensing the gusts of this first popular storm coming to break upon his lodgings, suddenly sent out to them two of the citizens (some of whom were with him) with new and milder terms to be proposed in their council, terms he had improvised then and there to meet his need. These two diverted the first tempest, carrying the enraged crowd back to the town hall to hear and consider what they had to say. The deliberation was short; a second storm arose as violent as the first. Whereupon he dispatched four new mediators of the same standing to meet them, protesting that he had now better conditions to present, ones that would entirely satisfy them; by this means the tumult was again calmed, and the people once more turned back to the council chamber. In short, by this dispensation of distractions, one after another, diverting their fury and dissipating it in frivolous consultations, he at last laid it to sleep until day broke — which was his principal aim.

Who saved both himself and others in the city of Liege by an ingenious evasion, the Duke of Burgundy having sent him in to execute the articles of the promised surrender.

## modern-en · origen · 69:476

Origen makes them eternally come and go from a better to a worse state. The opinion Varro mentions is that, after a revolution of four hundred and forty years, they are reunited to their first bodies. Chrysippus held that this would happen after some unknown and undefined span of time. Plato, who claims to have taken this belief from Pindar and the ancient poets — that we undergo infinite vicissitudes of change, for which the soul is prepared, having neither punishment nor reward in the other world that is not temporal, just as its life here is temporal — concludes that the soul has a singular knowledge of the affairs of heaven, hell, and the world, through all of which it has passed and re-passed and made stays on its various voyages — all matters for its memory. Watch his account of its progress elsewhere: "The soul that has lived well is reunited to the star to which it is assigned; the one that has lived badly is moved into a woman; and if it does not reform there, is moved again into a beast of a kind suited to its vicious habits, and will see no end of its punishments until it has returned to its natural constitution and, by the force of reason, purged itself of those gross, stupid, elementary qualities it was polluted with." But I will not skip the Epicureans' objection against this transmigration from one body to another; it is a fine one. They ask what is to be done if the number of those dying happens to exceed the number of those being born. For the souls turned out of their old lodgings will jostle and shove to be first into the new ones. And further, what do they do with their time while waiting for new quarters to be made ready? Or conversely, if more animals are born than die, the body, they say, would be in poor shape while it waited for a soul to be infused into it — and you would end up with some bodies dying before they had ever been alive.

## modern-en · strato · 69:268

Xenophon reports a similar perplexity in Socrates's teaching: at one point men are not to inquire into the form of God, then a moment later he makes him hold that the sun is God, and the soul God; that there is only one God, and then that there are many. Speusippus, Plato's nephew, makes God a certain power that governs all things, and says he has a soul. Aristotle says at one time it is the spirit, at another the world; at one time he gives the world another master, at another he makes God the heat of heaven. Xenocrates makes eight: five named among the planets; a sixth composed of all the fixed stars as so many members; the seventh and eighth, the sun and moon. Heraclides Ponticus does nothing but float between opinions, finally stripping God of sense and making him shift from one form to another, until in the end he calls him heaven and earth. Theophrastus wanders in the same indecision among his fancies, attributing the superintendence of the world now to understanding, now to heaven, now to the stars. Strato says it is nature, having the power of generation, increase, and diminution, without form or sentience. Zeno says it is the law of nature, commanding good and forbidding evil — which law is an animal; and he sets aside the customary gods, Jupiter, Juno, Vesta. Diogenes of Apollonia, that it is air. Xenophanes makes God round, seeing and hearing, not breathing, and having nothing in common with human nature. Aristo thinks the form of God incomprehensible, strips him of sense, and does not know whether he is an animal or something else. Cleanthes at one time supposes it to be reason, at another the world, at another the soul of nature, at another the supreme heat rolling and surrounding all. Perseus, Zeno's disciple, was of the opinion that men have given the title of god to those who have been useful and added some notable advantage to human life — even to useful things themselves. Chrysippus made a confused heap of all the preceding theories, and counted, among a thousand forms of gods he invents, men who have been deified. Diagoras and Theodorus flatly denied that there were any gods at all. Epicurus makes the gods shining, transparent, and air-permeable, lodged as between two forts, between two worlds, safe from blows, clothed in human shape and with members like ours — members that serve them no purpose:

Whose book Of Carnal Conjunction Montaigne names among the grave writers on the subject; and who, in the Apology, makes God have neither sense nor form, and holds Nature to be the mistress of all things.

The Egyptian ladies, in their Bacchanalia, each carried one finely carved of wood about their necks, as large and heavy as she could so carry; besides which, the statue of their god presented one which surpassed all the rest of his body in size. The married women in the region where I live make of their kerchiefs the figure of one upon their foreheads, to glorify themselves in their enjoyment of it, and on becoming widows they throw it behind and cover it with their head-cloths. The most modest matrons of Rome thought it an honour to offer flowers and garlands to the god Priapus, and they made the virgins, at the time of their espousals, sit upon his shameful parts. And I am not sure I have not in my own time seen some air of similar devotion. What was the meaning of that ridiculous bit of our forefathers' clothing — and still worn by our Swiss? Why do we make a show of our equipment in figure under our breeches, and often, even worse, above its natural size, by falsehood and imposture? I have half a mind to believe that this sort of garment was invented in those better, more conscientious ages, that the world might not be deceived, and that every man should give a public account of his proportions. The simple peoples wear them still, and around their real size. Back then, the tailor took measure of it as the shoemaker now does of a man's foot. That worthy man who, when I was young, gelded so many noble and ancient statues in his great city, so they should not corrupt the eyesight of the ladies — following the advice of this other ancient worthy:

The god to whom the most modest matrons of Rome thought it an honour to offer flowers and garlands.

Before the Peloponnesian War there was no great talk of this science. Hippocrates brought it into repute; whatever he laid down, Chrysippus overturned; after him, Erasistratus, Aristotle's grandson, overturned what Chrysippus had written; after these, the Empirics came forward, who took the opposite line from the ancients in handling this art; when the credit of these began a little to fade, Herophilus set up another sort of practice, which Asclepiades in turn rose up against, and overturned. Then, in their turn, the opinions first of Themison, and then of Musa, and after that those of Vectius Valens, a physician famous through his dealings with Messalina, came into fashion. The empire of medicine in Nero's time was established in Thessalus, who abolished and condemned everything held until his day. His doctrine was refuted by Crinas of Marseilles, who was the first to bring all medical operations under the calendars and motions of the stars, and reduced eating, sleeping, and drinking to hours most pleasing to Mercury and the moon. His authority was soon afterwards displaced by Charinus, a doctor from the same city of Marseilles, who not only challenged all the ancient methods of medicine but also the use of hot baths that had been generally common for so many ages. He made men bathe in cold water, even in winter, and plunged his sick patients in the natural water of streams. No Roman until Pliny's time had ever stooped to practise medicine; that work was done only by Greeks and foreigners, just as today among us French it is done by those who can rattle off some Latin. For, as a very great doctor says, we do not easily accept the medicine we understand, any more than we do the drugs we ourselves gather. If the nations from which we import guaiacum, sarsaparilla, and China wood have physicians, how much value can we imagine they set, by the same recommendation of strangeness, rarity, and high price, on our own cabbage and parsley? — for who would dare to look down on things fetched from so far and obtained at the hazard of so long and dangerous a voyage?
