## modern-en · gregory-xiii · 100:16

The strangeness of these inventions puts another thought in my head: that it is a kind of weakness in monarchs, and evidence that they don't sufficiently understand what they are, when they go in for being honoured and looking great through extravagant expense. It might be forgivable in a foreign country, but among their own subjects, where they hold sovereign power and can do whatever they like, it takes away from their dignity at the very pinnacle of honour they can reach: just as, it seems to me, it is unnecessary for a private gentleman to dress lavishly at home — his house, his servants, his kitchen answer for him well enough. The advice Isocrates gives his king seems to me grounded in reason: that he should be splendid in plate and furniture, because it is an expense of long duration that passes on to his successors, and that he should avoid all kinds of grandeur that will soon be forgotten. I loved to dress finely when I was a younger brother, for want of any other ornament, and it suited me well; there are some on whom rich clothes practically weep. We have strange stories of the personal frugality of our kings — kings who were great in reputation, courage, and fortune. Demosthenes was passionately against the law of his city that set aside public money for the splendour of their public games and festivals: he wanted their greatness to be displayed in numbers of well-equipped ships and well-provisioned armies; and there is good reason to condemn Theophrastus, who in his Book on Riches takes the contrary view, holding that sort of expense to be the true fruit of abundance. These are pleasures, says Aristotle, that please only the lower sort of people and vanish from memory as soon as the crowd has had its fill, and no serious or judicious man can have any respect for them. This money would, in my opinion, be much more royally — and also more usefully, justly, and lastingly — spent on ports, harbours, walls, and fortifications, on grand buildings, churches, hospitals, colleges, and on the improvement of streets and highways — and Pope Gregory XIII will leave a fine memory to future ages for just this; and our Queen Catherine would have left to posterity proof of her natural generosity and munificence, had her means matched her inclinations. Fortune has done me a great injury by interrupting the noble work on the Pont-Neuf of our great city, and depriving me of the hope of seeing it finished before I die.

Who will leave a laudable memory to future times, Montaigne says, for laying money out on ports, havens, walls, fortifications, churches, hospitals, colleges and the reforming of streets and highways rather than on public shows. The pope who reformed the calendar in 1582, so that France passed at one step from the 9th to the 20th of December.

There is no heart so effeminate that the rattle and sound of our drums and trumpets will not inflame it with courage; nor so sullen that the harmony of our music will not rouse and cheer it; nor a soul so stubborn that it will not feel itself struck with some reverence in considering the gloomy vastness of our churches, the variety of ornaments, and the order of our ceremonies, and in hearing the solemn music of our organs and the grave and devout harmony of our voices. Even those who come in with contempt feel a certain shivering in their hearts, and something of dread that makes them begin to doubt their opinions. For my part, I do not think myself strong enough to hear an ode of Horace or Catullus sung by a beautiful young mouth without being moved; and Zeno was right to say "that the voice is the flower of beauty." Someone once tried to make me believe that a certain person, whom all we French know, had imposed on me in reciting some verses he had made — that they were not the same on paper that they were in the air, and that my eyes would judge them differently from my ears: so great is the power of pronunciation to give shape and value to works that are left to the efficacy and modulation of the voice. That is why Philoxenus was not so much to blame, when he heard someone giving a poor accent to one of his compositions, for kicking and smashing certain earthen vessels of his, saying: "I break what is yours, because you corrupt what is mine." To what end did those men who, with firm resolve, killed themselves turn their faces away so as not to see the blow they themselves had appointed? And those who, for their health, ask and command incisions to be made on them and cauteries applied — why can they not endure the sight of the preparations, the instruments, and the operations of the surgeon, when the eye plays no part in the pain? Are not these proper examples to verify the authority the senses have over the imagination? It is to no purpose that we know these tresses were borrowed from a page or a lackey, that this rouge came from Spain and this pearl-powder from the Ocean Sea. Our sight will still compel us to confess the subject more agreeable and more lovely against all reason — for in that there is nothing of its own:

The poet whom Dionysius, because he could not equal him in poesy, condemned to the quarries; and who, hearing a man give an ill accent to a composition of his, spurned and broke certain earthen vessels of the man’s, saying: I break what is thine, because thou corruptest what is mine.

And so men proceed: we let the laws and precepts go their own way; we ourselves keep another course, not only by debauchery of manners, but often by judgment and contrary opinion. Just listen to a philosophical lecture: the invention, eloquence, and pertinency strike the mind at once and move you; there is nothing that touches or stings your conscience; it is not that they are addressing. ## modern-en · ctesibius · 103:268

I have seen elsewhere houses in ruins, and statues of gods and men: these are still men. It is all true; and yet, for all that, I cannot so often revisit the tomb of that so great and so powerful city without admiration and reverence. The care of the dead is commended to us; now, I have been brought up from my infancy with these dead; I knew the affairs of Rome long before I knew those of my own house; I knew the Capitol and its layout before I knew the Louvre, and the Tiber before I knew the Seine. The qualities and fortunes of Lucullus, Metellus, and Scipio have always run in my head more than those of anyone of my own country; they are all dead; so is my father, as absolutely dead as they, and is removed as far from me and life in eighteen years as they are in sixteen hundred — whose memory, friendship, and society, nevertheless, I do not cease to embrace and make use of, with a perfect and lively union. Indeed, of my own inclination, I pay more service to the dead; they can no longer help themselves, and therefore, it seems to me, the more require my assistance: it is there that gratitude appears in its full lustre. The benefit is not so generously bestowed where there is retrogradation and reflection. Arcesilaus, going to visit Ctesibius, who was sick, and finding him in a very poor condition, very finely slipped some money under his pillow, and, by concealing it, also acquitted him of the acknowledgment due for such a benefit. Those who have deserved from me friendship and gratitude have never lost it by being no more; I have better and more carefully paid them when they were gone and ignorant of what I did; I speak most affectionately of my friends when they can no longer know it. I have had a hundred quarrels in defence of Pompey and for the cause of Brutus; this acquaintance still continues between us; we have no other hold even on present things but by fancy. Finding myself of no use to this age, I throw myself back upon that other, and am so enamoured of it that the free, just, and flourishing state of that ancient Rome (for I love it neither in its birth nor its old age) interests and impassions me; and therefore I cannot so often revisit the sites of their streets and houses, and those ruins deep down even to the Antipodes, without being moved. Is it by nature, or through error of fancy, that the sight of places we know to have been frequented and inhabited by persons whose memories are commended in story moves us more, in some way, than to hear an account of their acts or to read their writings?

## modern-en · tigellinus · 103:195

To finish accounting for my poor humours, I confess that in my travels I seldom reach my inn without it crossing my mind to consider whether I could there be sick and dying at my ease. I want to be lodged in some private part of the house, away from all noise, bad smells, and smoke. I try to flatter death by these trivial circumstances — or, to put it better, to discharge myself of every other encumbrance, so that I may have nothing to do, nor be troubled with anything but that which will weigh heavily enough on me without any other load. I would have my death share in the ease and conveniences of my life; it is a great part of life, and of great importance, and I hope it will not in future contradict the past. Death has some forms that are easier than others, and takes on different qualities according to every man's fancy. Among the natural deaths, the one that comes from weakness and stupor I think most favourable; among the violent ones, I can less easily think of a precipice than of the fall of a house that will crush me in a moment, and of a wound by a sword than of an arquebus shot; I should rather poison myself with Socrates than stab myself with Cato. And though it amounts to the same thing, my imagination makes as great a difference as that between death and life, between throwing myself into a burning furnace and plunging into the channel of a river — so emptily does our fear concern itself more with the means than the effect. It is but an instant, true; but an instant of such weight that I would willingly give many days of my life to pass it over after my own fashion. Since every man's imagination renders it more or less terrible, and since every man has some choice among the various forms of dying, let us try a little further to find one that is wholly clear of any offence. Might one not render it even voluptuous, like the Commorientes of Antony and Cleopatra? I set aside the brave and exemplary efforts produced by philosophy and religion; but among men of little mark there have been some, like Petronius and Tigellinus at Rome, condemned to despatch themselves, who have, so to speak, rocked death to sleep with the delicacy of their preparations; they made it slip and steal away in the midst of their accustomed diversions, among girls and good fellows; not a word of consolation, no mention of making a will, no ambitious affectation of constancy, no talk of their future condition; amid sport, feasting, wit and mirth, common and indifferent conversation, music, and amorous verses. Could we not imitate this resolution after a more decent fashion? Since there are deaths good for fools and deaths good for the wise, let us find ones fit for those between the two. My imagination suggests one that is easy, and, since we must die, to be desired. The Roman tyrants thought they granted a criminal his life when they gave him the choice of his death. But was not Theophrastus, that so delicate, modest, and wise philosopher, compelled by reason when he dared utter this verse, translated by Cicero:

With Petronius, one of the two men of little mark at Rome who, condemned to despatch themselves, rocked death asleep with the delicacy of their preparations, and made it slip away amongst girls and good fellows, with not a word of consolation nor any mention of a will.

"But, at your age, you will never come back from so long a journey." What do I care? I undertake it neither to come back, nor to finish it; my business is only to keep myself in motion while motion pleases me; I only walk for the walk's sake. They who chase after a benefit, or a hare, do not really run; only they run who run at base, and to exercise their running. My design is divisible throughout: it is not founded on any great hopes; every day concludes my expectation: and the journey of my life is carried on the same way. And yet I have seen places far enough off where I would gladly have stayed. And why not, if Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes, Zeno, Antipater — so many sages of the sourest sect — readily abandoned their country, without any cause for complaint, and only for the enjoyment of another air. In earnest, what most displeases me in all my travels is that I cannot resolve to settle where I would most like to, but must always look ahead to coming back, to fitting in with the common humour.

The Stoic, named in the succession of the sourest sect — Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Diogenes, Zeno, Antipater — all of whom readily abandoned their country for the enjoyment of another air. Not the Cynic, nor the atheist, nor the Apolloniate.

## modern-en · metrocles · 69:574

that swells in this way and fortifies itself by growing old. Just look into the ancient considerations that first set in motion this famous torrent so full of dignity, awe, and reverence — you will find them so light and weak that it is no wonder if these people, who weigh and reduce everything to reason, and who admit nothing on authority or on trust, have judgments often very remote from those of the public. It is no wonder if people who take their pattern from the first image of nature should in most of their opinions swerve from the common path. As for example, few of them would have approved the strict conditions of our marriages, and most of them have been for having wives in common, without obligation. They would refuse our ceremonies. Chrysippus said that a philosopher would do a dozen somersaults — yes, and without his breeches — for a dozen olives. That philosopher would hardly have advised Cleisthenes to refuse to give the fair Agarista, his daughter, to Hippoclides, for having seen him stand on his head on a table. Metrocles, somewhat indiscreetly, broke wind backwards while disputing in the presence of a great audience in his school, and hid in his own house for shame until Crates came to visit him and, adding to his arguments and consolations the example of his own liberty by setting himself to compete with him as to who could be louder, cured him of that scruple, and drew him into his own Stoic sect — freer than the more reserved Peripatetic one he had been in until then. What we call decency — not daring to do in public what it is decent enough to do in private — the Stoics call foppishness; and to mince matters, and to be so modest as to conceal and disown what nature, custom, and our desires publish and proclaim of our actions, they treated as a vice. The others thought it was to undervalue the mysteries of Venus to draw them out of their private chapel and expose them to public view, and that to bring them out from behind the curtain was to debase them. Modesty is a thing of weight; secrecy, reserve, and circumspection are part of esteem. Pleasure was wonderfully ingenious when, under the mask of virtue, she sought not to be prostituted in the open streets, trodden under foot, exposed to public view, lacking the dignity and convenience of her private rooms. Hence some say that to abolish public brothels is not only to scatter fornication into every place where it had been confined to one, but also, by the difficulty, to incite wild and idle people to this vice:

Who broke wind backwards somewhat indiscreetly while disputing before a great auditory in his school, and kept himself hid at home for shame until Crates came to visit him; and who slept in winter abroad amongst sheep and in summer in the cloisters of churches.

## modern-en · chremonides · 104:71

Let us not attempt these examples; we shall never come up to them. They set themselves resolutely, and without agitation, to watch the ruin of their country, which possessed and commanded all their will: that is too much, and too hard a task for our more ordinary souls. Cato gave up the noblest life that ever was on this account; we lesser spirits must run from the storm as far as we can; we must provide for feeling, not for endurance, and dodge blows we cannot meet. Zeno, seeing Chremonides, a young man he was fond of, come up to sit beside him, suddenly jumped up, and when Cleanthes asked why he did so, said: "I hear that physicians especially prescribe rest, and forbid disturbance, in all swellings." Socrates does not say: "Do not surrender to the charms of beauty; stand your ground, and do everything you can to resist it." "Flee from it," he says; "avoid the sight and encounter of it, as you would of a powerful poison that shoots its arrows and wounds at a distance." And his fine pupil, inventing or recounting — in my opinion rather recounting than inventing — the rare perfections of the great Cyrus, makes him distrustful of his own strength to resist the charms of the divine beauty of that illustrious Panthea, his captive, and so he commits the visiting and keeping of her to another, who could not have so much liberty as himself. The young man Zeno loved, at whose drawing near to sit down by him Zeno suddenly started up — and told Cleanthes, who asked why, that he heard the physicians prescribe rest above all things and forbid emotion.

## modern-en · perrete · 104:107

Our people nowadays are so trained up to bustle and show that good nature, moderation, equability, constancy, and other such quiet and obscure qualities are no longer thought of or noticed. Rough bodies make themselves felt; smooth ones are handled imperceptibly; sickness is felt, health little or not at all, any more than the oils that soothe us, compared with the pains for which we are soothed. It is acting for one's own reputation and profit, not for the public good, to refer to the public square what could be done in the council chamber, or to noonday what could have been done the night before; or to be jealous to do oneself what one's colleague can do as well as you; some surgeons of Greece used to perform their operations on platforms in plain sight of the people, to attract more practice and more profit. They think that good rules cannot be understood except by the sound of a trumpet. Ambition is not a vice of small people or of such modest means as ours. Someone said to Alexander: "Your father will leave you a great dominion, easy and at peace"; this young man was envious of his father's victories and the justice of his rule; he would not have enjoyed the empire of the world in ease and peace. Alcibiades, in Plato, would rather die young, beautiful, rich, noble, and learned, with all this at the very peak, than fall short of such a condition; this disease is, perhaps, excusable in so strong and so full a soul. But when wretched, dwarfish little souls flatter and deceive themselves, and think to spread their fame for having given a correct judgment in some matter, or maintained discipline at the guard of a city gate, the more they think to raise their heads, the more they show their tails. This petty doing-good has neither body nor life; it vanishes in the first mouth, and goes no further than from one street to another. Brag of it by all means to your son or your servant, like the old fellow who, having no other audience for his praises or witness to his valour, boasted to his chambermaid, crying: "O Perrette, what a fine, clever man you have for a master!" At worst, talk of it to yourself, like a councillor of my acquaintance who, having disgorged a whole cartful of legal jargon with great heat and equal folly, on coming out of the council chamber to relieve himself, was heard quite contentedly muttering between his teeth:

The chambermaid to whom an old fellow, having no other auditor of his praises, boasted: O Perrete, what a brave, clever man hast thou for thy master! The modern edition spells her Perrette.

I would have the advantage on our side; but if I do not get it, I will not go mad. I am heartily for the right party; but I do not want to be picked out as an especial enemy to others, beyond the general quarrel. I deeply resist this vicious form of opinion: "He is for the League because he admires the grace of Monsieur de Guise; he is impressed by the energy of the King of Navarre, therefore he is a Huguenot; he criticises this or that in the king, therefore he is seditious in his heart." And I did not grant even to the magistrate that he was right in condemning a book because it had placed a heretic among the best poets of the age. Are we not to dare say of a thief that he has a handsome leg? If a woman is a prostitute, must she necessarily smell foul? In the wisest ages, did they revoke the proud title of Capitolinus that they had conferred on Marcus Manlius as preserver of religion and public liberty, and stifle the memory of his liberality, his feats of arms, and the military honours granted to his valour, because he afterwards aspired to sovereignty against the laws of his country? If we conceive a hatred of a lawyer, will he not be allowed the next day to be eloquent? I have spoken elsewhere of the zeal that has pushed worthy men into similar errors. For my part, I can say, "Such a man does this thing badly, and another thing virtuously and well." In the same way, when affairs go badly, they would have everyone in their party be blind or a blockhead, and our judgment and conviction subservient not to the truth but to the project of our desires. I would rather lean toward the other extreme, so much do I fear being bribed by my own wishes; to which may be added that I am slightly distrustful of things I want to be true.
